structures.name: Sole trader (current structure)
structures.summary: The individual runs the trade personally. Profits arising in the tax year are taxed at Income Tax rates plus Class 4 NIC, whether or not drawn. No Corporation Tax and nothing to file at Companies House. Liability is unlimited (GOV.UK: 'personally responsible for all of the debts of the business'). Class 2 NIC is treated as paid at or above the Small Profits Threshold (SPT); below it, voluntary Class 2 can be paid. Admin: Self Assessment, plus MTD for Income Tax once qualifying income passes the threshold. Figures are rUK rates; Scottish taxpayers pay Scottish rates on non-savings income.
pros: Lightest admin of all structures; no Companies House fees or filings
Usually cheapest at low and moderate profits once company running costs are counted
Outside IR35 (no intermediary); Class 2 treated as paid at or above the SPT (NIM70350)
Cash basis is the default from 2024-25, with full deduction of most kit costs when paid
cons: Unlimited personal liability, so insurance matters
Profit cannot be retained at a lower rate; all profit taxed in the year it arises
Above about £50,270 of profit: 40% Income Tax plus 2% Class 4 (42% combined); 62% in the £100,000-£125,140 taper band
MTD ITSA quarterly reporting once qualifying income exceeds the threshold
structures.costs: No Companies House fees. Self Assessment; MTD-compatible software once in MTD ITSA. Accountancy and software costs: null (no official figure).
structures.when_it_fits: Baseline for every comparison. Usually cheapest at low and moderate profits. Above about £50,270 of profit a company begins to be worth testing (see incorporation-rule-of-thumb and company-vs-sole-extraction).
structures.risks: Unlimited liability. A sole trader is outside IR35, but a client can still be found to be the direct employer under the general status tests, and the agency rules (ITEPA Part 2 Ch 7) can apply through crewing agencies. Scottish taxpayers pay Scottish rates on non-savings income.

figures.2024-25: Personal Allowance £12,570 (tapered above £100,000). Basic 20% on £1-£37,700 taxable, higher 40% to £125,140, additional 45% above. Class 4: 6% on £12,570-£50,270, 2% above. Class 2 SPT £6,725; voluntary Class 2 £3.45/week.
figures.2025-26: Same Income Tax bands and Class 4 as 2024-25. Class 2 SPT £6,845; voluntary £3.50/week.
figures.2026-27: Same Income Tax bands and Class 4. Class 2 SPT £7,105; voluntary £3.65/week.
figures.2027-28: Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026) OOTLAR Annex A: bands unchanged (20/40/45; PA £12,570). Class 4 6%/2% on £12,570/£50,270. Class 2 SPT £7,355; voluntary £3.80/week (announced).

structures.status: Law for 2024-25, 2025-26 and 2026-27. Class 2 reform in force since 6 April 2024 (NIM70350). 2027-28 partly law: PA £12,570 and basic rate limit £37,700 frozen to 5 April 2031 (FA 2021 s5 as extended by FA 2026 s10). 2027-28 main rates 20/40/45 announced for Finance Bill 2026-27. Class 2 SPT £7,355 and £3.80/week announced only, for affirmative secondary legislation in early 2027. Class 4 limits stay frozen. Budget 2026 press release 28 Oct 2026; OOTLAR Annex A updated 5 Nov 2026.
structures.relevance: The baseline. At low and moderate profits it is usually cheapest once company running costs are counted.

structures.name: Private limited company (personal service company)
structures.summary: A separate legal person owned by shareholders and run by directors; owners are 'responsible for business debts only up to the value of their financial investment' (GOV.UK). Pays Corporation Tax on its profits, including equipment hire income. Money is extracted by (1) salary through PAYE with employee and employer Class 1 NIC; (2) dividends, only from available profits, with no NIC but dividend tax; (3) director's loans, with s455 tax on loans outstanding 9 months after the year end and beneficial-loan benefit-in-kind rules. Profits left in the company bear only Corporation Tax until extracted. Register at Companies House (at least one director, one shareholder, PSC details, registered office, SIC code); directors and PSCs must verify identity (from 18 Nov 2025); add Corporation Tax to the business tax account; register as an employer to run PAYE. Each year: accounts and CT600 by commercial software (HMRC's free service closed 31 March 2026), and a confirmation statement.
pros: Limited liability for contracts actually made by the company
Profits can be retained at 19% CT (26.5% marginal between £50,000 and £250,000; 25% above), deferring personal tax
Employer pension contributions are CT-deductible with no NIC and no income tax (strongest lawful reason to incorporate once there is surplus profit)
Spouse can hold ordinary shares outright (Jones v Garnett; ITTOIA s626)
Tax-free AMAPs, trivial benefits (£300 cap for directors) and commercial interest on director loans are available
cons: On full extraction the saving is small or nil: from 2026-27 (dividends 10.75%/35.75%) essentially nil
IR35 / off-payroll rules can remove most of the benefit
No Employment Allowance for a sole-director company where the director is the only employee paid above the ST
Higher running costs, filing deadlines and automatic penalties
s455 tax on overdrawn director's loans (33.75%, or 35.75% for loans from 6 April 2026)
Restricted goodwill relief on related-party incorporation (CTA 2009 s879K)
structures.costs: Companies House from 1 Feb 2026: digital incorporation £100, digital confirmation statement £50, no fee for annual accounts (1 May 2024 - 31 Jan 2026: £50 and £34). CT600 needs commercial software from 1 April 2026; software-only accounts filing at Companies House from 1 April 2028 (announced). PAYE/RTI if salary paid. Accountancy and software: null (no official figure). See company-running-costs for penalties.
structures.when_it_fits: Worth modelling once profits regularly exceed about £50,000-£60,000 and there is surplus profit to retain or put into a pension, or a spouse who can genuinely hold ordinary shares, or limited liability is valued. If main clients are medium/large and treat the role as inside IR35, most of the benefit is lost.
structures.risks: IR35/off-payroll (ITEPA Part 2 Ch 8 and Ch 10). s455 at 33.75% (35.75% for loans from 6 April 2026). Settlements legislation (ITTOIA Part 5 Ch 5) where income is shifted to family. No Employment Allowance for a sole director-only payroll. Restricted goodwill relief (CTA 2009 s879K). Higher running costs and penalties. Proposed only: distributions framework reform (draft legislation 2027, intended effect April 2028) covering reductions of capital, demergers, purchase of own shares, Transactions in Securities, non-UK distributions and loans, unlawful distributions; it does not change ordinary salary or dividend extraction.

figures.2024-25: CT FY2024: 19% to £50,000; 25% above £250,000; marginal relief fraction 3/200 between. Dividends: £500 allowance; 8.75% / 33.75% / 39.35%. Employer NIC 13.8% above ST £175/week (£9,100/year). Employee NIC 8% from PT £242/week to UEL £967/week, 2% above.
figures.2025-26: CT FY2025: same 19%/25%, £50,000/£250,000, 3/200. Dividends 8.75% / 33.75% / 39.35%; allowance £500. Employer NIC 15% above ST £96/week (£5,000/year). Employment Allowance £10,500, but not for single-director companies.
figures.2026-27: CT FY2026: same. Dividends 10.75% / 35.75% / 39.35%; allowance £500. Employer NIC 15% above £96/week. PT £242/week; UEL £967/week.
figures.2027-28: Budget 2026: CT main rate 25% and small profits rate 19% (FY2027 is law, FY2028 announced). Dividend rates 10.75% / 35.75% / 39.35%. Class 1 thresholds frozen (PT £242, ST £96, UEL £967 per week; announced).

structures.status: Law: company form (Companies Act 2006); CT rates FY2024-FY2027 (FY2027 in Finance Act 2026 ss11-12); dividend rates 10.75%/35.75% from 2026-27 (FA 2026 s4, Royal Assent 18 March 2026); s455 35.75% for loans from 6 April 2026 follows automatically. Announced at Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026), not yet law: FY2028 CT rates (Finance Bill 2026-27); 2027-28 Class 1 thresholds (secondary legislation early 2027). Proposed: distributions framework reform (draft legislation 2027, intended effect April 2028).
structures.relevance: The main growth option; tax saving mainly from retention, employer pension contributions or a genuine spouse shareholding.

structures.name: General (ordinary) partnership
structures.summary: Two or more persons carrying on a business in common with a view of profit (Partnership Act 1890 s1). A partner can be a limited company. The partnership itself is not taxed: each partner pays tax on their own share. Individual partners pay Income Tax and Class 4 NIC on their share, charged separately on each partner (SSCBA 1992 Sch 2 para 4). A company partner pays Corporation Tax on its share instead (CTA 2009 ss1259-1262). Partners 'personally share responsibility' for losses and bills (GOV.UK). Each partner is jointly liable for all the firm's debts incurred while they are a partner (PA 1890 s9), and jointly and severally liable for the firm's wrongs (s12), so liability is unlimited. A nominated partner registers the partnership for Self Assessment (by 5 October in the business's second tax year), sends the partnership return and keeps the records. Each individual partner also registers (form SA401) and sends their own Self Assessment return. A company partner registers on form SA402 and reports its share on its own Company Tax Return (CT600), not on a Self Assessment return. If the partnership return is late, each partner has to pay a penalty. The partnership is not registered at Companies House (business.gov.uk).
pros: Profit is split between genuine partners, and each uses their own personal allowance, tax bands and Class 4 limits
No Companies House registration, fees or public accounts
Could suit a real two-person crew or kit-hire business

Partnerships do not yet have to use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax, and an individual partner's profit share does not count towards MTD qualifying income. HMRC will set a start date for partnerships later.
cons: Unlimited liability: each partner is liable for all the firm's debts and for wrongs done in the business by the other partners

No trading allowance against partnership trading income (ITTOIA s783AA(1)(a)). The allowance is also lost for the whole year on a partner's own side trade or miscellaneous income if that income includes any payment from the firm, and the same applies to anyone connected with a partner, such as their spouse (s783AP).

A spouse's share that is wholly or mainly a right to income (for example, a profit share with no share of capital) is taxed back on the other spouse under the settlements rules. A share given to a minor child is taxed on the parent.
Needs a partnership return as well as a return for every partner, and a late partnership return means a penalty for each partner
structures.costs: No Companies House fees. One partnership return plus each individual partner's Self Assessment return (a company partner reports its share on its CT600). The partnership registers for VAT as one business (GOV.UK gives the threshold as £90,000). A late partnership return means a penalty for each partner; the amounts are not settled in this item. Accountancy and software: null (no official figure).
structures.when_it_fits: Rarely useful for a solo technician. It can suit a real two-person crew or kit-hire business. It can also suit a spouse or partner who genuinely co-owns the kit and the business and shares in its capital and risk, provided clients contract with and pay the firm.
structures.risks: Unlimited joint liability. Settlements rules (ITTOIA Part 5 Ch 5): a spouse need not put in capital or do any work to be a partner (PM132400). Where the share is out of proportion to what they contribute and is wholly or mainly a right to income, s624 taxes it on the other spouse. Example: profits shared equally while the original owner keeps all rights to capital (TSEM4215 Example 10). An outright, unconditional share of both capital and income is normally protected by the s626 exemption for gifts between spouses (TSEM4215 Example 9). For adults who are not a spouse, the rules generally apply only where the share can revert to the giver (Example 11). A minor child's share given by a parent is taxed on the parent (s629, unless it is £100 or less a year). HMRC is likelier to challenge whether a partnership exists where there is no deed, or the deed is backdated by more than a few months (PM132400). Where a company is a partner, the mixed-membership rules (ITTOIA ss850C-850E) move part of the company's share to an individual partner only if Condition X (deferred profit) or Condition Y (excess share plus power to enjoy it) is met. IR35 can still apply to work done through a partnership. The partnership is an IR35 intermediary if any one of three conditions is met: the worker, alone or with relatives (spouse or civil partner, parent, child or remoter relation in the direct line, brother or sister), is entitled to 60% or more of the profits; most of the profits come from IR35 engagements with a single client, or a client and its associates; or the profit-sharing arrangements base any partner's income on the income that partner generates from such engagements (ITEPA 2003 s52(2) and s61P(1)). Splitting one business artificially to stay under the VAT threshold can be counteracted by an HMRC direction (VATA 1994 Sch 1 paras 1A-2).

figures.2024-25: Individual partners pay Income Tax and Class 4 on their profit share at the same rates and thresholds as a sole trader for the year (see rates block). A company partner pays Corporation Tax on its share. No trading allowance against partnership trading income (ITTOIA s783AA(1)(a)).
figures.2026-27: As 2024-25. Income Tax 20/40/45% (FA 2026 s2), with the higher rate from £37,701 and the additional rate over £125,140 of taxable income (Budget 2026 Annex A, 2026-27 column). Class 4: 6% on £12,570-£50,270 and 2% above (SSCBA 1992 s15(3) and (3ZA)).
figures.2027-28: Individual partners: same as a sole trader. Announced, not yet law: the 2027-28 Income Tax charge and main rates of 20/40/45%, to be set by Finance Bill 2026-27 (Budget 2026 OOTLAR 1.3, 28 Oct 2026). Already law: personal allowance £12,570 and basic rate limit £37,700 (FA 2021 s5, as amended by FA 2023 s5 and FA 2026 s10); higher rate limit £125,140 (ITA 2007 s10(5A): twice the personal allowance plus £100,000); Class 4 at 6% on £12,570-£50,270 and 2% above (SSCBA 1992 s15(3) and (3ZA), which have no end date; OOTLAR 2.1 keeps these limits at 2026-27 levels). Partners' shares of partnership savings or property income: the law now sets 22/42/47% for 2027-28 (FA 2026 ss5 and 7). Budget 2026 announced a rise to 24/44/49% from 6 April 2027 through Finance Bill 2026-27 (OOTLAR 1.1 and 1.2; the property rates are for England, Wales and Northern Ireland). The trading allowance rise to £3,000 from 6 April 2027 (announced, OOTLAR 1.5) would still not apply to partnership trading income.

structures.status: Law: Partnership Act 1890 ss1, 9 and 12; ITTOIA 2005 Part 9, including ss850C-850E (inserted by FA 2014 Sch 17); ITTOIA s783AA(1)(a) and s783AP (trading allowance); CTA 2009 ss1259-1262 (company partners); SSCBA 1992 s15 and Sch 2 para 4 (Class 4 on each partner's share); ITTOIA ss624, 626 and 629 (settlements); ITEPA 2003 ss52 and 61P; FA 2021 s5 as amended and ITA 2007 s10(5A) (2027-28 personal allowance and bands); FA 2026 ss5 and 7 (2027-28 savings and property rates of 22/42/47%). Guidance: GOV.UK 'Set up a business partnership'; HMRC PM132400, PM142000 and TSEM4215; GOV.UK MTD exemption page (updated 12 Nov 2026: partnerships 'do not currently need' MTD) and qualifying-income page. Announced only (Budget 2026, 28 Oct 2026; Finance Bill 2026-27): the 2027-28 Income Tax charge and main rates, savings and property rates of 24/44/49%, and the £3,000 trading allowance. Budget 2026 contains no partnership measure.
structures.relevance: Rarely helps a solo events technician. Agencies and production companies book and pay you personally, so a partnership only works with a genuine second partner (a crew-mate, or a spouse or partner who really co-owns the kit and the business) and with clients who contract with and pay the firm. See spouse-partnership for splitting profit with a spouse.

structures.name: Limited liability partnership (LLP)
structures.summary: A body corporate with legal personality separate from its members (LLP Act 2000 s1), incorporated at Companies House by two or more persons (s2). For income tax it is treated as a partnership: its activities are treated as carried on in partnership by its members (ITTOIA 2005 s863). Individual members pay Income Tax and Class 4 NIC on their profit share (SSCBA 1992 s15(3A)) and register for Self Assessment. A corporate member pays Corporation Tax on its share. Members 'are not personally liable for any debts the business cannot pay' (GOV.UK). An LLP needs at least 2 designated members at all times. It files annual accounts and a confirmation statement at Companies House and pays the same fee amounts as a company, but can incorporate or change its name only by software or paper. Salaried member rules (ITTOIA ss863A-863G; HMRC PM250000): an individual member is taxed as an employee if all three conditions are met. Condition A: it is reasonable to expect at least 80% of the amounts payable for their services to be 'disguised salary'. Condition B: the members' mutual rights and duties do not give them significant influence over the LLP's affairs. Condition C: their contribution is less than 25% of the disguised salary expected for the tax year. In HMRC v BlueCrest Capital Management (UK) LLP [2026] UKSC 18 (1 July 2026) the Supreme Court held that Condition B turns on the members' legally enforceable rights and duties under the LLP agreement, and that significant influence must be over the LLP's affairs as a whole. Informal influence does not count. Day-to-day operational decision-making is less likely to qualify, still less if it covers only part of the business, and responsibility for high-value day-to-day decisions is not in itself significant influence.
pros: Profit can be shared between genuine members, each using their own allowances and bands
Suits a genuine two-owner crew or kit-hire business
cons: Needs at least 2 members and at least 2 designated members at all times
No Corporation Tax deferral: all profit is taxed on the members as it arises, as for a sole trader
No tax saving over sole trading for a solo technician
No trading allowance against members' shares of LLP trading income (ITTOIA s783AA(1)(a) with s863)
Companies House fees, public accounts, confirmation statements and automatic late-filing penalties
structures.costs: From 1 Feb 2026 (SI 2025/1137): incorporation £100 software, £156 same-day software, £124 paper; confirmation statement £50 online/software, £110 paper; change of name £20 software, £85 same-day, £30 paper; voluntary strike-off £13 online, £18 paper. From 1 May 2024 to 31 Jan 2026 (SI 2024/155): incorporation £50 software, £78 same-day, £71 paper; confirmation statement £34 electronic, £62 paper; strike-off £33 electronic, £44 paper. There is no online (web) route for LLP incorporation or change of name, and no fee for filing accounts. Late accounts: £150 up to 1 month late, £375 up to 3 months, £750 up to 6 months, £1,500 over 6 months, doubled if late in 2 successive years. Also a partnership return plus each member's Self Assessment return. Accountancy: null.
structures.when_it_fits: Only if a genuine second owner joins (for example, a crew or kit-hire business with two working owners) and limited liability matters.
structures.risks: For a solo trader the second member is usually a spouse or partner. The main risks are then the settlements rules (a spouse's share that is wholly or mainly a right to income is taxed on the other spouse: TSEM4215) and whether the business is genuinely carried on in common. The salaried member rules are unlikely to apply where both members genuinely share profits and the LLP agreement gives each real rights over the LLP's affairs as a whole (Conditions A and B, as read in BlueCrest). A member on a fixed or profit-independent return with no governance rights could, however, be taxed as an employee. IR35 can apply to work supplied through an LLP (ITTOIA s863(2) treats an LLP as a partnership for income tax). The LLP is an IR35 intermediary if any one of three conditions is met: the worker, alone or with relatives, is entitled to 60% or more of the profits; most of the profits come from IR35 engagements with a single client, or a client and its associates; or a member's profit share is based on the income that member generates from such engagements (ITEPA 2003 s52(2)(a)-(c) and s61P(1)(a)-(c)). HMRC Spotlight 50 (26 Mar 2019) says contractor arrangements using a personal service company and an offshore LLP to get round the loan charge 'do not work'. Spotlight 66 (23 Oct 2024) says the employer 'Partnership Model', which moves employees into an LLP, does not work. Individual members must have verified their identity at Companies House (LLP Act s2(2)(ea)); verification for corporate members is to come 'at a later date'. Designated members can be prosecuted for failing to file.

figures.2024-25: Individual members pay Income Tax and Class 4 on their profit share at the same rates as a sole trader; a corporate member pays Corporation Tax. LLP fees 6-30 April 2024 (SI 2012/1907 Sch 1 para 10 before amendment): incorporation £10 electronic, £30 same-day electronic, £40 paper (£100 same-day paper); confirmation statement £13 electronic, £40 paper; strike-off £10. From 1 May 2024 (SI 2024/155): incorporation £50 software, £78 same-day software, £71 paper; confirmation statement £34 electronic, £62 paper; strike-off £33 electronic, £44 paper.
figures.2025-26: Members taxed as in 2024-25. Fees from 6 April 2025 to 31 January 2026: incorporation £50 software, £78 same-day, £71 paper; confirmation statement £34 online, £62 paper. From 1 February 2026 (SI 2025/1137): incorporation £100 software, £156 same-day software, £124 paper; confirmation statement £50 online/software, £110 paper; strike-off £13 online, £18 paper.
figures.2026-27: Members taxed as in 2024-25. Incorporation £100 software, £156 same-day software, £124 paper; confirmation statement £50 online/software, £110 paper (fees page updated 25 Sept 2026).
figures.2027-28: Individual members: same as a sole trader. Announced, not yet law: the 2027-28 Income Tax charge and main rates of 20/40/45%, to be set by Finance Bill 2026-27 (Budget 2026 OOTLAR 1.3, 28 Oct 2026). Already law: personal allowance £12,570 and basic rate limit £37,700 (FA 2021 s5 as amended); higher rate limit £125,140 (ITA 2007 s10(5A)); Class 4 at 6% on £12,570-£50,270 and 2% above (SSCBA 1992 s15(3) and (3ZA), applied to LLP members by s15(3A); OOTLAR 2.1 keeps these limits at 2026-27 levels). Budget 2026 contains no LLP or salaried-member measure. Companies House fees: null (no change announced; no fee regulations after SI 2025/1137 found on legislation.gov.uk on 24 Nov 2026).

structures.status: Law: LLP Act 2000 ss1-2; ITTOIA 2005 s863 and ss863A-863G (inserted by FA 2014 Sch 17, from 6 April 2014), as interpreted in HMRC v BlueCrest Capital Management (UK) LLP [2026] UKSC 18 (1 July 2026; appeal dismissed, Condition B sent back to the First-tier Tribunal); SSCBA 1992 s15(3A) (Class 4 on members). Fees: SI 2012/1907 Sch 1 para 10 as amended by SI 2024/155 (1 May 2024) and SI 2025/1137 (1 Feb 2026). Identity verification has been law for individual members since 18 Nov 2025; the 12-month transition ended (GOV.UK update 19 Nov 2026); corporate members are not yet covered. 2027-28: personal allowance, bands and Class 4 already law; Income Tax main rates announced only (Budget 2026, 28 Oct 2026; Finance Bill 2026-27). Budget 2026 contains no LLP measure.
structures.relevance: Only worth considering if a genuine second owner joins (for example, a crew-mate, or a spouse who co-owns the kit-hire side) and limited liability matters. For a solo technician it adds Companies House costs and filings with no tax saving over sole trading.

structures.name: Limited liability: what it does and does not protect
structures.summary: A company or LLP is a separate legal person; owners are generally not liable beyond what they put in (company owners liable 'only up to the value of their financial investment'; LLP members 'not personally liable for any debts the business cannot pay', LLP Act 2000 s1). A sole trader has unlimited liability; ordinary partners 'personally share responsibility'. Directors keep statutory duties and 'may be fined, prosecuted or disqualified'. Protection applies only to contracts actually made by the company/LLP: the registered name must appear on POs, invoices, receipts, letters and websites; registered number, registered office and part of the UK on letters, order forms and websites (SI 2015/17 regs 24-25). It does not protect against personal guarantees or personal loans (Start Up Loans are unsecured personal loans), wrongful trading contributions (IA 1986 s214), HMRC joint and several liability notices on directors (avoidance, evasion, repeated insolvency), or personal criminal/regulatory liability. Acting as a director without verified identity is an offence (CA 2006 s167M, from 18 Nov 2025).
pros: Protects personal assets from business debts on contracts made by the company/LLP
cons: Does not remove director duties or personal criminal and regulatory exposure
Personal guarantees and personal loans remain personal
Insurance (public liability, equipment, professional indemnity) still needed in every structure
structures.costs: No monetary figures. Insurance costs: null.
structures.when_it_fits: HMRC research found limited liability the most common reason for incorporating (36% in a 2025 survey). For an events technician site, equipment or injury claims are the main risk, so insurance may matter more than incorporating.
structures.risks: Since 18 Nov 2025 it is an offence to act as a director without verified identity; the company and any director who lets an unverified director act can also offend; first convictions reported 17 Sep 2026.

figures.current: No monetary figures.

structures.status: Law: Companies Act 2006; LLP Act 2000 s1; Partnership Act 1890; CA 2006 s167M (inserted by ECCTA 2023 s43, fully in force 18 Nov 2025 under SI 2025/1118, 12-month transition for existing directors tied to next confirmation statement); trading disclosures SI 2015/17 regs 24-25.
structures.relevance: Expend should check that POs, invoices and hire agreements are in the company's name if the user incorporates.

techniques.name: Company/LLP running costs, filing deadlines and late-filing penalties
techniques.summary: Companies House fees changed on 1 Feb 2026 (SI 2025/1137, made 28 Oct 2025). Incorporation is £100 online/software (£156 same-day by software, £124 paper). The confirmation statement is £50 online/software (£110 paper). Voluntary strike-off is £13 online (£18 paper). LLPs pay the same amounts. There is no fee for filing annual accounts. From 1 May 2024 to 31 Jan 2026 (SI 2024/155) the fees were: incorporation £50, confirmation statement £34, strike-off £33 online. Deadlines for private companies and LLPs: later accounts are due 9 months after the accounting reference date (ARD). First accounts covering more than 12 months are due 21 months from incorporation or 3 months from the ARD, whichever is longer; first accounts of 12 months or less follow the normal 9-month rule. A shortened accounting period can bring the deadline forward. For companies only: Corporation Tax (non-large) is payable 9 months and 1 day after the period end, and the CT600 is due 12 months after it. HMRC's free joint accounts/CT600 service closed on 31 March 2026, so a CT600 now needs commercial software (paper only with a reasonable excuse, or in Welsh). Amended or re-filed returns can still be sent by software, on paper or through an agent for now. Companies House late accounts penalties (private company or LLP): £150, £375, £750 or £1,500, doubled if accounts are late in 2 successive years. FA 2026 s265 doubled the HMRC flat CT600 penalties for returns with a filing date on or after 1 April 2026: £200, or £400 if more than 3 months late; £1,000 or £2,000 for a third successive failure. The tax-related penalty is unchanged: 10%, or 20% if the return is delivered more than 2 years after the period end, of the tax unpaid 18 months after the period end. Announced, not yet in force: filing at Companies House restricted to identity-verified company officers or employees, or Authorised Corporate Service Providers (ACSPs) and their employees, from no sooner than November 2027; software-only accounts filing for all companies from 1 April 2028 (the announcements do not say whether LLP accounts are covered); and mandatory online filing of amended Company Tax Returns from 1 April 2028, by HMRC directions (Budget 2026 OOTLAR 2.40, 28 Oct 2026).
techniques.conditions: Companies House fees, deadlines and late accounts penalties apply to companies and LLPs alike. Corporation Tax, the CT600 and its penalties apply to companies only: an LLP's members are taxed as partners (ITTOIA 2005 s863), and the LLP files a partnership return instead. Sole traders and ordinary partnerships pay none of these Companies House fees.
techniques.risks: Late accounts bring automatic penalties. Not filing accounts or confirmation statements is a criminal offence for directors and LLP designated members. A late confirmation statement can also bring a financial penalty, and Companies House can strike the company off. If a CT600 is 6 months late, HMRC issues a tax determination, which cannot be appealed. Running costs reduce, and at this user's profit level usually remove, any tax saving from incorporating.
techniques.data_needed: Whether the business is a company or an LLP; ARD and period end; incorporation date; any notice shortening the accounting reference period; actual filing dates of accounts and CT600; whether the previous financial year's accounts were late; whether CT600 flat penalties arose for the two previous accounting periods; Corporation Tax still unpaid 18 months after the period end.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Penalty estimator, not a saving. Companies House accounts penalties (private company or LLP), measured from the filing deadline: up to 1 month late £150; over 1 to 3 months £375; over 3 to 6 months £750; over 6 months £1,500. Double the penalty if the previous financial year's accounts were also late. The CT600 flat penalty depends on the return's filing date, normally 12 months after the period end. Filing date on or after 1 April 2026: £200 if late, or £400 if delivered more than 3 months after the filing date; for a third successive failure £1,000, or £2,000 if more than 3 months late. Filing date before 1 April 2026: £100 or £200, and £500 or £1,000 for a third successive failure. If the return is not delivered within 18 months after the period end, add a tax-related penalty. It is 10% of the tax unpaid at that point if the return arrives within 2 years of the period end, and 20% if it arrives later (FA 1998 Sch 18 para 18). Add the fees on the dates they are paid (they changed on 1 May 2024 and 1 Feb 2026) to any comparison of sole trading and a company.

figures.2024-25: 6-30 April 2024 (SI 2012/1907 Sch 1 before amendment): company incorporation £12 web, £10 software, £30 same-day software, £40 paper, £100 same-day paper; confirmation statement £13 electronic, £40 paper; voluntary strike-off £10. LLP incorporation was £10 electronic, £30 same-day electronic, £40 paper. From 1 May 2024 (SI 2024/155): incorporation £50 web/software, £78 same-day software, £71 paper; confirmation statement £34 electronic, £62 paper; change of name £20 electronic, £83 same-day electronic, £30 paper; voluntary strike-off £33 electronic, £44 paper. LLPs paid the same amounts. Companies House late accounts (private company or LLP): £150 / £375 / £750 / £1,500, doubled if late in 2 successive financial years. HMRC CT600 late filing (filing date before 1 April 2026): £100; £200 if more than 3 months late; £500 / £1,000 for a third successive failure. Plus 10% (20% if delivered more than 2 years after the period end) of tax unpaid 18 months after the period end.
figures.2025-26: 6 April 2025 to 31 January 2026: the fees from 1 May 2024 applied. That means incorporation £50 digital, £78 same-day, £71 paper; confirmation statement £34 digital, £62 paper; change of name £20, £83 same-day, £30 paper; strike-off £33 electronic, £44 paper. From 1 Feb 2026 (SI 2025/1137): incorporation £100 online/software, £156 same-day (software), £124 paper; confirmation statement £50 online/software, £110 paper; change of name £20 online/software, £85 same-day, £30 paper; strike-off £13 online, £18 paper. LLPs pay the same amounts but can incorporate and change name only by software or paper. CT600 penalties at £100 / £200 / £500 / £1,000 apply to filing dates before 1 April 2026, normally periods ending before 1 April 2025. The doubled rates apply from filing dates on or after 1 April 2026.
figures.2026-27: Fees as from 1 Feb 2026 (GOV.UK fees page updated 25 Sept 2026); no fee for annual accounts. Companies House late accounts penalties as above. HMRC CT600 late filing for a filing date on or after 1 April 2026 (FA 2026 s265): £200; £400 if more than 3 months late; for a third successive failure £1,000, or £2,000 if more than 3 months late. Plus 10% or 20% of tax unpaid 18 months after the period end. Earlier filing dates keep £100 / £200 / £500 / £1,000.
figures.2027-28: Companies House fees: null (no change announced; no fee regulations after SI 2025/1137 found on legislation.gov.uk on 24 Nov 2026). Announced, not yet in force: from no sooner than November 2027, with at least 6 months' notice, only identity-verified company officers or employees, or ACSPs and their employees, may file at Companies House, including incorporation, confirmation statements and accounts (the campaign page describes this for companies and does not say how it applies to LLPs). Company accounts filed on or after 1 April 2028 must use commercial software (iXBRL), and the web and paper routes close for accounts; GOV.UK says 'all companies' and does not say whether LLP accounts are covered. Abridged and filleted accounts continue, and the small and micro company P&L filing requirement is paused. HMRC: amended Company Tax Returns must be filed online from 1 April 2028, by directions (Budget 2026 OOTLAR 2.40, 28 Oct 2026); until then they can still be sent on paper. Accountancy and software costs: null.

techniques.status: Law: Companies House fees under SI 2012/1907 Sch 1, as amended by SI 2024/155 (from 1 May 2024) and SI 2025/1137 (from 1 Feb 2026). Filing periods under CA 2006 s442. Late accounts civil penalty under CA 2006 s453 and SI 2008/497; amounts as in the Companies House guidance updated 16 Jan 2026. CT600 flat penalties under FA 1998 Sch 18 para 17, as amended by FA 2026 s265 for filing dates on or after 1 April 2026 (policy paper 26 Nov 2025). Tax-related penalty under para 18. HMRC's joint filing service closed on 31 March 2026. Announced, not in force: Companies House filing restrictions (not before November 2027); software-only accounts filing for companies from 1 April 2028 (Companies House news, 23 Oct 2026; LLP coverage not stated); mandatory online filing of amended Company Tax Returns from 1 April 2028 by HMRC directions (Budget 2026 OOTLAR 2.40, 28 Oct 2026).
techniques.relevance: If the user incorporates or forms an LLP, these fees, deadlines and automatic penalties feed the late-filing estimator and must be added to the company side of any comparison. With all profit drawn, a company saves little or nothing from 2026-27 (see company-vs-sole-extraction), so at this user's turnover the running costs usually make incorporating more expensive.

techniques.name: Companies House identity verification (ECCTA 2023)
techniques.summary: Since 18 Nov 2025 directors and PSCs must verify identity (CA 2006 s167M, inserted by ECCTA 2023 s43, in force under SI 2025/1118). New directors verify and give their personal code at incorporation/appointment. Directors appointed before 18 Nov 2025 had to deliver a verification statement with the next confirmation statement during the 12-month transition (18 Nov 2025 - 17 Nov 2026), which GOV.UK said on 19 Nov 2026 'has now passed'. New PSCs give their code when first added or within 14 days. Free via GOV.UK One Login (biometric passport from any country, UK photo driving licence, BRP, BRC or Frontier Worker permit; or bank/building society details plus NI number and security questions; or in person at a participating Post Office). An Authorised Corporate Service Provider (AML-supervised accountant/solicitor) may charge. Acting as a director unverified is an offence for the director, the company and every officer in default; Companies House may issue financial penalties, annotate the register, prosecute or refer to the Insolvency Service.
techniques.conditions: Photo ID, or bank details plus NI number, or Post Office in person. A personal code per person and a verification statement per role.
techniques.risks: Offence to act as an unverified director; first convictions secured. A confirmation statement cannot be filed without each director's personal code.
techniques.data_needed: Whether the user (and any co-director/PSC) has a Companies House personal code.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Not a saving. Cost £0 via GOV.UK One Login; ACSP fee null. Flag as a one-off step before or at incorporation.

figures.2025-26: Mandatory from 18 Nov 2025. Free via GOV.UK One Login; ACSP fees: null.
figures.2026-27: Transition period for existing directors ended 17 Nov 2026.
figures.current: Cost via GOV.UK One Login £0.

techniques.status: Law. CA 2006 s167M fully in force 18 Nov 2025 (SI 2025/1118 reg 2(1)(g), subject to reg 4). Transition ended (GOV.UK update 19 Nov 2026). Companies House expects every company to have complied or be on a compliance or enforcement pathway by end of March 2027.
techniques.relevance: Small one-off admin step for the company or LLP route.

techniques.name: Companies House accounts filing reforms (April 2028)
techniques.summary: From 1 April 2028 all UK registered companies must file their accounts at Companies House in iXBRL using commercial software, whether they file themselves or through an agent or accountant. There is no transition period: any accounts filed after that date, including revised accounts, must use software. Web and paper filing close for accounts only; web filing stays for confirmation statements and other filings. Three other changes also apply from April 2028. A company claiming an audit exemption must include a strengthened statement on the balance sheet: the directors name the exemption and confirm the company qualifies. The component parts of accounts and reports must be filed together. A business reason is needed to shorten the accounting reference period more than once within 5 years. On 23 Oct 2026 the government paused, with no end date, the planned requirement for small and micro companies to file a profit and loss account. During the pause it will look at joining up Companies House and HMRC filing ('tell Government once'). Abridged and filleted accounts (without the P&L) therefore remain allowed. The 1 April 2028 software-only date was added to guidance on 9 June 2026 and reconfirmed on 23 Oct 2026. Separately, the government has said it intends to remove the requirement for any company to prepare a directors' report, under its Modernising Corporate Reporting programme. That is not yet law.
techniques.conditions: Applies to all UK registered companies for accounts filed on or after 1 April 2028; the trigger is the filing date, not the accounting period. The announcements refer to companies; they do not say whether LLP accounts are covered.
techniques.risks: Adds a software or accountant cost for a company that would otherwise file its own accounts online. There is no transition period, so accounts filed late, or re-filed after rejection, after 1 April 2028 must also go by software. Directors remain legally responsible even when an agent files.
techniques.data_needed: Whether the user has incorporated and who files accounts.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Not a saving; add a software cost (null, no official figure) to company running costs from 1 April 2028.

figures.2027-28: Software-only (iXBRL) filing for all company accounts filed on or after 1 April 2028 (the last days of tax year 2027-28; first day of CT financial year 2028). Software cost: null.

techniques.status: ECCTA 2023 is law, but its accounts provisions are in force only for the purpose of making regulations (s219(2)(b)). These are ss53-54 (P&L filing), s57 (audit-exemption statement) and s58 (removal of abridged accounts). None of the commencement regulations on legislation.gov.uk (the latest is No. 7, SI 2026/57, January 2026) brings them into force. The power to require electronic delivery by registrar's rules (CA 2006 s1068(4A), inserted by ECCTA s75) has been in force since 4-5 March 2024. The power to require documents to be delivered together (ECCTA s78) has been in force since 4 March 2024. No enacted limit on shortening the accounting reference period was found: CA 2006 s392 limits only extensions. Announced: software-only accounts filing from 1 April 2028 (GOV.UK guidance updated 9 June 2026; Companies House news and Written Ministerial Statement HLWS419, both 23 Oct 2026). The small and micro company P&L filing requirement was paused on 23 Oct 2026 with no end date.
techniques.relevance: Only matters if the user incorporates. From 1 April 2028 the company's accounts must be filed through commercial software or an accountant, so the app should budget for that. Small companies can still keep their profit and loss account off the public register by filing filleted accounts.

techniques.name: Incorporation relief (TCGA 1992 s162)
techniques.summary: Where a non-company transfers a business as a going concern with all its assets (or all except cash) to a company wholly or partly for shares, gains on the assets are deducted from the base cost of the new shares, deferring tax until the shares are sold. If part of the consideration is not shares, only A/B is relieved (A = cost of new shares, B = total consideration); the rest is chargeable. For transfers on or after 6 April 2026 the relief must be claimed and the s162A election to disapply is repealed (FA 2026 s39).
techniques.conditions: Whole business transferred as a going concern with all its assets (cash may be kept); shares issued to the transferor. Claim content (CG65735): description of the business; company name and CRN; number, type and date of shares; chargeable assets and values; non-share consideration; relief claimed; base cost of new shares. No share valuation required.
techniques.risks: Relief restricted if consideration is a loan-account credit or cash. All assets must go, so unsuitable if the van or kit is to be kept personally. For a technician, gains are usually small (equipment often stands at a loss; personal goodwill may have little transferable value), so the relief may not be needed. Share base cost is reduced.
techniques.data_needed: List of business assets with cost and market value at transfer; consideration split (shares vs loan account/cash); transfer date.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Gain deferred = sum of gains on chargeable assets x A/B; tax deferred = that gain (after the £3,000 annual exempt amount if otherwise unused) x CGT rate (18%/24%).

figures.2024-25: Relief automatic. s162A election to disapply due by the second anniversary of the 31 Jan after the tax year of transfer, or the first anniversary if the shares are disposed of by the end of the following tax year.
figures.2025-26: Same as 2024-25 for transfers before 6 April 2026.
figures.2026-27: Claim required. Deadline: first anniversary of the 31 Jan after the tax year of transfer (e.g. transfer on 19 July 2026 must be claimed by 31 Jan 2029). Usually in the SA return (SA108 box 54 or an attachment).
figures.2027-28: Same claim regime. Budget 2026 announced no change.

techniques.status: Law. Finance Act 2026 (c.11) s39 (18 March 2026) splits s162(1) into (a)/(b), adds s162(6) and omits s162A, for transfers on or after 6 April 2026 (s39(5)). Announced at Budget 2025 (OOTLAR para 1.33, 28 Nov 2025). Budget 2026 OOTLAR has no measure on it.
techniques.relevance: Only if business assets stand at a gain; do not miss the claim for 2026-27 transfers.

techniques.name: Incorporation relief (TCGA 1992 s162) now has to be claimed
techniques.summary: Procedural point: for transfers of a business on or after 6 April 2026 s162 relief applies only if claimed; the s162A election to disapply is abolished.
techniques.conditions: Whole business transferred as a going concern with all its assets (cash may be kept), consideration at least partly shares; relief proportionate to the share part (s162(4)).
techniques.risks: If the claim is missed, gains on equipment transferred at market value are chargeable. Capital allowance balancing adjustments and VAT on the transfer need separate checks.
techniques.data_needed: Transfer date; tax year of transfer; asset values.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Deadline calculator: claim by the first anniversary of the 31 January following the tax year of transfer (2026-27 transfer: 31 January 2029, derived).

figures.2025-26 and earlier: Automatic relief; s162A election available to disapply
figures.2026-27: Claim required by the first anniversary of the 31 January following the tax year of transfer (e.g. transfer in 2026-27: claim by 31 January 2029, derived)
figures.2027-28: Claim required (same rule)

techniques.status: Law. FA 2026 (c.11) s39, Royal Assent 18 March 2026; applies to transfers on or after 6 April 2026 (s39(5)). TCGA s162 on legislation.gov.uk (revised to 23 Nov 2026) includes s162(1)(b) and s162(6); s162A omitted.
techniques.relevance: Procedural trap if the user incorporates the sole trade and its equipment from 2026-27.

techniques.name: Gift (hold-over) relief on business assets (TCGA 1992 s165)
techniques.summary: Applies when an individual disposes of a qualifying asset otherwise than by a bargain at arm's length (a transfer to a connected person or own company counts as not at arm's length). Transferor and transferee claim jointly (transferor alone for settlement trustees). Both the transferor's gain and the transferee's base cost are reduced by the held-over gain. Qualifying assets: (a) assets used in a trade carried on by the transferor, their personal company (at least 5% of votes) or a trading group member whose holding company is their personal company; (b) unlisted (AIM counts) trading company shares or shares in the personal company. Consideration exceeding the s38 cost is chargeable at once (s165(7)). No relief: gifts of shares to a company (s165(3)(ba)); non-resident transferee (s166) unless UK land (s167A); company controlled by connected non-residents (s167); where s260 applies; settlor-interested settlements (s169B, clawback s169C). Donee emigrating within 6 years triggers the held-over gain (s168). Restrictions for non-trade use (Sch 7 paras 5-6) and non-business assets (para 7). A sole trader can use it at incorporation to move chosen assets (e.g. goodwill or equipment) into the company at undervalue without meeting s162 conditions (follows from statute; not described in HMRC's manual).
techniques.conditions: Joint claim by transferor and transferee on form HS295, separately for each disposal. Not for share transfers to a company or companies controlled by connected non-residents.
techniques.risks: Restricted where the asset was not used in the trade throughout ownership or only partly used. Consideration above cost is taxed. The company inherits a low base cost. Undervalue sales need proper valuation.
techniques.data_needed: Asset cost, market value, consideration paid, business-use history.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Held-over gain = (market value - cost) less any excess of consideration over cost (taxed now); deferral value = held-over gain x CGT rate.

figures.2024-25: No monetary limits; the relief defers gains.
figures.2026-27: As above.
figures.2027-28: Budget 2026: Sch 7 para 7(2)(b) restriction formula for shares modernised from 6 April 2027 to include assets within the intangibles regime or SSE (Finance Bill 2026-27).

techniques.status: s165 is law for 2024-25 to 2026-27. The Sch 7 para 7(2)(b) change was announced at Budget 2025 (26 Nov 2025), published in draft 23 June 2026, confirmed at Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026) for Finance Bill 2026-27; applies to disposals on or after 6 April 2027; not enacted at 23 Nov 2026.
techniques.relevance: Alternative to s162 when incorporating but keeping some assets personally; only relevant where assets stand at a gain.

techniques.name: Capital allowances on incorporation: CAA 2001 s265 market value v s266 connected-party election
techniques.summary: On incorporation the company succeeds to the trade and the sole trader stops carrying it on, so CAA 2001 s265 applies (s265(1)(b), (1A)). For income tax the sole trade is treated as permanently discontinued (CA29030). Without an election: plant that passes to the company without being sold is treated as sold to it at market value (s265(2)-(3)). This gives a balancing charge or allowance in the final sole-trade period, with each item's disposal value capped at its original cost (s62). The company gets writing-down allowances only, with no AIA and no FYA (s265(4); CA29030). Because the deemed sale is between connected persons (ss213-214), the company's qualifying expenditure is capped at the trader's disposal value (s218(2)), so its WDA base is the lower of market value and the trader's original cost. Plant actually sold to the company: the sole trader's disposal value is the net sale price (s61 table item 1). The company gets no AIA or FYA (s217), and its qualifying expenditure is capped at that disposal value (s218(2)). With a joint s266 election: plant passes at a price that gives neither a balancing allowance nor a balancing charge (s267(2)), so pools transfer at their tax written-down value (CA29040). The company is treated as having done everything the sole trader did (s267(4)), and s265 does not apply (s266(7)). The election needs connected parties (for example, the trader controls the company), both within the UK tax charge on the profits, a company that is not a dual resident investing company, and notice to HMRC within 2 years of the succession (s266(1), (4), (5)). It is not available where s561 applies (s266(8)). Fixtures need a separate joint s198 election, for no more than the s266 amount (CA29040). Kit bought in the final sole-trade period gets no AIA (s38B general exclusion 1) and no FYA (s46 general exclusion 1). Cash basis, the default from 2024-25 unless the trader elects for GAAP accounts (ITTOIA 2005 ss24A, 25C; BIM72005): there are no capital allowances, charges or disposal values except for cars (CAA s1A(2)-(5)), so kit whose cost was deducted is not in a pool. Its actual sale proceeds are a trading receipt of the final period (ITTOIA s96A(3), (3I); BIM72020). If the trader stops using an item in the trade without disposing of it, its market value is the receipt (s96A(4)). s266 contains no cash-basis exclusion, so a connected cash-basis trader and company can still make the joint election. But no source opened settles what s267 then means for kit already deducted under the cash basis. HMRC's only guidance on s266 and the cash basis (BIM72068) covers the reverse case: a predecessor on accruals and a successor on the cash basis.
techniques.conditions: s266: predecessor and successor connected (s266(5): one is a body corporate and the other controls it, or connected under s575); both within the charge to UK tax on the profits of the activity; successor not a dual resident investing company; joint notice to an officer of HMRC within 2 years after the succession takes effect (s266(4)). The election can be made whether or not any plant is actually sold or transferred (s266(3)). Fixtures need a separate joint s198 election. s266 has no cash-basis exclusion, but its effect on kit already deducted under the cash basis is not settled (see figures_disputed). A trader who elects for GAAP accounts for the final tax year (ITTOIA s25C) leaves the cash basis. The kit then enters a pool at its unrelieved portion, usually nil (CAA s66A(4); BIM72073), and s265 or s266 applies to it in the usual way. Leaving the cash basis also brings the other change-of-basis adjustments for that year (ITTOIA Part 2 Chapter 17; BIM72070), so take advice first.
techniques.risks: If the 2-year deadline is missed, market value treatment applies. The company gets no AIA or FYA on kit taken over from the sole trade, whether it passes by election (s267(4): the company stands in the trader's shoes, with no new expenditure), by transfer without sale (s265(4)) or by sale (ss214, 217). The 40%/50% main-rate FYA also needs unused, not second-hand plant (s45U). New kit the company buys after incorporation qualifies in the normal way. Kit bought in the last sole-trade period gets neither AIA nor FYA, so time large purchases. An election is not always better: if market value is below the pool value, not electing gives a balancing allowance at the trader's income tax plus Class 4 rate. Cash basis: s96A taxes actual sale proceeds whatever is elected, and the effect of a s266 election on kit already deducted is not settled, so take advice before relying on one. Leaving the cash basis does not reverse earlier deductions, because the kit enters the pool at its unrelieved portion, usually nil (s66A(4); BIM72073). The sources opened do not settle how a gift of cash-basis kit to the company, with no proceeds, is treated under s96A, so record a sale at market value or take advice.
techniques.data_needed: Accounting basis of the sole trade (cash basis or accruals); for pooled assets, the tax written-down value of the main pool and any single-asset pools; for each item of kit, its original cost, market value at incorporation, purchase date, and whether it is bought or transferred and at what price; whether any kit was bought in the final sole-trade period; incorporation (succession) date, for the 2-year deadline; the trader's marginal income tax and Class 4 rate in the final period and the company's expected CT rate.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Accruals basis (pooled kit). Let base = sum over items of min(market value, original cost). Without an election: balancing figure = base - pool TWDV. A positive figure is a balancing charge taxed at the trader's income tax + Class 4 marginal rate in the final period; a negative figure is a balancing allowance. The company then claims main-rate WDAs on base (s218(2) with s62), at its CT rate. With an election: no balancing figure, and the company continues WDAs on the TWDV. The value of the election is roughly the trader's tax on the balancing charge minus the present value of the CT relief on the company's extra WDAs ((base - TWDV) x WDA rate x CT rate each year, on a reducing balance). Company WDA rate: 14% for CT chargeable periods beginning on or after 1 April 2026, with the hybrid rate for periods straddling that date (FA 2026 s28(2)(a), (3)-(6)). 12% is announced (not law) for periods beginning on or after 1 April 2027, again with a hybrid. Cash basis: the final-period receipt is the actual sale proceeds (market value where an item stops being used in the trade without a disposal), taxed at income tax + Class 4. The company claims WDAs only, on its connected-party cost capped at the lowest of market value and the trader's original cost (s218(3)). No saving can be computed for a s266 election on cash-basis kit, because its effect is not settled.

figures.2024-25: AIA £1,000,000 (s51A(5), F(No.2)A 2023 s8). Main-rate WDA 18%; special rate 6% (s104D). No AIA or FYA for the company on kit passing on the succession.
figures.2025-26: AIA £1,000,000. Main-rate WDA 18% for chargeable periods ending before 1 Apr 2026 (CT) / 6 Apr 2026 (IT). Straddling periods use a hybrid rate: X = 18 x BRD/CP + 14 x ARD/CP, rounded up to 2 decimal places (FA 2026 s28(3)-(6)). Special rate 6%. 40% main-rate FYA (s45U and the s52(3) table, inserted by FA 2026 s29, Royal Assent 18 Mar 2026) for expenditure from 1 Jan 2026 on unused, not second-hand, non-special-rate plant. Cars are excluded (s46 GE2), as is kit bought in the final period (GE1). It is not company-only, so sole traders can claim it, and plant for leasing can qualify (s46(4B)).
figures.2026-27: AIA £1,000,000. Main-rate WDA 14% (law, FA 2026 s28) for chargeable periods beginning on or after 1 Apr 2026 (CT) / 6 Apr 2026 (IT); hybrid for straddling periods (e.g. a sole trader's 1 Apr 2026-31 Mar 2027 period: 14.06%). Special rate 6%. Main-rate FYA 40% (law: s45U and the s52(3) table, with no end date). Announced, not law: 50% FYA for expenditure from 1 Jan 2027, so 1 Jan-5 Apr 2027 would fall in 2026-27; hybrid 14%/12% WDA for periods straddling 1 Apr 2027 (CT) / 6 Apr 2027 (IT).
figures.2027-28: Announced, not law (Budget 2026, 28 Oct 2026, OOTLAR para 1.42; HMRC policy paper 29 Oct 2026; to be legislated in Finance Bill 2026-27): main-rate WDA 12% for chargeable periods beginning on or after 1 Apr 2027 (CT) / 6 Apr 2027 (IT), with a hybrid rate for straddling periods; main-rate FYA 50% for expenditure from 1 Jan 2027. The policy paper says the measure aims to give greater upfront relief to unincorporated businesses. Law until enacted: 14% WDA and 40% FYA. AIA £1,000,000 and special rate 6% (no change announced; the policy paper says special rate stays at 6%).

figures_disputed: Cash-basis kit given to the company with no payment: the sources opened do not settle whether the ITTOIA s96A receipt is nil or market value. s96A(3F) counts actual proceeds; s96A(4) uses market value only where the trader stops using the asset without disposing of it.

Effect of a s266 election where the sole trade is on the cash basis. s266(1)-(8) has no cash-basis exclusion, and s1A(2)-(3) stops the trader getting allowances or bringing in disposal values (cars apart). But no source opened says what s267(2) and (4) then give the company for kit already deducted under the cash basis, because BIM72068 covers only a predecessor on accruals and a successor on the cash basis. Do not compute it; refer to an adviser.
techniques.status: Law: CAA 2001 ss1A, 38B, 46, 52(3), 61-62, 66A, 213-218 and 265-267; AIA £1m (s51A(5), F(No.2)A 2023 s8(2)(a)); special rate 6% (s104D); 14% main WDA (FA 2026 c.11 s28); 40% main-rate FYA from 1 Jan 2026, with no end date (ss45U-45V and s52(3), FA 2026 s29; Royal Assent 18 Mar 2026). ITTOIA 2005: ss24A and 25C (cash basis the default from 2024-25; GAAP election) and s96A (cash-basis capital receipts). HMRC guidance: CA29030, CA29040, BIM72005, BIM72020, BIM72068, BIM72070, BIM72073. Announced only (Budget 2026, 28 Oct 2026, OOTLAR para 1.42; HMRC policy paper 29 Oct 2026; Finance Bill 2026-27, not yet enacted): 12% main WDA from 1 Apr 2027 (CT) / 6 Apr 2027 (IT) and 50% FYA for expenditure from 1 Jan 2027.
techniques.relevance: This matters only if the technician incorporates. On the cash basis (the default from 2024-25 unless they elect for accruals), kit is not pooled, so its sale price to the company is taxed as income of the last sole-trade period and the company gets writing-down allowances only, on the lower of market value and original cost; the s266 election clearly helps with a car or with kit pooled under accruals accounting, but its effect on cash-basis kit is not settled, so take advice before relying on it.

techniques.name: Cessation of the sole trade on incorporation, after basis period reform
techniques.summary: From 2024-25 trade profits are taxed on the tax-year basis (ITTOIA s7(1) amended; ss7A-7D inserted by FA 2022 Sch 1). Periods of account not matching the tax year are apportioned by days (or another reasonable consistent measure); 31 March and 1-4 April year ends are not apportioned. ITTOIA Pt 2 Ch 15 (including s202 final year and s205 overlap relief) was omitted for 2024-25 onwards; all overlap relief was given in 2023-24, so none remains for a later cessation. Transition profits are spread 20% a year over 2023-24 to 2026-27 with the balance in 2027-28 (FA 2022 Sch 1 para 72). On permanent cessation (which incorporation usually is) the whole unspread balance is charged in the year of cessation (para 72(5)-(6), BIM81310). Acceleration election (para 73) deadline: first anniversary of the normal SA filing date (31 Jan 2027 for 2024-25; 31 Jan 2028 for 2025-26; 31 Jan 2029 for 2026-27). Transition profits are excluded from net income for benefits/allowances (para 75) but the tax is still computed as if included, so the PA taper and higher rates bite.
techniques.conditions: Only relevant if the trader had transition profits in 2023-24 (a non-5 April/31 March year end before the reform).
techniques.risks: Incorporating in 2024-25 to 2026-27 can bunch unspread transition profits into one year and push them into higher-rate bands. Late accounting date rules do not apply in the year of cessation.
techniques.data_needed: Whether the user had transition profits in 2023-24 and how much remains unspread; proposed cessation date; other income in the cessation year.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Unspread balance charged on cessation = transition profit x (1 - 0.2 x number of spreading years already taxed). Extra tax = marginal-rate difference from bunching vs normal spreading.

figures.2024-25: Ceasing in 2024-25: illustratively, of £20,000 of transition profits, £16,000 is charged (extrapolation from BIM81310).
figures.2025-26: BIM81310 Example 20: transition profits £20,000, cessation 12 Feb 2026: £4,000 taxed in 2023-24, £4,000 in 2024-25, £12,000 balance in 2025-26.
figures.2026-27: Ceasing in 2026-27: balance after three 20% slices, i.e. £8,000 of £20,000 (extrapolation).
figures.2027-28: Fifth spreading year: ceasing does not accelerate, as the final 20% is due anyway.

techniques.status: Law. FA 2022 (c.3) Sch 1 paras 2, 3, 8, 61(1) (effect from 6.4.2024); spreading and cessation para 72; acceleration para 73; tax computation para 75; tax years 2023-24 to 2027-28. Later announced changes could not be checked (search budget ran out).
techniques.relevance: Check for unspread transition profits before choosing an incorporation date.

techniques.name: Trade losses carried forward after incorporation (ITA 2007 s86)
techniques.summary: Where an individual transfers a trade to a company for consideration wholly or mainly in shares, unused carry-forward trade losses can be set against income from the company (dividends, salary, interest, rent), treated as profits of the trade (s86(2), (5); BIM85060). No monetary cap; the s24A cap does not apply. Conditions: in the transfer year, beneficial ownership of the allotted shares and the company carrying on the trade throughout from transfer to the next 5 April; in later years, both throughout the whole tax year (s86(3)-(4)). Set-off order (ss83-84) is year by year with no skipping, so losses can be wasted against income the PA or dividend allowance would have covered. For 2024-25 to 2026-27 within a year the general s25(2) rule applies (greatest tax reduction). From 2027-28, s25(3A) (FA 2026 s6) requires Step 2/3 reliefs to be set against non-property/savings/dividend income first, i.e. salary before dividends.
techniques.conditions: Consideration wholly or mainly shares; individual keeps beneficial ownership; company carries on the trade throughout the relevant periods.
techniques.risks: Lost if shares are sold or the company stops the trade. HMRC practice (not law, BIM85060): relief not refused while shares representing more than 80% of the consideration are retained. Losses stay with the individual and cannot be used by the company.
techniques.data_needed: Unused trade losses carried forward; consideration split; income received from the company each year.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Tax saved = min(loss remaining, income from company in the year) x marginal rate on that income, taking care that losses absorbed against income otherwise covered by allowances save nothing.

figures.current: No monetary cap stated in s86.

techniques.status: Law: ITA 2007 s86 in force with no outstanding effects (checked 24 Nov 2026). FA 2026 s6 inserted ITA s25(3A) for 2027-28 onwards. HMRC's 80% retention is practice (BIM85060), not statute.
techniques.relevance: Only if the sole trade has unused losses, e.g. after a heavy equipment year; structure the transfer for shares.

techniques.name: VAT on incorporation: transfer of a going concern (VAT Notice 700/9)
techniques.summary: If the business is transferred as a going concern, the transfer is 'not treated as a supply' and no VAT is charged on the assets. TOGC rules are compulsory ('You cannot choose to opt out'). Form VAT68 lets the company keep the sole trader's VAT number, but the company then takes on liability for VAT outstanding on that registration and the seller loses rights to repayments.
techniques.conditions: Assets sold as part of a business; buyer intends to carry on the same kind of business; no significant break in trading; if the seller is VAT-registered the buyer must be registered or required to register.
techniques.risks: Notice 700/9 does not address incorporation specifically (HMRC treats the company as buyer; worth confirming). Taking over the VAT number takes over historic VAT liabilities.
techniques.data_needed: VAT registration status; value of assets transferred; whether the VAT number is to be transferred.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: VAT not charged = 20% of asset transfer value (cash-flow effect; usually recoverable anyway by a VAT-registered company).

figures.current: VAT registration threshold £90,000 (see vat-registration-threshold).

techniques.status: Law: VAT (Special Provisions) Order 1995 (SI 1995/1268) art 5; VATA 1994 s49; VAT Regulations 1995 reg 6. Notice 700/9 section 10 (VAT68) has force of law. Notice last updated 23 May 2025.
techniques.relevance: Only if the technician is VAT-registered when incorporating.

techniques.name: Rule of thumb: profit level at which a company beats sole trading (2024-25 to 2027-28)
techniques.summary: No current official rule of thumb exists, so the decision must be calculated. The OTS (closed 2023) found in 2019 (para 3.17, 2018-19 rates) that 'the slight advantage for companies at most income bands would be outweighed by the additional administration costs of running a company'. Illustrative calculation from GOV.UK rates (rUK taxpayer; single-director company; salary £12,570; no Employment Allowance; all post-CT profit paid as dividends in the same year; no pension, student loan or other income; running costs excluded): on full extraction the company saves only in a narrow band, and from 2026-27 (dividends 10.75%/35.75%) essentially nil. Remaining advantages: retention (defers dividend tax), employer pension contributions (salary-sacrifice NIC cap of £2,000 from 2029-30 does not affect direct employer contributions), and a spouse's outright ordinary shareholding (s626). Exit costs are rising: BADR 14% (2025-26), 18% from 6 April 2026; lifetime limit to £500,000 from 6 April 2027 (announced).
techniques.conditions: Recalculate with actual figures: retained v extracted profit, spouse's position, pension contributions, IR35 status of each engagement, Scottish residence, student loans, running costs (Companies House £50 a year plus accountancy and software).
techniques.risks: Not official figures. Inside-IR35 income removes the advantage. Retention is deferral, not permanent saving. The distributions reform (April 2028) content is set out in the distributions-framework-reform-2028 item; do not overstate it.
techniques.data_needed: Annual profit forecast; how much the user needs to draw; spouse income; pension plans; client IR35 profile.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Compute sole-trader tax (IT + Class 4) v company total (employer NIC on salary above ST + CT on profit after salary and employer NIC + dividend tax on extracted dividends), using the rates block; add running costs; model retention separately.

figures.2024-25: Company (salary £12,570; employer NIC 13.8% above £9,100) beats sole trader only for profits of about £52,430-£73,680 (max saving about £1,140 at about £59,590), plus a tiny band of about £122,900-£127,680 from the PA taper. At £80,000: sole trader £22,289 v company £22,876 (tax).
figures.2025-26: Company ahead only for profits of about £55,480-£70,250; max saving about £759 at about £60,250. At £60,000: sole trader £13,889 v company £13,169. At £100,000: sole trader £30,689 v company £33,457 (full extraction).
figures.2026-27: Company ahead only at about £60,150-£60,500 (max about £15): effectively no full-extraction advantage. Retention example (extract only up to £50,270 total income): at £100,000 profit, current-year tax £24,253 v sole trader £30,689, with £29,476 left in the company after CT and taxed on later extraction.
figures.2027-28: Rates unchanged per Budget 2026 Annex A, so as 2026-27. Running costs and accountancy fees (null) reduce any saving further.

techniques.status: Illustrative calculation, not official. 2024-25 to 2026-27 rates are law; 2026-27 dividend rates set by FA 2026 s4. Much of 2027-28 already law (PA/BRL freeze FA 2021 s5 extended by FA 2026 s10; dividend rates FA 2026 s4; CT FY2027 FA 2026 ss11-12). Announced only (Budget 2026, 28 Oct 2026): 2027-28 income tax charge (Finance Bill 2026-27 measure 1.3), NIC uprating (early 2027 SI), BADR limit cut (6 Apr 2027), distributions reform (Apr 2028).
techniques.relevance: For this technician, incorporation rarely pays on tax alone if all profit is drawn; the app's structure calculator should model retention, not just full extraction.

techniques.name: Company vs sole trader: combined rates and when a company actually saves tax
techniques.summary: With all profit drawn every year, a company usually does not beat sole trading in 2024-25 to 2026-27 after the 2025 employer NIC changes and the 2026 dividend rise. Exception in 2024-25 and 2025-26 just above the higher-rate threshold: CT is deducted before the dividend is tested against £50,270, keeping more in the basic-rate dividend band. Salary £12,570 plus dividends: company ahead by up to about £1,130 for profits of about £52.5k-£73.5k (2024-25), and up to about £760 for £55.5k-£70k (2025-26). From 2026-27 the gain disappears apart from about £15 near £60k. A company otherwise saves mainly by retention (19%; 26.5% marginal £50k-£250k; 25% above), employer pension contributions, or smoothing dividends into low-income years. Retained profits stay taxable when extracted.
techniques.conditions: Derived figures assume single director-shareholder, no Employment Allowance, no other income, England, no associated companies, profits taxed in the same year, no accountancy/payroll/Companies House costs. Partial extraction is a deferral; retained profits are taxed on later payment (dividend rates or, on qualifying liquidation, possibly CGT/BADR subject to the TAAR).
techniques.risks: IR35 can remove the dividend route. Company money belongs to the company; drawing without a dividend or salary creates a director's loan (s455). Shares to a spouse are subject to the settlements rules. s162 relief must be claimed for transfers from 6 Apr 2026.
techniques.data_needed: Profit; drawings needed; IR35 status of engagements; spouse shareholding; pension intentions.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Combined rate on profit drawn as dividend = 1 - (1 - CT rate) x (1 - dividend rate). Compare with sole trader 26% basic / 42% higher. Then add running costs.

figures.2024-25: Derived combined rate: basic 26.0875% (19% CT then 8.75%) v sole trader 26% (20% + 6%); higher 46.3375% (19% CT), 50.3125% (25%), 51.30625% (26.5% marginal) v sole trader 42%. Profit £80,000, full extraction, salary £12,570: company net £57,124.15 v sole trader £57,711.40.
figures.2025-26: Combined rates as 2024-25. Profit £80,000 full extraction: company £56,804.40 v sole trader £57,711.40. Partial extraction (salary £12,570 plus £37,700 dividends): tax now £18,208.54 v sole trader £22,288.60, with £14,776.46 retained and still taxable later.
figures.2026-27: Derived combined rate: basic 27.7075% (19% CT then 10.75%); higher 47.9575% (19%), 51.8125% (25%), 52.77625% (26.5%) v sole trader 26% / 42%. Profit £80,000 full extraction: company £55,764.87 v sole trader £57,711.40. Partial extraction (salary £12,570 plus £37,700 dividends): tax now £18,952.54 (employer NIC £1,135.50 + CT £13,818.04 + dividend tax £3,999.00) v sole trader £22,288.60 (income tax £19,432.00 + Class 4 £2,856.60); £14,776.46 retained.
figures.2027-28: Dividend rates unchanged at 10.75% / 35.75% / 39.35%; CT 19% / 25%; NIC thresholds frozen; comparison as 2026-27 before admin costs.

techniques.status: Rates 2024-25 to 2026-27 are law; 2026-27 dividend rise FA 2026 s4 (2026-27 and subsequent years); CT FY2026 FA 2025 ss13-14 and FY2027 FA 2026 ss11-12. Still to come for 2027-28: income tax charge and main rates (Finance Bill 2026-27, OOTLAR 1.3), NIC limits (OOTLAR 2.1, legislation early 2027). Announced, not law: BADR limit £500k from 6 Apr 2027 (OOTLAR 1.33); distributions reform from Apr 2028 (OOTLAR 2.15). All monetary outputs are derived.
techniques.relevance: Core answer to 'should I incorporate?': revisit when about £15,000+ a year can be left in the business or profits approach the £100,000 taper.

techniques.name: Choosing the director's salary: secondary threshold vs LEL vs primary threshold
techniques.summary: In a one-director company with no Employment Allowance, each £1 of salary between the ST and PT costs employer NIC (15%; 13.8% in 2024-25) but no employee NIC, is tax-free if the PA is otherwise unused, and is CT-deductible with the NIC. Salary beats a dividend for that slice whenever the CT rate exceeds n/(1+n): 13.04% at 15%, 12.13% at 13.8%. As CT is at least 19% when profits are taxable, salary at the PT (£12,570) is generally optimal with no other income. Above the PT, salary bears 20% IT + 8% employee NIC + 15% employer NIC, so dividends are cheaper.
techniques.conditions: RTI payroll; directors use an annual earnings period. Assumes no other income using the PA, England bands, no student loan, no Employment Allowance, company taxable profit at least equal to the salary. Salary at or above the LEL gives a State Pension qualifying year (SSCBA s6A).
techniques.risks: If the company has little or no taxable profit the CT saving disappears and salary above the ST simply costs 15% NIC. Other income using the PA changes the answer. IR35 deemed payments override this planning. Recompute every year.
techniques.data_needed: Company profit; director's other income; Employment Allowance eligibility; whether a qualifying year is wanted.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Net gain per £1 of salary between ST and PT v dividend = (1 - d) x [1 - (1 + n)(1 - c)], d = marginal dividend rate, n = employer NIC rate, c = marginal CT rate. Example 2026-27, c = 19%, d = 10.75%: 0.8925 x 0.0685 = 6.11p per £1, so £462.80 on the £7,570 slice. With Employment Allowance available, n is effectively 0.

figures.2024-25: ST £9,100, LEL £6,396, PT £12,570. Salary £9,100: no NIC, qualifying year. Salary £12,570: employer NIC £478.86 (13.8% x £3,470). Derived (pre-salary profit £50,000, all post-tax profit as dividend, England, no other income): salary £9,100 net £39,677.59; £12,570 net £39,925.26; sole trader £40,268.20.
figures.2027-28: Announced: ST £5,000, LEL £6,916, PT £12,570; employer NIC at LEL £287.40, at PT £1,135.50 (derived).

techniques.status: Law for 2024-25 to 2026-27. 2027-28 NIC thresholds announced at Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026), awaiting regulations; LEL £6,916 derived from £133/week. Net-income figures are derived, not HMRC-published.
techniques.relevance: Default salary decision if the user incorporates: normally £12,570; LEL minimum for a qualifying year; £5,000 avoids all NIC but loses the qualifying year.

techniques.name: Employment Allowance: single-director company exclusion
techniques.summary: A company cannot claim the Employment Allowance (EA) for a tax year if every payment of earnings for which it is the secondary contributor goes to the same employee who is a director when each payment is made (NICA 2014 s2(4A), from 6 April 2016, SI 2016/344). GOV.UK: the director 'must not be the only employee liable for secondary Class 1 National Insurance'. EA can never be set against NIC on an IR35 deemed employment payment (s2(4)). Per NIM06545 the company becomes eligible once another employee (not the director) is paid at or above the ST, or more than one director is paid above it; two directors where only one is above the threshold are still excluded. If the qualifying employee leaves, EA can be used for the rest of that year but not the next unless another qualifying person is employed. Main-purpose anti-avoidance (s2(10)-(13)); one claim per connected group.
techniques.conditions: Applies only to bodies corporate where the sole earner above the ST is a director.
techniques.risks: Paying a family member above the ST only to unlock EA must be genuine work at a commercial rate or it will be challenged (wholly and exclusively; settlements; s2(10) anti-avoidance).
techniques.data_needed: Number of employees and directors paid above the ST.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Solo director salary £12,570 costs employer NIC 15% x (12,570 - 5,000) = £1,135.50 in 2025-26 and 2026-27 with no EA.

figures.2024-25: EA £5,000; ST £9,100/year (£175/week); employer rate 13.8%.
figures.2027-28: EA £10,500; ST £96/week; 15% (Budget 2026 Annex A).

techniques.status: Law since 6 April 2016 (NICA 2014 s2(4A), SI 2016/344). EA £10,500 and 15% in force from 6 April 2025 (NIC (Secondary Class 1 Contributions) Act 2025). 2027-28 figures announced in Budget 2026 Annex A (28 Oct 2026).
techniques.relevance: Explains the £1,135.50 employer NIC cost of a solo director's £12,570 salary.

techniques.name: Employment Allowance (and the single-director exclusion)
techniques.summary: Reduces an eligible employer's secondary Class 1 NIC bill by up to a fixed annual amount. Rose from £5,000 to £10,500 from 6 April 2025, when the £100,000 employer-NIC eligibility limit (and State aid conditions) was removed. A company cannot claim if all earnings go to one person who is a director (s2(4A)). A sole trader employing a spouse is not excluded by that rule.
techniques.conditions: Not if all earnings paid by a company go to one director. One company per connected group, one payroll. Deemed IR35 payments excluded (s2(4)). Public authorities and domestic employers (other than care and support workers) cannot claim.
techniques.risks: Main-purpose anti-avoidance (s2(10)-(12)). Employing a spouse or relative only to unlock EA risks this rule; pay must be commercial for real work. Does not reduce employee NIC.
techniques.data_needed: Employer secondary Class 1 liability for the year; employees on payroll.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Saving = min(EA cap, employer secondary Class 1 for the year).
