figures.2024-25: £5,000 per year. Employers with secondary Class 1 at or above £100,000 in the previous year could not claim (NICA 2014 s2(4B)-(4G)).
figures.2025-26: £10,500; £100,000 limit and State aid conditions removed from 6 April 2025 (NICSCCA 2025 s3).
figures.2027-28: £10,500 (current law NICA 2014 s1(2)(a); Budget 2026 Annex A).

techniques.status: Law. NICA 2014 s1(2)(a) £10,500 as substituted by NICSCCA 2025 s3(2) from 6 April 2025; s2(4A) from 6 April 2016; ss(4B)-(4G) omitted from 6 April 2025. Confirmed in Budget 2026 OOTLAR Annex A (28 Oct 2026).
techniques.relevance: A one-person company gets no EA; a genuine employee paid above £5,000 unlocks up to £10,500 of relief.

techniques.name: Modernising the distributions framework (from April 2028)
techniques.summary: Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026) and HMRC's summary of responses (same day; consultation 23 Jun - 14 Sep 2026) confirm all seven proposals to modernise taxation of distributions and repayments of capital to individuals and trusts, so transactions are taxed consistently 'regardless of legal form, company residence or transaction structure' and to 'reduce opportunities for well-advised taxpayers to structure how profits are taken out'. Strands: (1) after a share reorganisation (e.g. new holding company), capital treatment on buyback or reduction of capital limited to capital originally subscribed (listed companies out of scope); (2) non-UK company payments and loans aligned with UK rules, including a temporary s455-like charge on loans to individuals; (3) Purchase of Own Shares relief modernised with mechanical conditions and tranche payments; (4) statutory demerger relief expanded; (5) Transactions in Securities rules reformed, possibly brought into self-assessment. Unchanged: dividend and CGT rates, ordinary dividends, CGT on ordinary share sales; genuine changes of ownership including family succession keep capital treatment.
techniques.conditions: Mainly affects shareholders who control how profits are paid out.
techniques.risks: Capital-treatment exit routes for retained profits (e.g. buybacks via a holding company) may be taxed as income from 2028. Treatment of liquidations and MVLs not stated; detail not yet published.
techniques.data_needed: Whether the user has or plans a company with retained profits.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Not a saving. Do not assume retained profits can later be extracted at CGT/BADR rates.

figures.2027-28: Draft legislation for technical consultation in 2027. Effective April 2028 (2028-29).

techniques.status: Announced at Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026) with HMRC consultation outcome the same day. Draft legislation 2027; changes start 6 April 2028. Not law.
techniques.relevance: A company's advantage depends on retaining and later extracting cheaply; this reform may close capital-treatment exits.

techniques.name: Distributions framework reform (April 2028) and participator-payments reporting (dropped)
techniques.summary: Budget 2026 confirmed the distributions reform (draft legislation 2027, effect from April 2028). Separately, proposed new reporting requirements for close company payments to participators (consulted March - June 2026) will not be implemented 'at this time' (OOTLAR 2.44).
techniques.conditions: Detail in draft legislation in 2027.
techniques.risks: What counts as a distribution, and possibly s455 interactions, may change from April 2028; re-check company extraction planning then.
techniques.data_needed: None now; watch item.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Not applicable.

figures.2027-28: No change yet
figures.2028-29: Distributions framework changes from April 2028 (details not yet published: null)

techniques.status: Announced, not law. Budget 2026 OOTLAR (28 Oct 2026, updated 5 Nov 2026) para 2.15 (distributions) and para 2.44 (participator reporting dropped for now). Technical consultation 2027; commencement intended from April 2028 (exact day not given).
techniques.relevance: Watch item for any company structure.

techniques.name: Business Asset Disposal Relief rate and limit changes; proposed Founders' Relief
techniques.summary: BADR reduces CGT on qualifying disposals of a business or shares in a personal trading company. Rate 10% to 14% to 18%; lifetime limit falls to £500,000 from 6 April 2027 (announced). Budget 2026 also proposed Founders' Relief: 10% CGT on up to £10m of lifetime gains on qualifying share disposals from 6 April 2027, aimed at founders of and early investors in high-growth companies (see founders-relief).
techniques.conditions: BADR: personal company (5% or more of shares, votes and economic rights), trading, officer or employee, for 2 years. BADR excluded on goodwill transferred to one's own close company (s169LA).
techniques.risks: With BADR at the 18% basic CGT rate, the company exit advantage is much smaller. Founders' Relief is unlikely to fit a one-person service company. Anti-phoenix TAAR and distributions rules apply.
techniques.data_needed: Expected gain on disposal; prior BADR claims.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: BADR saving = qualifying gain (within lifetime limit) x (24% - BADR rate) where the gain would otherwise be higher-rate; nil where it would be taxed at 18% anyway from 2026-27.

figures.2024-25: BADR 10%; lifetime limit £1m.
figures.2026-27: BADR 18%; £1m.
figures.2027-28: BADR 18%; lifetime limit £500,000 for disposals from 6 April 2027 (announced, with transitional rules for earlier contracts). Founders' Relief proposed at 10% up to £10m (consultation closes 30 Nov 2026).

techniques.status: BADR rates are law (FA 2025 s8 amending TCGA s169N(3)); £1m limit law (s169N(4)-(4A), FA 2020). £500,000 limit announced at Budget 2026 (OOTLAR 28 Oct 2026) for Finance Bill 2026-27; not law. Founders' Relief proposed: technical consultation 28 Oct - 30 Nov 2026; legislation by amendment to Finance Bill 2026-27 for disposals on or after 6 April 2027.
techniques.relevance: Weakens the 'retain then exit cheaply' argument for a PSC.

techniques.name: Business Asset Disposal Relief: rates and lifetime limit
techniques.summary: BADR taxes qualifying gains on selling or closing a business or selling shares in a personal trading company at a reduced CGT rate up to a lifetime limit. 14% from 6 April 2025; 18% from 6 April 2026; lifetime limit cut from £1m to £500,000 for disposals on or after 6 April 2027 (announced). From 2026-27 BADR equals the basic CGT rate, so it only benefits gains otherwise taxed at 24%.
techniques.conditions: Sole trader/partner: owned the business at least 2 years up to the sale; on closure, assets disposed of within 3 years. Shares: for 2 years, employee or officer, trading company (or holding company of trading group), personal company (at least 5% of shares and votes plus 5% of profits and assets or of sale proceeds). Associated disposals qualify. Must be claimed.
techniques.risks: MVL then restarting the same trade within 2 years can turn the distribution into income (ITTOIA s396B; see winding-up-taar). Significant cash or investments can taint trading status. Lifetime limit counts all earlier claims.
techniques.data_needed: Gains, ownership periods, prior BADR used.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Saving = min(gain, remaining lifetime limit) x (24% - 18%) from 2026-27 for gains above the basic-rate band.

figures.2024-25: 10% (disposals on or before 5 April 2025); lifetime limit £1 million
figures.2026-27: 18% (from 6 April 2026; TCGA s169N(3)); lifetime limit £1 million
figures.2027-28: 18%; lifetime limit £500,000 for disposals on or after 6 April 2027 (announced; Finance Bill 2026-27, transitional rules for contracts before 6 April 2027 not completed)
figures.comparison: Main CGT rates 2026-27 and 2027-28: 18% basic, 24% higher; annual exempt amount £3,000.

techniques.status: Rates law: TCGA s169N(3) 18% (FA 2025 s8(4),(6)); current to 23 Nov 2026. £1m limit law (FA 2020 Sch 3). £500,000 announced at Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026; HMRC Agent Update 149; TIIN 29 Oct 2026); Finance Bill 2026-27 (OOTLAR 1.33); not yet law.
techniques.relevance: On retirement, sale of business or kit, or winding up a future company; plan large gains before 6 April 2027 if over £500,000 (unlikely).

techniques.name: New CGT Founders' Relief (from 6 April 2027)
techniques.summary: Announced at Budget 2026: 10% CGT on qualifying disposals of shares or securities up to a £10m lifetime limit per individual, for disposals on or after 6 April 2027, reduced by any BADR or Investors' Relief claimed from 6 April 2027. Proposed conditions (TIIN and HMT technical consultation): individual held at least 25% of ordinary share capital (with matching votes and economic rights) when the trade or preparation began; held the shares at least 5 years; UK resident at least 5 continuous tax years. Company: in UK CT scope with substantial UK presence for 5 periods; trading company still carrying on the original trade; not an EIS-excluded trade; turnover at least £10m and at least 15 qualifying full-time employees (35+ hours a week, at least NMW; directors, contract and agency workers excluded) in the period before disposal; at least 2 of 3 tests: 25% compound turnover growth over 3 periods (from at least £10m), 25% compound headcount growth over 3 periods (from at least 15), at least £1.5m qualifying R&D spend in 3 years. Claimed via SA with a supplementary form; TAARs planned; withdrawn with interest if an R&D claim fails.
techniques.conditions: Under consultation (closes 30 Nov 2026); added to Finance Bill 2026-27 by amendment.
techniques.risks: A one-person events-technician company cannot qualify (£10m turnover, 15 employees). Do not plan around it.
techniques.data_needed: None for this user.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Treat as not available to this user.

figures.2026-27: Not applicable
figures.2027-28: 10% rate; £10 million lifetime limit (announced)

techniques.status: Announced at Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026); consultation closes 30 Nov 2026; to be legislated by amendment to Finance Bill 2026-27; not law at 23 Nov 2026.
techniques.relevance: Low; only for a scalable production company with outside investment.

techniques.name: Corporation tax: small profits rate, main rate, limits and marginal relief fraction
techniques.summary: Companies pay 19% on augmented profits up to the lower limit (£50,000), 25% above the upper limit (£250,000), and the main rate reduced by marginal relief in between. Unchanged since FY2023 and enacted to FY2027. CT runs by financial year (1 April - 31 March); the tax-year keys map to the financial year starting 1 April in that tax year.
techniques.conditions: UK-resident company, not a close investment-holding company (CTA 2010 s18B(1)(b), s18N). Limits use augmented profits (taxable total profits plus exempt distributions from non-group companies); reduced for periods under 12 months and divided by (1 + number of associated companies). Straddling periods are apportioned, but rates are identical FY2023-FY2027.
techniques.risks: Splitting a business across companies does not multiply the £50,000 band (associated companies). A CIC pays 25% on all profits. Retained profits are taxed again on extraction, so the low rate is a deferral.
techniques.data_needed: Company augmented profits; period length; number of associated companies.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: CT = 19% x A if A <= L; 25% x A if A > U; else 25% x N - 3/200 x (U - A) x N/A (see ct-marginal-relief-formula).

figures.2024-25: FY2024 (1 Apr 2024 - 31 Mar 2025): small profits rate 19% (augmented profits up to £50,000); main rate 25% (above £250,000); lower limit £50,000; upper limit £250,000; standard marginal relief fraction 3/200
figures.2028-29: FY2028: 25% and 19% announced at Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026) for Finance Bill 2026-27; Annex A shows £50,000 / £250,000 and 3/200.

techniques.status: Law FY2023-FY2027 (FY2026: FA 2025 ss13-14; FY2027: FA 2026 ss11-12, 18 March 2026). FY2028 announced (OOTLAR 1.38), not law.
techniques.relevance: Core inputs for any incorporate-or-not calculation; marginal rate 26.5% between £50,000 and £250,000.

techniques.name: Corporation tax marginal relief formula and the 26.5% marginal rate
techniques.summary: Where augmented profits (A) fall between the limits, CT is charged at 25% then reduced by marginal relief = F x (U - A) x (N / A), F = 3/200, U = upper limit, N = taxable total profits. This gives an effective 26.5% on each pound between £50,000 and £250,000.
techniques.conditions: Only where A exceeds the lower limit and does not exceed the upper limit (CTA 2010 s18B); U and L adjusted for associates and short periods first.
techniques.risks: Calculators must use augmented profits for the band test. Each extra deductible pound (salary, employer pension, capital allowances) in the band saves 26.5%, so timing deductions into high-profit periods is valuable.
techniques.data_needed: Taxable total profits; exempt distributions; associated companies; period length.

figures.current: CT at exactly £50,000 = £9,500; at £250,000 = £62,500; the £200,000 difference bears £53,000, a 26.5% marginal rate (HMRC CTM03925). Worked example (derived, no associates, 12-month period, no exempt distributions, profits £80,000): 25% x £80,000 = £20,000 less 3/200 x £170,000 = £2,550, so CT = £17,450 (effective 21.8125%). HMRC example: profits £90,000 plus £8,000 exempt distributions gives MR £2,094 and CT £20,406.

techniques.status: Law. CTA 2010 s18B (formula) and s18D (limits), inserted by FA 2021 Sch 1 para 3 from FY2023. Rates: FY2024 F(No.2)A 2023 ss5-6; FY2025 F(No.2)A 2024 ss12-13; FY2026 FA 2025 ss13-14; FY2027 FA 2026 ss11-12. ss18B and 18D up to date to 21 Nov 2026.
techniques.relevance: Needed for exact CT once company profits pass £50,000; shows why pension contributions and kit spending are worth most in that band.

techniques.name: Associated companies: sharing the £50,000 and £250,000 limits
techniques.summary: If a company has associated companies in an accounting period, the lower and upper limits are divided by (N + 1), N = number of associated companies. Companies are associated if one controls the other or both are under the control of the same person(s) ('control' per CTA 2010 ss450-451).
techniques.conditions: Associated for any part of the period counts (s18E(1)); companies with no trade or business in the period (or the associated part) are ignored (s18E(3)); certain passive holding companies treated as not carrying on business (s18F); associates' rights (spouse, relatives) attributed only where there is 'substantial commercial interdependence' (s18G); fixed-rate preference shares and certain loan-creditor links ignored (ss18H-18I).
techniques.risks: A second company for equipment hire under the technician's control is associated: each gets £25,000 / £125,000, so splitting saves no CT. A spouse's separate company is not usually associated unless there is substantial commercial interdependence. Dormant companies do not count.
techniques.data_needed: Other companies the user (or associates, where interdependent) controls.

figures.current: 1 associate: £25,000 / £125,000; 2 associates: £16,666.67 / £83,333.33; 3 associates: £12,500 / £62,500 (HMRC example). Limits also reduced proportionately for periods under 12 months (s18D(4)).
figures.2024-25: same rule
figures.2026-27: same rule
figures.2027-28: same rule (no change announced)

techniques.status: Law. CTA 2010 Part 3A ss18A-18N (FA 2021 Sch 1 para 3), effect for FY2023 onwards. Corporate Tax Roadmap (30 Oct 2024) commits to retaining SPR and marginal relief for this Parliament.
techniques.relevance: Matters if the user considers separate hire and labour companies, or a family member's company that trades with his.

techniques.name: Dividend allowance and dividend tax rates (rise from 6 April 2026)
techniques.summary: Dividends above the allowance are taxed at the ordinary, upper and additional rates according to the band they fall in; dividends are the top slice of income. From 6 April 2026 ordinary and upper rates rose 2 points; additional unchanged.
techniques.conditions: The £500 allowance is a 0% band that still uses up the basic-rate band. Dividend rates apply UK-wide (incl. Scotland). Unused PA covers dividends at 0%. From 6 April 2027 reliefs and allowances are set first against income other than property, savings and dividends (ITA s25(3A)). Dividends must be lawful distributions of profits.
techniques.risks: The 2026-27 rise makes full extraction worse than sole trading at basic and higher rates. Spouse/children shareholdings can be caught by the settlements rules. s455 rate is tied to the upper rate and also rose to 35.75%.
techniques.data_needed: Salary and other income; dividends paid.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Dividend tax = (dividends in each band - unused allowance) x band rate, after PA and dividend allowance.

figures.2024-25: Dividend allowance £500; ordinary 8.75%; upper 33.75%; additional 39.35%
figures.2027-28: £500; 10.75%; 35.75%; 39.35% (current law; Budget 2026 Annex A confirms)

techniques.status: Law. ITA 2007 s8 amended by FA 2026 (c.11) s4 (18 Mar 2026) for 2026-27 and later years. £500 allowance ITA s13A (FA 2023 s7) from 2024-25. ITA s25(3A) (FA 2026 s6(6),(8)) from 2027-28. Announced only: distributions reform from 6 Apr 2028; ACT abolished from 1 Apr 2031.
techniques.relevance: From 2026-27 a basic-rate director pays a combined 27.7075% (19% CT then 10.75%) v 26% as a sole trader.

techniques.name: Class 1 employee (primary) NIC: LEL, primary threshold, UEL and rates
techniques.summary: Employees (including directors) pay primary Class 1 above the PT, at 8% up to the UEL and 2% above. Earnings between the LEL and the PT bear no NIC but build State Pension qualifying years (SSCBA s6A).
techniques.conditions: Directors use an annual earnings period (SS(C)R 2001 reg 8): standard annual or alternative method (NIM12003). Married women's reduced rate 1.85% between PT and UEL.
techniques.risks: Lump-sum director pay does not avoid NIC. Salary below the LEL earns no qualifying year.
techniques.data_needed: Director/employee annual earnings.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Employee NIC = 8% x (min(pay, UEL) - PT) + 2% x max(0, pay - UEL).

figures.2027-28: Announced (Budget 2026): LEL £6,916 (£133/wk); PT £242/wk (£12,570); UEL £967/wk (£50,270); 8% / 2%. PT and UEL frozen to April 2031 (Budget 2025).

techniques.status: Law for 2024-25 to 2026-27. 2027-28 announced only (Budget 2026 OOTLAR 28 Oct 2026, updated 5 Nov 2026; affirmative SI early 2027). PT/UEL freeze April 2028 - April 2031 announced at Budget 2025.
techniques.relevance: Sets the director's tax- and NIC-free salary (to £12,570) and the minimum salary for a qualifying year (LEL).

techniques.name: Class 1 employer (secondary) NIC: secondary threshold and rate; Class 1A
techniques.summary: Employers pay secondary Class 1 on each employee's earnings above the ST, with no upper limit, including the company's own director. From 6 April 2025 the rate rose from 13.8% to 15% and the ST fell from £9,100 to £5,000. Class 1A on benefits uses the same rate.
techniques.conditions: Deductible for the company. Applies to a sole director's salary. Employment Allowance can offset it where available.
techniques.risks: Since 2025-26 the ST (£5,000) is below the LEL (£6,500 / £6,708), so any salary that earns a qualifying year costs some employer NIC without EA.
techniques.data_needed: Employee earnings; EA eligibility.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Employer NIC = rate x max(0, pay - ST), less EA where available.

figures.2024-25: ST £9,100 (£175/wk, £758/month); 13.8% above ST; Class 1A and 1B 13.8%
figures.2027-28: ST £96/wk (£5,000) announced to be maintained until April 2031 (Budget 2025 OOTLAR s2.2; Budget 2026 Annex A); rate 15% (law)
figures.other zero-rate thresholds: Upper secondary threshold for under-21s and apprentices under 25: £50,270 (£967/wk). Freeport and Investment Zone UST: £25,000 (£481/wk).

techniques.status: Law for 2024-25 to 2026-27: NIC (Secondary Class 1 Contributions) Act 2025 (c.11), Royal Assent 3 April 2025 (s1 rate 15% from 6 April 2025, no end date; s2 ST £96/£417/£5,000 for 2025-26, unchanged for 2026-27). 2027-28 ST announced only (Budget 2026 OOTLAR s2.1/Annex A; affirmative SI early 2027).
techniques.relevance: Cost of paying a director above £5,000 (£9,100 in 2024-25); main reason the optimal salary changed in 2025-26.

techniques.name: Income tax: personal allowance, bands and the £100,000 taper (England, Wales and NI)
techniques.summary: PA and basic rate band frozen to 2030-31. Higher rate starts at £50,270 total income with a full PA; additional rate above £125,140 taxable income. PA withdrawn £1 for every £2 of adjusted net income over £100,000.
techniques.conditions: Taper uses adjusted net income (ITA 2007 ss35, 58); gross personal pension contributions and Gift Aid reduce it; employer pension contributions never enter it. Scottish non-savings bands differ: 2026-27 starter 19% to £3,967, basic 20% to £16,956, intermediate 21% to £31,092, higher 42% to £62,430, advanced 45% to £125,140, top 48% above. Dividends and savings use UK bands.
techniques.risks: Fiscal drag with frozen thresholds. The £100,000-£125,140 band is the most expensive and the main target for pension contributions or retaining profit in a company.
techniques.data_needed: Total income, Scottish residence flag, pension contributions, Gift Aid.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: PA = max(0, 12,570 - max(0, ANI - 100,000)/2). Effective marginal rate £100,000-£125,140 = 60% (62% with Class 4).

figures.2024-25: PA £12,570; basic 20% on first £37,700 taxable; higher threshold £50,270; higher 40% on £37,701-£125,140 taxable; additional 45% above £125,140; PA reduced by half the excess of ANI over £100,000, nil at £125,140
figures.derived: Effective marginal rate on non-savings income £100,000-£125,140 = 60%; 62% for a sole trader with 2% Class 4.

techniques.status: Law. FA 2021 s5 (PA £12,570, BRL £37,700, no indexation), extended by FA 2023 s5 (to 2027-28) and FA 2026 s10 (18 Mar 2026, to 2030-31). ITA s10(5A) fixes ART at 2 x PA + £100,000 = £125,140. 2026-27 rates law (FA 2026 ss1-2). 2027-28 main rates announced for Finance Bill 2026-27; thresholds already law.
techniques.relevance: Base for every comparison; £100,000 taper is a key trigger point for pension contributions.

techniques.name: Class 4 and Class 2 NIC for the self-employed
techniques.summary: Sole traders pay Class 4 at 6% between the lower and upper profits limits and 2% above. Since 6 April 2024 Class 2 is not payable above the small profits threshold (treated as paid); below it, voluntary Class 2 can be paid.
techniques.conditions: Class 4 on taxable trading profits; pension contributions do not reduce Class 4 profits. Above the SPT a qualifying year is given without paying Class 2.
techniques.risks: In a company comparison, the sole trader pays only 6%/2% against 8% employee + 15% employer on salary above the thresholds.
techniques.data_needed: Taxable trading profit.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Class 4 = 6% x (min(profit, 50,270) - 12,570) + 2% x max(0, profit - 50,270). Voluntary Class 2 = weekly rate x 52 if profit below SPT and the user wants the qualifying year.

figures.2024-25: Class 4: LPL £12,570, UPL £50,270, 6% between, 2% above. Class 2: SPT £6,725; £0 above it (treated as paid); voluntary £3.45/wk below it
figures.2027-28: Announced: Class 4 £12,570 / £50,270, 6% / 2%; Class 2 SPT £7,355, voluntary £3.80/wk; Class 3 £19.05/wk. LPL and UPL maintained to April 2031.

techniques.status: Law for 2024-25 to 2026-27 (SSCBA 1992 s15; HMRC rates page updated 6 April 2026). 2027-28 SPT, Class 2 and Class 3 announced at Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026) for affirmative SI early 2027; LPL/UPL freeze to April 2031 announced at Budget 2025 and repeated.
techniques.relevance: The baseline NIC the user pays today.

techniques.name: Income tax and Class 4 thresholds (frozen to 5 April 2031)
techniques.summary: PA £12,570 and basic rate limit £37,700 (higher-rate threshold £50,270); additional rate above £125,140. Class 4 6% between £12,570 and £50,270, 2% above. Frozen to 5 April 2031, so reliefs matter more each year as profits rise.
techniques.conditions: Scottish non-savings bands differ.
techniques.risks: Fiscal drag: rising profits face the same thresholds.
techniques.data_needed: Profit forecast by year.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Use the rates block for each tax year.

figures.2026-27: Same; Class 2 SPT £7,105; voluntary Class 2 £3.65/wk
figures.2027-28: PA £12,570; BRB £37,700; Class 4 6%/2%; Class 2 SPT £7,355; voluntary £3.80/wk (Budget 2026 Annex A)

techniques.status: Law for 2024-25 to 2026-27. PA/BRL law through 2030-31 (FA 2021 s5 as amended by FA 2023 s5 and FA 2026 s10, Royal Assent 18.3.2026). Class 4 limits in SSCBA s15 (changeable by order). 2027-28 income tax charge and main rates announced for Finance Bill 2026-27; Class 2 SPT £7,355 and £3.80 announced at Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026) for SI early 2027.
techniques.relevance: Base figures for the app's calculations in every year.

techniques.name: Director's loan account: s455 tax on loans to participators
techniques.summary: If a close company lends to a participator (e.g. director-shareholder) or associate and the loan is outstanding 9 months after the end of the accounting period, the company pays temporary tax equal to the dividend upper rate for the tax year the loan was made; refunded (s458) when the loan is repaid, released or written off.
techniques.conditions: Due 9 months and 1 day after the end of the accounting period of the loan (s455(3)). Loans repaid before then trigger nothing. For repayment on or after the due date, relief is given 9 months after the end of the accounting period of repayment (s458(4)-(5)); claim within 4 years from the end of the financial year of repayment. CA 2006 s197: loans to a director need members' approval unless aggregate value is £10,000 or less (s207).
techniques.risks: Anti-bed-and-breakfasting (s464ZA from 30 Oct 2024). Write-off taxed on the participator (ITTOIA s415). Loans over £10,000 create a beneficial-loan benefit with Class 1A unless interest is paid at the official rate. Repeated overdrawn accounts suggest disguised remuneration.
techniques.data_needed: Director's loan account balance at each period end and 9 months later; loan dates; repayments and redraws.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: s455 = rate (by tax year of loan) x balance outstanding at 9 months + 1 day after period end (refundable later).

figures.2024-25: 33.75% of loans or advances made in 2024-25
figures.2026-27: 35.75% of loans made on or after 6 April 2026 (dividend upper rate raised by FA 2026 s4)
figures.2027-28: 35.75% (tied to the dividend upper rate; no change announced at Budget 2026)

techniques.status: Law. CTA 2010 s455(2) (FA 2016 s50) ties the rate to ITA s8(2): 33.75% from 2022-23 (FA 2022 s4(1)(b)); 35.75% from 2026-27 (FA 2026 s4(1)(b),(2)). Budget 2026 OOTLAR Annex A shows 35.75% for 2027-28. s464ZA inserted by FA 2025 s81 from 30 Oct 2024; old s464C omitted.
techniques.relevance: A short-term director's loan repaid within 9 months of year end is a lawful cash-flow tool; left outstanding it costs 35.75% (refundable) plus a BIK above £10,000.

techniques.name: If incorporated: s455 charge on loans to director-shareholders, and the beneficial loan official rate
techniques.summary: s455 charge on close-company loans to participators at the dividend upper rate for the tax year of the loan; not payable if repaid, released or written off before 9 months after period end; s458 relief within 4 years, given 9 months after the end of the period of repayment. Bed-and-breakfasting countered by CTA 2010 ss464ZA-464ZB (replacing ss464C-464D from 30 Oct 2024, FA 2025 s81): £5,000+ repaid and re-borrowed within 30 days in a later period is matched; where £15,000+ is owed and new loans of £5,000+ were arranged, also matched. FA 2025 repealed s464B relief for return payments. Interest-free/cheap director loans are a taxable benefit (ITEPA s175) at the official rate minus interest paid, unless loans stay at or below £10,000 throughout the year (s180). From 2025-26 HMRC can change the official rate in-year (EIM26104). Budget 2026: close-company participator payment reporting will not be implemented 'at this time'.
techniques.conditions: Close company; borrower a participator or associate.
techniques.risks: Using company loans instead of salary or dividends is the main HMRC target. Applies only after incorporation.
techniques.data_needed: Loan balances, dates and interest paid; official rate in force.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: BIK = (official rate - interest rate paid) x average balance (if over £10,000 at any time); Class 1A = 15% x BIK.

figures.2024-25: s455 33.75%; official rate 2.25%; £10,000 threshold
figures.2025-26: s455 33.75%; official rate 3.75% (from 6 Apr 2025; can now change in-year)
figures.2026-27: s455 35.75% for loans on or after 6 April 2026 (FA 2026 s4); official rate 3.75% from 6 Apr 2026; £10,000 threshold
figures.2027-28: Dividend upper rate 35.75%, so s455 35.75% (Budget 2026 Annex A)

techniques.status: Law. CTA 2010 s455; FA 2026 s4 (2026-27 onwards, so 2027-28 already law); official rate by Treasury regulations, in-year changes possible from 6 April 2025 (EIM26104); ITEPA s180 £10,000; FA 2025 s81 (ss464ZA/464ZB from 30 Oct 2024). Participator reporting decision announced at Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026), not legislation.
techniques.relevance: If the user incorporates and is tempted to draw money as a director's loan.

techniques.name: Beneficial (cheap) loans to directors: £10,000 threshold and the official rate of interest
techniques.summary: An interest-free or cheap employment-related loan is a taxable benefit equal to interest at the official rate less interest actually paid. No charge if total such loans do not exceed £10,000 at any time in the tax year (ITEPA s180). Employer pays Class 1A on the benefit.
techniques.conditions: £10,000 test on the aggregate outstanding at all times; separate £10,000 test for non-qualifying loans (s180(1)(b)); qualifying loans (interest deductible) excluded; normally averaging method.
techniques.risks: Since 6 April 2025 the official rate can change during the year (commitment withdrawn at Autumn Budget 2024). Loans over £10,000 need members' approval (CA 2006 s197/s207) and may trigger s455.
techniques.data_needed: Loan balances through the year; interest paid; official rate.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Budget 3.75% x loan as a taxable benefit plus 15% Class 1A on that benefit (2025-26, 2026-27).

figures.2024-25: Threshold £10,000; official rate 2.25%; Class 1A 13.8%
figures.2026-27: Threshold £10,000; official rate 3.75% from 6 April 2026 (EIM26104, updated 3 Nov 2026, no in-year change); Class 1A 15%
figures.2027-28: Threshold £10,000 (law). Official rate: null, not yet published.

techniques.status: Law. ITEPA ss175-183; s180 (FA 2014 s22(1)) up to date to 22 Nov 2026; s181 and FA 1989 s178 (Treasury regulations). In-year change policy from 6 Apr 2025 (EIM26104, updated 3 Nov 2026).
techniques.relevance: Director's loans up to £10,000 are benefit-free (s455 can still apply).

techniques.name: Trivial benefits exemption (£50 each; £300 annual cap for close-company directors)
techniques.summary: A non-cash benefit costing £50 or less is exempt if not cash or a cash voucher, not under salary sacrifice or contractual obligation, and not in recognition of particular services. Directors and office holders of a close company, and their family or household, are capped at £300 a tax year.
techniques.conditions: ITEPA s323A Conditions A-E; £300 cap for close-company directors (s323B). From 6 April 2016.
techniques.risks: A benefit costing £50.01 is fully taxable. Cash, gift cards that work as cash vouchers, and regular contractual perks fail. CT deductibility follows normal rules (not addressed by the source).
techniques.data_needed: Cost per benefit; running total per director per year.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Up to £300 a year per director tax- and NIC-free (company only).

figures.2024-25: £50 per benefit; £300 annual cap for close-company directors/office holders and family or household
figures.2027-28: £50; £300 cap (no change announced)

techniques.status: Law: ITEPA ss323A-323C (FA 2016 s13), 2016-17 onwards; up to date to 23 Nov 2026. Budget documents could not be searched for 2027-28 announcements.
techniques.relevance: Small, company-only.

techniques.name: Employer pension contributions: deductible for CT, no NIC, no income tax
techniques.summary: A company's contribution to a registered pension scheme for its director or employee is CT-deductible if wholly and exclusively for the trade, not taxable on the employee (ITEPA s308) and not earnings for Class 1 NIC (SS(C)R 2001 Sch 3 Pt 6 para 2(a)). It counts towards the annual allowance.
techniques.conditions: BIM46035: accept the deduction where salary plus pension is comparable with unconnected staff for similar duties; relief in the period of payment (PTM043100) with spreading for large increases. Carry forward unused AA from 3 previous years. Member's own contributions relievable only up to the greater of £3,600 or relevant UK earnings (FA 2004 ss189-190); dividends are not relevant earnings, so employer contributions are the main route for a low-salary director.
techniques.risks: Annual allowance charge above the available AA. Contributions for a family member who is not a genuine employee are not exempt (EIM01570). Locked until minimum pension age. Unused pension funds come into IHT from April 2027. Salary-sacrificed contributions above £2,000 attract NIC from 6 April 2029 (direct employer contributions unaffected).
techniques.data_needed: Company profits; director salary; pension inputs in prior 3 years; membership history.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Cost to shareholder of a £10,000 employer contribution = net dividend forgone (see derived example).

figures.2024-25: AA £60,000; taper where threshold income > £200,000 and adjusted income > £260,000, minimum £10,000; MPAA £10,000; employer and employee NIC 0% on the contribution
figures.2027-28: AA £60,000; MPAA £10,000; tapered AA adjusted-income threshold £260,000 (Budget 2026 Annex A); Lump Sum Allowance £268,275
figures.derived example 2026-27: A £10,000 employer contribution costs the shareholder the net dividend it replaces: higher-rate £5,204.25 at 19% CT, or £4,722.38 at the 26.5% marginal rate; basic-rate at 19% CT £7,229.25. A sole trader putting £10,000 gross into a personal pension gives up £6,000 net (higher rate) or £8,000 net (basic rate), and Class 4 is still due on that profit.

techniques.status: Law. ITEPA s308; SS(C)R 2001 Sch 3 Pt VI para 2(a); FA 2004 ss189-190, s228A. Figures on GOV.UK rates page (6 Apr 2026) and Budget 2026 OOTLAR Annex A (28 Oct 2026, updated 5 Nov 2026). IHT on unused pensions from 6 Apr 2027 enacted (FA 2026 ss66-71). Salary-sacrifice NIC cap enacted (NIC (Employer Pensions Contributions) Act 2026 c.15 s1, £2,000 from 2029-30).
techniques.relevance: One of the strongest lawful reasons to incorporate once there is surplus profit.

techniques.name: Salary-sacrifice pension contributions above £2,000 to attract NIC from 6 April 2029
techniques.summary: From 6 April 2029 (tax year 2029-30 onwards), salary or bonus given up under an optional remuneration arrangement (salary or bonus sacrifice) in return for an employer pension contribution counts as earnings for employee (primary) and employer (secondary) Class 1 NIC, to the extent it exceeds a contributions limit of £2,000 for a tax year. The charge is in SSCBA 1992 s4(6A)-(6E), inserted by the National Insurance Contributions (Employer Pensions Contributions) Act 2026 s1 (s2 does the same for Northern Ireland). It works through regulations that have not yet been made. Income tax relief on pension contributions is unchanged, and ordinary employer contributions made without any sacrifice stay free of NIC with no limit.
techniques.conditions: Applies only where the pension contribution is provided under optional remuneration arrangements as defined in ITEPA 2003 s69A. Type A: the employee gives up a right to salary or bonus in return. Type B: the employee agrees to take the contribution rather than an amount of earnings. Amounts up to the £2,000 limit for a tax year are not treated as earnings (SSCBA s4(6B)). The regulations may set pay-period equivalents of the limit (up to £1 above the arithmetical equivalent), decide when the deemed earnings count as paid, and in prescribed cases treat an amount other than the sum given up as earnings (s4(6C)-(6D)). The Act says only 'for a tax year'. It does not say whether the limit is per employment or per person; the Budget 2025 document says both 'per employee' and 'per person', so the regulations will decide. HMRC's policy paper says sacrifice cannot take pay below the National Minimum Wage, and the effect of sacrifice on adjusted net income does not change.
techniques.risks: A company director who formally gives up salary or a bonus, or is offered a pension contribution instead of a bonus, falls within s69A (Type A or B). From 2029-30, anything above £2,000 a year then attracts employee and employer NIC. A contribution the company decides to make, with no salary or bonus given up and no cash alternative, is outside optional remuneration arrangements and stays NIC-free. It still counts towards the annual allowance and must be wholly and exclusively for the trade to be deductible. The detailed rules (pay-period limits, timing, more than one employment) are not yet in regulations, so recheck any 2029-30 plan once they are made. Reducing the £2,000 limit later needs approval by both Houses (SSCBA s176(1)(zza)).
techniques.data_needed: Whether any pension contribution is, or would be, funded by giving up salary or a bonus; the amount given up in each tax year; the employee's other Class 1 earnings in the year, to place the excess against the thresholds.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: This is a future cost, not a saving. From 2029-30: excess = max(0, salary or bonus given up in the tax year - £2,000). Employee NIC = excess x the employee's marginal Class 1 rate. At 2026-27 rates (and the announced 2027-28 rates) that is 8% between the primary threshold and the upper earnings limit and 2% above it. Employer NIC = excess x the secondary rate (15% above the secondary threshold at the same rates). NIC rates for 2029-30 are not yet set, so use the rates in force for that year. Paying the same amount as a direct employer contribution, with no sacrifice, avoids both charges.

figures.2024-25: No limit: pension contributions under salary sacrifice are free of Class 1 NIC
figures.2026-27: No limit
figures.2027-28: No limit
figures.2028-29: No limit (the Act has effect only from 2029-30, s1(3))
figures.2029-30: Contributions limit £2,000 for a tax year. Any amount given up above it is Class 1 earnings for employee and employer NIC. Law: NIC (Employer Pensions Contributions) Act 2026 s1(3)-(4) and s2(3)-(4). The regulations setting the detail are not yet made.

techniques.status: Law. National Insurance Contributions (Employer Pensions Contributions) Act 2026 (c. 15), Royal Assent 29 April 2026, in force on the day it was passed (s3(2)). The amendments have effect for 2029-30 and later tax years (s1(3), s2(3)), and the first regulations must set the limit at £2,000 (s1(4), s2(4)). No regulations under SSCBA s4(6A) found on legislation.gov.uk on 24 Nov 2026. Announced at Budget 2025 (26 Nov 2025). The HMRC policy paper of 4 Dec 2025 has not been updated and still says primary legislation 'will be introduced'. Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026) treats the cap as an existing decision and announced no change.
techniques.relevance: No effect while the technician is a sole trader, because there is no salary to give up. If they later run a company, it can pay pension contributions for them as director directly, with no NIC and no £2,000 cap. Only a salary or bonus swap above £2,000 a year would bear NIC from April 2029.

techniques.name: Charging the company interest on money the director lends it
techniques.summary: A director can lend money to their company (e.g. cash introduced, or kit sold and left on loan account) and be paid a commercial rate of interest. For the director it is savings income, which can be covered by the 0% starting rate for savings (up to £5,000, reduced £1 for £1 by non-savings income above the PA, gone at £17,570) and the personal savings allowance (£1,000 basic, £500 higher, £0 additional). A company paying yearly UK interest must deduct income tax at source (ITA 2007 s874): 'the basic rate' (20%) for 2024-25 to 2026-27; 'the savings basic rate' from 2027-28 (FA 2026 s6(8), Sch 1 para 29): 22% in law (FA 2026 s5), 24% if Budget 2026 is enacted. The company reports and pays via CT61; the director gets credit through Self Assessment. Interest above a reasonable commercial return is a distribution (CTA 2010 s1000(1) para E). Close-company interest to a participator not paid within 12 months after period end is deductible only when paid (CTA 2009 ss373, 375).
techniques.conditions: Genuine, documented loan at a commercial rate. With a £12,570 salary and no other non-savings income, up to £5,000 + £1,000 = £6,000 of interest can be tax-free in 2026-27 (derived).
techniques.risks: Above-commercial interest challenged. Company must operate s874 deduction and report. Savings rates rise from 2027-28. Loan relationships treatment of the company's deduction not reviewed.
techniques.data_needed: Loan balance, interest rate, director's other income.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Saving = interest x (company marginal CT rate) + interest covered by starting rate/PSA x director's savings rate otherwise payable, compared with extracting the same amount as dividend.

figures.2024-25: Savings rates 20% / 40% / 45%; starting rate 0% on up to £5,000 (full only where non-savings income does not exceed £12,570; lost at £17,570); PSA £1,000 basic / £500 higher; company deducts 20%
figures.2026-27: Savings 20% / 40% / 45%; starting rate limit £5,000 (FA 2026 s9 freezes it to 2030-31); PSA £1,000 / £500; deduction at 20%
figures.2027-28: Savings rates enacted at 22% / 42% / 47% (FA 2026 s5); Budget 2026 announced 24% / 44% / 49% from 6 April 2027 (Finance Bill 2026-27); starting rate £5,000; PSA £1,000 / £500; s874 deduction at the savings basic rate in force

techniques.status: Law: ITA s874 (basic rate to 2026-27; savings basic rate from 2027-28 by FA 2026 s6(8), Sch 1 para 29); FA 2026 s3 (2026-27 savings 20/40/45), s5 (2027-28 22/42/47), s9 (starting rate £5,000 frozen 2026-27 to 2030-31). Announced only: 24/44/49 for 2027-28 (Budget 2026 28 Oct 2026; HMRC policy paper 29 Oct 2026; Finance Bill 2026-27).
techniques.relevance: Lawful extraction route if the user incorporates and lends the company working capital or transferred equipment value.

techniques.name: Approved mileage allowance payments (director/employee) and simplified mileage (self-employed)
techniques.summary: An employer, including the director's own company, can pay an employee or director approved mileage allowance payments (AMAPs) for business travel in a car, van, motorcycle or cycle that is not a company vehicle. Payments up to the approved amount (business miles x the statutory rate) are free of income tax (ITEPA ss229-230). For NIC, payments up to the highest rate x all business miles are free of Class 1 (SS(C)R 2001 reg 22A). From 2026-27 the car and van rate is 55p a mile for the first 10,000 business miles in the tax year and 25p after. This comes from ITEPA s230(2) as amended by the Taxation (Energy and Vehicles) Act 2026 s2 (Royal Assent 15 July 2026), with effect for 2026-27 and later years and no end date. The same section raised the self-employed simplified mileage rate for cars and goods vehicles (ITTOIA s94F) to 55p for the first 10,000 miles. If the employer pays less than the approved amount, the employee can claim mileage allowance relief on the shortfall (ITEPA s231). Announced, not law: Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026; OOTLAR 2.7) said the rate above 10,000 miles rises from 25p to 35p for AMAPs and simplified mileage from 6 April 2027, by a statutory instrument not yet made. Where IR35 (Chapter 8) or off-payroll working (Chapter 10) applies to an engagement through the director's company, ITEPA s339A treats each engagement as a separate employment. Travel to that client's site is then ordinary commuting, so AMAPs for it are taxable.
techniques.conditions: Only business travel qualifies: journeys whose cost would be deductible under ITEPA ss337-342, not ordinary commuting (s236(1)). The vehicle must not be a company vehicle (s229(4)(b), s236(2)), and the employee must be the driver, not a passenger (s229(4)(a)). The vehicle does not have to be legally owned by the employee. A van is a goods vehicle with a design weight of no more than 3,500 kg (s235(3)). For AMAPs, the 10,000-mile band counts all business miles by car or van in the tax year, in that employment and any associated employment (s230(1), (3)-(4)). Self-employed simplified mileage applies only to a car, motorcycle or goods vehicle that is not an 'excluded vehicle' (ITTOIA s94E). It is excluded if capital allowances have ever been claimed on providing it (Condition A), or if it is a goods vehicle (such as a van) or a motorcycle and any of its purchase cost has been deducted under the cash basis (Condition B; ss24A, 271D). For simplified mileage, the 10,000-mile band covers all business journeys by the cars and goods vehicles using the flat rate in the period for which the trade's profits are calculated (s94F(1), (3)-(4)). That period is the accounting period, which matches the tax year only if accounts end on 31 March or 5 April. Once used for a vehicle, simplified mileage must continue for as long as that vehicle is used in the trade (s94D(4)). Keep a mileage log.
techniques.risks: Payments above the approved amount are taxable on the excess, reported on a P11D or put through payroll. For NIC, anything above the highest rate x business miles in each earnings period is earnings (reg 22A). Mileage payments made under optional remuneration arrangements are fully liable to NIC (reg 22A(2A)). Travel to a permanent workplace is commuting. If an engagement through the director's company is inside IR35 or off-payroll, s339A makes travel to that client commuting, and AMAPs for it are taxable. Under Chapter 8, tax-free AMAPs paid by the company are deducted at Step 7 of the deemed payment calculation only so far as they were not already deducted as expenses at Step 3 (ITEPA s54(1) Step 7 and s54(7)), so each payment is deducted once, not twice. A sole trader who has expensed any of the purchase cost of a van or motorcycle under the cash basis cannot use simplified mileage for it (s94E Condition B). The 35p rate from 2027-28 is not yet law.
techniques.data_needed: Business miles by vehicle, kept cumulative per tax year for AMAPs and per accounting period for simplified mileage, for the 10,000-mile split; the business's accounting date; vehicle type and, for a van, its design weight; whether capital allowances have ever been claimed on the vehicle and, for a van or motorcycle, whether any of its purchase cost was deducted under the cash basis; a journey log with dates, places and purpose (can be linked to jobs or calendar entries); for a director, whether each engagement is inside IR35 or off-payroll.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Director (AMAP): approved amount = min(business miles in the tax year, 10,000) x first-band rate + max(0, miles - 10,000) x second-band rate, for cars and vans, counting miles across the employment and any associated employment. Motorcycles are 24p and cycles 20p on all miles. The company can pay up to this amount free of income tax and NIC and deduct it for corporation tax, in place of salary or dividends that would be taxed. If it pays less, the director claims mileage allowance relief on the gap at their marginal income tax rate. Sole trader: simplified mileage deduction = the same formula at the s94F rates (motorcycles 24p; there is no cycle rate), with the 10,000-mile band applied to business miles by all cars and goods vehicles on the flat rate in the accounting period, not the tax year, unless accounts end on 31 March or 5 April. Saving = deduction x (marginal income tax rate + Class 4 rate). Compare it with actual vehicle costs plus capital allowances before choosing, because the choice is then fixed for that vehicle.

figures.2024-25: AMAP: car or van 45p for the first 10,000 business miles, then 25p; NIC 45p for all business miles; motorcycle 24p; cycle 20p (law). Self-employed simplified mileage: car or goods vehicle 45p for the first 10,000, then 25p; motorcycle 24p
figures.2025-26: AMAP: car or van 45p for the first 10,000, then 25p; NIC 45p for all business miles; motorcycle 24p; cycle 20p (law). Self-employed simplified mileage: car or goods vehicle 45p for the first 10,000, then 25p; motorcycle 24p
figures.2026-27: AMAP: car or van 55p for the first 10,000, then 25p; NIC 55p for all business miles; motorcycle 24p; cycle 20p (law: ITEPA s230(2) as amended by TEVA 2026 s2). Self-employed simplified mileage (ITTOIA s94F): car or goods vehicle 55p for the first 10,000, then 25p; motorcycle 24p
figures.2027-28: Law now: car or van (and simplified-mileage car or goods vehicle) 55p for the first 10,000 miles with no end date, 25p after. Announced, not law (27-28 Oct 2026; OOTLAR 2.7; SI to follow): 35p above 10,000 miles for AMAPs and simplified mileage from 6 April 2027. NIC disregard under reg 22A(4) as it stands: 55p for all business miles, not 35p. Motorcycle 24p, cycle 20p: no change announced.

figures_disputed: 2027-28 NIC disregard for cars and vans: 55p for all business miles under reg 22A(4) as it stands. OOTLAR 2.7 says the 35p change 'will also apply' to the NIC disregard, so the effect cannot be confirmed until the SI is published.

2026-27 NIC disregard for AMAPs paid between 6 April and 14 July 2026: HMRC guidance (updated 5 June 2026) says 55p, but reg 22A(4) uses the s230(2) rate 'at the time when the payment is made', and s230(2) read 45p until TEVA 2026 received Royal Assent on 15 July 2026.
techniques.status: Law: 45p/25p for 2024-25 and 2025-26. Law: 55p/25p for 2026-27 and later years under the Taxation (Energy and Vehicles) Act 2026 (c.26) s2, Royal Assent 15 July 2026, which amended ITEPA s230(2) and ITTOIA s94F(2)-(3). The NIC disregard is in SS(C)R 2001 reg 22A. The GOV.UK employer rates page for 2026-27 was updated on 5 June 2026 to 55p for tax and NIC. Announced only: 35p above 10,000 miles from 6 April 2027 (announced 27 Oct 2026; Budget 2026, 28 Oct 2026, OOTLAR 2.7), to be made by SI under ITEPA s230(6) and ITTOIA s94F(6). No such SI was found on legislation.gov.uk on 24 Nov 2026.
techniques.relevance: As a sole trader the technician claims simplified mileage or actual costs, not AMAPs; AMAPs matter only if they incorporate and the company repays business miles driven in their own vehicle. Because they drive kit to venues across the UK, Expend must apply each year's rates and the running 10,000-mile split, and leave out commuting.

techniques.name: VAT registration and deregistration thresholds
techniques.summary: Registration compulsory when taxable turnover in the last 12 months exceeds £90,000 (register within 30 days of the end of that month; effective from the first day of the second month after crossing), or if expected to exceed £90,000 in the next 30 days alone (effective from the date you realised). Voluntary registration allowed. Same thresholds for sole traders and companies; each legal person has its own turnover.
techniques.conditions: Taxable turnover includes equipment hire and labour charges. Most production/event clients are VAT-registered and can recover VAT charged.
techniques.risks: Late registration: VAT due on past sales plus penalties. Artificially splitting a business (sole trade v company) to stay under the threshold can be challenged; HMRC can direct disaggregated businesses be treated as one.
techniques.data_needed: Rolling 12-month taxable turnover by month; forward 30-day expected turnover.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Monitor rolling 12-month turnover against £90,000; flag the month crossed and the registration deadline (30 days after month end).

figures.2024-25: From 1 April 2024: registration £90,000 (previously £85,000); deregistration £88,000 (previously £83,000).
figures.2026-27: Registration £90,000; deregistration £88,000.
figures.2027-28: Registration £90,000; deregistration £88,000 (Budget 2026 Annex A). Mandatory VAT e-invoicing roadmap for April 2029 (announced).

techniques.status: Law: VATA 1994 Sch 1 as amended by SI 2024/307 (in force 1 April 2024). No change in Budget 2025 or Budget 2026 Annex A. Mandatory e-invoicing from April 2029 announced only.
techniques.relevance: As profits grow turnover may cross £90,000; with B2B VAT-registered clients registration costs little and recovers VAT on kit.

techniques.name: VAT Flat Rate Scheme and the limited cost trader rule (VAT Notice 733)
techniques.summary: Pay a fixed percentage of VAT-inclusive turnover instead of netting input VAT. Single capital purchases of £2,000 or more incl. VAT reclaimed outside the scheme (Notice 733 s15.2); goods for resale, used up within a year, or for hire are not capital expenditure goods, so hire stock cannot be reclaimed this way (s15.1). Join if expected taxable turnover next year is £150,000 or less excl. VAT (HMRC must authorise). Leave if VAT-inclusive income in the year to the anniversary exceeds £230,000, or is expected to exceed £230,000 in the next 30 days; HMRC may allow staying after a one-off rise if next year is expected to be no more than £191,500; 12-month wait to rejoin. One sector rate for the main activity; 1 point lower in the first year of registration (limited cost rate 15.5%). Limited cost trader (regs 55A(4), 55KA, from 1 April 2017): 16.5% if relevant goods spend in the period is less than the higher of 2% of VAT-inclusive flat rate turnover or £1,000 a year pro rata (£250 a quarter); tested every return. Relevant goods exclude vehicles, parts and fuel (unless a transport business), food and drink for staff, capital goods, goods for resale/hire (unless main activity), promotional items, and all services.
techniques.conditions: HMRC acceptance; applies to the whole business.
techniques.risks: A labour-only technician with few goods purchases is likely a limited cost trader at 16.5%, close to the 16.67% (20/120) effective output VAT, and loses input VAT recovery, so usually not worthwhile. Kit purchases are capital and do not count towards the 2% test. Wrong sector or manipulated goods spend is an HMRC target.
techniques.data_needed: VAT-inclusive turnover by return period; relevant goods spend; sector; registration date; capital purchases.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Compare (turnover incl. VAT x flat rate) with (output VAT - input VAT) under standard accounting each period; apply 16.5% if the limited cost test is failed.

figures.2024-25: Rates as 2025-26 (unchanged).
figures.2025-26: Limited cost rate 16.5%. Sector rates: business services not listed elsewhere 12%; entertainment or journalism 12.5%; film, radio, TV or video production 13%; hiring or renting goods 9.5%; any other activity not listed 12%; photography 11%; labour-only construction 14.5%. Join <= £150,000; leave > £230,000.
figures.2026-27: Same rates. Notice 733 last updated 18 Dec 2025.
figures.2027-28: null: no change announced.

techniques.status: Law. VAT Regulations 1995 (SI 1995/2518) Part 7A regs 55A-55V; reg 55A(4) and 55KA inserted by SI 2017/295 from 1 April 2017. No outstanding effects. Budget 2026 OOTLAR announces no change.
techniques.relevance: Run the numbers once VAT-registered; standard accounting is often better for an equipment-owning technician.

techniques.name: Making Tax Digital: sole trader compared with a company
techniques.summary: MTD for Income Tax is governed by the Income Tax (Digital Obligations) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/336, in force 1 April 2026; reg 48 revoked SI 2021/1076 and SI 2024/167. It applies to an individual with self-employment and/or property income unless an exemption applies. The income exemption (Part 7 Chapter 2) looks two years back: you are in MTD for tax year Y if your qualifying income for Y-2 was more than the qualifying amount for Y-2 (regs 22, 23, 27). The amounts are £50,000 for 2024-25 (in from 6 April 2026), £30,000 for 2025-26 (in from 6 April 2027), and £20,000 for 2026-27 and later (in from 6 April 2028). On GOV.UK's wording, this is the return submitted in the previous tax year. Qualifying income is self-employment plus property income before expenses as entered on the return, counting only your share of jointly owned property. It excludes trustee receipts, visiting-performer payments and qualifying care receipts (regs 25-26), and HMRC also leaves out employment income, an individual partner's share of partnership profit, and dividends, including those from your own company. An amendment that increases qualifying income is ignored if made after the start of the year the exemption would cover (reg 26(c)), and periods other than 12 months are scaled (reg 26(d)). Once in, you stay in; from 2029-30 you leave only if qualifying income was at or below the amount in each of the three previous years (reg 24). Obligations: digital records, and quarterly updates for periods ending 5 July, 5 October, 5 January and 5 April, due 7 August, 7 November, 7 February and 7 May (reg 12; a calendar-quarters election is available, reg 11). The return is due by 31 January after the year. HMRC will not give penalty points for late quarterly updates in 2026-27 (GOV.UK). Budget 2026 announced the same for 2027-28 for those required to join in April 2027 (OOTLAR para 2.36; not law). Updates must still be sent before the return can be filed. Partnerships will need to join 'in the future' (no date). Companies: MTD for Income Tax does not cover company profits, and HMRC does 'not intend to introduce MTD for CT' (Transformation Roadmap, 21 July 2025). HMRC's free accounts and CT return filing service closed on 31 March 2026, so companies need commercial software from 1 April 2026. MTD for VAT covers every VAT-registered business (VAT Notice 700/22; extended to smaller VAT businesses from April 2022).
techniques.conditions: You are mandated for tax year Y if qualifying income for Y-2 was above the qualifying amount for Y-2 and no other exemption applies (e.g. digital exclusion). You need MTD-compatible software. Partnerships are not yet within MTD for Income Tax. When the sole trade ceases, for example on incorporation, the regulations provide a digital termination date and a final quarterly period ending with it (regs 6, 14).
techniques.risks: Quarterly reporting and software costs. Late-update penalty points apply from 2027-28 for April 2026 joiners, and from 2028-29 for April 2027 joiners if the announced easement is applied; late returns earn points in every year (see penalty-regime-domestic). Incorporating takes the trade's profits out of MTD for Income Tax, but the director can still be in through property income, and the company needs commercial software for its CT return, plus accounts, Companies House filings and payroll. Dividends do not count towards qualifying income. An upward amendment to an old return made after the relevant year starts does not bring you in early.
techniques.data_needed: Gross self-employment turnover and the user's share of property income for each tax year from 2024-25, as filed, with any amendments and their dates; any HMRC letter confirming a start date; quarterly update submission dates; whether a calendar-quarters election has been made; the sole-trade cessation date if incorporating.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: There is no tax saving; this is a compliance test. Mandation for tax year Y (2026-27 onwards): MTD applies if qualifying income(Y-2) > qualifying amount(Y-2), where the amount is £50,000 for 2024-25, £30,000 for 2025-26 and £20,000 for 2026-27 onwards. Once in, stay in; from 2029-30 the user is exempt again only if qualifying income(Y-3), (Y-2) and (Y-1) were each at or below that year's amount. Deadlines for year Y: 7 Aug, 7 Nov and 7 Feb within Y, 7 May after Y, and the return by 31 Jan after Y. In a structure comparison, set sole-trader MTD software cost against company accounts, CT software and payroll costs (company-running-costs).

figures.2024-25: Qualifying amount £50,000 (reg 27(a)). Over £50,000 in 2024-25: MTD from 6 Apr 2026 (reg 22).
figures.2025-26: Qualifying amount £30,000 (reg 27(b)). Over £30,000 in 2025-26: MTD from 6 Apr 2027 (reg 23).
figures.2026-27: First mandatory year for those over £50,000 in 2024-25. Quarterly deadlines 7 Aug 2026, 7 Nov 2026, 7 Feb 2027, 7 May 2027; return due 31 Jan 2028. No penalty points for late quarterly updates (HMRC policy, GOV.UK). Qualifying amount £20,000 (reg 27(c)): over £20,000 in 2026-27 means MTD from 6 Apr 2028.
figures.2027-28: Joiners are those over £30,000 in 2025-26. Quarterly deadlines 7 Aug 2027, 7 Nov 2027, 7 Feb 2028, 7 May 2028; return due 31 Jan 2029 (reg 12). No late-update penalty points in 2027-28 for April 2027 joiners: announced (Budget 2026, OOTLAR para 2.36), not law. The qualifying amount for 2027-28 income itself is £20,000, which decides entry from 6 Apr 2029.

techniques.status: Law: SI 2026/336, in force 1 April 2026 (reg 1); reg 48 revoked SI 2021/1076 and SI 2024/167; regs 22-27 set the income tests and amounts; reg 12 sets the quarterly deadlines. The 2026-27 late-update points easement is HMRC policy (GOV.UK 'Use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax', updated 18 Nov 2026). The 2027-28 easement for April 2027 joiners is announced only (Budget 2026, 28 Oct 2026, OOTLAR para 2.36). MTD for Corporation Tax: HMRC does not intend to introduce it (Transformation Roadmap, 21 July 2025). HMRC's CT online filing service closed on 31 March 2026.
techniques.relevance: If 2024-25 turnover was £50,000 or less, the technician was not brought in from April 2026. But 2025-26 turnover over £30,000 brings MTD from 6 April 2027, and 2026-27 turnover over £20,000 brings it from 6 April 2028, so Expend should test gross turnover from two years earlier and remind the quarterly deadlines. Incorporating would take the trade out of MTD for Income Tax but add company filing costs.

techniques.name: Pension annual allowance and the limit on relief for personal contributions
techniques.summary: The annual allowance (AA) is the most pension saving (gross personal plus employer/third-party contributions) across all registered schemes in a tax year without an AA charge; pension input period = tax year since 2016-17 (FA 2004 s238ZA). £60,000 for 2023-24 onwards (s228(1), F(No.2)A 2023 s20), lower if tapered or if the £10,000 MPAA is triggered. Unused AA from the previous 3 years can be carried forward (s228A). Income tax relief on personal contributions is capped at the higher of 100% of relevant UK earnings chargeable to income tax for the year or £3,600 gross (s190); relief on the basic amount only through relief at source (s191(7)). Relevant UK earnings for a sole trader = profits of a trade carried on personally, alone or as a partner (s189(2)(b), PTM044100); pensions, rent, interest, dividends and miscellaneous income do not count (FHL profits counted in 2024-25 only).
techniques.conditions: Personal contributions relieved up to 100% of relevant UK earnings (or £3,600 gross via relief at source). Relief in the tax year paid. Contributions above AA (after carry forward) taxed by the AA charge at the marginal rate.
techniques.risks: Personal contributions are not a trading expense: no reduction in trading profit or Class 4. Money locked until pension age. Cannot be backdated: pay by 5 April before profit is final. Carry forward does not lift the 100%-of-earnings cap. Kit-hire profit taxed as miscellaneous income is not relevant UK earnings.
techniques.data_needed: Relevant UK earnings (trading profit); contributions paid by date; employer contributions; prior 3 years' unused AA and membership.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Relief = gross contribution x marginal income tax rate (20% at source + extra via SA), limited to relevant UK earnings; net cost at higher rate 60p per £1, about 40p in the £100,000-£125,140 band.

figures.2024-25: AA £60,000; basic amount £3,600 gross (£2,880 net)
figures.2026-27: AA £60,000; basic amount £3,600 gross
figures.2027-28: AA £60,000 (Budget 2026 OOTLAR Annex A)

techniques.status: Law. FA 2004 Part 4; s228(1) (F(No.2)A 2023 s20) £60,000 for 2023-24 and later; s190(4) £3,600. Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026) OOTLAR Annex A confirms £60,000 for 2026-27 and 2027-28; no change announced. (The main Budget document's Annex A covers financing, not rates.)
techniques.relevance: The main legal way for a growing freelancer to cut tax; also lowers adjusted net income for the HICBC, PA taper and childcare limit.

techniques.name: Carry forward of unused annual allowance (3 years)
techniques.summary: Unused AA from the previous 3 tax years can be added to the current year's AA. Current year used first, then the earliest unused year. Lets a large contribution be made in a high-profit year without an AA charge.
techniques.conditions: Must have been a member of a registered pension scheme at some point in each earlier year carried forward. Tapered years carry forward only the reduced AA. If the MPAA applies, carry forward adds only to the £50,000 alternative AA.
techniques.risks: Personal contributions still relieved only up to 100% of relevant UK earnings in the year of payment, so carry forward mainly helps in an exceptional profit year or for company employer contributions. Records of past inputs needed; errors trigger the AA charge.
techniques.data_needed: Pension inputs and membership for each of the last 3 years.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Available AA = current AA + sum of unused AA for the 3 prior years (earliest first), limited for personal contributions by relevant UK earnings.

figures.2026-27: Current £60,000 plus up to £60,000 for each of 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26: theoretical maximum £240,000
figures.2027-28: Current £60,000 plus up to £60,000 for each of 2024-25, 2025-26 and 2026-27: theoretical maximum £240,000

techniques.status: Law. FA 2004 s228A (FA 2011 Sch 17) from 2011-12; 3-year look-back from 2019-20 (4 years 2016-17 to 2018-19). AA £60,000 (s228(1)); MPAA £10,000; alternative AA £50,000 (s227ZA, s227B(2)). Budget 2026 OOTLAR Annex A confirms £60,000 for 2026-27 and 2027-28; no change to carry forward announced.
techniques.relevance: Open a registered personal pension or SIPP now, even with a small contribution, so each year's unused AA is available later.

techniques.name: Relief at source on personal pension contributions (self-employed)
techniques.summary: A self-employed member of a relief-at-source scheme pays contributions net of basic-rate tax; the provider reclaims 20% (£80 becomes £100 gross), including for Scottish/Welsh taxpayers and Scottish starter-rate payers. Relief limited to gross contributions up to 100% of relevant UK earnings, or £3,600 gross (£2,880 net) with low or no earnings. Higher and additional rate relief is claimed via Self Assessment (basic and higher rate limits extended by the gross contribution, s192(4); Scotland s192(4A); Wales s192(4B)): a further 20% on income taxed at 40%, 25% at 45%. Extra relief is lost only if not claimed in the return/amendment or within 4 years (TMA s43). Gross contributions reduce adjusted net income and threshold income but not trading profit or Class 4.
techniques.conditions: Relief-at-source scheme (personal, stakeholder, most SIPPs); paid within the tax year; net contribution capped at 80% of relevant UK earnings; extra relief claimed on the return.
techniques.risks: Unclaimed extra relief is lost. Use the gross contribution in ANI and threshold income calculations. No Class 4 reduction. Scottish rates and bands differ.
techniques.data_needed: Net contributions paid and dates; marginal rate.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Gross = net / 0.8; extra relief = gross contribution falling in the higher band x 20% (25% in the additional band); Scotland per GOV.UK percentages.

figures.2024-25: Provider adds 20% (net £80 becomes £100 gross); no-earnings limit £2,880 net (£3,600 gross)
figures.2025-26: 20% added at source; £2,880 net no-earnings limit
figures.2026-27: 20% added at source; extra relief via SA: 20% (40% payer) or 25% (45% payer). Scottish extra relief per GOV.UK: 1% on income taxed at 21%, 22% at 42%, 25% at 45%, 28% at 48%
figures.2027-28: No change announced

techniques.status: Law: FA 2004 ss188, 190, 192 (and ss192(4A)/(4B)). No change announced at Budget 2025 (26 Nov 2025) or Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026). Scottish rates for 2027-28 not confirmed (null).
techniques.relevance: How the user gets pension relief as a sole trader; most valuable at 40% and above.

techniques.name: Using pension contributions to restore the personal allowance (£100,000 to £125,140)
techniques.summary: The PA falls £1 for every £2 of ANI over £100,000 and is nil at £125,140, giving an effective 60% rate in that band. Gross relief-at-source contributions are deducted from ANI (ITA s58 Step 3) and grossed-up Gift Aid at Step 2. Each £100 gross contribution in the band saves about £60 (£20 at source, £20 band extension, £20 restored allowance), net cost about £40.
techniques.conditions: ANI per ITA s58. Higher-rate relief claimed on the return. Contribution paid in the same tax year.
techniques.risks: Profits must be estimated before 5 April (no carry back); Gift Aid can be carried back (s426). EIS, SEIS and VCT relief do NOT lower ANI. Scottish rates differ.
techniques.data_needed: Forecast ANI for the year; contributions paid to date.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Gross contribution needed to reach £100,000 = ANI - 100,000 (max £25,140); saving approx 60% of that amount (rUK).

figures.2024-25: PA £12,570; taper above £100,000; nil at £125,140; a £25,140 gross contribution takes ANI from £125,140 to £100,000
figures.2027-28: PA £12,570, income limit £100,000, additional rate above £125,140 (Budget 2026 Annex A); PA and BRL frozen to 5 April 2031

techniques.status: Law. ITA s35 (£12,570; s35(2) £100,000 not indexed under s57); s58 (ANI); s10(5A) (£125,140); FA 2004 s192(4). PA/BRL freeze to 2030-31 enacted by FA 2026 s10 (18 March 2026). Budget 2026 OOTLAR Annex A confirms 2027-28.
techniques.relevance: High-value once profits pass £100,000; also protects Tax-Free Childcare and the 30 hours.

techniques.name: Enacted pension changes: salary-sacrifice NIC limit (2029-30) and inheritance tax on unused pensions (from 6 April 2027)
techniques.summary: Two changes, both already enacted, affect pension planning. (1) The National Insurance Contributions (Employer Pensions Contributions) Act 2026 (c.15, Royal Assent 29 April 2026) inserts s4(6A)-(6E) into SSCBA 1992. For 2029-30 onwards, regulations may treat pay given up under optional remuneration (salary or bonus sacrifice) arrangements for employer pension contributions as earnings for Class 1 NIC, above a 'contributions limit'. The first regulations must set that limit at £2,000 a year (s1(4)). Later regulations can reduce it, but only with the approval of both Houses (s1(2); SSCBA s176(1)(zza)). No regulations had been made by 24 November 2026. HMRC's policy paper (4 December 2025) says employee (primary) and employer (secondary) Class 1 NIC will be due on the excess. Income tax relief is unchanged, ordinary employer contributions made without sacrifice keep their NIC relief, and sacrifice still reduces adjusted net income. (2) Finance Act 2026 (c.11, Royal Assent 18 March 2026) ss66-71 bring most unused pension funds and death benefits into the estate for inheritance tax for deaths on or after 6 April 2027 (new IHTA s150A). Excluded are benefits payable only as: dependants' scheme pensions; trivial commutation lump sums that replace them; dependants' or nominees' annuities bought together with the member's lifetime annuity; and benefits paid because the member was in employment at death (death-in-service). The spouse or civil partner and charity exemptions still apply (s69). Budget 2026 announced further technical amendments from 6 April 2027 (OOTLAR 1.27); these are not yet law.
techniques.conditions: The NIC limit affects only employees, including company directors, who give up pay in return for employer pension contributions. A sole trader cannot use salary sacrifice, and a sole trader's personal contributions never had NIC relief. The limit would matter for a spouse employed by the business who sacrifices pay. It would also matter for the freelancer as a director after incorporating, if they chose sacrifice rather than direct employer contributions. The IHT change applies to deaths on or after 6 April 2027 where the estate plus the pension exceeds the available nil-rate bands and the pension does not pass to an exempt beneficiary such as a spouse, civil partner or charity.
techniques.risks: Later regulations can lower the £2,000 limit. The operating detail (pay-period equivalents, timing, several employers) waits for regulations not yet made. From 6 April 2027 pensions stop sheltering wealth from IHT where they pass to non-exempt beneficiaries such as children. Income tax on inherited pensions is not covered here. The Budget 2026 technical amendments are announced, not law.
techniques.data_needed: Whether any pension is funded by salary or bonus sacrifice (a spouse employee, or the freelancer as a future director), and how much is sacrificed each tax year. For estate planning only: pension values and the intended beneficiaries.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Not a saving: a cost check. From 2029-30, extra NIC = (pay sacrificed in the tax year - £2,000, if positive) x (employee Class 1 rate on that slice + employer Class 1 rate), using the rates then in force and subject to the regulations. Direct employer contributions made without sacrifice: no NIC. IHT: for deaths on or after 6 April 2027, add unused pension funds (less excluded benefits) to the estate; there is no IHT on the part that passes to a spouse, civil partner or charity.

figures.2024-25 to 2028-29: No limit: pay sacrificed for employer pension contributions is not earnings for Class 1 NIC (HMRC policy paper, 'Current law').
figures.2029-30: £2,000 a year contributions limit. Class 1 primary and secondary NIC on sacrificed pay above it (NIC (Employer Pensions Contributions) Act 2026 s1(3)-(4); s2 for Northern Ireland). The Act is law, but the charge only works once the regulations are made, and none had been made by 24 November 2026.
figures.2027-28: Unused pension funds and most death benefits count in the IHT estate for deaths on or after 6 April 2027 (FA 2026 ss66 and 71; IHTA s150A). Spouse, civil partner and charity exemptions extended to notional pension property (FA 2026 s69).
figures.budget_2026: OOTLAR 1.27 (announced 28 October 2026, for Finance Bill 2026-27, effective 6 April 2027): a prospective personal representative may direct scheme administrators to pay the IHT, and personal representatives may choose how notional pension property is treated when working out the reduced charity rate.

techniques.status: Law: National Insurance Contributions (Employer Pensions Contributions) Act 2026 c.15 (Royal Assent 29 April 2026, in force that day under s3(2); has effect for 2029-30 onwards; no regulations found on legislation.gov.uk as at 24 November 2026). Finance Act 2026 c.11 ss66-71 (Royal Assent 18 March 2026; deaths on or after 6 April 2027). Announcement history: the salary-sacrifice limit was first announced at Budget 2025 (26 November 2025; OOTLAR measure 2.9). IHT on unused pensions was first announced at Autumn Budget 2024 (30 October 2024), with a technical consultation published the same day. Budget 2025 OOTLAR measure 1.16 restated it and added the withholding and payment mechanics. Announced only: Budget 2026 (28 October 2026) OOTLAR 1.27 technical amendments for Finance Bill 2026-27, from 6 April 2027.
techniques.relevance: Little effect today: as a sole trader the freelancer cannot use salary sacrifice and keeps full income tax relief on personal contributions. It matters if they employ a spouse through a sacrifice scheme or incorporate (a director should use direct employer contributions, which stay free of NIC), and for family estate planning from April 2027.

techniques.name: ISA subscription limits
techniques.summary: Up to £20,000 a year into ISAs (cash, stocks and shares, innovative finance, Lifetime). Interest, dividends and gains inside are free of income tax and CGT; ISA income is outside ANI and does not use the PSA or dividend allowance. Junior ISA limit £9,000.
techniques.conditions: UK resident; one overall adult limit across all ISA types per tax year.
techniques.risks: No upfront relief; subscriptions do not reduce ANI. Unused allowance cannot be carried forward.
techniques.data_needed: Subscriptions per tax year by ISA type.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Tax saved = interest/dividends/gains sheltered x the rate that would otherwise apply (after PSA, dividend allowance, AEA).

figures.2024-25: Adult £20,000; Junior ISA £9,000; Lifetime ISA £4,000 within the £20,000
figures.2026-27: Adult £20,000; Junior ISA £9,000; Child Trust Fund £9,000
figures.2027-28: Adult £20,000; Junior ISA £9,000 (Budget 2026 Annex A); cash ISA limit kept at £20,000 for all savers (Budget 2026)

techniques.status: Law. ISA Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/1870) reg 4ZA(1) £20,000, 4ZA(1A) £4,000 LISA, 4ZB(1) £9,000 JISA; no end date (Budget 2025 policy: kept to 5 April 2031). £12,000 cash ISA cap (SI 2026/1018) revoked by SI 2026/1218 (made 18 Nov 2026, in force 6 Apr 2027). LISA charge 20% above £450,000 cap from 29 Oct 2026; First Time Buyer ISA from April 2029 announced only.
techniques.relevance: Keep the tax reserve in a cash ISA, especially from 2027-28 when savings rates rise and a higher-rate payer's PSA is only £500.

techniques.name: Cash ISA limit: £12,000 cut announced, then cancelled at Budget 2026
techniques.summary: Budget 2025 (OOTLAR 2.3) announced a £12,000 cash ISA limit within £20,000 from April 2027 (over-65s exempt), legislated by SI 2026/1018 (made 10 Sep 2026; due in force 6 April 2027) with anti-circumvention rules (including a charge on interest on cash in stocks and shares/IF ISAs at 'the savings basic rate', given as 22% in the TIIN of 17 Sep 2026). Budget 2026 (OOTLAR 2.5, 28 Oct 2026) reversed it: cash ISA limit stays £20,000 for all savers over 18. SI 2026/1218 (made 18 Nov 2026, laid 19 Nov 2026, in force 6 April 2027) reg 12 revokes SI 2026/1018, so neither the cap nor the anti-circumvention rules take effect.
techniques.conditions: None; overall ISA limit £20,000 in 2026-27 and 2027-28.
techniques.risks: Data still showing £12,000 is out of date; use £20,000.
techniques.data_needed: None.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Use £20,000 cash ISA capacity for 2027-28.

figures.2026-27: Cash ISA limit the full £20,000
figures.2027-28: Cash ISA limit £20,000 (the £12,000 cut is cancelled)

techniques.status: Revocation is law: SI 2026/1218 made 18 Nov 2026, laid 19 Nov 2026, in force 6 April 2027 (reg 12 revokes SI 2026/1018). Announced at Budget 2026 (OOTLAR 2.5, 28 Oct 2026); HMRC policy paper 19 Nov 2026.
