techniques.relevance: Up to £20,000 a year of cash (tax reserve, emergency fund) sheltered in 2027-28 and later.

techniques.name: Lifetime ISA (and the planned First Time Buyer ISA)
techniques.summary: Open aged 18-39 (first payment before 40); pay in up to £4,000 a year until 50, within the £20,000 ISA allowance (both frozen to 5 April 2031). Government bonus 25% (up to £1,000 a year). No charge for a qualifying first home at £450,000 or less, from age 60, terminal illness or death; otherwise a 25% charge. From 29 October 2026 (SI 2026/1130) the charge is 20% where the withdrawal would qualify except that the price exceeds £450,000. Qualifying purchase: first-time buyer, at least 12 months after first payment, mortgage-funded (not a private loan from a relative/spouse), paid via conveyancer. From 6 April 2029 a First Time Buyer ISA replaces the LISA for new savers (announced): from 18 with no upper age, £4,000 a year, 25% bonus on the final balance at exchange for homes up to £450,000, total bonus cap £20,000, held 1 year, mortgage required, no withdrawal charge.
techniques.conditions: First payment before 40; 12-month wait; conveyancer; mortgage not from relatives; each joint buyer needs their own LISA.
techniques.risks: The 25% charge takes back more than the bonus: £4,000 + £1,000 bonus = £5,000; 25% charge £1,250 leaves £3,750, a £250 loss (6.25% of own money). Contributions do not reduce ANI. For a higher-rate retirement saver a pension gives more relief.
techniques.data_needed: Age; first-time buyer status; intended property price.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Bonus = 25% x contribution (max £1,000/yr); net loss on non-qualifying withdrawal = 6.25% of contributions.

figures.2024-25: £4,000 limit; 25% bonus (max £1,000); £450,000 property cap; 25% withdrawal charge
figures.2026-27: Same, except charge for a first home above the cap is 20% from 29 October 2026
figures.2027-28: No change announced
figures.2029-30: First Time Buyer ISA planned from April 2029: £4,000 a year, 25% bonus, cumulative bonus cap £20,000, homes up to £450,000 (announced)

techniques.status: LISA law (Savings (Government Contributions) Act 2017; ISA Regs 1998 Schedule). 20% over-cap charge law (SI 2026/1130, made 27 Oct, in force 29 Oct 2026). First Time Buyer ISA announced (consultation 22 Jun - 18 Aug 2026; Budget 2026 28 Oct 2026; government response 18 Nov 2026); no legislation yet.
techniques.relevance: Worth considering if under 40 and a first-time buyer.

techniques.name: Venture Capital Trust (VCT) income tax relief
techniques.summary: Subscribing for new VCT shares gives an income tax reduction on up to £200,000 a year: 30% to 5 April 2026, 20% for shares issued on or after 6 April 2026 (FA 2026 amending ITA s263(2)). VCT dividends tax-free; disposals CGT-exempt. Relief is the lower of rate x amount subscribed and the amount reducing liability to nil. Company limits doubled from 6 April 2026.
techniques.conditions: New shares in an approved VCT; 5-year holding; relief only in the year of issue (no carry back); no linked loan (s264); reduced by linked sales within 6 months either side (s264A).
techniques.risks: Clawback on disposal within 5 years. Capital at risk, illiquid, high charges. A tax reducer: does NOT lower ANI (no help with HICBC, PA taper or childcare). Risk-to-capital condition (s286ZA). At 20% it is no better than basic-rate pension relief.
techniques.data_needed: Income tax liability; amount subscribed; issue date.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Relief = min(rate x subscription (max £200,000), income tax liability).

figures.2024-25: Relief 30%; maximum subscription £200,000; minimum holding 5 years
figures.2026-27: Relief 20% (shares issued from 6 April 2026); £200,000; 5 years; company limits: annual £10m (knowledge-intensive £20m), lifetime £24m (£40m), gross assets £30m before and £35m after issue
figures.2027-28: Relief 20%; no further rate change announced

techniques.status: Law: FA 2026 (c.11) s15 (commencement s15(9)) from 6 April 2026. Announced only: clawback at the rate applying at issue for shares issued from 6 April 2026 (Budget 2026, 28 Oct 2026, OOTLAR 1.36; Finance Bill 2026-27, backdated). Until enacted ITA s266(4) still says 30%.
techniques.relevance: Only after pensions are maximised and with a large income tax bill; risk money only.

techniques.name: Enterprise Investment Scheme (EIS) income tax relief
techniques.summary: Subscribing for new shares in a qualifying unquoted trading company gives 30% income tax relief on up to £1m a year (£2m if at least £1m in knowledge-intensive companies); can be carried back one year. Gains can be deferred by reinvesting; CGT exemption on disposal after 3 years if income tax relief was given; loss less relief can be set against income. Company limits doubled from 6 April 2026.
techniques.conditions: Investor not connected (not an employee; not more than 30% of shares, votes or assets; paid directors generally excluded unless payments permitted). 3-year holding. Company must hold an HMRC compliance certificate.
techniques.risks: Relief limited to income tax liability; does not reduce ANI or NIC. Risk-to-capital condition (s157A). High risk of loss and illiquidity. Withdrawn on early disposal. A founder cannot normally claim EIS on their own company.
techniques.data_needed: Income tax liability current and prior year; subscription.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Relief = min(30% x subscription, income tax liability of the chosen year).

figures.2024-25: Relief 30%; £1m (£2m with knowledge-intensive companies); 3-year holding
figures.2026-27: Relief 30%; £1m/£2m; 3 years; company annual limit £10m (KIC £20m), lifetime £24m (£40m), gross assets £30m before and £35m after
figures.2027-28: No rate change announced

techniques.status: Law. ITA 2007 Part 5; s158(2A) 30%; s158(2ZA) £1m/£2m (from 6 April 2018); shares issued before 6 April 2035 (s157(1)(aa), FA 2024 s11). Company limits FA 2026 s14 (Royal Assent 18 March 2026, from 6 April 2026). Technical changes from 6 April 2027 announced at Budget 2026 for Finance Bill 2026-27 (not law).
techniques.relevance: For later high-profit years; not for the user's own company.

techniques.name: Seed Enterprise Investment Scheme (SEIS) income tax relief
techniques.summary: 50% income tax relief on up to £200,000 a year in new shares of very early-stage companies; carry back available. Reinvestment relief exempts 50% of a reinvested gain on up to £200,000 invested (max £100,000 of gain). CGT-free disposal after 3 years; loss relief against income.
techniques.conditions: Investor not an employee (directors may claim); not more than 30% of the company; 3-year holding; company meets SEIS conditions.
techniques.risks: Very high risk. Relief capped at income tax liability; does not reduce ANI. Risk-to-capital condition (s257AAA). Clawback if a condition is broken.
techniques.data_needed: Income tax liability; subscription.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Relief = min(50% x subscription, income tax liability).

figures.2024-25: Relief 50%; £200,000 a year; 3-year holding
figures.2026-27: Relief 50%; £200,000; 3 years (no SEIS change from 6 April 2026 listed)
figures.2027-28: Technical fixes only (Budget 2026 OOTLAR 1.36)

techniques.status: Law: ITA 2007 Part 5A; TCGA Sch 5BB; £200,000 limit since 6 April 2023 (FA 2023 s15). 2027-28 technical changes announced (Budget 2026 OOTLAR 1.36 and TIIN, 28 Oct 2026) for Finance Bill 2026-27.
techniques.relevance: Only risk capital at high profit levels; not for a founder holding more than 30% of their own company.

techniques.name: Gift Aid: higher and additional rate relief
techniques.summary: A Gift Aid gift is treated as paid after deduction of basic-rate tax (ITA 2007 s414(2)(a)). The charity or CASC claims 25p for every £1 given, so a £100 gift is worth £125 gross. The donor's basic rate limit and higher rate limit both go up by the gross gift (s414(2)(b)). Income that would have been taxed at 40% is then taxed at 20%, and income that would have been taxed at 45% is taxed at 40%. On rest-of-UK non-savings income, a higher-rate payer therefore gets extra relief of 20% of the gross gift (GOV.UK example: £25 back on a £100 gift), and an additional-rate payer gets 25% (20% + 5%). This applies only to the extent the donor has income in the bands that move. The gross gift is also deducted from adjusted net income (s58 Step 2), which can reduce the High Income Child Benefit Charge or restore a tapered personal allowance. Extra relief is claimed through Self Assessment or by asking HMRC to change the tax code. A gift can be carried back to the previous tax year by election (s426; see gift-aid-carry-back).
techniques.conditions: Each gift must be a qualifying donation (s416), meeting Conditions A to F, including Condition EA. Condition A: it is a payment of money, so free work or kit does not count. Condition B: it is not repayable. Condition C: it is not given through payroll giving. Condition D: it is not deductible in calculating any income, so it cannot also be claimed as a business expense. Condition E: it is not linked to the charity acquiring property from the donor or a person connected with the donor. Condition EA: it is not, and does not amount in substance to, the donor waiving money the charity owes them on an amount advanced to it for which social investment relief (ITA Part 5B) was obtained (s416(6A)). Condition F: any benefits to the donor are within the limits in ss417-421. The donor gives a Gift Aid declaration to a charity or CASC with an HMRC charity reference number. The donor must pay income tax or CGT for the year at least equal to the basic-rate tax treated as deducted, which in practice means net gifts of no more than 4 times the tax paid (GOV.UK). Scottish taxpayers: the Scottish band limits move as well (s414(2)(b)). With the 2026-27 Scottish rates, extra relief is 22% for a 42% higher-rate payer, 25% for a 45% advanced-rate payer, 28% for a 48% top-rate payer and 1% for a 21% intermediate-rate payer (derived). s414A adjusts the relief where a devolved basic rate differs from the UK basic rate.
techniques.risks: If tax paid is less than the basic-rate tax treated as deducted, HMRC charges the donor the difference (s424). Tainted donations (ITA Part 13 Ch 8): a donation is tainted only if all of Conditions A, B and C in s809ZJ are met. Condition A: the donor or a connected person enters into arrangements, and it is reasonable to assume that the donation and the arrangements would not have been made independently of each other (s809ZJ(2)). Condition B (for donations made on or after 6 April 2026, FA 2026 s56 replaced the old main-purpose test with this outcome test): a linked person who is not a charity receives financial assistance under or in connection with those arrangements, directly or indirectly, from the charity or a connected charity (s809ZJ(5)). 'Financial assistance' includes a loan, a guarantee, an indemnity or any form of investment, whether or not on arm's length terms (s809ZJ(8)). Arm's length payments by the charity for work done for it, or for the expenses of that work, are ignored (s809ZL(2A)), so being paid a normal rate to work on a charity's event does not by itself count. Condition C: the donor is not a charity-owned company or linked housing provider. If a donation becomes tainted in the tax year it is made, the relief and the deduction from adjusted net income are lost (s809ZM(1), (2) and (6); s58(4)). If it becomes tainted in a later tax year, income tax is charged for that later year equal to the extra tax that would have been due for the donation year, with late-payment interest running from 1 February after the donation year (s809ZMA). Relief on associated donations made under the same arrangements is removed or clawed back in the same way (s809ZMB). Donations made before 6 April 2026 follow the old rules (main-purpose test; relief removed under the old s809ZM). The gift is a real cost, and the relief is always less than the gift. Gift Aid does not reduce Class 4 NIC, because it is not a deduction from trading profits.
techniques.data_needed: For each gift: net amount, date, recipient and whether there is a declaration. Also: whether the user or anyone connected with them has any arrangement with the charity, or receives loans, guarantees, indemnities, investment or other payments from it (other than arm's length pay for work); whether the user is a Scottish taxpayer; taxable income in each band; income tax and CGT for the year; adjusted net income before gifts (for the HICBC and the £100,000 taper); whether any gift is to be carried back under s426.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Gross gift = net / 0.8. Extra relief to the donor (rest of UK) = 20% of the part of the gross gift that fits within income above the basic rate limit, plus a further 5% of any part within income above the additional-rate threshold. For Scottish taxpayers, use the marginal Scottish rate minus 20%. Then reduce adjusted net income by the gross gift. In the HICBC band the charge falls by 1% of Child Benefit per £200 (2026-27: about 7.2% of the gross gift with one child, 11.9% with two). In the £100,000-£125,140 taper a further 20% of the gross gift comes back through the restored personal allowance, so the donor gets 40% in all and tax relief covers 60% of the gross gift once the charity's 20% is counted. There is no Class 4 saving.

figures.2024-25: Basic rate 20% (law; HMRC income tax rates page). Gross-up: net / 0.8. On rest-of-UK non-savings income, extra relief is 20% of the gross gift for a higher-rate payer and 25% for an additional-rate payer. The old purpose test for tainted donations applies.
figures.2025-26: Same: basic rate 20% (law). The old purpose test for tainted donations applies to donations made before 6 April 2026.
figures.2026-27: Basic rate 20%, higher 40%, additional 45% (FA 2026 s2), so extra relief is 20% and 25% (rest of UK). Scottish (GOV.UK 2026-27 rates): 22% at the higher rate (42%), 25% at the advanced rate (45%), 28% at the top rate (48%), 1% at the intermediate rate (21%). Dividends shifted from the 35.75% upper rate to the 10.75% ordinary rate: 25% (OOTLAR Annex A dividend rates). For donations from 6 April 2026 the outcome test applies, with same-year removal (s809ZM) and later-year clawback (s809ZMA) (FA 2026 s56(8) and Sch 9).
figures.2027-28: Announced, not law: basic 20%, higher 40%, additional 45% (Budget 2026, 28 Oct 2026, sections 3.6 and 3.9; Budget 2026 OOTLAR Annex A). Parliament must set the rates for each year (ITA s6(2)), and FA 2026 s1 charges income tax for 2026-27 only, so this needs Finance Bill 2026-27. If enacted, the gross-up stays net / 0.8 (s415 uses the main basic rate). Property rates are 22/42/47% in law (FA 2026 s7), and Budget 2026 proposes 24/44/49% for property and savings income. Both keep 20-point and 5-point gaps, so extra relief on that income is the same.

techniques.status: Law: ITA 2007 Part 8 Ch 2 (ss414, 414A, 415, 416 including Condition EA in s416(6A), 424, 426); s58 Step 2, with s58(4) substituted by FA 2026 Sch 9 para 23(3); Part 13 Ch 8 tainted donations: s809ZJ (Condition B substituted and 'financial assistance' defined by FA 2026 s56), s809ZL (s809ZL(2A) inserted by FA 2026 Sch 9), s809ZM (subsection (1) substituted by FA 2026 Sch 9 para 7(3): same-year tainting only), s809ZMA (later-year clawback) and s809ZMB (associated donations), both inserted by FA 2026 Sch 9 para 8. These changes apply to donations made on or after 6 April 2026 (FA 2026 s56(8)). legislation.gov.uk shows no outstanding effects on ss414, 416, 424, 426 or 58. The basic rate is 20% in law for 2024-25 to 2026-27 (FA 2026 s2 for 2026-27). The 2027-28 rates are announced only (Budget 2026, 28 Oct 2026; Finance Bill 2026-27). The rates annex is the Budget 2026 OOTLAR Annex A; the main Budget document's own Annex A covers financing.
techniques.relevance: With turnover under £50,000 the user's profit usually sits in the basic-rate band. The charity then gets 25p per £1, but the user gets no extra relief. Gift Aid becomes worth claiming once profit passes £50,270, and especially in the £60,000-£80,000 Child Benefit charge band or the £100,000-£125,140 taper, for cash the user would give anyway.

techniques.name: Gift Aid carry back (ITA 2007 s426)
techniques.summary: A donor can elect to treat a Gift Aid donation made in the current year as made in the previous tax year, getting relief at the previous year's rates and reducing that year's ANI (s58 Step 2 covers s426 gifts). E.g. a gift in December 2026 can be carried back to 2025-26 if the election is made in the 2025-26 return filed by 31 January 2027.
techniques.conditions: Election on or before delivery of the year P return and no later than the normal filing date (s426(6)); year P charged amount must be at least the increased total of gifts (s426(2)).
techniques.risks: Late return = no carry back. Pension contributions have no equivalent.
techniques.data_needed: 2025-26 ANI; gift dates; return filing date.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Gross gift needed to bring prior-year ANI to £60,000 or £100,000; saving = reduction in HICBC or restored PA at prior-year rates plus higher-rate relief.

figures.2025-26: A gift made between 6 April 2026 and filing can be carried back to 2025-26; election in a return filed by 31 January 2027 (online deadline)
figures.2026-27: A gift made in 2027-28 before the 2026-27 return is filed can be carried back; deadline 31 January 2028

techniques.status: Law. ITA 2007 s426 in force; s426(8) omitted by FA 2012 s50; no outstanding effects. FA 2026 Sch 9 para 23(3) substituted s58(4) (tainted/associated donations excluded at Step 2).
techniques.relevance: Act now (before 31 Jan 2027): a donation carried back can cut the 2025-26 HICBC or restore 2025-26 personal allowance.

techniques.name: Trading allowance (£1,000, rising to £3,000 from 2027-28)
techniques.summary: One allowance per individual per tax year, against gross receipts of all relevant trades (carried on alone, not in partnership, not rent-a-room) plus Part 5 Ch 8 miscellaneous income (ss783AA-783AC). £1,000 for 2024-25 to 2026-27 (s783AD). Full relief (automatic unless elected out under s783AL): if relevant income is no more than the allowance it is treated as nil. Partial relief (election s783AM, by the first anniversary of the normal SA filing date): profit = gross receipts minus the allowance, with no actual expenses or capital allowances (s783AI; BIM86050) and no loss. Exclusions deny ALL relief for that whole year (BIM86030) if relevant income includes any payment from the individual's or spouse's employer (s783AO), a firm in which the individual is or is connected with a partner (s783AP), or a close company where the individual is a participator or associate (s783AQ); also s783AN cases.
techniques.conditions: Not for partnership trading income, employer/spouse's employer income, or income from a company the person or a connected person controls; excludes rent-a-room receipts. Partial relief gives up all actual expenses and capital allowances.
techniques.risks: Main trade receipts share the same single allowance, so substantial sales leave nothing for side income like kit hire. If ever on PAYE with a client and also invoicing it, or spouse employed by a client, the allowance is lost for that year. After incorporation, payments from the user's own close company knock it out.
techniques.data_needed: Gross receipts of all trades and miscellaneous income; payer relationships.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: If gross relevant income <= allowance: income treated as nil. Else compare (receipts - allowance) with (receipts - actual expenses - capital allowances) and choose the lower profit.

figures.2027-28: £3,000 (announced 28 October 2026; Finance Bill 2026-27); SA trading income reporting threshold also £3,000

techniques.status: £1,000 law: ITTOIA s783AD(1) (F(No.2)A 2017 Sch 3), up to date to 22-24 Nov 2026. £3,000 announced (HMRC TIIN 'Increasing the trading allowance', 28 Oct 2026; effect 6 April 2027; Finance Bill 2026-27); not law.
techniques.relevance: Limited use while the main trade runs; relevant to a family member's small side income or a very low year.

techniques.name: Trading allowance rises from £1,000 to £3,000 (2027-28)
techniques.summary: The trading allowance (trading and miscellaneous income) rises from £1,000 to £3,000 from 6 April 2027, and the SA reporting threshold for trading income also rises to £3,000.
techniques.conditions: Used instead of actual expenses; full relief only where the allowance covers all relevant income.
techniques.risks: No use for the main trade where profits exceed £3,000 and expenses are higher.
techniques.data_needed: Gross trading/miscellaneous receipts.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: As trading-allowance with £3,000 for 2027-28.

figures.2027-28: £3,000 (announced)

techniques.status: Announced at Budget 2026 (OOTLAR 28 Oct 2026, updated 5 Nov 2026) for Finance Bill 2026-27, effect 6 April 2027. Not law: ITTOIA s783AD still reads £1,000.
techniques.relevance: Marginal; only for small side income separate from the main trade.

techniques.name: Property allowance (£1,000)
techniques.summary: A £1,000 tax-free allowance for income from land and buildings in a property business (ITTOIA s783BD), separate from and claimable alongside the trading allowance. Gross property income of £1,000 or less: full relief automatic (elect out to claim a loss). Above £1,000: elect to deduct £1,000 instead of actual expenses (no loss). Elections by the first anniversary of the normal SA filing date. Lost for the whole year if income includes payments from the person's or spouse's employer, a firm in which the person is or is connected with a partner, or a close company where the person is a participator or associate; or if the s274A finance-cost reducer is claimed; or if rent-a-room expenses are deducted instead of rent-a-room relief. Letting a home or land to a film crew is property income (PIM1051); hiring out equipment is not.
techniques.conditions: Not for income from a controlled company/partnership or employer; not with the finance-cost reducer or with rent-a-room where expenses are deducted; cannot create a loss. Gross income £1,000-£2,500: contact HMRC; over £2,500: Self Assessment.
techniques.risks: Records still needed. Location-letting income is property income, not trading income.
techniques.data_needed: Gross property income (location fees, storage, parking).
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: If gross <= £1,000: nil taxable. Else taxable = max(gross - £1,000, gross - expenses) choosing the lower.

figures.2027-28: £1,000 (no change announced); property income taxed at property rates 22%/42%/47% under FA 2026 s7, proposed to rise to 24%/44%/49%

techniques.status: Law: ITTOIA Part 6A Ch 2 (ss783B-783BQ; F(No.2)A 2017 Sch 3); s783BD £1,000 every year. FA 2026 s7 property rates 22/42/47 for 2027-28 (law); 24/44/49 announced at Budget 2026 (Finance Bill 2026-27).
techniques.relevance: Covers small location fees, storage or parking lets; not kit hire.

techniques.name: Rent a Room relief (£7,500)
techniques.summary: Rent-a-room relief (ITTOIA 2005 Part 7 Ch 1) exempts an individual's gross receipts for furnished residential accommodation in their only or main UK home, up to £7,500 a year (s789(4)). Receipts include charges for meals, cleaning and laundry (s786). The limit is tested on the 'total rent-a-room amount': receipts plus any relevant balancing charges, with no deduction for expenses (s788). The limit is halved to £3,750 unless the exclusive receipts condition is met (s790). The condition fails if anyone else receives receipts for letting accommodation in the same home (or for meals, cleaning or laundry with it) at a time when it is the individual's main home, during a relevant period. The relevant periods are: the income period (the tax year, or the part of it during which the letting runs, s786(4)); the 12 months beginning when the income period begins; and the 12 months ending when it ends (s790(2)). For a letting that runs all tax year, all three periods are the tax year itself. For a part-year letting, the test reaches up to 12 months forward from the letting's start and back from its end. At or below the limit the relief is automatic. The individual can elect out for that year (s799), for example to claim a loss. Above the limit, the default is the normal method (method A: receipts less expenses). The individual can instead elect for method B (s800): tax on receipts plus balancing charges over the limit, with no expenses or capital allowances. A method B election continues for later years until withdrawn. If the total rent-a-room amount is at or below the limit in any year, the election is treated as withdrawn for that year and all later years, so a fresh election is needed if receipts later go back over the limit (s800(4) and (6)). The relief covers lodgers and bed-and-breakfast or guest-house income in the home, whether that income is trading or property income and whether the home is owned or rented. It does not cover homes converted into separate flats, unfurnished lettings, or rooms let as an office, store or other business space (PIM4002). It is for individuals only, not companies or partnerships (PIM4001).
techniques.conditions: The accommodation must be furnished, in a UK residence that is the individual's only or main residence for some or all of the income period (s786). The individual must not also get other taxable income from the same trade, letting or agreement (s785). Elections under s799 or s800, and their withdrawal, are made to HMRC in writing. No special form is needed, and the right entries on the return are enough (PIM4050). The deadline is one year after the normal 31 January filing date: 31 January 2027 for 2024-25 and 31 January 2028 for 2025-26 (s799(3), s800(5)). HMRC can accept a late election. A tax return is needed if receipts exceed the limit (GOV.UK).
techniques.risks: Receipts are counted gross (rent plus meals, cleaning, laundry and any balancing charges). A lodger paying £150 a week (£7,800 a year) is therefore over the £7,500 limit whatever the costs. Receipts from all rent-a-room sources (for example a lodger and a B&B) count towards one limit, which under method B is split between the sources in proportion to their receipts (ss796-798; PIM4030). A method B election lapses for good after any year at or below the limit, so it must be made again if receipts rise later. The £1,000 property allowance cannot apply to a property business made up only of rent-a-room receipts (s783BA). In any year in which rent-a-room expenses are deducted in a property business (a s799 election, or receipts over the limit without a s800 election), no property allowance is available at all (s783BM). Location or filming fees for the home are not rent-a-room receipts.
techniques.data_needed: Gross receipts, including meals, cleaning and laundry charges, and any balancing charges; letting start and end dates; whether anyone else (a partner, joint owner or other) receives letting income from the home while it is the user's main home, during the income period, the 12 months from its start or the 12 months to its end; whether the home is the main residence; expenses (to compare methods A and B); whether an s800 election is in force and whether it lapsed in an earlier year at or below the limit; whether the letting is a trade (B&B) or property income.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Limit L = £7,500, or £3,750 if the s790 condition is not met. Total rent-a-room amount X = gross receipts R plus any relevant balancing charges, with no deduction for expenses (s788). If X is L or less, taxable income is 0 (unless a s799 election is made to use a loss). If X is more than L: method A = receipts minus allowable expenses (the default); method B = receipts plus balancing charges minus the deductible amount (needs an s800 election in force; no expenses or capital allowances). The deductible amount is L, shared out between source types (a trade, a UK property business, Part 5 Ch 8 income) in proportion to each type's receipts out of R, and capped at that type's receipts (ss796-798). Saving = tax on the profit without the relief minus tax on the figure chosen, at the marginal rate. Property income pays income tax only; a B&B trade also pays Class 4.

figures.2024-25: Basic amount £7,500 (s789(4), set by SI 2015/1539, with effect for 2016-17 onwards); £3,750 if the s790 exclusive receipts condition is not met. Election deadline 31 January 2027.
figures.2026-27: £7,500 / £3,750. Election deadline 31 January 2029. Property income is taxed at the main rates this year (Budget 2026 OOTLAR Annex A).
figures.2027-28: £7,500 / £3,750 under current law; the Budget 2026 documents make no change. Any taxable rent-a-room profit in a UK property business (method A or B) is 'property income' (ITA s17A, inserted by FA 2026 s6 for 2027-28) and is taxed at the property rates. In law these are 22%/42%/47% (FA 2026 s7). Budget 2026 proposes 24%/44%/49% and says these will apply across England, Wales and Northern Ireland (Finance Bill 2026-27; not law). Devolved rates from 2027-28 (FA 2026 s8 and Sch 2, in force 16 September 2026 with 2027-28 as the first tax year, SI 2026/1023): the Scottish Parliament may set separate property rates for Scottish taxpayers (Scotland Act 1998 s80C(2B), substituted by FA 2026 Sch 2 para 1); for Welsh taxpayers the property rates are the UK property rates less 10 points plus any Welsh rate set by Senedd Cymru (ITA s6B(1A), Step 3 substituted by FA 2026 Sch 2 para 2). Profit from a B&B or guest-house trade, and Part 5 Ch 8 income, is not property income and stays at the main rates.

techniques.status: Law: ITTOIA 2005 Part 7 Ch 1 (ss784-802). s789(4) is £7,500, set by SI 2015/1539 with effect for 2016-17 onwards. legislation.gov.uk is up to date to 24 November 2026, and its only listed pending change does not affect these sections. HMRC guidance: PIM4001, PIM4002, PIM4030, PIM4050. Property income rates for 2027-28 are law (FA 2026 ss6-7). Scottish and Welsh property rates: FA 2026 s8 and Sch 2, in force 16 September 2026 for 2027-28 onwards (SI 2026/1023). The further 2-point rise to 24/44/49 is announced only (Budget 2026, 28 Oct 2026; Finance Bill 2026-27).
techniques.relevance: Lets the user take in a lodger, or host visiting crew in their own home, and keep up to £7,500 a year tax-free (£3,750 if a partner or anyone else also gets letting income from the home), separately from the trade. Fees for using the home as a filming location, office or kit store are not covered; they are property income (see property-allowance).

techniques.name: Personal savings allowance
techniques.summary: Interest up to the allowance is taxed at 0%: £1,000 basic-rate, £500 higher-rate, nil additional-rate. Interest still counts in ANI.
techniques.conditions: Allowance depends on the highest marginal band; joint account interest split equally.
techniques.risks: Crossing £50,270 halves it; over £125,140 removes it. Interest on the tax reserve can quietly use it up.
techniques.data_needed: Interest received by account; total income.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Taxable interest = max(0, interest - PSA - unused starting-rate band) at savings rates.

figures.2027-28: £1,000 / £500 (Budget 2026 Annex A); savings rates 22%/42%/47% in FA 2026 s5, proposed to rise to 24%/44%/49%

techniques.status: Law: ITA ss12A-12B (FA 2016 s4), amounts fixed in s12B(2)-(4). Savings rates 20/40/45 law for 2024-25 (F(No.2)A 2024 s3), 2025-26 (FA 2025 s3), 2026-27 (FA 2026 s3); 2027-28 22/42/47 law (FA 2026 s5); 24/44/49 announced at Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026; TIIN 29 Oct 2026) for Finance Bill 2026-27.
techniques.relevance: For a higher-rate sole trader the £500 allowance is small; keep the tax reserve in a cash ISA.

techniques.name: Starting rate for savings (0% on up to £5,000)
techniques.summary: Up to £5,000 of interest taxed at 0%, reduced £1 for £1 by taxable non-savings income above the PA (e.g. trading profit); nil once other income reaches £17,570. Applies on top of the PSA.
techniques.conditions: Other (non-savings, non-dividend) income below £17,570. GOV.UK example: wages £16,000 leave £3,430 above the PA, so starting rate band is £1,570.
techniques.risks: Trading profit counts as other income.
techniques.data_needed: Non-savings income; interest.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Band = max(0, 5,000 - max(0, other income - 12,570)).

figures.2027-28: £5,000 at 0% (Budget 2026 Annex A)

techniques.status: Law. ITA s12(3) £5,000; indexation off and £5,000 confirmed by F(No.2)A 2024 s4 (2024-25), FA 2025 s4(1) (2025-26), FA 2026 s9 (2026-27 to 2030-31). 2027-28 figure is law.
techniques.relevance: Useful in a low-profit year or for a lower-earning spouse holding savings (outright gift only).

techniques.name: Separate savings and property income tax rates from 2027-28
techniques.summary: FA 2026 (Royal Assent 18 March 2026) inserts ITA ss6D and 11CA (property rates) and s7 sets 2027-28 property rates at 22%/42%/47%. Savings rates (ITA s7A) are 20/40/45 for 2026-27 (FA 2026 s3(2)) and 22/42/47 for 2027-28 (FA 2026 s5). Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026; HMRC policy paper 29 Oct 2026) announced Finance Bill 2026-27 will raise both to 24%/44%/49% from 6 April 2027, with property and savings trust rates of 49%. Dividend rates from 2026-27 are 10.75/35.75/39.35. Equipment hire income is not property income.
techniques.conditions: Property rates apply in England, Wales and NI; savings rates UK-wide.
techniques.risks: Rates not final until Finance Bill 2026-27 passes; show both figures with status.
techniques.data_needed: Savings and property income by year.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Hold both the enacted (22/42/47) and announced (24/44/49) values for 2027-28 and switch on Royal Assent.

figures.2026-27: Savings 20%/40%/45%; property income at main rates; dividends 10.75%/35.75%/39.35%

techniques.name: Keeping adjusted net income at £100,000 or less to protect childcare support
techniques.summary: Tax-Free Childcare and the 30 hours both use ANI (ITA s58: net income less grossed-up Gift Aid and gross relief-at-source pension contributions). A gross pension contribution that brings expected ANI to £100,000 keeps both schemes and also gets about 60% relief in the taper band. Example: profits £110,000 and a £10,000 gross contribution (£8,000 net) gives ANI £100,000, saving about £6,000 in tax and keeping up to £2,000 per child of top-up plus the 30 hours.
techniques.conditions: Test is expected ANI for the current tax year; contribution paid before 5 April; reconfirm every 3 months and update estimates.
techniques.risks: Lumpy self-employed income can push ANI over £100,000 late in the year; plan contributions in time; declarations must be honest. VCT/EIS/SEIS relief does not reduce ANI.
techniques.data_needed: Forecast ANI for each parent; children's ages; childcare costs.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Gross contribution needed = expected ANI - 100,000; value = tax relief (~60% in band) + childcare support retained (up to £2,000 per child TFC plus 30 hours value, null).

figures.2024-25: £100,000 limit for each parent
figures.2027-28: £100,000 (no change announced)

techniques.status: Law. ITA s58; Childcare Payments Act 2014 s10 and SI 2015/448 reg 15 (UK-wide TFC); SI 2022/1134 regs 4 and 14(3)(c) (30 hours, England). Budget 2026 announced no change.
techniques.relevance: Highest-value planning step for a parent with profits around £100,000-£125,140.

techniques.name: Kit hire income: trading income or miscellaneous income
techniques.summary: HMRC generally accepts that leasing chattels is a trade; non-trading 'special leasing' only in exceptional cases with very little evidence of trading, e.g. a single asset with no personal involvement (BLM00305). Hire profits fall under the miscellaneous sweep-up (ITTOIA s687) only where not otherwise taxable (BIM100220). Hiring kit with the technician operating it is a supply of services within the trade.
techniques.conditions: For a technician who regularly hires owned kit to production companies, often with own labour, the hire is most likely part of the trade or a second trade. Trading: cash basis kit deductions (s33A) or AIA; trading losses usable against other income; counts as relevant UK earnings for pensions. Miscellaneous: no cash basis; special leasing allowances only against special leasing income (CAA s258); losses only against miscellaneous income; not relevant UK earnings.
techniques.risks: Labelling trading hire as miscellaneous to avoid Class 4 is contrary to HMRC's presumption. Kit with operator is a service. After incorporation, kit kept personally and hired to the user's company must be at arm's length; that income cannot use the trading allowance and its allowances go only against that special leasing income.
techniques.data_needed: Hire bookings (with or without operator), clients, kit used, frequency; ledger category 'kit hire'.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Default: treat as trading income (Class 4 applies: 6% £12,570-£50,270, 2% above).

figures.current: If trading: cash basis is the standard method; Class 4 applies (6% between £12,570 and £50,270, 2% above). If miscellaneous: no Class 4; shares the single trading allowance (£1,000; £3,000 from 2027-28 if enacted).

techniques.status: Law: ITTOIA Part 2, s687, Part 6A (s783AD £1,000); CAA 2001 ss19, 258; ITA s152; FA 2004 s189; SSCBA s15. HMRC BLM00305; BIM100220 (updated 4 Aug 2026). Announced: trading allowance £3,000 from 6 April 2027 (Budget 2026; Finance Bill 2026-27).
techniques.relevance: Default: treat kit hire as trading income.

techniques.name: Capital allowances and cash-basis deductions for equipment (including kit for hire)
techniques.conditions:
Cash basis: the deduction is taken when the cost is paid, and the asset must be acquired for continuing use in the trade; part private use needs a just and reasonable split.

Accruals:
- AIA: available on any plant except the s38B exclusions. It is reduced for part private use (s205), scaled up or down for chargeable periods longer or shorter than 12 months (s51A(6)), and shared between related businesses under common control (ss51B-51N).
- First-year allowance (s45U): the plant must be unused and not second-hand, not special-rate and not a car. It is not available in the period the trade permanently stops (s46 general exclusion 1). Plant for leasing or hire (general exclusion 6) qualifies only if s46(4B) is met: the hirer uses it wholly or almost wholly to earn income within the charge to UK tax, or the hirer is UK-resident and does not use it to a significant extent to earn untaxed foreign income. It is also denied for spending connected with disqualifying arrangements (s45V). Both tests must be met: a main purpose of the arrangements is to get the s45U allowance, and it is reasonable to regard them as contrived, abnormal or lacking a genuine commercial purpose, or as getting round the intended limits of the relief. Buying needed kit sooner to get the allowance is not caught by its purpose alone. It is also denied for spending linked to another person's change of trade (general exclusion 7).
- Personal kit brought into the trade is treated as bought at market value, capped at its original cost (s13). It gets writing-down allowances only.

Vehicles: a car, van or motorcycle whose costs are claimed at the simplified mileage rate gets no other deduction or allowance for its purchase (ITTOIA s94D; CAA s38ZA).

Special leasing (hire outside any trade): each item is a separate qualifying activity (s19(4)). Allowances are set against the person's income from any special leasing. Where the hirer does not use the item for a qualifying activity, such as their own trade, for all or part of the year, the allowance (or a proportionate part) is set only against income from that leasing. Any excess is carried forward against income of the same kind (s258(2), (3) and (5)).
techniques.risks: Selling kit, receiving insurance money for it, or taking it out of business use creates taxable income: a receipt under the cash basis (s96A, at market value if the kit is kept but no longer used in the trade), or a disposal value under capital allowances. Where the AIA covered the whole cost, the sale price can be a balancing charge in full (see unreported-kit-sales-balancing-charges). Second-hand kit gets no first-year allowance. There is no AIA or first-year allowance in the period the trade permanently stops, which matters on incorporation (see caa-s266-election). The 50% first-year allowance and 12% WDA are not law until Finance Bill 2026-27 is enacted. Moving between the cash basis and accruals needs transitional adjustments.
techniques.data_needed: For each kit purchase: date paid, cost, new or second-hand, car or not, VAT, supplier, and private-use share. Also: whether the item was owned personally before being brought into the trade; the accounting basis (cash or accruals) and period-of-account dates; pool balances, including first-year allowance balances waiting to enter the pool; whether any vehicle uses simplified mileage; hire bookings (in the trade or outside it, and whether the hirer uses the kit in their own business); and disposals with proceeds.

figures.2024-25: Cash basis is the default (s24A). AIA £1,000,000 (s51A(5)). Main WDA 18%; special rate 6% (s104D); small pool limit £1,000 (s56A). No 40% first-year allowance (it starts on 1 January 2026).
figures.2025-26: AIA £1,000,000. Main WDA 18% for periods of account ending before 6 April 2026 (such as 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026); hybrid rate for periods spanning 6 April 2026. Special 6%. 40% first-year allowance (law) for new, unused main-rate plant (not cars) bought from 1 January 2026 within the 2025-26 period of account (FA 2026 s29; CAA s45U, s52(3)).
figures.2026-27: AIA £1,000,000. Main WDA 14% for periods beginning on or after 6 April 2026 (FA 2026 s28). A period spanning 6 April 2026 uses X = 18 x BRD/CP + 14 x ARD/CP, rounded up to 2 decimal places; for 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027 that is 14.06%. Special rate 6%. First-year allowance 40% (law). 50% is proposed for spending from 1 January 2027, which falls in the 2026-27 period for a 5 April or 31 March year end; 40% applies until it is enacted.
figures.2027-28: AIA £1,000,000. Proposed (Budget 2026, 28 Oct 2026; TIIN 29 Oct 2026; OOTLAR 1.42; Finance Bill 2026-27; not law): main WDA 12% for periods beginning on or after 6 April 2027, with a hybrid rate for spanning periods, and a first-year allowance of 50%. Current law: 14% and 40%. Special rate 6%.
figures.note: Budget 2026 OOTLAR Annex A (corporation tax table) lists the AIA at £1m, the main rate at 14% / 12% and the special rate at 6% / 6% for FY2026-27 / FY2027-28, and the main-rate first-year allowance at 40% / 50%. The 50% still needs Finance Bill 2026-27. For income tax, the £1m comes from s51A(5), and the chargeable period is the period of account (CAA s6). Under the cash basis, capital allowances are claimed only for cars.

techniques.status: Law: cash basis default from 2024-25 (ITTOIA s24A, inserted by FA 2024 Sch 10) and s33A; AIA £1m (CAA s51A(5), F(No.2)A 2023 s8); 14% main WDA and 40% first-year allowance (FA 2026 ss28-29, Royal Assent 18 March 2026); special rate 6% (s104D); pooling rules CAA s58(4A) and (5); special leasing CAA s258. legislation.gov.uk lists no pending change that affects these sections. Announced, not law: 50% first-year allowance for spending from 1 January 2027, and 12% WDA from 6 April 2027 (income tax) / 1 April 2027 (corporation tax) (Budget 2026, 28 Oct 2026; TIIN 29 Oct 2026; OOTLAR 1.42; Finance Bill 2026-27).
techniques.relevance: Kit the user buys to keep using in the business is deducted in full in the year it is paid for under the default cash basis. Buying needed kit just before 5 April therefore brings the relief forward a year. Kit hired out as part of the trade is treated the same way, and selling kit later creates taxable income.

techniques.name: Plant and machinery: new 40% FYA (2026), 50% from 2027, WDA cut to 14% then 12%
techniques.summary: Law (Finance Act 2026, c. 11, Royal Assent 18 March 2026). s28 cut the main-pool writing-down allowance (WDA) from 18% to 14% (CAA 2001 s56(1)) for chargeable periods beginning on or after 6 April 2026 for income tax (1 April 2026 for corporation tax). A period that spans that day uses X = 18 x BRD/CP + 14 x ARD/CP, rounded up to 2 decimal places (s28(3)-(6)). For income tax the chargeable period is the period of account (CAA s6). So a sole trader's year to 31 March 2027 gets 14.06%, a calendar year 2026 gets 15.05% and a year to 30 April 2026 gets 17.73%, while a period starting on 6 April 2026 gets 14%. s29 added a 40% first-year allowance (FYA) (CAA ss45U, 52(3)) for expenditure incurred on or after 1 January 2026 on plant or machinery that is unused, not second-hand and not special-rate expenditure. Two sets of rules exclude it. s45V excludes expenditure under arrangements whose main purpose, or one of whose main purposes, is to secure the FYA and which are contrived, abnormal or lacking a genuine commercial purpose, or exploit shortcomings in the Act. The s46 general exclusions that matter to a sole trader are: GE1, expenditure in the period the trade permanently ceases; GE2, cars; GE6, plant for leasing, where hiring an asset out counts as leasing; GE7, plant connected with a change in another person's trade where getting an FYA is a main benefit; and GE8, plant brought into the trade after being acquired for other purposes (s13, which covers personal kit), plant provided for long funding leasing (s13A) and gifts (s14). s46 also contains GE5 (long-life asset transitional expenditure), which is not relevant here. New s46(4B) lets leased or hired-out plant qualify in either of two cases: the hirer uses it wholly or almost wholly to earn income within the charge to UK tax, or the hirer is UK-resident and does not use it to a significant extent to earn foreign income outside the charge to UK tax. Unlike full expensing (s45S, companies only), the FYA is open to sole traders and partnerships. The 60% left after the FYA is not pooled in the period of purchase; it joins the main pool in a later chargeable period, normally the next (s58(5)). If a disposal event happens before any of that balance has been pooled, for example the kit is sold in the period of purchase, the balance goes into the pool for the period of the disposal (s58(6)-(7)). An asset that is also used privately goes in a single-asset pool (s206), and its FYA is cut to a just and reasonable business share (s205). The balance carried forward is still worked out as if the FYA had not been cut (s205(3)). On a sale, the disposal value, capped at cost (s62), comes off the pool. In an ordinary period a balancing charge arises only if disposal values exceed the pool balance (ss55(3), 56(6)). In the final chargeable period of the main pool, which is the period in which the trade permanently ceases (s65(1)), there is no WDA: any balance left gives a balancing allowance, and a balancing charge arises only if disposal values exceed the balance (ss55(2)-(4), 56(6)-(7)). A single-asset pool ends on its first disposal event (s65(2)), so selling a private-use asset gives a balancing allowance or a balancing charge in that period, reduced to the business share (s207). Two limits matter most for a sole trader. First, on the cash basis (the standard basis for sole traders since 2024-25, ITTOIA s24A) no capital allowances are given except on cars (CAA s1A; GOV.UK), so kit is simply deducted when paid. Second, under accruals the £1,000,000 annual investment allowance (AIA, s51A) gives 100% on the same kit, including second-hand and hired-out kit; the AIA and the FYA cannot both be claimed on the same cost (s52A). Announced only (Budget 2026, 28 October 2026, OOTLAR para 1.42; HMRC policy paper 29 October 2026), and now in Finance Bill 2026-27 (Bill 173, as introduced 4 November 2026) clauses 20 and 21: the FYA rises to 50% for expenditure incurred on or after 1 January 2027 (clause 20 changes only the rate in s52(3)), and the main WDA falls to 12% for chargeable periods beginning on or after 6 April 2027 (income tax) or 1 April 2027 (corporation tax). A period that spans the change would use X = (14 x pre-CD + 12 x post-CD) / CP, rounded up to 2 decimal places; an income tax period that began before 6 April 2026 would use X = (18 x TY25 + 14 x 365 + 12 x post-CD) / CP (clause 21). The special-rate WDA stays at 6%.
techniques.conditions: For the FYA, all of these must hold. Expenditure incurred on or after 1 January 2026. Plant or machinery that is unused and not second-hand. Main-rate expenditure, not special-rate. Not a car (GE2). Not incurred in the period the trade permanently ceases (GE1). Not plant brought into the trade after being acquired for other purposes, such as personal kit, and not a gift (GE8; ss13, 14). Kit bought to hire out or lease qualifies only within s46(4B), meaning use to earn UK-taxable income or a UK-resident hirer not using it significantly for untaxed foreign income. Not incurred under disqualifying arrangements (s45V). The trader must be on the accruals basis, because under the cash basis only cars get capital allowances (CAA s1A). The allowance is claimed on the tax return and may be claimed for the whole or part of the cost (s52(4)). The AIA and the FYA cannot both be claimed on the same cost (s52A); only the part not relieved by them goes into a pool for WDAs (s58(4A), (5)).
techniques.risks: Claiming the 40% FYA where the AIA would give 100% on the same cost delays relief. Second-hand kit, cars, kit first acquired for private use and gifted kit get no FYA. Kit hired to a non-UK hirer for use abroad can fall outside s46(4B). Kit used partly for private purposes gets a reduced allowance in a single-asset pool, and selling it closes that pool with a balancing allowance or charge (ss65(2), 207). For pooled kit, proceeds (capped at cost) reduce the pool, with a balancing charge only if they exceed the pool balance; when the trade ceases the pool closes with a balancing allowance or, if disposal values exceed the balance, a balancing charge (ss55, 56(6)-(7), 65(1)). If kit is sold before the post-FYA balance has been pooled, the balance is pooled in the period of sale (s58(6)). If the trader is on the cash basis, sale proceeds of kit whose cost was deducted are taxable receipts instead (ITTOIA s96A). The 50% FYA and 12% WDA are in Finance Bill 2026-27 but are not law and could change before Royal Assent. There is anti-avoidance in s45V.
techniques.data_needed: Accounting basis (cash or accruals) for each year; period of account start and end dates; for each item: date the expenditure was incurred, cost, new or second-hand, car or not, main or special rate, whether bought to hire out and to whom (UK or overseas hirer), private-use share, whether brought in from personal use or received as a gift; AIA already used in the period; main pool, special rate pool and single-asset pool balances brought forward; disposal dates and proceeds; whether and when the trade permanently ceases.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: This applies only on the accruals basis; on the cash basis deduct the cost when paid. (1) AIA first: allowance = min(cost, £1,000,000 pro-rated for a period that is not 12 months), all in the period of purchase. (2) For cost not covered by the AIA, FYA = rate x cost. The rate is 40% for expenditure from 1 January 2026; 50% is announced for expenditure from 1 January 2027, but 40% is the law until Finance Bill 2026-27 is enacted. Reduce the FYA for private use. The balance (cost minus the unreduced FYA) enters the main pool, or a single-asset pool, from the next period, or in the period of disposal if the kit is sold first (s58(6)). (3) WDA each period = rate x (pool brought forward + additions - disposal values). The rate depends on the period of account: 18%, then the s28 hybrid, then 14%, then 12% (announced, with the clause 21 hybrid). Scale it for periods that are not 12 months. If the main pool or special rate pool is £1,000 or less, the whole balance may be claimed (s56A). In the period the trade permanently ceases, give a balancing allowance of the remaining balance, or a balancing charge if disposal values exceed it, instead of a WDA. (4) Tax saved = allowance x the marginal rate of income tax plus Class 4 NIC (6% main, 2% upper) in the tax years to which that period's profits are apportioned.

figures.2025-26: Main WDA 18% for periods of account ending before 6 April 2026; a period spanning 6 April 2026 uses the s28 hybrid (year to 30 April 2026: 17.73%). FYA 40% (law) for qualifying expenditure from 1 January 2026. Special 6%; AIA £1,000,000.
figures.2026-27: Main WDA 14% (law) for periods of account beginning on or after 6 April 2026; hybrid for spanning periods (year to 31 March 2027: 14.06%; calendar year 2026: 15.05%). FYA 40% (law) for expenditure 6 April 2026 to 31 December 2026; for 1 January to 5 April 2027, 50% is announced (Finance Bill 2026-27 clause 20) but 40% remains the law until enacted. Special 6%; AIA £1,000,000.
figures.2027-28: Announced only (Budget 2026; Finance Bill 2026-27 clauses 20 and 21, not law): main WDA 12% for periods beginning on or after 6 April 2027 (IT) / 1 April 2027 (CT), hybrid for spanning periods; FYA 50% for expenditure from 1 January 2027. Current law: 14% WDA and 40% FYA. Special 6%; AIA £1,000,000 (Budget 2026 Annex A).

figures.hybrid_examples_2026_derived: Year to 31 March 2027: 14.06%; calendar year 2026: 15.05%; year to 30 April 2026: 17.73%

techniques.status: Law: FA 2026 (c. 11, Royal Assent 18 March 2026). s28 sets the 14% main WDA (CAA s56(1)). s29 sets the 40% FYA (CAA ss45U, 45V, 46(4B)-(4G), 52(3)). The £1m AIA is in CAA s51A; s52A bars AIA and FYA on the same cost. The cash-basis bar on allowances other than for cars is CAA s1A, with the cash basis the standard basis from 2024-25 (ITTOIA s24A). Announced only: 50% FYA from 1 January 2027 and 12% WDA from 6 April 2027 (IT) / 1 April 2027 (CT), from Budget 2026 (28 October 2026; OOTLAR para 1.42, updated 5 November 2026) and the HMRC policy paper of 29 October 2026, in Finance Bill 2026-27 (Bill 173, printed as introduced 4 November 2026; clause 20 FYA rate, clause 21 WDA rate and hybrid). The Bill had its first reading on 3 November 2026 and second reading on 23 November 2026, with Committee of the whole House listed for 30 November and 1 December 2026. It is not law.
techniques.relevance: On the default cash basis this changes nothing for the user, because kit is deducted when paid. If the user opts into accruals, the £1m AIA already gives 100% on new or second-hand kit, including kit hired out, so the 40%/50% FYA only matters above £1m of spending or in a structure that cannot claim the AIA (such as a partnership with a company member), and the lower WDA mainly slows relief on any pool balance carried forward.

techniques.name: Other Budget 2026 changes noted (mileage, trading allowance, capital allowances)
techniques.summary: (1) Mileage: 55p for the first 10,000 business miles in a car, van or goods vehicle is law for 2026-27 and every later year (TEVA 2026 s2, Royal Assent 15 Jul 2026, amending ITEPA s230(2) and ITTOIA s94F(2)-(3); HCWS421 of 27 Oct 2026 calls it permanent). The rate above 10,000 miles rises from 25p to 35p from 6 Apr 2027 by SI (OOTLAR 2.7), also for the NIC disregard. 2024-25 and 2025-26: 45p/25p. (2) Trading allowance and SA trading reporting threshold rise from £1,000 to £3,000 from 6 Apr 2027 (OOTLAR 1.5; Finance Bill 2026-27). (3) Capital allowances: 14% WDA from 6 Apr 2026 (IT) and 40% FYA from 1 Jan 2026 are law; 50% FYA from 1 Jan 2027 and 12% WDA from 6 Apr 2027 announced (OOTLAR 1.42). Exclusions: cars (GE2); plant for leasing (GE6) unless s46(4B) applies; period of cessation; s45V.
techniques.conditions: Mileage changes by SI; others by Finance Bill 2026-27.
techniques.risks: Announced items not yet law.
techniques.data_needed: Business miles; kit purchases.

Main WDA 14% (periods from 6 Apr 2026; blended for straddling periods). FYA 40% for new unused main-rate plant from 1 Jan 2026. ANNOUNCED, NOT LAW: 50% FYA for spending from 1 Jan 2027.

techniques.name: Interest on business borrowing as a trading expense (BIM45650 onwards)
techniques.summary: Interest is deductible for trading profits if incurred wholly and exclusively for the trade (ITTOIA s34), e.g. borrowing to buy plant, vans or for working capital. What matters is how the money is used while interest accrues (BIM45665; Scorer v Olin Energy). An identifiable business share of a loan is allowable (s34(2), BIM45690). Incidental costs of obtaining finance are deductible under s58 when the interest is. It is a deduction in computing profit, so it reduces Class 4 too and is not subject to the s24A cap.
techniques.conditions: Borrowing funds business spending or assets. Keep loan agreements and interest statements; separate business account where possible. Mixed-use assets: business proportion only. HP/credit interest on allowable purchases allowed by business-use proportion.
techniques.risks: Swapping capital for a loan does not by itself make interest deductible (BIM45700). An overdrawn capital account funded by borrowing points to private drawings and interest will be restricted (BIM45705; Silk v Fletcher [2000] SpC 201). Interest funding private spending not allowable (BIM45690). Interest on late income tax/CGT not deductible (BIM45740). Upward revaluation does not increase deductible borrowing.
techniques.data_needed: Loan agreements, interest paid, use of funds, capital account balance.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Interest x business-use share x (marginal IT rate + Class 4 rate).

figures.2024-25: No monetary cap on accruals or cash basis
figures.2026-27: No monetary cap
figures.current: Deduction equals interest on the business-use portion of borrowing

techniques.status: Law. ITTOIA ss25, 29, 34 (incl. s34(2)), 58-59. Cash-basis £500 cap (s51A) omitted by FA 2024 Sch 10 from 2024-25. BIM45690 section updated 1 July 2026. BIM70040 is out of date (still shows £500 cap).
techniques.relevance: Applies to loans or HP for kit, vans or working capital at every profit level.

techniques.name: Cash basis: £500 interest cap removed from 2024-25 (Finance Act 2024 s16, Sch 10)
techniques.summary: From 2024-25 the cash basis is the default for eligible sole traders, turnover limits are gone, and the £500 cash-basis interest cap (ITTOIA s51A, s57B) is removed: interest is deductible on the same wholly-and-exclusively basis as accruals. Cash-basis losses can be relieved like accruals losses. BIM70040 (still showing £500) applies only to years ending on or before 5 April 2024; use BIM72000 onwards. Capital expenditure on education or training is never deductible on the cash basis (s33A, BIM72035).
techniques.conditions: Trade uses the cash basis (default) and is not excluded; interest wholly and exclusively for the trade. To use accruals tick 'traditional accounting' on SA103.
techniques.risks: Ensure the app does not apply the £500 cap or old turnover tests for 2024-25 onwards. Mixed-purpose loans must now be apportioned.
techniques.data_needed: Accounting basis election; interest paid.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: No cap from 2024-25; for 2023-24 cap interest and finance costs at £500 (purchase interest not capped).

figures.2023-24: Cash basis interest and finance costs capped at £500 a year (s57B); interest on purchases (HP, trade credit, credit card on allowable purchases) not capped
figures.2024-25: No £500 cap; cash basis default unless electing accruals
figures.2026-27: No cap

techniques.name: Qualifying loan interest relief: loan to invest in or lend to a close company (ITA 2007 s383, ss392-395)
techniques.summary: An individual can deduct (Step 2, s383(4)) interest on a personal loan used to buy ordinary shares in, or lend to, a close company that is not a close investment-holding company, where the money is used wholly and exclusively for its business (or an associated close company's). Counts towards the s24A cap. From 2027-28 s25(3A) (FA 2026 s6) sets the relief against non-property/savings/dividend income first. Conditions: company close when the loan is applied (s392(2)); not a CIC when interest is paid (s393(1)(a)); capital recovery condition (s393(2), s406); either material interest (>5% of ordinary share capital or assets on a winding up, alone or with associates, s394) or full-time working (holds some shares and spends the greater part of time managing the company, s393(3)). Lost for shares if the borrower or spouse claims EIS (s392(3)); lost entirely if SITR is claimed (s392(3A)); s392 does not mention SEIS. No relief for overdrafts or credit cards (s384(1)) or above-commercial interest (s384(2)). Claim in box 5 'Other tax reliefs' SA101 (HS340). The company can pay commercial interest on a director's loan (savings income; company deducts tax under s874 at basic rate to 2026-27, savings basic rate from 2027-28).
techniques.conditions: As in summary; keep the lender's interest certificate; make a claim.
techniques.risks: Recovering capital from the company reduces relief. s24A cap. Non-genuine loans or above-commercial interest challenged. 2027-28 savings rate rise (24/44/49 announced) erodes the advantage of the company paying interest to the director.
techniques.data_needed: Personal loan details and interest; use of funds; shareholding %; time spent in company.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Relief = eligible interest (subject to s24A cap) x marginal rate.

figures.2024-25: Relief = eligible interest, capped by s24A at the greater of £50,000 and 25% of adjusted total income; material interest threshold more than 5%
figures.2026-27: Same
figures.2027-28: Same cap. From April 2027 Step 2 and 3 reliefs apply to non-savings, non-dividend, non-property income first (enacted: ITA s25(3A), FA 2026 s6(6),(8)).

techniques.status: Law: ITA ss383, 384, 392-395, 393A, 406, 24A; no outstanding effects. s25(3A) enacted by FA 2026 s6(6),(8). Savings rates 2027-28: 22/42/47 enacted (FA 2026 s5); 24/44/49 announced (Budget 2026). HS340 (2026) added 6 April 2026; HS340 (2025) added 6 April 2025.
techniques.relevance: If the user incorporates: borrow personally (e.g. Start Up Loan) and on-lend to the company for kit, keeping income tax relief on the interest.

techniques.name: Qualifying loan interest relief: loan to invest in a partnership (ITA 2007 ss398-399)
techniques.summary: Interest on a personal loan used to (a) buy an existing partner's share (SAIM10280), (b) contribute capital or a premium, (c) lend to the partnership, or (d) repay an earlier qualifying loan, is deductible at Step 2 (s383(4)), where funds in (b)/(c) are used wholly for the firm's trade. Must be a partner (or s399(5) senior employee) throughout from use of the loan to payment of interest; not a limited partner in an LP or member of an investment LLP. Capital withdrawn counts as repayment (s399(3), ss406-407). Claim required; no overdraft/credit card interest (s384(1)); no above-commercial interest (s384(2)); denied where only insignificant risk of not making a post-tax profit (s384A). Counts towards s24A. Film partnerships: only 40% eligible (s400). s384B blocks certain loans where the partnership's property business uses the cash basis. Residential letting interest gets a s399B tax reduction instead: 20% for 2024-25 to 2026-27, property basic rate 22% from 2027-28 (FA 2026).
techniques.conditions: Condition A (partner throughout, s399(2)); Condition B (no capital recovered, s399(3), s406); claim; s384B and s399A/B restrictions.
techniques.risks: Drawing capital reduces relief. s24A cap. Spouse partnership must be genuine (settlements rules; TSEM4320). Do not claim the same interest twice (s387).
techniques.data_needed: Loan, interest, partnership capital account.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Relief = eligible interest x marginal rate, subject to s24A.

figures.2024-25: Capped by s24A (greater of £50,000 and 25% of adjusted total income); film partnerships: only 40% of interest eligible (s399(4))
figures.2026-27: Same

techniques.status: Law: ITA ss383, 384, 384A, 384B, 387, 398-400, 406, 24A (revised to 16 Sep 2026, no outstanding effects). FA 2024 Sch 10 para 8 narrowed s384B from 2024-25. FA 2026 s6(8), Sch 1 para 21 and s7 set the s399B reducer at the property basic rate (22%) from 2027-28 (law). Autumn Budget 2026 not checked for new changes (search budget).
techniques.relevance: Only if the user forms a partnership or LLP.

techniques.name: Cap on 'unlimited' income tax reliefs (ITA 2007 s24A)
techniques.summary: For individuals, certain Step 2 deductions taken together ('Amount A') must not exceed 'Amount B' = the greater of £50,000 and 25% of adjusted total income (if total income is under £200,000 the limit is always £50,000). Capped (s24A(6)): trade loss relief against general income (s64); early trade losses (s72); post-cessation trade relief (s96); property loss relief against general income (s120); post-cessation property relief (s125); employment loss relief (s128); share loss relief; qualifying loan interest; ITEPA s555; ITTOIA s446 and s454(4). Excluded (s24A(7)): BPRA-attributable relief; (6)(a)-(e) relief against profits of the same trade/property business; share loss relief on EIS, SEIS or SITR shares. Adjusted total income (s24A(8)): total income + payroll giving - gross relief-at-source pension contributions - net-pay excess relief (FA 2004 s193(4)) and s194(1) relief. Losses carried forward (s83) and interest deducted as a trading expense are outside the cap; blocked qualifying loan interest cannot be carried forward or back.
techniques.conditions: Applies automatically to listed reliefs.
techniques.risks: Large first-year allowances creating a loss set sideways can hit the cap; carry-forward against the same trade is uncapped.
techniques.data_needed: Total income; payroll giving; gross pension contributions; capped reliefs claimed.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Cap = max(£50,000, 25% x adjusted total income); capped reliefs above it are disallowed.

figures.2024-25: Cap = greater of £50,000 and 25% of adjusted total income
figures.2026-27: Same

techniques.status: Law. Inserted by FA 2013 Sch 3 para 1 (2013-14). s24A(7)(c) (overlap relief) omitted from 6 April 2024 (FA 2022 Sch 1 paras 39, 61(1)). s24A(7)(d)(iii) inserted from 17 July 2014 (FA 2014 Sch 11 para 5). No outstanding effects. HS204 (2025) and (2026). 2027-28 announcements not checked (search budget).
