techniques.name: Tax treatment of grants received by a self-employed trader: revenue vs capital (BIM40451, CA14100, CA14200)
techniques.summary:
Grants follow the normal tax rules, supplemented by ITTOIA 2005 s105 (BIM40451). Revenue grants meet revenue costs (BIM40451's own example is interest payable) and are normally trading receipts (Smart v Lincolnshire Sugar [1937] 20 TC 643; Burman v Thorn Domestic Appliances [1981] 55 TC 493). Grants with no specific purpose ('undifferentiated receipts') are treated as revenue (Poulter v Gayjon Processes [1985] 58 TC 350; Ryan v Crabtree Denims [1987] 60 TC 183). Capital grants, paid to acquire capital assets, are normally not trading receipts (Seaham Harbour Dock v Crook [1931] 16 TC 333).

Accruals basis with capital allowances: CAA 2001 s532 treats expenditure as not incurred to the extent that it is met, directly or indirectly, by a public body (the Crown or any government, public or local authority) or by any other person. This applies even if the grant arrives after the purchase (Cyril Lord Carpets v Schofield 42 TC 637; CA14100). A loan is not a contribution (CA14100). The exceptions are in ss534-536; s533 deals only with dredging. Insurance or compensation money for an asset that has been destroyed, demolished or put out of use is not a contribution (s535; CA14200).

The s536 exception (CA14200): a contribution is NOT deducted if the payer is not a public body and can neither get a contribution allowance under CAA 2001 Part 11 Chapter 2 nor deduct the payment in calculating the profits of a trade or 'relevant activity' it carries on (s536(2), (3)). For plant and machinery, a relevant activity is a UK or overseas property business, a profession or vocation, a concern listed in ITTOIA s12(4) (mines, transport undertakings and so on), or managing an investment company (s536(5)(a)). A contribution allowance needs the contribution to be made for a trade or relevant activity carried on by the payer (s538(1)(b)). When testing for a contribution allowance, a tax-exempt payer such as a charity is assumed to be within the charge to tax (s536(4)).

In practice: an Arts Council England grant reduces qualifying expenditure. ACE is an executive non-departmental public body (GOV.UK) and calls itself a public authority, but no HMRC page names it, so treating it as a public body is an inference. A grant that a charity or private person pays from its own funds normally does not reduce qualifying expenditure, so the full cost qualifies, unless the money is in fact met indirectly by a public body.

Cash basis (the default from 2024-25, BIM72005): kit is deducted when paid under s33A, so capital allowances do not apply to kit, and nor does the s532 netting (cars stay in capital allowances). s96A brings into profit any 'capital refund' on an asset deducted under the cash basis; s96A(3G) defines this as an amount that is in substance a refund of capital expenditure. HMRC guidance (BIM72020) does not say whether a third-party grant towards kit counts as one. Industrial Development Act 1982 grants are receipts on the cash basis even if designated for capital expenditure (s105(2A)); s105 does not apply to professions or vocations. A voluntary or personal payment is taxable only if it attaches to the trade, judged by its character in the recipient's hands (BIM41810).
techniques.conditions: Classify each grant by purpose from the award letter: revenue, capital or personal need. Split mixed awards, for example a course plus a laptop. Record who pays: a public body; a charity or private person paying from its own funds; or a payer who gets tax relief for the payment (a contribution allowance, or a deduction in a trade or relevant activity it carries on). Record whether the business uses the cash basis or accruals.
techniques.risks: Avoid double relief. Where s532 applies (a public-body payer, or a payer who gets relief for the payment), do not claim AIA, FYA or WDA on the grant-funded part of the kit. Do not leave out a revenue grant while deducting the cost it paid for. Do not net off a grant that a charity or private person paid from its own funds: under s536 that understates capital allowances. A grant that is a trading receipt but pays for a non-deductible personal cost, such as childcare (ITTOIA s34), adds taxable income with no matching deduction. A grant for personal or household need may not be a trading receipt at all (BIM41810), so flag such grants for review instead of taxing them automatically. A training grant nets to nil only if the course is deductible (BIM35660: it must update existing expertise or give new expertise in the existing business area). On the cash basis, capital spending on education or training is not deductible (s33A(3)). The treatment of a kit grant on the cash basis is not settled.
techniques.data_needed: Award letter and application, showing purpose; payer and payer type (public body; charity or private person paying from its own funds; or a payer who gets relief); what the grant pays for, split between revenue, capital and personal items; date received; accounting basis (cash or accruals).
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Revenue grant: add to trading receipts in the year received (cash basis) or as GAAP requires (accruals). It nets to nil only where the funded cost is itself deductible. Capital grant on accruals: qualifying cost = cost minus grant if the payer is a public body (for example a council, or Arts Council England, treated as one although HMRC does not name it) or gets relief for the payment (for example a client business that deducts it). Otherwise the full cost qualifies and the grant is ignored. Capital grant on the cash basis: there is no settled answer. The conservative course is to deduct the full cost and add the grant as a receipt, which has the same effect as deducting only the net cost; flag it for review. Personal or hardship grant: do not add it automatically; ask what it was for (see hardship-grants-voluntary-payments).

figures.revenue_grant: taxable trading receipt: on the cash basis when received (BIM72015); on accruals as GAAP requires
figures.capital_grant_accruals_public_body_or_re: qualifying expenditure = cost minus grant (CAA 2001 s532; CA14100)
figures.capital_grant_accruals_non_public_payer_: full cost qualifies where the payer is not a public body and gets neither a contribution allowance nor a deduction in a trade or relevant activity it carries on (CAA 2001 s536(2)-(5); CA14200); the grant is not deducted and is not a trading receipt (BIM40451)
figures.industrial_development_grant_cash_basis: receipt even if designated for capital expenditure (ITTOIA s105(2A)); trades only

figures_disputed: capital_grant_cash_basis: HMRC guidance (BIM72020) does not say whether a third-party grant towards kit deducted under s33A is a s96A(3G) 'capital refund'; left null
techniques.status: Law. The rule is unchanged in substance from 2024-25 to 2026-27. The s536(5)(a) list of relevant activities was amended by Finance Act 2025 Sch 5 paras 8(18) and 12(3), which abolished the furnished holiday lettings rules, for income-tax periods of account beginning on or after 6 April 2025. That amendment does not affect grants to a sole trader. Budget 2026 (OOTLAR, published 28 Oct 2026 and updated 5 Nov 2026) announces no change to the grant or contribution rules for 2027-28. Sources: case law; ITTOIA 2005 ss33A, 34, 96A and 105 (including s105(2A)); CAA 2001 ss532-536 and 538 (revised text on legislation.gov.uk, checked 24 Nov 2026). HMRC guidance, with each section's own last-change date from the GOV.UK content API: BIM40451 (14 Dec 2018), CA14100 (19 Aug 2019), CA14200 (3 Jan 2017), BIM41810 (16 Oct 2018), BIM72020 (7 Apr 2025) and BIM35660 (6 Mar 2024).
techniques.relevance: If the technician gets a bursary or grant (ScreenSkills, Arts Council, a charity), money for courses, travel or running costs is normally taxable income. On the accruals basis, money for kit reduces capital allowances only if it comes from a public body such as Arts Council England or from a payer that gets tax relief for it, such as a client business; a charity grant or private gift normally leaves the full cost claimable. On the default cash basis the treatment of kit grants is unsettled, so keep the award letter.

techniques.name: Hardship and personal welfare grants from industry charities: when they are not trading receipts (BIM41810)
techniques.summary: BIM41810 case-law signposts: voluntary payments are not taxable unless attached to a source such as a vocation (Beynon v Thorpe); no trading relationship with the payer is needed (CIR v Falkirk Ice Rink); the character in the recipient's hands decides. A payment is a trading receipt if made to be used in the business, supplement receipts, keep the business going or solvent (Smart v Lincolnshire Sugar; BCINA v Mahany) or pay for inadequately paid services/lost profit (Rolfe v Nagel). If not a trading receipt consider CGT (BIM41801). Capital grants reduce qualifying expenditure; revenue grants are receipts; undesignated grants treated as revenue (BIM40451, CA14100). Personal injury compensation is not a trading receipt (BIM40105). A charity grant for personal need to pay household costs fits the non-taxable category reasonably well (e.g. Film and TV Charity Stop-Gap; Theatrical Guild short-term help; Backup Tech Medical/Hardship; Stage Hand). Grants towards business costs (e.g. Sir Horace Ové Grant: kit, travel to events, memberships, courses) are trading receipts or capital grants. COVID business grants were taxed under a specific statute (FA 2020 s106, Sch 16) covering public-authority schemes only (incl. Scottish 'hardship' funds), so a 'hardship' label alone is not decisive; Sch 16 does not apply to charity grants.
techniques.conditions: Grant made because of personal or financial hardship, illness or injury, not to fund trading or replace fees; keep the award letter showing purpose.
techniques.risks: Not confirmed by HMRC guidance. Grants replacing trading income or funding kit, travel to work, courses or memberships are likely trading receipts or capital contributions. Consider a white-space note on the return if treated as non-taxable.
techniques.data_needed: Grantor, award letter, purpose.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Do not auto-add to turnover; ask what the grant was for and classify.

figures.current: null: HMRC has no specific guidance or figure for industry-charity hardship grants

techniques.status: Settled case law with HMRC guidance; not a statutory relief. BIM41810 content last changed 16 Oct 2018 (manual updated 4 Aug 2026). Charity scheme details from Film and TV Charity guidance June 2026.
techniques.relevance: Expend should ask the purpose of any grant received in a quiet spell, illness or injury before treating it as turnover.

techniques.name: Tax treatment of Arts Council awards and bursaries (BIM50710, EIM50200, 1978 Revenue-Arts Council agreement)
techniques.summary: BIM50710: taxability depends on the award's 'quality in the hands of the recipient'; an award coming as an incident of the person's profession or vocation (including part-time) is normally a taxable professional receipt (Temperley v Smith; Smart v Lincolnshire Sugar; Duff v Williamson; CIR v Falkirk Ice Rink; McGowan v Brown and Cousins), even without an application or refund undertaking. Exceptions: an unsolicited prize given as a mark of honour or public esteem is not taxable; an award may instead be employment income, casual miscellaneous income or an annual payment. EIM50200: Arts Council awards are employment income or, more usually, trading income. The 1978 Inland Revenue/Arts Council agreement is not reproduced on GOV.UK. A 9 June 2020 DCMS written answer (UIN 53581) gave the Arts Council's understanding that 'buying time' development grants should not be taxable and project grants are; it was corrected by WMS HCWS717 on 24 March 2022 after HMRC ruled ACE Emergency Response Fund grants to individuals were taxable trading receipts (they replaced lost revenue). Net: a genuine development award may be arguable as non-taxable; project and income-replacing grants are taxable; HMRC decides case by case.
techniques.conditions: Treatment depends on the purpose in the application and award; keep both. DYCP-type development awards may fall in the 'buying time' category; NLPG project grants are taxable.
techniques.risks: The agreement is not public, has no legal force and is applied case by case. Development grants that fund trading work or replace fees are taxable. Equipment bought with a taxable grant is subject to the contribution rule (CA14100). Disclose the treatment on the return.
techniques.data_needed: Application and award documents; purpose.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Default: treat as a trading receipt unless clearly a 'buying time' development award; flag for review.

figures.current: null: no statutory figure; treatment depends on each award

techniques.status: Non-statutory. BIM50710 and EIM50200 metadata last updated 14 Dec 2018. Written answer of 9 June 2020 (UIN 53581) corrected by HCWS717 (24 March 2022). No change announced.
techniques.relevance: Relevant if the user applies to Arts Council England as a creative technician.

techniques.name: Deductibility of the proprietor's own training (BIM35660, BIM42526)
techniques.summary: A sole trader's own training is revenue and deductible if it updates existing expertise or gives new expertise in the existing business area, including keeping pace with technology and industry practice; ancillary courses (e.g. bookkeeping, digital skills) may be allowable. Training to start a new business or move into an unrelated area is unlikely to be allowable (capital or not for the existing trade: Dass v Special Commissioner [2006] EWHC 2491 (Ch)). Officers should not take an overly narrow view of 'updating' (BIM42526). On the cash basis, capital expenditure on education or training is never deductible (s33A, BIM72035).
techniques.conditions: Wholly and exclusively for the trade carried on when the training is done; related to the existing business area.
techniques.risks: Retraining for an unrelated trade not deductible. Keep course outlines. A bursary that paid for the course is a receipt. Start Up Loans cannot be used for training.
techniques.data_needed: Course details and link to current work (lighting, sound, video, rigging, safety).
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Course cost x (marginal IT + Class 4) if allowable.

figures.current: No monetary limit. BIM35660 last updated 6 March 2024 (GOV.UK metadata); any 2026 update null.

techniques.status: Law 2024-25 to 2026-27: ITTOIA s33, s34, s33A(3) (F(No.2)A 2017). HMRC BIM35660 and BIM42526. No announced 2027-28 change found (search budget ran out).
techniques.relevance: Courses that update skills in lighting, sound, video, rigging or safety used in current work are likely allowable.

techniques.name: Independent Loan Charge Review 2025 (Ray McCann) and the government response
techniques.summary: Announced at Budget 2024; Ray McCann appointed January 2025; final report and government response published 26 November 2025 (Budget 2025). Report found 2017-2020 settlement terms 'were never capable of generating the levels of voluntary settlement HMRC hoped for'. Nine recommendations; all accepted except 4b (10-year plan with write-off), and the government went further: relevant liability written off at settlement; loans 'unstacked' to years received; reduction for promoter fees; accrued late payment interest written off; penalties not sought as standard (but deliberate-and-concealed penalties can be a condition); IHT charges from the scheme trust written off if arising up to 3 months after the offer; extra £5,000 deduction for all; write-off capped at £70,000 (IHT write-off outside the cap). Promoters, introducers and their directors excluded. Now law: FA 2026 ss25-27 and SI 2026/821 (in force 5 August 2026). Pre-1 June 2021 contract settlements excluded.
techniques.conditions: Only liabilities within loan charge scope; must also settle all other disguised remuneration avoidance; those already settled and paid are unaffected.
techniques.risks: One-off concession for historic users, not a precedent. Non-engagement leads to existing loan charge enforcement. Deliberate misrepresentation voids the settlement.
techniques.data_needed: Only if the user or family ever used a loan scheme.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: See loan-charge-settlement-scheme formula.

figures.current: Review's promoter-fee allowance: suspend up to 10% (tapered by income) of gross scheme income a year. £5,000 deduction for all: HMRC estimates about 10,000 individuals (about 30% of those in scope) could have liabilities removed. Write-off cap £70,000 (about the 80th percentile). In scope: about 23,000 individuals and 4,000 employers not settled, plus about 10,000 individuals and 1,000 employers not fully paid. Cost about £365m to 2030-31. Payment plans up to 5 years without further information, longer by agreement. HMRC to contact everyone in scope by end of 2027-28.

techniques.status: Law. Report and response published 26 Nov 2025. FA 2026 (c.11) ss25-27 (18 March 2026). SI 2026/821 made 14 July 2026, laid 15 July 2026, in force 5 August 2026.
techniques.relevance: Only if the user or a family member ever used a loan or umbrella loan scheme.

techniques.name: Loan Charge Settlement Scheme (Finance Act 2026 ss25-27; SI 2026/821)
techniques.summary: FA 2026 s25 requires a scheme under which HMRC offers settlements to people liable to loan charge amounts; on acceptance the covered amounts stop being payable and a lower settlement amount is due. Settlement = extra income tax and NIC from attributing loans to the years received (unstacking), reduced by promoter-fee allowances and a further £5,000, subject to the £70,000 cap. Offer excludes late payment interest, IHT and most penalties; IHT charges arising (or within 3 months of the offer letter) written off. Acceptance is a binding contract closing covered checks; the acceptance form must be returned even if the offer is £0.
techniques.conditions: Liable to unpaid loan charge amounts. HMRC need not offer to suspected promoters/introducers or their (shadow) directors (s25(2)(b)). Employer settled first where PAYE should have applied. Contact 0300 322 9494; CAGetHelpOutOfTaxAvoidance@hmrc.gov.uk.
techniques.risks: Not accepting leaves the full liability plus interest. Liabilities outside the loan charge not reduced. A remaining trust can still trigger future IHT.
techniques.data_needed: Loan amounts by year; loan charge gross liability.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Per tax year: starting amount reduced by 10% of the first £50,000 and 5% of the next £100,000 attributed to that year; sum; reduce by £5,000 (not below nil); settlement cannot be more than £70,000 below the loan charge gross liability.

figures.current: s25(6): per tax year reduce the starting amount (not below nil) by 10% of the first £50,000 plus 5% of the next £100,000 attributed to that year; then total reduced by £5,000; if the result is more than £70,000 below gross liability, settlement = gross liability - £70,000. Payment plans up to 5 years (possibly longer) with interest on instalments. Settlements agreed before 1 June 2021 excluded (s25(4)). Other DR liabilities included only if an enquiry or assessment existed on or before 26 November 2025.

techniques.status: Law. FA 2026 (c.11) ss25-27, enacted 18 March 2026; SI 2026/821 made 14 July 2026, laid 15 July 2026, in force 5 August 2026. HMRC guidance first published 17 July 2026, updated 5 Nov 2026.
techniques.relevance: Only for historic loan charge exposure; shows HMRC pursues these schemes for decades.

techniques.name: Domestic penalty regime: inaccuracy, failure to notify, late filing, late payment, MTD points and interest
techniques.summary: Inaccuracy penalties (FA 2007 Sch 24) are a % of potential lost revenue (PLR) by behaviour and prompted/unprompted disclosure, reduced for quality of disclosure (telling up to 30%, helping up to 40%, access up to 30%; restricted to 10 points above the minimum if disclosure takes 3+ years); careless penalties can be suspended up to 2 years. Failure to notify (FA 2008 Sch 41) works similarly. Legacy SA late filing and payment penalties (FA 2009 Schs 55 and 56) apply to years before joining MTD. MTD ITSA replaces them with points-based late submission penalties and percentage late payment penalties (FA 2021 Schs 24-26). Late payment interest = Bank of England base rate + 4% since 6 April 2025.
techniques.conditions: No inaccuracy penalty with reasonable care. No failure-to-notify penalty for non-deliberate failure with reasonable excuse remedied without delay. Unprompted disclosure lowers the minimum. Points under the threshold expire after 24 months.
techniques.risks: Company officers can be liable for a company's deliberate penalties. Deliberate behaviour extends assessment time limits to 20 years. Late filing is a civil default; deliberate omission of income is evasion.
techniques.data_needed: Filing due dates and actual dates; tax due and payment dates; whether the user is in MTD ITSA; missed submission count in the last 24 months; behaviour category and disclosure type for any error; base rate history.
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Penalty/fine estimator. Legacy SA late return: £100; after 3 months £10/day up to £900; at 6 months greater of 5% of tax due or £300; again at 12 months. Legacy late payment: 5% of unpaid tax at 30 days, 6 months, 12 months. MTD (2026-27): 1 point per missed deadline; at 4 points (2 for annual filers from April 2027 per guidance) £200 and £200 per further miss; late payment 3% at day 15, +3% at day 30, then 10% a year from day 31 (first-year grace 30 days). Interest = unpaid tax x (base + 4%) x days/365 using the dated rate table. Inaccuracy = PLR x % within the behaviour range.

figures.current: Inaccuracy: careless 0-30% unprompted, 15-30% prompted; deliberate 20-70% / 35-70%; deliberate and concealed 30-100% / 50-100%. Failure to notify (non-deliberate): 0-30% unprompted within 12 months, 10-30% unprompted after 12 months, 10-30% prompted within 12 months, 20-30% prompted after 12 months; deliberate 20-70% / 35-70%; deliberate and concealed 30-100% / 50-100%. Legacy late filing: £100; then £10 a day after 3 months up to £900; then greater of 5% or £300 at 6 months and again at 12 months. Legacy late payment: 5% of unpaid tax at 30 days, 6 months, 12 months. Late payment interest 8.00% from 24 November 2026; repayment interest 3.00%.
figures.2024-25: Legacy SA penalties. Late payment interest: 7.75% (from 22 Aug 2023), 7.50% from 20 Aug 2024, 7.25% from 26 Nov 2024, 7.00% from 25 Feb 2025.
figures.2025-26: Legacy SA penalties, including the return due 31 January 2027. Late payment interest: 8.50% from 6 Apr 2025, 8.25% from 28 May 2025, 8.00% from 27 Aug 2025, 7.75% from 9 Jan 2026.
figures.2026-27: MTD ITSA mandatory from 6 April 2026 where 2024-25 qualifying income exceeded £50,000. MTD penalties: 1 point per missed deadline, 4-point threshold, £200 at the threshold and for each later miss; no points for late quarterly updates in the first year; quarterly deadlines 7 Aug, 7 Nov, 7 Feb, 7 May. Late payment: nothing up to 15 days; 3% at day 15; another 3% at day 30; then 10% a year from day 31 for up to 2 years; first-year grace period 30 days. Interest 7.75% then 8.00% from 24 Nov 2026.
figures.2027-28: MTD threshold: more than £30,000 qualifying income (2025-26 return); more than £20,000 from 6 April 2028. Late payment penalties per HMRC guidance: 4% at day 15, plus 4% at day 30, plus 10% a year from day 31 (NOT shown in law: FA 2021 Sch 26 para 5 still reads 3%). From April 2027 new penalties for all personal SA filers, annual filers 2-point threshold (guidance only; the only appointment order found, SI 2026/370, covers MTD users).

techniques.status: Law: FA 2007 Sch 24; FA 2008 Sch 41; FA 2009 Schs 55-56; FA 2021 Schs 24-26 in force from 1 April 2026 for MTD users for 2026-27 onwards (SI 2026/370); 3%/3%/10% rates (SI 2025/589, in force 31 May 2025, income tax 2025-26 onwards); MTD thresholds (SI 2026/336 reg 27); interest base + 4% from 6 April 2025. Guidance only, not found in law: 4%+4% for 2027-28; new penalties for all SA filers from April 2027; first-year 30-day grace, 2-year limit on the 10% charge and no first-year update points. Pages: CC/FS7a 21 Jul 2026; CC/FS11 19 Mar 2026; MTD penalties guidance 19 Nov 2026; HMRC interest rates 6 Nov 2026.
techniques.relevance: Core data for Expend's late-filing and late-payment fines estimator at all profit levels. Also: gov.uk/self-assessment-tax-returns/penalties; gov.uk/guidance/penalties-for-making-tax-digital-for-income-tax; HMRC interest rates page; CC/FS11.

techniques.name: Mandatory registration of paid tax advisers with HMRC (FA 2026 s223 onwards)
techniques.summary: FA 2026 Part 7 Chapter 1 (ss223-249, Schs 20-21; Royal Assent 18 March 2026). A 'tax adviser' is an organisation, or an individual sole trader, that in the course of a business assists others with their tax affairs by advising on tax, acting as their agent, or helping with documents HMRC is likely to rely on (s224). From the appointed day for its tranche, an adviser may not interact with HMRC about a client's tax affairs unless registered or a Sch 20 exception applies (s223(1)). Interacting covers phone, post, email, online messages, filing returns, claims, notices or other documents, and any other communication (s223(2)); HMRC's guidance also lists making payments. It applies even if the adviser or the client is outside the UK (s223(3)). The bar starts tranche by tranche under SI 2026/807 reg 4. Tranche 1 (everyone not in a later tranche) starts on 18 August 2026. Tranche 2, 18 November 2026: no agent services account (ASA) but an HMRC online Self Assessment or Corporation Tax account immediately before 18 August 2026. Tranche 3, 18 February 2027: payroll services only. Tranche 4, 1 April 2027: a business consisting substantially of FSMA regulated activities, or serving such a group. Advisers who had an ASA immediately before 18 August 2026 are treated as registered from that date (reg 5) and need not register again. HMRC's 3-month registration windows are administrative and close on those dates. Sch 20 exceptions (as amended by SI 2026/815 from 17 August 2026): software providers; customs and connected excise or import VAT; VAT, IOSS, NI tax and UK representatives; taxes not payable to HMRC, such as council tax or business rates; Valuation Office matters; group undertakings; court or tribunal appeals; complying with a statutory obligation; and replying to an HMRC information request. Unpaid help for family or friends is outside the regime because it is not given in the course of a business (s224; HMRC guidance). Sanctions: HMRC must first allow 30 days for representations and then give a compliance notice (s233). Each later prohibited interaction costs £5,000, or £10,000 where the adviser has been assessed 4 or more times in the 2 years ending with the contravention or is under an ineligibility order (s234). Relevant individuals of an organisation can be liable instead (s235), and there are temporary and permanent ineligibility orders (ss236-237).
techniques.conditions: Applies only to people or firms paid, in the course of a business, to deal with HMRC about someone else's tax. It does not apply to the user dealing with their own tax, or to a spouse, partner or friend helping for free.
techniques.risks: An 'adviser' who cannot give an Agent Reference Number (ARN) may find HMRC will not discuss the client's affairs. An unregistered 'adviser' who is also offering a tax scheme is a red flag. An ARN confirms registration only, not identity or authority to act for the client; HMRC still runs its usual identity and client-authorisation checks.
techniques.data_needed: The accountant's or bookkeeper's ARN: 11 characters, 4 letters including 'ARN' followed by 7 digits (for example XARN1234567).
techniques.how_to_estimate_saving: Not applicable: this is a compliance check on the user's adviser, not a saving.

figures.registration_windows_open: online service from 18 May 2026 (first window closed 18 August 2026); SA/CT account holders from 18 August 2026; payroll-only from 18 November 2026; financial services from 31 December 2026 (HMRC guidance)
figures.higher_penalty_trigger: 4 or more penalty assessments in the 2 years ending with the contravention, or an ineligibility order in force

techniques.status: Law: FA 2026 c.11 Part 7 Ch 1 (Royal Assent 18 March 2026), commenced by SI 2026/807 (made 13 July 2026). In force: 14 July 2026 (s247 power only), 18 August 2026 (tranche 1) and 18 November 2026 (tranche 2). Appointed but not yet in force at 24 November 2026: 18 February 2027 (tranche 3) and 1 April 2027 (tranche 4). Sch 20 amended by SI 2026/815 from 17 August 2026. Guidance: 'Check if and when you need to register as a tax adviser with HMRC' (updated 17 Nov 2026); sanctions page (30 Apr 2026).
techniques.relevance: The technician does not need to register to deal with HMRC about their own tax. Any accountant or bookkeeper they pay to deal with HMRC should be able to quote an ARN, and a spouse or friend helping for free is outside the rules.

family_and_trusts.name: Settlements legislation: ITTOIA 2005 Part 5 Chapter 5 (ss619-648)
family_and_trusts.summary: Main anti-avoidance code against income shifting within a family: income arising under a 'settlement' is taxed as the settlor's. s620(1): settlement = 'any disposition, trust, covenant, agreement, arrangement or transfer of assets' (charitable loan arrangements excluded); settlor includes anyone who made it, provided funds directly or indirectly, or made a reciprocal arrangement (s620(2)-(3)). s624(1): income from property in which the settlor has an interest is the settlor's alone. s625(1): settlor has an interest if property or related property may benefit the settlor or spouse/civil partner; s625(4) excludes court-order/agreement or likely-permanent separated spouses, widows/widowers and future spouses. s629: income paid to or for the settlor's unmarried minor child or stepchild is the settlor's unless the child's relevant settlement income from that parent is £100 or less (s629(3)). s619A: such income is the top slice of the settlor's income; trust expenses cannot reduce it (s624(1A)). Exceptions: s626 outright spouse gifts; s627 (e.g. divorce/separation provision); s628/s630 charity gifts. Bounty required (Jones v Garnett [2007] UKHL 35 at [7]; Lord Walker at [48]: avoidance intent not essential but readily inferred). HMRC test (TSEM4320): would the same payments be made to an arm's-length acquirer? TSEM4325 indicators: disproportionate returns on capital; share classes letting dividends go only to lower-rate holders; dividend waivers; income moved from the profit-maker to a lower-rate relative; par/gifted shares with restricted rights; a limited partnership share gifted or transferred below value; dividends only on certain classes; dividends to minor children/stepchildren. FA 2025 Sch 12 (2025-26 onwards) deleted only the protected foreign-source income exceptions (ss628A-628C, 630A).
family_and_trusts.conditions: Applies where there is (1) an arrangement with bounty; (2) income arising under it; and (3) settlor or spouse can benefit (s624) or income goes to the settlor's unmarried minor child (s629). No formal trust needed. Arm's-length commercial transactions fall outside (TSEM4320).
family_and_trusts.risks: Income taxed on the settlor at top rate; discovery assessments for earlier years (Donovan & McLaren). Works alongside the GAAR and the managed service company rules.

figures.current: s629(3) de minimis: £100 per child per parent per tax year.

family_and_trusts.status: Law, in force; Chapter up to date to 23 Nov 2026 (only outstanding effect relates to s168). s619A and s624(1A) from 6 April 2007 (ITA 2007 Sch 1). FA 2025 Sch 12 Part 1 (2025-26 onwards) deleted ss628A-628C and 630A and references in s624(3) and s629(5); charity exceptions s628/s630 unchanged. FA 2026 s54 amended s636(7).
family_and_trusts.relevance: Test every family proposal against ss620, 624, 626 and 629; bites hardest above £50,270 or in the £100,000-£125,140 taper.

family_and_trusts.name: Outright gifts between spouses or civil partners (ITTOIA 2005 s626)
family_and_trusts.summary: s624(1) does not apply to an outright gift of property between spouses or civil partners if Condition A (gift carries the right to the whole income) and Condition B (property not wholly or substantially a right to income) are met. Not outright if subject to conditions or if the property or related property is, will or may become payable to or applicable for the giver's benefit (s626(4)). HMRC examples: TSEM4205 Ex 4 let property gifted outright (rent is the spouse's); Ex 4a giver can require return (caught); Ex 5 non-voting, no-capital B shares (caught; Young v Pearce [1996] STC 743); Ex 6 all shares in a one-man IT company gifted to the wife (not caught; Jones v Garnett); TSEM4355 Ex 20, 21, 23 (quoted shares, shares in asset-rich companies, not caught). CGT: no CGT on gifts to a spouse unless separated and not living together all year, or goods for their business to sell; recipient takes over base cost. IHT: s18 exemption unlimited unless transferor is long-term UK resident and spouse is not (capped at the 'exemption limit' from 6 April 2025, FA 2025 Sch 13; amount not confirmed). Jointly owned let property is taxed 50:50 unless Form 17 is filed with evidence of unequal beneficial shares.
family_and_trusts.conditions: Legally married or civil partners, not separated (s625(4)). Genuinely outright, unconditional, carries the whole income, asset with real capital rights (ordinary shares, cash, quoted investments, full partnership share of capital and income, let property), no route back to the giver.
family_and_trusts.risks: Conditions, reverters, side agreements or income-only rights defeat it. Not for settlements of income (dividend waivers; dividends voted only on the spouse's class: TSEM4225 Ex 12, 13). Gift then loan-back or lease-back of equipment to the giver's business is high risk under s626(4)(b) (statutory reading; no HMRC example). The asset really belongs to the spouse on divorce or death. Covers spouses/civil partners only; minor children under s629; cohabitees outside the spouse limb but s624 still applies if the settlor can benefit.

figures.current: No monetary figures. From 2027-28 savings and property rates 22/42/47% (FA 2026, law); 24/44/49% announced (Budget 2026).

family_and_trusts.status: Law, unchanged since 5 Dec 2005 (civil partner wording SI 2005/3229); up to date to 23 Nov 2026, no pending change to ss625-626. History: ICTA 1988 s685(4A)-(4C) (FA 1989 s108), s660A(6) (FA 1995 Sch 17), rewritten as ITTOIA s626 (6 April 2005).
family_and_trusts.relevance: Cleanest statutory route to move investment income to a lower-taxed spouse; for trading profit it helps only via a genuine partnership share (TSEM4215 Ex 9) or ordinary shares after incorporation.

family_and_trusts.name: Parental settlements: income paid to the settlor's minor children (ITTOIA 2005 s629, s631)
family_and_trusts.summary: Income under a parent's settlement paid to or for the parent's 'relevant child' (child or stepchild under 18, unmarried, not in a civil partnership), or that would otherwise be the child's income, is taxed on the parent unless the child's relevant settlement income from that parent is £100 or less in the year (s629(3)). If exceeded, ALL is taxed on the parent (TSEM4310 Ex 18: £105 all taxed); each parent has a separate £100 (Ex 19). Covers non-trust gifts (cash in a building society, shares in the family company), bare trusts whether or not income is paid out (TSEM4300 Ex 14), IIP trusts with a minor life tenant (Ex 15), discretionary payments (Ex 16). s631 catches retained income later paid out.
family_and_trusts.conditions: Settlor is a parent or step-parent; child unmarried minor. Gifts from grandparents/others are outside s629 unless the parent is in substance the settlor (TSEM4300: Mr J lets his mother subscribe for 40% of his company at par, she gifts to grandchildren, dividends taxed on Mr J) or there are reciprocal arrangements (s620(3)).
family_and_trusts.risks: Indirect gifts via grandparents or friends caught; shares in a parent's company given to children caught; income retained in a bare trust still caught; once over £100 the whole amount is the parent's top slice (s619A).

figures.2025-26: £100 de minimis per child per parent
figures.2026-27: £100 de minimis per child per parent

family_and_trusts.status: Law for 2024-25 to 2026-27; no 2027-28 change announced. Pre-9 March 1999 settlements: Sch 2 para 133 removes s629(1)(b) (TSEM4305). FA 2025 Sch 12 paras 6, 7, 70(1) deleted the s630A reference from s629(5) for 2025-26 onwards; s630 charity exception unchanged.
family_and_trusts.relevance: Rule for Expend: parental gifts to a child earning over £100 of interest/dividends a year go on the parent's return; use a Junior ISA instead.

family_and_trusts.name: Employing a spouse or partner at a reasonable wage (BIM47105 onwards)
family_and_trusts.summary: Wages to a relative are deductible under ITTOIA s34 if there is no non-trade purpose and the amount is not set by the relationship; 'equal pay for equal value' is fully allowable (BIM47105). HMRC compares the whole package (salary, benefits, pension) with unconnected staff (BIM47105, BIM47106). Only an identifiable excessive part is disallowed (s34(2); Earlspring Properties v Guest [1995] 67 TC 259). Must be genuine (Moschi v Kelly [1952] 33 TC 442: 'wife's wages' credited to the husband's drawings disallowed for lack of reliable evidence). Accruals: s36 allows remuneration paid more than 9 months after the period end only when paid; not under the cash basis (BIM47130), where wages are deducted when paid. Uncommercial pay to a spouse or minor child may also be taxed under the settlements rules (BIM47106, TSEM4320). Pension contributions for a family employee allowable if the package is comparable (BIM46035). Worked example 2026-27 (rUK): spouse paid £12,570 evenly via payroll, no other income: no income tax, no employee NIC; employer NIC 15% x (£12,570 - £5,000) = £1,135.50, which an eligible employer can offset with the £10,500 Employment Allowance (a sole trader employing a spouse is not excluded); deduction worth 26% (£3,268.20) at basic, 42% (£5,279.40) at higher, 62% (£7,793.40) if all within the taper. Pay at or above the LEL (2026-27: £129/wk, £559/month, £6,708/yr) up to the PT gives the spouse a qualifying year with no employee NIC. Marriage Allowance interaction: if the spouse's income is below £12,570, transferring £1,260 saves 20% x (£12,570 - spouse income), max £252 at £11,310 or below, nil at £12,570; unavailable if the freelancer is higher-rate.
family_and_trusts.conditions: Real work the business needs (bookkeeping, invoicing and chasing POs, scheduling, travel booking, kit prep and maintenance, driving kit). Written statement of employment particulars; timesheets; rate comparable to an unconnected person; paid into the spouse's own account on time, via payroll where thresholds require; consistent year to year.
family_and_trusts.risks: Disallowance if above market rate, round sum unrelated to work, not actually paid, taken back, or implausible hours (e.g. spouse has a full-time job). Excess may be taxed on the freelancer under the settlements rules. Payroll duties (RTI, auto-enrolment above £10,000, employer NIC).

family_and_trusts.relevance: Most practical family measure for a sole trader whose spouse genuinely helps; value rises at 42% and about 62% in the taper.

family_and_trusts.name: National Minimum Wage rates and the family-business exemption
family_and_trusts.summary: Rates apply from 1 April each year (not the tax year). NMW Regulations 2015: reg 57 (family household) and reg 58 (family business): work is not 'work' if the worker is a member of the employer's family, lives in the family home and participates in running the business (reg 58). Worker must be at least school leaving age for NMW.
family_and_trusts.conditions: All three reg 58 conditions at once; if the family member lives elsewhere NMW applies in full. Whether 'member of the employer's family' covers a cohabiting partner: unconfirmed.
family_and_trusts.risks: Underpaying a non-exempt worker brings arrears and penalties. NMW exemption does not make a rate deductible; the BIM47105 commercial test still governs. Paying at or near NMW/NLW for documented hours is good evidence of reasonableness.

figures.2027-28: From 1 Apr 2027 (announced): 21+ £13.21; 18-20 £11.27; under 18 £8.31; apprentice £8.31

family_and_trusts.status: Regs 57-58 (SI 2015/621) law since 6 April 2015; reg 57 amended from 1 April 2024 (SI 2024/75). April 2026 rates law (SI 2026/357). April 2027 rates announced only (Government accepted LPC recommendations 28 Oct 2026); no amending SI as at 24 Nov 2026.
family_and_trusts.relevance: Benchmark hourly rate for a spouse's wage; hours x rate should reconcile to payroll.

family_and_trusts.name: Payroll, RTI and Class 1 NIC thresholds for employing family
family_and_trusts.summary: Register as an employer before the first payday (not more than 2 months before). Report pay on or before each payday (RTI). GOV.UK gives two triggers: the PAYE guide says register if any employee is paid £96+ a week, gets expenses/benefits, gets a pension, has another job, or has received JSA, ESA or Incapacity Benefit; the 'Register as an employer' tool asks about £129 or more a week. Use £96 (the ST) as the safe trigger. Keep payroll records even if not registering. Employment Allowance: business doing less than half its work in the public sector; excludes domestic workers (except care/support workers) and IR35 off-payroll earnings; one payroll; one company per connected group. The single-director rule applies only to companies. 2024-25 only: EA needed prior-year employer Class 1 below £100,000.
family_and_trusts.conditions: Below LEL: no qualifying year. LEL to PT: qualifying year with no employee NIC. Employer NIC above ST.
family_and_trusts.risks: Late RTI filings and payments attract penalties. Conflicting GOV.UK triggers: do not rely on the higher one. Auto-enrolment duties separate.

figures.2027-28: Announced (Budget 2026 Annex A, 28 Oct 2026): LEL £133/wk; PT £242/wk; ST £96/wk; UEL £967/wk; employer 15%; EA £10,500

family_and_trusts.status: 2024-25 to 2026-27 in force (HMRC rates pages). 2027-28 announced (Budget 2026 OOTLAR Annex A, updated 5 Nov 2026), not yet law.
family_and_trusts.relevance: Common spouse wage sizes: £5,000 (no NIC, no credit); £6,708-£12,570 in 2026-27 (credit, no employee NIC, employer NIC usually absorbed by EA).

family_and_trusts.name: Automatic enrolment duties when employing a spouse or family member
family_and_trusts.summary: A spouse, civil partner or other relative employed by the sole trader under a contract is a 'worker'. The trader has automatic enrolment duties from the day the first employee starts work (the 'duties start date'), even if nobody has to be enrolled (The Pensions Regulator, TPR). A jobholder must be automatically enrolled if they work or ordinarily work in Great Britain, are aged at least 22 and under State Pension age, and are paid earnings of more than £10,000 in a 12-month pay reference period (Pensions Act 2008 ss1(1), 3(1)). GOV.UK says 'at least £10,000', but the statute says 'more than'. For shorter pay reference periods the trigger is pro-rated (s3(6B)) and replaced by rounded figures: more than £833 a month, £192 a week or £768 per 4 weeks (SI 2021/314 art 3; TPR). So £10,000 a year paid in equal monthly amounts (£833.33) is over the monthly trigger. Northern Ireland has a parallel Act (Pensions (No. 2) Act (Northern Ireland) 2008 s3, same £10,000). Minimum contributions are 8% in total, of which at least 3% comes from the employer, on qualifying earnings between £6,240 and £50,270 a year (ss13, 20(1)(b)-(c)); in monthly terms that is £520 to £4,189. Some workers can join without being automatically enrolled. Jobholders aged 16 to 74 who earn above £6,240 but are not eligible can opt in, and the employer must then contribute (s7). Workers earning £6,240 or less can ask to join a scheme, without an employer contribution (s9). TPR lists the employer's duties: assess staff on the duties start date (assessment can be postponed for up to three months); write to each one within 6 weeks; complete a declaration of compliance within 5 months even if no one is enrolled; re-enrol and re-declare every three years. Example (derived, 2026-27): a wage of £12,570 paid evenly gives an employer minimum of 3% x (£12,570 - £6,240) = £189.90 a year, and a total minimum of 8% = £506.40. For a sole trader, wages and employer pension contributions for a relative are deductible if the whole package is comparable with what an unconnected employee would get for work of similar value (BIM47105). BIM46035 says the same about pension contributions and expressly covers an employee who is a close relative of the proprietor of an unincorporated business. Employer contributions are deducted in the period of account in which they are paid (FA 2004 s196(2)(b)).
family_and_trusts.conditions: The relative must be a genuine employee doing real work for the business, paid through payroll. Automatic enrolment applies if they are aged 22 to State Pension age and their earnings in the pay reference period are over the trigger: more than £833 in a monthly period, £192 in a weekly period or £768 in a 4-weekly period. The £10,000 figure applies as such only to a 12-month pay reference period. The employer must also act on opt-in requests (s7) and joining requests (s9). The scheme must meet the quality requirement of at least 3% employer and 8% total on qualifying earnings (s20). The employer may pay the full 8% itself.
family_and_trusts.risks: TPR penalties: a £400 fixed penalty (SI 2010/5 reg 12), and escalating daily penalties from £50 a day for an employer with 1-4 staff up to £10,000 a day for 500 or more (reg 13). Contributions missed because the scheme was set up late must be backdated (TPR). The commonest slip in a one-employee family business is forgetting the letter to the employee or the declaration of compliance. Paying £10,000 a year in equal monthly instalments (£833.33) triggers enrolment, because the monthly trigger is £833. Irregular pay, such as one large month, can push earnings over £833 in that pay period and trigger enrolment even if the annual total is under £10,000. An excessive pay-and-pension package for a relative can be partly disallowed (BIM47105, BIM46035).

figures.2027-28: Trigger £10,000; £6,240 to £50,270 (DWP review published 3 November 2026: values kept while the Pensions Commission completes its work, final report expected early 2027; the statutory figures simply continue)

family_and_trusts.status: Law (Great Britain): Pensions Act 2008 ss1, 3, 7, 9, 13, 20. £10,000 since 6 April 2014 (SI 2014/623); £6,240 since 6 April 2020 (SI 2020/372); £50,270 and the current per-period rounded figures since 6 April 2021 (SI 2021/314). Northern Ireland: Pensions (No. 2) Act (Northern Ireland) 2008. Penalties: SI 2010/5 regs 12-13. DWP reviews keep the figures unchanged to 2027-28 (latest published 3 November 2026). The Pensions (Extension of Automatic Enrolment) Act 2023 s1 powers (to lower the age of 22 and to reduce or remove the £6,240 lower limit) are prospective and not in force (s2(3): commencement by regulations).
family_and_trusts.relevance: If the user employs a spouse or partner, paying no more than £833 a month (£9,996 a year) or £192 a week keeps them below the automatic enrolment trigger (£10,000 paid monthly is £833.33 and is over it), though the user must still write to them within 6 weeks and file a declaration of compliance within 5 months. Paying more, such as £12,570, means enrolling them if they are aged 22 to State Pension age, at a deductible minimum employer cost of £189.90 a year; TPR penalties feed the fines estimator.

family_and_trusts.name: Employing your children: legal limits and the pocket-money trap
family_and_trusts.summary: Dollar v Lyon [1981] 54 TC 459 (BIM37737): farming parents paid children aged 14, 11, 9 and 7 £2 a week each plus £250 of savings certificates (about £354 a year each); only £104 cash to the eldest (the only one lawfully employable) was allowed; the rest was pocket money. Illegality does not by itself bar a deduction, but an innocent explanation is preferred; equal sums and an eight-year-old's 'contract' were 'strange and unconvincing'. Genuine pay for lawful work at a commercial rate is deductible (s34; BIM47106). England and Wales: part-time from 14 (13 where byelaws allow light work); council permit may be needed; hour limits (e.g. 12 hours a week in term time; no work before 7am or after 7pm); performance licence for paid performances/modelling; full-time only from minimum school leaving age. School-age children and family members living in the employer's home are outside the NMW. Under-16s pay no NIC but go on payroll if income exceeds the PA; from 16 RTI reporting. Pay with no bounty is the child's own income (TSEM4105/4355); excess pay is not deductible and may fall under s629 (over £100 per parent).
family_and_trusts.conditions: Lawful employment (byelaws, permits), real age-appropriate tasks, commercial rate, paid to the child, recorded; payroll from 16 where thresholds met.
family_and_trusts.risks: Equal round sums, pocket-money amounts or implausible contracts for young children disallowed and may fall under s629. Unlawful employment weighs against the deduction.

figures.current: Dollar v Lyon: £2/week each plus £250 savings certificates (~£354/yr per child); £104 allowed. s629 de minimis £100 per parent per child. Term-time limit example 12 hours a week.

family_and_trusts.status: Law: ITTOIA s34; s629; CYPA 1933 s18 and local byelaws (E&W). Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026 (c.21, Royal Assent 29 April 2026) s28 replaces CYPA ss18/18A with national regulations and a compulsory permit; in force only for regulation-making powers (s78(1)(a)); main changes await commencement. BIM37737 (1 April 2016), BIM47106 (14 Dec 2018), TSEM4105/4300/4310 current.
family_and_trusts.relevance: Marginal: teenagers (14+) could be paid small sums for genuine kit prep, cleaning, packing or warehouse help.

family_and_trusts.name: Taking a spouse or civil partner into partnership: profit-sharing and HMRC's view
family_and_trusts.summary: PM132400: HMRC 'cannot challenge the apportionment of profits, as you can a wage, by reference to the value of the partners' contribution'. A spouse partner need not contribute capital, manage, or do the main work; with a deed and accounts allocating profit, challenges rarely succeed; tax motive alone does not make it a sham. Challenges likelier with no deed or backdating beyond a few months. Settlements rules still apply (TSEM4215; PM132400 citing s619): bounty where the share is 'out of all proportion' to contribution; s626 applies if the spouse takes an unlimited share of assets and income with no conditions; caught if wholly or mainly a right to income. TSEM4215: Ex 10 sleeping-partner wife gets half the income of an £80,000 architect's practice but no capital, so her £40,000 is taxed on him; Ex 9 wives admitted to an equal four-way share of profits and capital of a car dealership (premises, stock) within s626; Ex 8 sleeping partner with £10,000 capital at risk not caught. PM132400 flags businesses depending on one person's personal skills.
family_and_trusts.conditions: Written deed before the period; spouse gets a real share of capital (e.g. kit, goodwill) and income with no reverter; clients contract with and are invoiced by the firm; partnership return and both SA returns; each partner pays Class 4 on their share. A share between the SPT and £12,570 with no other income attracts no tax or NIC yet Class 2 is treated as paid.
family_and_trusts.risks: Income-only shares or capital reserved to the freelancer caught by s624 (Ex 10). Backdating challenged. POs remaining with the individual undermine the partnership. Spouse becomes jointly and severally liable; owns their capital on separation. Unmarried partner: outside s624 unless income returns to the settlor, but no CGT/IHT spouse relief. Capital allowance consequences of transferring kit into a partnership not researched.

figures.2024-25: Class 4: 6% on £12,570-£50,270, 2% above; Class 2 SPT £6,725
figures.2026-27: Class 4: 6% / 2%; SPT £7,105; voluntary Class 2 £3.65/wk
figures.2027-28: Announced (Budget 2026 Annex A): SPT £7,355; Class 4 limits £12,570/£50,270

family_and_trusts.status: Law: ITTOIA ss619-648 (ss620, 624, 626 up to date Nov 2026); Partnership Act 1890 (s9 checked). PM132400 updated 7 Oct 2026; TSEM4215 10 Sep 2026. 2027-28 SPT £7,355 and £3.80 announced (affirmative regs early 2027). No Budget 2026 change to settlements or partnership taxation.
family_and_trusts.relevance: Main lawful route for a sole trader to split trading profit with a spouse above about £50,270, but weak where clients book this particular technician unless the spouse genuinely co-owns the kit and clients contract with the firm.

family_and_trusts.name: Unmarried (cohabiting) partners: what changes
family_and_trusts.summary: s624 only applies where the settlor or spouse/civil partner can benefit (s625); s625(4)(d) excludes a person the settlor may later marry, so a cohabitee is not a 'spouse'. HMRC: the legislation 'will not apply where the recipient is another individual unless there are arrangements' to benefit the settlor or spouse (TSEM4320; also TSEM4220, TSEM4215). An outright gift of an income-producing asset (e.g. hire equipment) to a cohabitee is generally outside the settlements rules. Cohabitees do not get: Marriage Allowance; CGT spouse treatment (gift is a market-value disposal; cohabitees not connected under TCGA s286; s165 hold-over can apply to trade assets); IHT spouse exemption (gifts are PETs; IHT only if death within 7 years and gifts exceed £325,000, taper 3-7 years; £3,000 annual exemption). HICBC still applies to the higher earner ('partner' includes cohabitees). Wages must pass the commercial test (BIM47105). Partnership shares: for a non-spouse, legislation applies only with reverter arrangements (TSEM4215 Ex 11), but the partnership must be genuine. s629 still catches gifts to the settlor's own minor children above £100. If the couple later marry, review income from assets gifted before marriage (s626 wording).
family_and_trusts.conditions: Outright gift with no route back to the giver or spouse; commercial, documented wage or profit share.
family_and_trusts.risks: CGT on gifts at market value; IHT if death within 7 years of large gifts; loss of the asset if the relationship ends; arrangements returning value bring s624 back.

figures.current: IHT nil-rate band £325,000; annual exemption £3,000; 7-year PET rule with taper 3-7 years.

family_and_trusts.status: Law: ITTOIA ss624, 625, 626, 629 (up to date 22-23 Nov 2026); TCGA ss17, 286, 165; IHT gift rules. TSEM4320, TSEM4215, TSEM4220 updated 10 Sep 2026. No change found, but Budget documents could not be searched (search budget ran out).
family_and_trusts.relevance: For a long-term unmarried partner: investment income can be moved by outright gift, at the cost of CGT/IHT spouse reliefs and Marriage Allowance.

family_and_trusts.name: Marriage Allowance (transferable personal allowance)
family_and_trusts.summary: The lower-earning spouse/civil partner elects to give up £1,260 of PA (10% of £12,570 rounded up to £10, ITA s55B(4)-(5)); the other gets a basic-rate tax reduction (20%, also for Scottish taxpayers, s55B(3)) of up to £252, not below nil. Recipient must not be liable above the basic rate (GOV.UK: income usually £12,571-£50,270; Scotland up to the intermediate rate, usually income up to £43,662 in 2026-27). Transferor: GOV.UK says income 'normally' below the PA; legal test for UK residents (s55C(1)(c)) is not liable above basic rate after losing £1,260. Practically: transferor income at or below £11,310 gives the full £252 net gain; between £11,310 and £12,570 the gain shrinks 20p per £1; above £12,570 nothing. Not for unmarried couples; not with Married Couple's Allowance; election within 4 years after the year end (s55D(1)): claims can go back to 2022-23, but a 2022-23 claim must be made by 5 April 2027; backdated elections cover one year (s55D(3)); carries forward until withdrawn while conditions are met, ending if the recipient gets no reduction in a year (s55D(5)). If both file SA, transferor files at least 3 days before the recipient.
family_and_trusts.conditions: Married/civil partners; transferor income below the PA (practically); recipient not higher/additional rate.
family_and_trusts.risks: Lost in any year the recipient becomes higher-rate; a spouse wage or profit share above £11,310 reduces the gain; with savings/dividend income HMRC advises checking who should claim.

figures.2024-25: £1,260 transferable; max saving £252
figures.2027-28: £1,260 (Budget 2026 Annex A); PA £12,570 (frozen to 2030-31 by FA 2026 s10)

family_and_trusts.status: Law: ITA Part 3 Ch 3A (ss55A-55E), FA 2014 s11. 2027-28 £1,260 law via the frozen PA (FA 2021 s5 as amended by FA 2023 s5 and FA 2026 s10). £252 max for 2027-28 assumes the announced 20% basic rate.
family_and_trusts.relevance: Worth £252 a year only while the freelancer is basic-rate and the spouse earns below £12,570; Expend should check backdating to 2022-23 (deadline 5 April 2027 for that year).

family_and_trusts.name: Pension contributions for a non-earning spouse or child (relief at source)
family_and_trusts.summary: Under relief at source a member with no earnings still gets 20% relief on contributions up to £3,600 gross a year (£2,880 net + £720 relief). The freelancer can fund a personal pension for a spouse or child and the government adds the relief.
family_and_trusts.conditions: Registered relief-at-source personal pension; contribution in the member's name; £2,880 net limit without earnings; locked until minimum pension age.
family_and_trusts.risks: No deduction against business profits (gift out of taxed income). Use IHT annual or normal-expenditure exemptions. From 6 April 2027 unused pension funds form part of the member's estate for IHT.

figures.current: Non-earner limit £2,880 net (£3,600 gross, derived); relief up to 100% of earnings for earners

family_and_trusts.status: Law: FA 2004 ss188-191 (basic amount £3,600 in s190(4), in force since 6.4.2006; relief above earnings only via RAS, s191(7)). IHT on pensions law: FA 2026 ss66-71 (IHTA s150A) for deaths on or after 6 April 2027.
family_and_trusts.relevance: A small top-up of £720 per family member per year; does not reduce the freelancer's own tax.

family_and_trusts.name: Loans from family members to the business: interest deduction, the lender's tax and the gift-and-loan-back problem
family_and_trusts.summary:
A spouse, partner, parent or other relative can lend their own money to the business on commercial terms.

The trader's side:
- Interest is a revenue item (ITTOIA s29). It is deductible from trading profit if the borrowed money is used wholly and exclusively for the trade, for example to buy kit or a van or as working capital (s34; BIM45665).
- What counts is how the money is used while the interest accrues (BIM45665, Scorer v Olin Energy). Where use is mixed, only the business part is allowed (s34(2); BIM45670).
- Swapping capital already taken out of the business for loan finance does not on its own pass the test (BIM45700). Borrowing that funds private drawings or an overdrawn capital account is restricted (BIM45705; Silk v Fletcher).
- The £500 cash-basis interest cap was removed from 2024-25 (ITTOIA s51A omitted by FA 2024 Sch 10).
- A sole trader pays the interest gross. The duty to deduct tax from yearly interest (ITA s874(1)) applies only to payments by a company, a local authority or a partnership with a company member, or to a lender whose usual place of abode is outside the UK (SAIM9080).

The lender's side:
- The lender is taxed on the interest as savings income, but may pay nothing if it is covered by their personal allowance, the 0% starting rate for savings and the personal savings allowance.
- Starting rate: up to £5,000, reduced £1 for £1 by other taxable non-savings income above the personal allowance. It is nil once that income reaches £17,570 with a standard £12,570 allowance.
- Personal savings allowance (ITA s12B): £1,000 for basic-rate, £500 for higher-rate and nil for additional-rate taxpayers.
- From 2027-28, reliefs and allowances must be set against income other than savings, property and dividend income first (ITA s25(3A), FA 2026 s6(6)).

Gift-and-loan-back and children:
- If the trader first gives the money to a spouse who lends it back, the gift is likely not to be an 'outright gift' under ITTOIA s626(4)(b), because there are circumstances in which the property is 'applicable for the benefit of the giver'. The settlements rules can then treat the interest as the trader's own income (s624). No HMRC guidance or case deals with gift-and-loan-back directly. The closest guidance is TSEM4205 example 4a (a gift the giver can require to be returned is not outright) and TSEM4210 (look at the whole arrangement).
- If a parent gives money to their own minor child, who lends it on, the interest is taxed as the parent's once it exceeds £100 a year. All of it is then taxed, and the limit applies per parent (s629(3); TSEM4310).
family_and_trusts.conditions:
- The lender's own money, not money the trader has given them.
- A written loan agreement at a commercial interest rate, with repayment terms.
- The money is used for the business (kit, vehicles, working capital), not for drawings.
- Interest is actually paid into the lender's own account and recorded.
- The lender deals with their own tax on the interest. GOV.UK's savings guidance relies on banks and building societies telling HMRC about the interest they pay. Interest on a private loan does not come through that route, so the lender should not wait for an HMRC letter.
  - If any of the interest is taxable, because it is not all covered by the lender's personal allowance, starting rate and PSA, and the lender has not been sent a notice to file a return, they must tell HMRC by 5 October after the tax year (TMA 1970 s7(1), (1C)). The savings-income exemption in s7(3) and (6ZA) applies only if none of it is taxed at the savings basic, higher or additional rate.
  - Savings interest over £10,000 needs a Self Assessment return (GOV.UK 'Check if you need to send a Self Assessment tax return').
  - GOV.UK gives later dates for contacting HMRC when no letter arrives: the end of November in 'Tax on savings interest', and 31 March in the Self Assessment checker. Both assume a bank has reported the interest, so use the statutory 5 October deadline.
family_and_trusts.risks:
- Gift-and-loan-back: money that came from the trader is likely to make the interest the trader's own income (s624, s626(4)(b)), so there is no saving.
- Interest above a commercial rate: the excess is unlikely to be wholly and exclusively for the trade (s34), and may involve bounty (a settlement needs an element of bounty: TSEM4105, CIR v Plummer). No HMRC guidance sets a rate for family loans, so use a rate a lender at arm's length would charge.
- Interest on money used privately is disallowed (BIM45700, BIM45705).
- The lender's tax on interest rises from 2027-28. Savings rates of 22/42/47% are law (FA 2026 s5). Rates of 24/44/49% were announced at Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026, OOTLAR 1.1) for Finance Bill 2026-27 and are not yet law.
- If the business later becomes a company, the company must deduct income tax from yearly interest paid to an individual (ITA s874(1)(a); SAIM9070).
  - Up to 2026-27 the deduction is at the basic rate, 20%.
  - From 2027-28 it is at the savings basic rate: s874(2) as amended by FA 2026 Sch 1 para 29, which s6(7) introduces and s6(8) applies from 2027-28. That is 22% under current law, or 24% if Finance Bill 2026-27 enacts the Budget 2026 rate.
  - OOTLAR 1.12 also flags further deduction-at-source amendments from 6 April 2027.
- In a company, the interest deduction follows the corporation tax loan relationship rules, not ITTOIA s34 (BIM45665).

Announced only: savings rates of 24/44/49% for 2027-28 and the related deduction-at-source amendments (Budget 2026, 28 Oct 2026; OOTLAR 1.1 and 1.12). Finance Bill 2026-27 is not yet law: it had its Commons second reading on 23 Nov 2026, and Committee of the whole House is due on 30 Nov and 1 Dec 2026, followed by a Public Bill Committee.
family_and_trusts.relevance: Useful when the business needs money for kit or a van and a lower-earning spouse, partner or parent has savings of their own. The user deducts the interest at their marginal income tax rate plus Class 4, while the lender may pay little or no tax on it. It does not work with money the user has given them first.

family_and_trusts.name: Commercial loan from a family member to the business (interest deductible to the trader, possibly tax-free for the lender)
family_and_trusts.summary: A relative with their own savings lends to the business at a commercial rate; the trader deducts interest (BIM45665) at marginal rate plus Class 4; the lender's interest may be sheltered by PA, the £5,000 starting rate (other taxable income below £17,570) or the PSA. A sole trader paying yearly interest to a UK-resident individual does not deduct tax at source (ITA s874 applies only to companies, local authorities, partnerships with a company member, or payees abroad).
family_and_trusts.conditions: Lender's own money; written agreement at a reasonable commercial rate; used for business spending or assets; interest actually paid.
family_and_trusts.risks: Circular arrangements (trader gifts money to relative to lend back) are not wholly and exclusively and can trigger the settlements rules. Above-commercial interest contains bounty and is disallowed. After incorporation, the company must deduct tax on yearly interest (s874(1)(a)). Savings rates rise from 2027-28.

figures.2025-26: Starting rate 0% on up to £5,000 (nil once other income reaches £17,570); PSA £1,000 / £500 / £0 (ITA s12B); savings rates 20/40/45% (FA 2025 s3). Company deduction on yearly interest (s874(2)): 20%.
figures.2026-27: Starting rate limit £5,000 (FA 2026 s9); PSA £1,000 / £500 / £0; savings 20/40/45% (FA 2026 s3). Company deduction 20%.
figures.2027-28: Starting rate £5,000 (frozen to 2030-31); PSA £1,000 / £500 / £0; savings 22/42/47% (FA 2026 s5, law); 24/44/49% announced (Finance Bill 2026-27). Company deduction at the savings basic rate (s874(2) as amended by FA 2026 s6(8), Sch 1 para 29): 22% enacted, 24% if the proposal is enacted.

family_and_trusts.status: Law: ITTOIA s34; ITA s12B; FA 2026 ss3, 5, 9 and Sch 1 para 29; FA 2025 s3. Announced only: 24/44/49 (Budget 2026, 28 Oct 2026).
family_and_trusts.relevance: Useful once the user is higher-rate and a lower-income relative has savings; saving = trader's marginal rate + Class 4 minus any tax the lender pays.

family_and_trusts.name: Family-level income thresholds: High Income Child Benefit Charge, £100k allowance taper and Tax-Free Childcare
family_and_trusts.summary: Three family thresholds test each person's own adjusted net income (ANI), not the household's. ANI is net income less grossed-up Gift Aid and gross relief-at-source pension contributions (ITA 2007 s58). (1) High Income Child Benefit Charge: if either partner's ANI is over £60,000 and either of them gets Child Benefit, the partner with the higher ANI repays 1% of the Child Benefit for every £200 over £60,000. The percentage and the charge are rounded down, and the charge reaches 100% at an ANI of £80,000 (ITEPA 2003 ss681B-681C). 'Partner' includes an unmarried partner you live with as if married. (2) Personal allowance: reduced by £1 for every £2 of the individual's ANI over £100,000, reaching nil at £125,140 (ITA s35(2)). (3) Tax-Free Childcare: the government adds £2 for every £8 paid in, up to £500 per child every 3 months (£2,000 a year), or £1,000 (£4,000 a year) for a disabled child. It is lost if either partner's expected ANI for the tax year is over £100,000. Each partner must also normally expect to earn at least 16 hours a week at their minimum wage over the next 3 months (aged 21 or over: £2,643.68 in 2026-27). Someone self-employed for less than 12 months is exempt from this minimum. A partner who is not working can still qualify only in limited cases, such as getting Carer's Allowance or certain incapacity benefits while the other partner works. Because the tests are per person, some steps can keep each partner below the thresholds: gross pension contributions, Gift Aid, and income that genuinely belongs to a spouse or partner (a commercial wage for real work, or a real partnership share). For example, if one partner has ANI of £120,000 and the other earns £20,000, the couple repays all their Child Benefit and loses Tax-Free Childcare, and the higher earner loses £10,000 of personal allowance. If the same £140,000 were split £75,000 and £65,000, they would repay 75% of the Child Benefit and keep the full personal allowance and Tax-Free Childcare.
family_and_trusts.conditions: Each lever must be genuine. Spouse or partner wage: deductible only if it has no non-trade purpose and the amount is not decided by the relationship. HMRC's test is 'equal pay for equal value'. It applies to the whole package of salary, benefits and pension contributions, and only the part that is not wholly and exclusively for the trade is disallowed (BIM47105). Spouse or civil partner partnership: a share out of all proportion to the spouse's contribution shows bounty, so the arrangement is a settlement. But the outright-gift exception still applies if the spouse gets an unconditional share in both the partnership's capital and its income (ITTOIA s626; TSEM4215). In TSEM4215 Example 9 the wives do no work, yet their equal shares of capital and profits are exempt. The trader is taxed on the spouse's share (under s624) only in two cases: what the spouse receives is wholly or substantially a right to income (s626(3)), or the gift is not outright because it has conditions or could revert to the giver (s626(4)). TSEM4215 Example 10: a sole-trader architect takes his wife into partnership with half the income profits, but he alone keeps the rights to capital profits. She does no work and puts in no capital, so her share is taxed on him. A spouse's share must therefore carry real rights to capital as well as income. For an unmarried partner the settlements rules apply only where the property can revert to the settlor (TSEM4215), but the s626 spouse exception and Marriage Allowance are not available. Pension contributions and Gift Aid are reliefs Parliament intended and reduce ANI directly (s58). Tax-Free Childcare uses expected ANI, which must be reconfirmed every 3 months, and declarations must be honest.
family_and_trusts.risks: Moving income can make the other partner the higher earner, and the charge always falls on the partner with the higher ANI once it is over £60,000. A wage above the commercial rate is partly disallowed. An income-only or conditional partnership share is taxed back on the trader, and penalties may follow. If a partner's earnings fall below the Tax-Free Childcare minimum (16 hours a week at their minimum wage), the family loses Tax-Free Childcare unless an exception applies. The exceptions are a business started less than 12 months ago, or, while the other partner works, Carer's Allowance, Incapacity Benefit, Severe Disablement Allowance, contribution-based ESA or National Insurance credits. Tax-Free Childcare is a cliff edge: £1 of expected ANI over £100,000 for either partner removes it. Contrived steps risk the GAAR (see gaar-family-arrangements).

TFC: £2 per £8, up to £2,000 a year per child (£4,000 disabled); £100,000 expected-ANI limit per partner. TFC minimum (21+): £2,379.52 per 3 months (derived: 16 h x 13 weeks x £11.44 National Living Wage from 1 April 2024; not quoted on a current GOV.UK page).

family_and_trusts.status: Law: ITEPA 2003 ss681B-681H (£60,000 and £200 from 2024-25, F(No.2)A 2024 s5); ITA 2007 ss35 and 58; PA and basic rate limit frozen to 2030-31 (FA 2021 s5 as amended by FA 2026 s10); Childcare Payments Act 2014 and SI 2015/448 (Tax-Free Childcare). Guidance: BIM47105, TSEM4215, GOV.UK Tax-Free Childcare eligibility pages. Announced only (Budget 2026, 28 October 2026): offsetting Child Benefit overpayments against the HICBC, backdated to January 2013 (Budget document para 6.184; OOTLAR 1.88; Finance Bill 2026-27). The April 2027 minimum wage rates are also announced only. The 2027-28 rates come from Budget 2026 OOTLAR Annex A (rates and allowances, updated 5 November 2026); Annex A of the main Budget 2026 document is about financing, not rates.
family_and_trusts.relevance: Central for a freelancer with children as profits pass £60,000 and £100,000. Gross pension contributions, and income that genuinely belongs to a spouse or partner who works in the business, can keep Child Benefit, the personal allowance and Tax-Free Childcare. These are worth far more than the tax rate alone suggests.

family_and_trusts.name: Bare (simple) trusts
family_and_trusts.summary: In a bare (simple) trust each beneficiary has an immediate and absolute title to capital and income (TSEM1563). They can take the assets at 18 in England and Wales, or 16 in Scotland (GOV.UK, Types of trust). The beneficiary, not the trustees, is taxed on the income and gains and reports them; trustees need not file a trust return (TSEM1563). For CGT the assets are treated as the beneficiary's, including a child's (TCGA s60), so the beneficiary's own annual exempt amount (£3,000, TCGA s1K(2)) and rates apply. The trusts' £500 tax-free amount does not apply, but the beneficiary's own Personal Allowance does (GOV.UK, Trusts and Income Tax). For IHT, a gift into a bare trust is a gift to the beneficiary and therefore a potentially exempt transfer (IHTA s3A(1A), (2)). It is outside the donor's estate if the donor survives 7 years, and the assets form part of the beneficiary's estate. Parental bare trusts: income from a parent's gift to their own unmarried minor child (including a stepchild) is taxed on that parent even if it is kept in the trust (ITTOIA s629; TSEM4300 Example 14). The exception is where the child's total income from that parent's settlements is £100 or less in the tax year. Above £100, ALL of it, not just the excess, is the parent's (s629(3)-(4); TSEM4310 Examples 18-19). Each parent has a separate £100. Bare trusts made before 9 March 1999 are caught only on income actually paid out. Income from funds a parent adds to such a trust on or after 9 March 1999 is the parent's even if retained, subject to the £100 limit (TSEM4305 Example 17). s629 does not tax gains, so a parent-funded bare trust shelters only gains, using the child's £3,000 AEA. Gifts from grandparents or others are not caught unless the parent is the real settlor, for example by providing the funds indirectly or through a reciprocal arrangement (s620(3); TSEM4125). Trust Registration Service (TRS): every UK express trust, including a bare trust, must register unless it is excluded (TRSM22010). The deadline is 90 days from creation for non-taxable trusts created after 6 October 2020. There are three relevant exclusions. (1) A trust created as a requirement of opening a cash deposit account for a child (MLR 2017 Sch 3A para 6A, from 9 March 2022). This does not cover investments held for a child (TRSM23160). (2) A pilot trust holding £100 or less and created before 6 October 2020 (para 6). (3) From 30 June 2026 only, a general exclusion (para 23A, inserted by SI 2026/621 reg 35(5)). It applies to one such trust per settlor that holds no UK land, holds assets of appreciable worth (art, antiques, collectibles, jewellery and similar) of no more than £2,000 in total, has never held property worth more than £10,000 cumulatively since creation, has income of no more than £5,000 a year, and has no UK tax liability (GOV.UK, Check if you need to register a trust). A Junior ISA is not a trust and needs no registration (TRSM23160).
family_and_trusts.conditions: The beneficiary must be absolutely entitled now: there are no conditions to meet, only deferred payment (TSEM1563 Examples 1-3). The gift cannot be taken back. The trustees cannot withhold the assets from a beneficiary aged 18 (16 in Scotland). An income tax benefit needs the money to come from someone other than the parent (for example a grandparent, without reciprocal arrangements), or the trust must produce no more than £100 of income a year from each parent's gifts.
family_and_trusts.risks: If a parent funds the trust, income over £100 a year is taxed on the parent, and the whole amount, not just the excess. Money a parent adds to a pre-9 March 1999 bare trust is caught on the same basis. Control is lost at 18 (16 in Scotland). The gift is permanent and sits in the child's estate. Indirect or reciprocal funding by a parent counts as the parent's settlement. TRS: register within 90 days unless excluded. HMRC can charge a £5,000 fixed penalty if a failure is not put right within the time it sets. The para 23A exclusion did not exist before 30 June 2026.
