family_and_trusts.status: Law in force: TCGA s60; IHTA s3A; ITTOIA ss620, 629; TCGA s1K(2) £3,000 from 2024-25 (FA 2023 s8; s1K(3) omitted from 2025-26 by FA 2025). MLR 2017 Sch 3A para 6 (from 6 October 2020), para 6A (from 9 March 2022, SI 2022/137) and para 23A (from 30 June 2026; SI 2026/621 made 9 June 2026, reg 35(5), in force 21 days after making). Guidance: TSEM1563, TSEM4300, TSEM4305, TSEM4310, TSEM4125, TRSM22010, TRSM23160; GOV.UK 'Check if you need to register a trust' (https://www.gov.uk/guidance/check-if-you-need-to-register-a-trust, published 30 June 2026, last updated 13 July 2026 to add a Welsh translation; the old 'Register a trust as a trustee' URL now redirects there). No changes announced for 2027-28.
family_and_trusts.relevance: This only matters if the user or the grandparents want to put money aside for the children; it does nothing for the user's trading income. A grandparent-funded bare trust uses the child's own allowances, while a parent-funded one shelters only gains and sends income over £100 a year back onto the parent's return, so for most families a Junior ISA (no tax, no registration) is simpler.

family_and_trusts.name: Interest in possession (IIP) trusts
family_and_trusts.summary: Trustees must pass trust income (net of expenses) to the income beneficiary. Trustees pay 20% on non-dividend income and 8.75% (to 5 April 2026) / 10.75% (from 6 April 2026) on dividends; the beneficiary is taxed at their own rates with credit. Income can be mandated to the beneficiary. From 2027-28 property and savings income in non-discretionary trusts taxed at 22% (FA 2026), 24% announced. IHT: lifetime IIP trusts created on or after 22 March 2006 are generally relevant property (entry, ten-year and exit charges) unless a disabled person's interest; a will life interest is taxed as part of the life tenant's estate (40% on death). Settlor-interested income is the settlor's (s624); a settlor's minor child life tenant means the parent is taxed (s629; TSEM4300 Ex 15).
family_and_trusts.conditions: Deed or will; trustees; TRS registration; trust returns.
family_and_trusts.risks: Settlor-interested and parental rules redirect income tax; relevant property charges for lifetime trusts; professional set-up and running costs.

figures.2024-25: Trustees: 20% other income; 8.75% dividends
figures.2026-27: Trustees: 20% other income; 10.75% dividends
figures.2027-28: Property and savings 22% (law, FA 2026) or 24% (announced, Budget 2026); dividends 10.75%; other 20%

family_and_trusts.status: Law for 2024-25 to 2026-27. 2027-28 22% property/savings basic rates law (FA 2026 ss5, 6, 7, Sch 1; ITA ss11CC, 11DA; Royal Assent 18 March 2026). 24% announced (Budget 2026 28 Oct 2026; TIIN 29 Oct 2026) for Finance Bill 2026-27. 2027-28 20% default basic rate announced (needs annual charge). 10.75% dividend ordinary rate permanent text (FA 2026 s4).
family_and_trusts.relevance: Mainly a will-planning tool; does nothing for the freelancer's own income tax.

family_and_trusts.name: Discretionary and accumulation trusts: income tax at the trust rates
family_and_trusts.summary: Trustees decide who benefits and when, and can accumulate income. If net income is at or below the de minimis (£500 from 2024-25, divided as £500 / number of the settlor's qualifying trusts, minimum £100 with 5 or more), no tax; above it ALL income is taxable. Accumulated/discretionary income taxed at the trust rate (45%), dividends 39.35% (no dividend allowance). Income used for trust management expenses taxed at 20% (dividends 8.75% to 2025-26, 10.75% from 2026-27). Payments to beneficiaries carry a 45% credit; non-taxpayers and basic/higher-rate beneficiaries can reclaim (R40/SA), except a settlor's spouse from a settlor-interested trust; payments to the settlor's minor children taxed on the settlor (s629). From 2027-28 property and savings trust rates: 47% in law (FA 2026; ITA s9(1A)-(1B)), 49% announced; TME on property/savings at the property and savings basic rates (announced 24%); s498 tax pool amendments from 6 April 2027 announced.
family_and_trusts.conditions: Deed, trustees, TRS registration. Exclude settlor and spouse to avoid s624; s629 still applies to the settlor's minor children. Relevant property IHT regime.
family_and_trusts.risks: Among the highest rates in the system; IHT entry, ten-year and exit charges; admin costs; settlor-interested status.

figures.2024-25: Trust rate 45%; dividend trust rate 39.35%; tax-free amount £500 (divided among the settlor's trusts, minimum £100)
figures.2026-27: Trust rate 45%; dividend trust rate 39.35%; TME 20% / 10.75% (dividends); £500
figures.2027-28: Other income 45%; dividend trust rate 39.35%; property trust rate and savings trust rate 47% (law, FA 2026) or 49% (announced, Budget 2026); £500

family_and_trusts.status: Law 2024-25 to 2026-27: ITA s9 (45%, 39.35%); s24B £500 (F(No.2)A 2023 Sch 2); FA 2026 s4 (10.75%). 2027-28 47% law (ITA s9(1A)-(1B), FA 2026 s6 and Sch 1 para 4, 18 March 2026). 49% and s498 change announced (Budget 2026 OOTLAR Annex A, 28 Oct 2026; Finance Bill 2026-27).
family_and_trusts.relevance: Cannot shelter trading income; a wealth-stage tool for invested capital passed to the next generation.

family_and_trusts.name: IHT relevant property regime: 20% entry charge, 6% ten-yearly charge, exit charges
family_and_trusts.summary: A lifetime transfer into a relevant property trust is immediately chargeable (IHTA s3(1), IHTM04067) at 20% on the excess over the available nil-rate band (£325,000 less chargeable transfers in the previous 7 years); grossed up if the settlor pays. Death within 7 years: recalculated at 40% with taper and credit ('a further 20%', trustees liable). Ten-year principal charge (s64) on value the day before, after debts and APR/BPR, at three-tenths of the effective rate (s66), up to 6% (IHTM42081). Exit (proportionate) charge (s65): s68/s69 rate x 1/40 per complete quarter, up to 6%; none in the first quarter after creation or after each ten-year anniversary (s65(4), IHTM42114). Special trusts (bereaved minors, disabled persons' interests) have no ten-year/exit charges (flat-rate charge if conditions fail); 18-25 trusts no ten-year charges but s71E charge between 18 and 25. FA 2026 Sch 12 (from 6 April 2026): 100% APR/BPR only within a £2.5m allowance, 50% above; pre-30 October 2024 trusts each have £2.5m from their first ten-year anniversary on or after 6 April 2026; trusts from 30 October 2024 share one £2.5m across the settlor's settlements (IHTA s124H); s69 exit rate computed ignoring APR/BPR and the s66(2) reduction (Sch 12 para 9). Budget 2026 (OOTLAR 1.26) announced rules on deducting trustees' liabilities from 28 October 2026 (Finance Bill 2026-27, not law).
family_and_trusts.conditions: Charges on transfers into most lifetime trusts, at each ten-year anniversary and on distributions. Bare trusts and disabled persons' trusts are PETs instead.
family_and_trusts.risks: Settling more than the available NRB triggers 20% immediately; complex calculations; gifts with reservation (IHTM04071); settlor-interested income tax rules.

figures.2024-25: NRB £325,000; lifetime rate 20%; ten-year charge max 6%

family_and_trusts.name: Trust standard rate band abolished; £500 tax-free amount from 6 April 2024
family_and_trusts.summary: Up to 2023-24 the first £1,000 of discretionary/accumulation trust income was taxed at basic/dividend ordinary rate (ITA s491), divided between the settlor's trusts (minimum £200). From 6 April 2024 this was withdrawn; most trusts and estates pay no income tax on income up to £500; above £500 the full amount is taxed (trust rates for discretionary trusts). £500 divided by the number of the settlor's discretionary/accumulation trusts, minimum £100 each with 5 or more. Not for bare trusts (beneficiary's allowances apply).
family_and_trusts.conditions: Trusts and estates with total income of all types up to £500. Cliff edge: £501 is fully taxable.
family_and_trusts.risks: Cliff edge; fragmentation reduces the per-trust amount; small cash trusts exceed £500 sooner as rates rise from 2027-28.

family_and_trusts.relevance: Mostly irrelevant unless the family sets up a small trust.

family_and_trusts.name: What trusts can and cannot do for a self-employed person's income tax
family_and_trusts.summary: Trading profits are taxed on 'the person receiving or entitled to the profits' (ITTOIA s8). A sole trader therefore cannot move the tax on day-rate earnings by paying, assigning or 'selling' future income to a trust. Any such arrangement is a 'settlement': s620 covers any disposition, trust, covenant, agreement, arrangement or transfer of assets, and the courts require an element of bounty (TSEM4105, citing IRC v Plummer and Jones v Garnett). Income from property from which the settlor or the settlor's spouse or civil partner can benefit is taxed on the settlor (ss624-625). Income paid to or for the settlor's own unmarried minor children (including stepchildren) is also taxed on the settlor unless it is £100 or less a year per child (s629(3)). Benefits such as loans routed through third parties in connection with a trade are taxed as trading profits under ITTOIA ss23A-23H. These were inserted by F(No.2)A 2017 s35 (Royal Assent 16 November 2017) and have effect for relevant benefits arising on or after 6 April 2017 (s35(4)). Loans and quasi-loans outstanding on 5 April 2019 are dealt with in F(No.2)A 2017 Sch 12 (s23A(10)). HMRC Spotlights 51 (10 May 2019) and 57 (17 December 2020, updated 26 May 2022) list self-employed people and partners among the users of remuneration trusts and revenue service trusts. Both say HMRC is considering whether the general anti-abuse rule (GAAR) applies; if it is applied, the penalty is 60% of the counteracted advantage (FA 2013 s212A). Spotlight 61 (22 December 2022) reports tribunal defeats for company remuneration-trust schemes. What trusts can legitimately do: IHT planning within the nil-rate band and exemptions; protecting assets for children or vulnerable people; controlling when beneficiaries get capital; will trusts. Income tax can be saved only on investment income from capital genuinely given away, with the settlor and spouse excluded, for beneficiaries taxed at lower rates who are not the settlor's own minor children. For example, grandchildren can reclaim part of the 45% credit on discretionary payments (ITA s494). Trust rates: a trust pays no income tax if its income is £500 or less, but above that ALL the income is taxed (ITA s24B; GOV.UK). The £500 is reduced only for a trust with accumulated or discretionary (trust-rate) income whose settlor has also made other such trusts. It becomes £500 divided by the number of those trusts, but not less than £100. Settlor-interested trusts, trusts for disabled or vulnerable beneficiaries (FA 2005 ss34-35) and pension or heritage maintenance trusts are left out of that rule (s24B(4)-(9)). Discretionary and accumulation trusts pay 45% (39.35% on dividends) in 2024-25 to 2026-27. For 2027-28 the law sets 47% on savings and property income (ITA s9(1A)-(1B), inserted by FA 2026 s6(8) and Sch 1 para 4), 45% on other income and 39.35% on dividends. Budget 2026 (28 October 2026) announced 49% on savings and property income (Finance Bill 2026-27 clause 4); that is not yet law. Interest in possession trustees pay 20% (dividends 8.75% to 2025-26, 10.75% from 2026-27). For 2027-28 their savings and property income is taxed at 22% in law (ITA ss11CC, 11DA, inserted by FA 2026 s6(8) and Sch 1 paras 10 and 12, at the basic rates set by FA 2026 ss5 and 7). 24% is announced (Finance Bill 2026-27 clause 3, which would also repeal FA 2026 ss5 and 7).
family_and_trusts.conditions: Capital genuinely given away; no possible benefit to the settlor or the settlor's spouse or civil partner (s625); beneficiaries not the settlor's own unmarried minor children, beyond the £100 de minimis (s629); income from investments, not from the settlor's trade or future earnings.
family_and_trusts.risks: Promoted trust schemes for the self-employed (remuneration trusts, revenue service trusts) do not work. The contributions are not deductible, and income tax, NIC and possibly IHT remain due, plus interest and penalties, including inaccuracy penalties for careless returns; the enablers' penalty regime targets promoters (Spotlights 51, 57, 61). A further 60% penalty is possible if HMRC applies the GAAR (FA 2013 s212A); Spotlights 51 and 57 say HMRC is considering this. ITTOIA ss23A-23H tax third-party benefits as trading profits. Legitimate trusts also carry risks: ss624/629 send income back to the settlor; gifts with reservation stay in the donor's estate (FA 1986 s102); IHT relevant property charges apply; above £500 all trust income is taxed; TRS registration is needed (a £5,000 penalty is possible); there are set-up and running costs; and trust rates on savings and property rise for 2027-28.

family_and_trusts.status: Law: ITTOIA ss8, 620, 624, 625, 629; ss23A-23H (F(No.2)A 2017 s35, Royal Assent 16 November 2017, effective for relevant benefits arising on or after 6 April 2017; Sch 12 for loans outstanding on 5 April 2019); ITA s9 (45% and 39.35%; 47% property and savings trust rates from 2027-28, inserted by FA 2026 s6(8) and Sch 1 para 4, Royal Assent 18 March 2026); ITA s24B (£500 from 2024-25); ITA ss11CC, 11DA (FA 2026 s6(8), Sch 1 paras 10, 12) with the 22% basic rates in FA 2026 ss5, 7; ITA ss494, 498; FA 2013 s212A; FA 1986 s102. Announced only (Budget 2026, 28 October 2026; OOTLAR 1.1, 1.2, 1.12 and Annex A): 49% property and savings trust rates (Finance Bill 2026-27, Bill 173, clause 4), 24/44/49% property and savings rates with repeal of FA 2026 ss5 and 7 (clause 3), and the tax-pool change (clause 39(4)), all from 6 April 2027. The Bill had its second reading on 23 November 2026 and is not law. Guidance: TSEM4105; Spotlights 51, 57 and 61 (current).
family_and_trusts.relevance: No trust can lower the tax on the user's day-rate earnings, and anyone offering a trust that 'takes income off your books' or pays the user back in loans is selling a scheme HMRC targets. Trusts become useful only later, for passing savings or property to children or grandchildren (mostly for IHT); for children's savings a Junior ISA is simpler.

family_and_trusts.name: Junior ISA compared with trusts for children
family_and_trusts.summary: Junior ISA (cash and/or stocks and shares): tax-free interest, dividends and gains; money belongs to the child; a parent/guardian opens it as registered contact (child can open own at 16-17 and become registered contact from 16); no withdrawals until 18 except terminal illness or death; becomes an adult ISA at 18. Child under 18 and UK-resident (abroad only if parent is a Crown servant). Max one cash and one S&S JISA; not alongside a CTF (CTF can transfer in). Anyone can pay in within £9,000 per child per year. JISA income is not income for any income tax purpose, including s629 (ISA Regs reg 22(1)(f)), and needs no TRS registration. Compare: parental bare trust (s629 above £100 per parent per child, ALL taxed; gains the child's; access at 18/16 Scotland; generally TRS registration; only cash-deposit trusts for minors excluded, TRSM23160, apart from the one-per-settlor de minimis); discretionary trust (£500 de minimis; 45% / 39.35% in 2024-25 to 2026-27; 49% announced for 2027-28 savings and property; trustees' gains 24% with £1,500 AEA; relevant property IHT; TRS; costs; control beyond 18). Grandparent gifts are the child's income (PA £12,570, £5,000 starting rate, £1,000 PSA) unless the parent is the true source (TSEM4125, TSEM4300). Regular contributions from surplus income can be IHT-exempt as normal expenditure out of income.
family_and_trusts.conditions: One cash and one S&S JISA per child; annual limit per child; money irrevocably the child's.
family_and_trusts.risks: Full access at 18; locked until then; avoid over-subscription.

family_and_trusts.name: IHT lifetime gift exemptions and nil-rate bands
family_and_trusts.summary: Annual exemption £3,000 (unused carries forward one year only). Small gifts up to £250 per person (unless another allowance used on that person). Wedding/civil partnership gifts: £5,000 to a child, £2,500 to a grandchild or great-grandchild, £1,000 to anyone else. Normal expenditure out of income: unlimited if regular, from income and leaving the giver able to meet usual living costs (e.g. rent for a child, payments into a child's savings). UK spouse/civil partner gifts exempt. Other gifts free of IHT if the giver survives 7 years; taper relief for gifts 3-7 years before death. Gifts into most trusts are chargeable. NRB £325,000; residence NRB £175,000 tapered above £2m; IHT 40%, or 36% if 10% or more of the net estate goes to charity.
family_and_trusts.conditions: Keep records; normal expenditure must be habitual, from income and not reduce the standard of living.
family_and_trusts.risks: 7-year rule; reservation of benefit; trust gifts are not PETs.

family_and_trusts.name: Inheritance tax on unused pension funds and death benefits from 6 April 2027
family_and_trusts.summary: For deaths on or after 6 April 2027 most unused pension funds and death benefits are 'notional pension property' in the estate (new IHTA s150A, FA 2026 s66), for registered schemes, QNUPS and s615(3) schemes, discretionary or not. Personal representatives report and pay; recipients can also be liable; scheme administrators only if they pay out in breach of a withholding notice or fail to act on a payment notice (s67). Excluded: dependants' scheme pensions (and replacing trivial commutation lump sums), dependants'/nominees' annuities bought with the member's lifetime annuity, death-in-service benefits. Spouse and charity exemptions apply (s69 amending IHTA ss18, 23). Withholding notice (s226A): each beneficiary limited to 50% until withdrawn, tax paid, or 15 months after the end of the month of death. Payment notice (s226B) for at least £1,000: administrator pays HMRC within 35 days. Government static estimates for 2027-28 (maximum): of about 213,000 estates with inheritable pension wealth, about 10,500 newly liable and about 38,500 pay more; average liability up about £34,000. Budget 2026 (OOTLAR 1.27) announced technical amendments from 6 April 2027 (prospective PRs can direct payment; PRs choose component treatment for the 36% charity rate).
family_and_trusts.conditions: Deaths on or after 6 April 2027 where the estate including pensions exceeds available NRBs and funds do not go to exempt beneficiaries.
family_and_trusts.risks: Pensions no longer an IHT shelter; beneficiaries can be jointly liable; income tax on inherited pensions not researched.

figures.current: Withholding: beneficiaries limited to 50% for up to 15 months after the end of the month of death. Payment notice minimum £1,000; administrator pays within 35 days. Estimates 2027-28: ~213,000 estates; ~10,500 newly liable; ~38,500 pay more; average +~£34,000.

family_and_trusts.status: Law: FA 2026 (c.11) ss66-71, Royal Assent 18 March 2026; s71 applies to deaths on or after 6 April 2027. Technical amendments announced only (Budget 2026, 28 Oct 2026, OOTLAR 1.27; Finance Bill 2026-27).
family_and_trusts.relevance: Pension contributions remain the strongest income tax relief; only the IHT advantage on death has gone (spouse still exempt).

family_and_trusts.name: Business Property Relief and Agricultural Property Relief: £2.5m 100% allowance from 6 April 2026
family_and_trusts.summary: From 6 April 2026 (FA 2026 s65, Sch 12) 100% APR and BPR together are limited to a £2.5m rolling allowance per individual (IHTA s124D), reduced by 100% relief used on chargeable transfers in the previous 7 years; 50% relief above. Unused allowance transfers to a surviving spouse (treated as 100% unused where the first death was before 6 April 2026), so a couple can pass up to £5m of qualifying property, or £5.65m with two NRBs (GOV.UK). Claim within 4 years from the end of the month the survivor dies, or 6 months from when PRs first act if later (s124F). Trusts: £2.5m allowance shared across the settlor's settlements made on or after 30 October 2024 (s124H); pre-30 October 2024 trusts each get £2.5m from their first ten-year anniversary on or after 6 April 2026. Fixed at £2.5m; CPI-indexed from 6 April 2031 (s124L). AIM and other unlisted shares get 50% only and do not use the allowance. Ten-year interest-free instalments for all APR/BPR property. Lifetime gifts from 30 October 2024 are under the new rules if the donor dies on or after 6 April 2026 within 7 years. History: £1m announced (Autumn Budget 2024); transferability (Budget 2025); £2.5m (23 Dec 2025). For this sole trader: the business or an interest in it, including kit used in the trade, qualifies at 100% after 2 years' ownership if trading and not mainly investment (s105(3)); excepted assets (s112) excluded; personally owned plant used by a partnership or controlled company gets 50% (s105(1)(d)); kit gifted separately from the business gets no BPR.
family_and_trusts.conditions: Trading, not mainly investment; owned 2 years before death or gift; used mainly for the business; claim the transferred allowance within the time limit.
family_and_trusts.risks: Excepted assets (e.g. surplus cash) may not qualify; personally held equipment outside a partnership gets only 50%; transitional rules for gifts from 30 October 2024.

family_and_trusts.name: Long-term UK residence test replaces domicile from 6 April 2025
family_and_trusts.summary: From 6 April 2025 excluded property status for non-UK assets depends on being a 'long-term UK resident', not domicile (IHTA s6(1),(1A), ss6A-6C, FA 2025 s44). Long-term resident if UK resident for at least 10 of the previous 20 tax years (SRT from 2013-14; split year counts as resident, IHTM47020). After leaving, in scope until non-resident for the 'required number' of consecutive years: 3 if 13 or fewer resident years in the 20 ending with the last UK-resident year, then 4 for 14, up to 10 for 20 (s6A(2)(b), (3)). Not long-term resident if non-resident for any 10 consecutive years within the previous 19 (s6A(2)(a)). Under-20s test (s6B), companies (s6C), elections (ss267ZC-267ZE). s267 deemed domicile omitted from 6 April 2025 (FA 2025 Sch 13). Remittance basis ended after 2024-25; from 2025-26 new arrivals non-resident for the previous 10 years can claim FIG relief (ITTOIA s845A onwards, FA 2025 s37) for 4 years, losing PA (s845E) and CGT AEA in claim years. Transitional rules (IHTM47021). For a UK-born, always-UK-resident sole trader none of this reduces tax.
family_and_trusts.conditions: Only relevant with a non-UK background, recent arrival, foreign assets or emigration plans.
family_and_trusts.risks: Overseas trusts of non-dom settlors lost protections (TSEM4705 onwards). Budget 2026 OOTLAR 1.28: CGT exit charge easement for temporarily migrating trusts from 28 October 2026 (announced).

figures.current: 10 of previous 20 tax years test; tail 3 to 10 years depending on resident years; FIG relief for 4 years after 10 years' non-residence.

family_and_trusts.name: General Anti-Abuse Rule (Finance Act 2013 Part 5) as it applies to family planning
family_and_trusts.summary: The GAAR (FA 2013 Part 5, ss206-215) lets HMRC counteract tax advantages from abusive tax arrangements. Arrangements are 'tax arrangements' if, having regard to all the circumstances, it would be reasonable to conclude that getting a tax advantage was the main purpose or one of the main purposes (s207(1)). They are 'abusive' if entering into or carrying them out 'cannot reasonably be regarded as a reasonable course of action' in relation to the tax provisions (s207(2)). HMRC's guidance calls this the 'double reasonableness' test (B12.1, C5.10). The tribunal considers whether the results fit the principles and policy objectives of the provisions, whether contrived or abnormal steps are used, and whether the arrangements exploit shortcomings in the law. s207(4) gives three indicators of abuse: income, profits or gains for tax purposes significantly below the economic amount; deductions or losses significantly above it; and claims to repay or credit tax that has not been and is unlikely to be paid. Each counts only if it is reasonable to assume the result was not anticipated when the provisions were enacted. An indicator against abuse (s207(5)) is that the arrangements follow established practice that HMRC had indicated it accepted when they were entered into. These examples are not exhaustive (s207(6)). Adjustments must be just and reasonable and can be made to any tax the GAAR covers (s209(2)-(3)). Their effect is suspended until HMRC has followed the procedure in Schedule 43, 43A or 43B (s209(6)(a)). Under Schedule 43, HMRC must refer the matter to the GAAR Advisory Panel (paras 5-6). The exception is where the taxpayer takes 'relevant corrective action' (amending the return or claim, or agreeing in writing to give up the advantage) before the closed period begins (para 4A). HMRC must consider any Panel opinion before its final notice (para 12). Under Schedules 43A and 43B (pooled, bound or generic cases), the Panel gives its opinion on the lead or other referred arrangements, or on a generic referral, not on each user's own arrangements. HMRC can also give a protective GAAR notice within the ordinary assessing time limits while the procedure runs (s209AA). The penalty is 60% of the counteracted advantage (s212A). It applies to arrangements entered into on or after 15 September 2016 where a return or other tax document relied on the advantage. The GAAR applies to arrangements entered into from 17 July 2013, and to NICs from 13 March 2014 (NICA 2014 s10).
family_and_trusts.conditions: HMRC's GAAR guidance names these as outside its target area: choosing to trade as a sole trader, in partnership or through a company; once incorporated, leaving profits to be paid out later as dividends instead of a larger salary now (B4.3, C5.6.4); ISAs, and outright gifts to children with no benefit kept (given as an IHT example); straightforward use of statutory reliefs (B4.4); and reasonable steps to obtain reliefs Parliament clearly intended, such as pension contributions (C5.6.2). The guidance does not name a spouse wage, a spouse partnership, Marriage Allowance or Junior ISAs. Treating them as outside the GAAR is a reasonable inference, but each must still pass its own rules. A wage must be at a commercial rate for real work (BIM47105). A gift to a spouse must be outright and not wholly or substantially a right to income (ITTOIA s626(3); TSEM4215). A parent's gift (or other settlement) may produce income for that parent's own child who is under 18 and not married or in a civil partnership ('child' includes a stepchild). If that income is more than £100 in the tax year, all of it is taxed on the parent, not just the excess. The £100 applies separately to each parent for each child (ITTOIA s629(1), (3), (4), (7)). The GAAR targets contrived multi-step arrangements, circular cash flows and 'loans' never meant to be repaid.
family_and_trusts.risks: Counteraction of the advantage, possibly by adjusting a different tax (s209(3)); the 60% penalty on top of the tax; interest; and the cost of the Panel process. The GAAR is a backstop: the targeted rules usually defeat a family scheme first. These include the settlements rules (ITTOIA ss619-648), the wholly and exclusively test, ITTOIA ss23A-23H and ITEPA Part 7A.

Applies to each parent for each child under 18 who is unmarried and not in a civil partnership, stepchildren included (s629(7))
figures.budget_2026: Budget 2026 document para 6.163 and OOTLAR para 2.35: a consultation 'shortly' on tackling the promotion and use of tax avoidance. According to the OOTLAR it will include new powers against 'serious and serial users of tax avoidance schemes'. Budget para 6.167 / OOTLAR 1.97: POTAS amendments in Finance Bill 2026-27. Neither proposes changes to the FA 2013 GAAR. Para 2.35 of the main Budget document is about property income reporting.

family_and_trusts.status: Law: FA 2013 Part 5 (ss206-215, Schs 43-43C) for arrangements from 17 July 2013; NICA 2014 s10 from 13 March 2014; s212A penalty (FA 2016 s158) for arrangements entered into on or after 15 September 2016; s209AA protective notices (inserted by FA 2020 Sch 14). Guidance: HMRC GAAR guidance Parts A-C, effective 16 July 2021. Announced only (28 October 2026): the avoidance consultation (Budget 2026 para 6.163, OOTLAR 2.35), not found on GOV.UK as at 24 November 2026; POTAS amendments for Finance Bill 2026-27 (Budget para 6.167, OOTLAR 1.97).
family_and_trusts.relevance: Matters if the freelancer later brings a spouse, partner or children into the business. Ordinary choices are safe: sole trader or company, a commercial wage, a genuine partnership, pension contributions. Anything sold as a scheme is not.

family_and_trusts.name: Candid verdict: which family and trust measures genuinely help this freelancer
family_and_trusts.summary: Ranking for a UK (rUK) sole-trader events technician with growing profits. (1) Pay a genuinely involved spouse or partner a documented, commercial wage for real admin, logistics or kit work, actually paid: saves income tax plus Class 4 at 26% (basic), 42% (higher), 62% (£100,000-£125,140) or 47% (additional); nothing below £12,570 of profit; best value from about £50,270. Spouse: no employee NIC below £12,570; employer NIC nil below the ST (£9,100 in 2024-25; £5,000 in 2025-26 and 2026-27), then 13.8% / 15%, offset by EA (£5,000 in 2024-25; £10,500 from 2025-26); wage at or above the LEL (£6,708 in 2026-27) earns a qualifying year. (2) Marriage Allowance: £1,260 transfer, up to £252 a year, backdatable to 2022-23; freelancer must be basic-rate and spouse below £12,570 (full £252 only at £11,310 or less); largely an alternative to (1). (3) At higher profits, a genuine spouse partnership with an unconditional share of capital, assets and profits, clients contracting with the firm (TSEM4215 Ex 9); in a skill-based business with modest kit HMRC may argue Ex 10 applies. (4) Outright gifts of savings or investments to a lower-rate spouse (s626); 2027-28 savings rates 22/42/47 law, 24/44/49 announced. (5) Junior ISAs (£9,000 per child in 2026-27); parental gifts producing over £100 per parent per child are wholly taxed on the parent; grandparent gifts not caught. (6) Pensions: relief at source plus SA higher-rate relief; reduce ANI (best lever for HICBC £60,000-£80,000 and the £100,000 taper) but not trading profit or Class 4; £2,880 net (£3,600 gross) for each non-earning family member. (7) If incorporated later: ordinary shares outright to the spouse (Jones v Garnett), no alphabet shares or waivers; IR35 still applies. Of no real use now: income tax trusts (45% trust rate; 47% legislated and 49% announced for 2027-28 savings/property); IHT trusts (100% APR/BPR within £2.5m, 50% above, transferable); non-dom planning. Never use: remuneration or revenue trusts (Spotlights 51, 56, 57, 61); dividend waivers; gift-and-loan-back; backdated partnerships; wages not paid or above the value of the work.
family_and_trusts.conditions: Genuine substance, contemporaneous documents and money actually moving; marital/civil partnership status decides availability.
family_and_trusts.risks: Settlements rules (s624, s629), wholly-and-exclusively disallowance, GAAR, NMW and payroll compliance, loss of control of gifted assets, relationship breakdown.

figures.current: Realistic savings: a few hundred pounds a year at basic rate, rising to several thousand at higher rates or with children near the £60,000-£100,000 thresholds, and only with a spouse or partner who genuinely works in or co-owns the business.

family_and_trusts.status: Verified 24 Nov 2026. Component measures mostly law (FA 2026 c.11: 22/42/47 savings and 47% trust rates for 2027-28; £2.5m APR/BPR allowance from 6 Apr 2026; ITTOIA ss624/626/629; Marriage Allowance backdating). Announced only (Budget 2026, 28 Oct 2026, Finance Bill 2026-27, from 6 Apr 2027): 24/44/49 and 49% trust rates.
family_and_trusts.relevance: The summary answer to 'can my family or a trust cut my tax?'.

funding.name: British Business Bank Start Up Loans (government-backed personal loan for business use)
funding.amount: £500 to £25,000 per individual, outstanding at any one time. At most £100,000 is lent to any one business in its lifetime (up to four partners at £25,000 each). Term 1 to 5 years with monthly repayments. The rate is fixed for the life of the loan: 7.5% a year for applications successful from 6 April 2026, and 6% for loans approved earlier (6% since 2012). There are no application, set-up or early-repayment fees. Successful applicants get free business-plan support and up to 12 months' free mentoring. It is an unsecured personal loan in the borrower's name, regulated under the Consumer Credit Act 1974, not a grant.
funding.how_taxed:
The loan is not income, and capital repayments are not expenses.
- Interest is a deductible trading expense to the extent the money is used wholly and exclusively for the trade (ITTOIA 2005 s34; BIM45665, BIM45690).
- Swapping capital already in the business for loan finance does not by itself make the interest deductible (BIM45700).
- Borrowing that funds private drawings, shown by an overdrawn capital account, is restricted (BIM45705).
- On the cash basis, the old £500 interest cap (ITTOIA s51A) was removed from 2024-25 by FA 2024 Sch 10, so the same rule applies on both bases.
If the user incorporates, the loan stays personal. Interest on money used to buy ordinary shares in, or lend to, their own close trading company can get qualifying loan interest relief (ITA 2007 ss383, 392), subject to these conditions:
- the conditions in s393: no capital recovered from the company, and either a material interest of more than 5% or holding shares and spending the greater part of their time running the company;
- the s24A cap, which applies with other reliefs: the greater of £50,000 or 25% of adjusted total income;
- the relief is lost if EIS or SITR relief is claimed on the same investment (s392(3), (3A)).
funding.risks:
The borrower is personally liable for the full loan even if the business fails, and missed payments harm their credit file. Interest is deductible only for the business-use share (BIM45690, BIM45700, BIM45705). The loan cannot fund training. Do not record the loan as income.
The loan counts as a subsidy (Minimal Financial Assistance, Subsidy Control Act 2022 s36). The subsidy value Start Up Loans confirms in writing counts towards the £315,000 limit over the current and two previous financial years. Keep that confirmation for at least 3 years and declare it on later grant or Growth Guarantee Scheme applications.

figures.2024-25: Fixed 6% (unchanged since 2012); first loan only if trading up to 36 months; £500-£25,000 per person; 1-5 years; no fees.
figures.2025-26: As 2024-25: 6%, 36-month limit. An application that passed the credit check before 6 April 2026 kept 6% if completed within 90 days. If a second credit check was needed on or after 6 April 2026, the rate is 7.5%.
figures.2026-27: From 6 April 2026: fixed 7.5% for successful applications; first loan if trading up to 60 months; £500-£25,000 per person outstanding; £100,000 lifetime per business; 1-5 years; no fees. Loans approved before 6 April 2026 stay at 6% for life. A Tranche B takes Tranche A's rate. A Second Loan takes the rate in force when it is applied for.
figures.2027-28: No change announced as at 24 Nov 2026; nothing in Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026).
figures.current:
Fixed 7.5%. From the official 7.5% table:
- £2,000 over 12 months: £82.18 interest (£173.51 a month).
- £2,000 over 24 months: £159.98 interest, £2,159.98 total, £90.00 a month.
- £2,000 over 36 months: £239.65 interest; over 48 months: £321.17; over 60 months: £404.55 (£40.08 a month).
- £5,000 over 60 months: £1,011.38 interest (£100.19 a month).
- £10,000 over 60 months: £2,022.77 interest (£200.38 a month).
- £25,000 over 60 months: £5,056.91 interest (£500.95 a month). The table shows a total of £30,056.92 because of rounding.
The calculator widget's default (£127.39 interest, £88.64 a month) is the 6%, 24-month figure mislabelled as 7.5%. Do not use it.

figures_disputed: Second Loan repayment condition: the Second Loans page says all repayments on schedule for the 3 months before applying (with the first loan drawn at least 6 months ago), but the loan FAQ says at least six months of full repayments. Treat 6 full repayments as the safe reading until the scheme confirms.
funding.status: Operating government-backed scheme run by the Start-Up Loans Company, part of the British Business Bank. Its terms are contractual scheme rules, not statute. The 7.5% rate and 60-month limit apply from 6 April 2026 (Start Up Loans FAQ and GOV.UK, read 24 Nov 2026). The tax treatment is law: ITTOIA 2005 ss34 and 58; s51A omitted from 2024-25 by FA 2024 Sch 10 paras 7(a) and 47; ITA 2007 ss383, 392-394 and 24A. The subsidy rules are in the Subsidy Control Act 2022 s36.
funding.relevance: Fixed-rate unsecured finance for kit, a van or working capital between purchase orders, but only if the business has traded for 60 months or less (from 6 April 2026), so a technician trading longer than that cannot get a first loan. The interest on the business-use share reduces taxable profit.

funding.name: Growth Guarantee Scheme (GGS)
funding.amount:
Up to £2m per business group. For businesses in scope of the Northern Ireland Protocol: £1m, or £285,000 in primary agriculture and £170,000 in fisheries and aquaculture.
Minimum facility: £1,000 for asset finance, invoice finance and asset-based lending; £25,001 for term loans and overdrafts.
Terms:
- term loans and asset finance: 3 months to 6 years, or up to 10 years for facilities up to £1.1m (NI £550,000) where the lender offers it; longer terms reduce the maximum facility;
- overdrafts, invoice finance and asset-based lending: 3 months to 3 years.
The government guarantees 70% of the outstanding balance to the lender after the lender's normal recovery process; the borrower stays 100% liable. Interest and fees are set by the lender, which must pass on the economic benefit of the guarantee. Upfront lender fees, including broker fees, are capped at 5%.
funding.how_taxed:
Sole trader:
- Interest, and the incidental costs of getting the finance (fees, commissions), are deductible if the borrowing is used wholly and exclusively for the trade (ITTOIA 2005 ss34, 58; BIM45665).
- A loan is not a 'contribution', so kit bought with it keeps its full cost for capital allowances (CA14100).
- The cash-basis £500 interest cap (s51A) no longer applies from 2024-25.
A company borrower is taxed under the corporation tax loan-relationship rules instead (BIM45665 refers to CFM).
funding.conditions: The borrower must give written confirmation that the facility will not take the business over its subsidy limit over a rolling 3-year period. Lenders run standard credit, fraud, AML and KYC checks, and every decision is at the lender's discretion. Not open to banks, building societies, insurers, public-sector bodies, state-funded schools or certain mining and extraction activities.
funding.risks: Lenders may take personal guarantees, but the principal private residence cannot be taken as security. The guarantee protects the lender, not the borrower. The facility counts as a subsidy and can reduce headroom for grants or a Start Up Loan. Interest on any private-use share is not deductible. Pricing varies by lender, so compare it with Start Up Loans and ordinary asset finance. For a small sole trader, term loans start at £25,001, so asset or invoice finance (from £1,000) is the realistic route.

figures.2024-25: Launched 1 July 2024, replacing RLS 3, to run until at least 31 March 2026 (HCWS502, 24 May 2024; Spring Budget 2024). 70% guarantee; maximum £2m (NI £1m); turnover limit £45m; minimums £1,000 for asset and invoice finance and £25,001 for loans and overdrafts (HCWS502). Maximum terms: 6 years for term loans and asset finance (the limit before the 2026 expansion, per HMT 13 Jul 2026), and 3 years for overdrafts and invoice finance.
figures.2025-26: Same terms. April 2025: about £500m of extra lending capacity announced for businesses with cash-flow pressures from changes in global tariffs. The 2025 Spending Review extended the scheme to 31 March 2030.
figures.current: 70% guarantee to the lender; borrower 100% liable; group turnover up to £54m; maximum £2m (NI £1m); minimum £1,000 (asset finance, invoice finance, ABL) or £25,001 (term loans, overdrafts); terms up to 6 years, or 10 years for facilities up to £1.1m where offered; overdrafts and invoice finance up to 3 years; upfront fees capped at 5%; runs to 31 March 2030.
figures.2027-28: No further change announced; scheduled to run to 31 March 2030.

figures_disputed: Start date of the £54m turnover limit and 10-year terms: no official date is published. Trade press reports either the end of October or the start of November 2026, and each lender adopts the terms in its own time, so check the lender's terms for any facility dated October to December 2026.
Scheme end date: BBB performance data and request-for-proposals pages say 31 March 2030, but one BBB press release (31 July 2025) says 5 April 2030.
funding.status: Live, non-statutory guarantee scheme administered by the British Business Bank on behalf of the Secretary of State for the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade. The contingent liability was notified to Parliament in HCWS502 (24 May 2024). Launched 1 July 2024 and extended to 31 March 2030 at Spending Review 2025. The expansion was announced in July 2026, is being adopted by lenders from about November 2026, and is funded through the Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026) BBB recapitalisation. The tax treatment is law: ITTOIA 2005 ss34 and 58, and CAA 2001 s532 (CA14100).
funding.relevance: Mainly relevant if the hire or kit side grows: an accredited lender may back asset finance on lighting, sound or video equipment from £1,000 with the guarantee if it would not lend otherwise. It cannot be applied for directly, and it does not change how the interest is taxed.

funding.name: Tax-Free Childcare
funding.amount: For every £8 the parent pays in, the government adds £2, so the top-up is 25% of the parent's payment (Childcare Payments Act 2014 s1(4)). The maximum per child is £500 per 3-month entitlement period, or £2,000 a year. For a disabled child it is £1,000 per period, or £4,000 a year. Payments into the account are capped at £2,000 per period (£4,000 for a disabled child) (s19(5)).
funding.how_taxed: The top-up is not a taxable receipt. HMRC pays it into the childcare account (Act s1(3)) and it can only be spent on childcare, so it does not go on the tax return. Eligibility uses adjusted net income (ITA 2007 s58(1), applied by reg 15(4)): net income less grossed-up Gift Aid and gross relief-at-source pension contributions.
funding.conditions:
(1) Minimum income: each partner expects income over the 3 months from the declaration of at least 16 hours a week at their national minimum wage rate on the declaration date, for 13 weeks (reg 2 'minimum weekly income'; reg 9(1), (4), (6)).
(2) Self-employed alternative: expected income over the whole tax year of the declaration of at least 16 hours x the rate for their age on 6 April x 52 weeks (reg 9(1)(b)(ii), (5), (5A)).
(3) What counts as income:
- Self-employed: expected receipts less expected expenses incurred wholly and exclusively for the trade, ignoring capital receipts and capital expenses (reg 10(3)-(4)). Buying kit therefore does not reduce it. A partner in a business partnership uses their share.
- Employed: the earnings (ITEPA s62 meaning) the person expects from employment, an office, or an engagement to which ITEPA Part 2 Chapters 7 to 10 apply (agency workers, IR35 intermediaries and managed service companies) (reg 10(1)-(2)). Unlike the 30-hours rules (SI 2022/1134 reg 18(3)), reg 10 does not expressly add amounts that are only treated as earnings, such as an IR35 deemed employment payment.
- Dividends, interest, property income and pensions do not count (GOV.UK).
(4) Start-up exemption: a self-employed person need not meet the income test for a first declaration made within 12 months of starting a trade, or for the three entitlement periods after that start-up period. A later start-up period can be used only once 48 months have passed since the end of the previous exempt period (reg 11).
(5) Treated as working without meeting the income test:
- Sickness and parental leave or pay (reg 12): statutory sick pay; Maternity Allowance; statutory maternity, paternity, adoption, parental bereavement or neonatal care pay; maternity, paternity, adoption, shared parental, statutory parental, parental bereavement or neonatal care leave. The person must have been in qualifying paid work immediately before (reg 12(3)) and is then treated as having income equal to the minimum. This applies to the self-employed too (reg 12(6)), so a self-employed parent on Maternity Allowance who met the test before stays eligible.
- New job or return from unpaid leave (reg 9(2)-(2A), for expected start dates from 16 Oct 2025): the person is treated as in paid work as an employed person from the 1 January, 1 April or 1 September before the start date (depending on when it falls) until the day before. The income test then looks at the 3 months from the start date (reg 9(4)(b)).
- A non-working person whose partner is in qualifying paid work counts as working if they get any of these (reg 13): incapacity benefit or severe disablement allowance; Carer's Allowance or Scottish carer's assistance; contributory ESA; NI credits for incapacity. The same applies if they are on carer's leave.
(6) Exclusions:
- Universal Credit payable to either partner, including a nil award, or a pending UC claim (Act s11).
- Being an eligible employee in an employer childcare voucher scheme or employer directly contracted childcare (ITEPA s270A and s318A schemes), unless the person intends to give the employer written notice to leave it within 3 months of the declaration (Act s12(1)(b), (4); GOV.UK says tell the employer within 90 days). Workplace nurseries under ITEPA s318 are not barred.
- Any other government payment towards childcare costs, such as a childcare bursary or grant (Act s13; GOV.UK).
- While tax credits existed, a valid declaration ended any tax credit award (Act s30).
(7) The child usually lives with the parent and is not fostered; the provider must be registered and signed up. Reconfirm every 3 months.
funding.risks:
Cliff edge: if either partner expects adjusted net income above £100,000 for the tax year, all of the top-up for that year is lost (reg 15). The test uses expected income at each 3-monthly reconfirmation, so forecast honestly and update the forecast.
Penalties:
- A careless or deliberate inaccuracy in a declaration costs 25% or 50% of the maximum top-up for the period (Act s42(2), (4), (5)). That is £125 or £250 per child for a standard 3-month period.
- The 25% penalty also applies if a person later finds an inaccuracy in a declaration and does not take reasonable steps to tell HMRC (s42(3), (5)). Self-employed income forecasts often change, so tell HMRC when one turns out to be wrong.
- Dishonestly obtaining top-ups: up to £3,000, or the amount obtained if greater (s46).
Universal Credit: claiming UC during an entitlement period without a change of circumstances, then re-declaring within 12 months, can bring a warning notice. A repeat within 4 years can bring disqualification for up to 3 years (ss33-34).
The minimum-income thresholds follow the minimum wage, which changes on 1 April, not 6 April.

figures.top_up_rate: 25% of the amount paid in (£2 per £8)
figures.2024-25: Top-up up to £500 per 3-month period (£2,000 a year) per child (£1,000 / £4,000 disabled). £100,000 adjusted net income limit per partner. Minimum expected income over 3 months, derived as 16 h x 13 wk x the NMW rates from 1 Apr 2024: £2,379.52 (21+, £11.44/h); £1,788.80 (18-20, £8.60/h); £1,331.20 (under 18 or apprentice, £6.40/h). Self-employed whole-year test (16 x 52, derived): £9,518.08, £7,155.20 or £5,324.80.
figures.2025-26: Same top-up and £100,000 limit. 3-month minimum, derived from the NMW rates from 1 Apr 2025: £2,539.68 (21+, £12.21/h); £2,080.00 (18-20, £10.00/h); £1,570.40 (under 18 or apprentice, £7.55/h). Whole-year test: £10,158.72, £8,320.00 or £6,281.60 (derived).
figures.2026-27: Same top-up and £100,000 limit. 3-month minimum: £2,643.68 (21+), £2,256.80 (18-20), £1,664.00 (under 18 or apprentice). These are confirmed on GOV.UK and equal 16 x 13 x £12.71 / £10.85 / £8.00. Whole-year test: £10,574.72 (21+, GOV.UK example), £9,027.20 or £6,656.00 (derived).
figures.2027-28: No Tax-Free Childcare measure in Budget 2026; the top-up and the £100,000 limit continue. Announced, not yet law: with the April 2027 NMW rates from Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026) of £13.21 / £11.27 / £8.31, the 3-month minimum becomes £2,747.68 / £2,344.16 / £1,728.48 and the whole-year test £10,990.72 / £9,376.64 / £6,913.92 (derived).
figures.threshold_switch_date: 1 April each year (the NMW change date). A declaration made 1-5 April already uses the new rate.

figures_disputed: 2027-28 minimum-income thresholds (£2,747.68 / £2,344.16 / £1,728.48 per 3 months; £10,990.72 / £9,376.64 / £6,913.92 a year) are provisional until the April 2027 National Minimum Wage amendment regulations are made. None were on legislation.gov.uk at 24 Nov 2026.
funding.status: Law: Childcare Payments Act 2014 (ss1, 11-13, 19, 30, 33-34, 42, 46) and the Childcare Payments (Eligibility) Regulations 2015 (SI 2015/448) regs 2, 5, 9-13 and 15. Amended by SI 2025/857, in force 15 Sep 2025, which aligned the application window with the 30-hours scheme; its new reg 9(2)-(2A) applies to expected work start dates on or after 16 Oct 2025, with transitional rules for start dates up to 31 Jan 2026 (regs 1(2), 3). Also amended by SI 2026/279 (from 6 Apr 2026), which corrects 'ends on' to 'ends with' in reg 9(2A). It also fills omitted cross-references in reg 12(7), so that EEA or Swiss equivalents of parental bereavement leave and pay count as qualifying paid work. Neither SI changes any figure. Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026) has no Tax-Free Childcare measure. The minimum-income amounts follow the NMW: April 2026 rates are in force (SI 2026/357); April 2027 rates are announced in Budget 2026 but not yet law.
funding.relevance: Worth up to £2,000 a year per child (£4,000 if disabled) on childcare the family already pays for. With lumpy day-rate work, the self-employed whole-year test, which uses profit after running costs but ignores kit purchases, usually keeps a freelancer eligible through quiet quarters; agency PAYE pay counts as employed income, and the £100,000 cliff matters mainly if a partner earns a lot or profits jump.

funding.name: Free childcare for working parents (30 hours, England)
funding.who: Working parents in England of a child aged from 9 months (SI 2022/1134 reg 13) until compulsory school age (Childcare Act 2016 s1(2)(a); GOV.UK says '9 months to 4 years'). Each parent and partner must meet the minimum-income test or an exception, and neither may expect adjusted net income above £100,000 for the tax year of the declaration (regs 14(3)(c), 15(3)(b)).
funding.amount:
Up to 1,140 hours a year over no fewer than 38 weeks (30 hours a week), funded through the local authority at a registered provider (reg 44(2)).
The 1,140 hours include any universal free early education under Childcare Act 2006 s7 (Childcare Act 2016 s1(6)(a); reg 44(3)). That is 570 hours a year (15 a week) for every child from the 1 January, 1 April or 1 September after their third birthday, and for eligible disadvantaged 2-year-olds (SI 2014/2147 regs 3-4). For those children the working-parent scheme adds 570 hours. Only children from 9 months who are not on the universal or disadvantaged 2-year-old offer depend on it for all 1,140 hours.
Providers may charge for extras such as meals, nappies and trips. No cash is paid to the parent. The cash value depends on local provider charges and is not verified. It can be used together with either Tax-Free Childcare or Universal Credit childcare, but Tax-Free Childcare and UC childcare cannot be had at the same time (GOV.UK).
funding.how_taxed: Not a taxable receipt: the local authority funds the provider, and nothing is paid to the parent. Eligibility uses adjusted net income (ITA 2007 s58), which gross pension contributions and grossed-up Gift Aid reduce.
funding.conditions:
England only.
- Minimum income: each parent expects to earn at least 16 x their national minimum wage hourly rate x 13 weeks over the 3 months from the declaration (reg 18(1), (3)).
- Self-employed people may test the tax year of the declaration instead (reg 18(3) 'relevant period'). GOV.UK's example is £10,574.72 a year for 21+ in 2026-27, using 52 weeks.
- Self-employed income is expected non-capital receipts less expected non-capital expenses incurred wholly and exclusively for the trade: expected profit, not turnover. Kit purchases are ignored (reg 18(3)).
- Employed income is earnings under ITEPA s62 plus amounts treated as earnings under ITEPA Part 2 Chapters 7 to 10 (agency workers, IR35 intermediaries and managed service companies) (reg 18(3)).
- Someone both employed and self-employed may count both, or self-employed income alone if that makes them eligible (reg 18(2); GOV.UK).
- Dividends, interest, property income and pensions do not count (GOV.UK).
- Start-up rule: no minimum income is needed for 12 months from the declaration if the person is in a start-up period. That means their first 12 months of self-employment, and only if they started no other self-employment in the previous 5 years (reg 17(3)(b), (4)).
- A non-working partner can qualify if the other parent works and the partner has limited capability for work, gets a specified benefit (e.g. Carer's Allowance, contribution-based ESA, the UC carer element) or is on carer's leave (regs 14(4), 15(4); GOV.UK).
- Applications can be made from when the child is 23 weeks old. Hours start on 1 January, 1 April or 1 September after the child turns 9 months, and the deadline is the day before (GOV.UK).
- Reconfirm every 3 months.

figures.2024-25: £100,000 adjusted net income limit per parent (reg 14(3)(c)). 3-month minimum, derived from reg 18 and the NMW from 1 Apr 2024: £2,379.52 (21+; £183.04 a week), £1,788.80 (18-20; £137.60 a week), £1,331.20 (under 18 or apprentice; £102.40 a week). Tax-year test for 21+: £9,518.08 (52 weeks, derived). Hours: the working-parent entitlement under these Regulations was 570 hours a year (15 a week over 38 weeks) until 31 Aug 2025 (reg 44(2)(b) before SI 2023/1330 reg 2(8)(a)). Parents of 2-year-olds became eligible from 1 Apr 2024, and of children from 9 months from 1 Sep 2024 (SI 2023/1330 reg 2(5)(a)-(b)). Children from the term after their third birthday had the universal 570 hours on top, making 30 hours a week. For eligible disadvantaged 2-year-olds the universal 15 hours counted towards the 570 (reg 44(3)(a) as then in force), so the scheme added nothing for them.
figures.2025-26: £100,000 limit. 3-month minimum, derived from the NMW from 1 Apr 2025: £2,539.68 (21+; £195.36 a week), £2,080.00 (18-20; £160.00 a week), £1,570.40 (under 18 or apprentice; £120.80 a week). Tax-year test for 21+: £10,158.72 (derived). Hours: 570 a year until 31 Aug 2025, then up to 1,140 a year (30 a week over 38 weeks) from 9 months, from 1 Sep 2025 (SI 2023/1330 reg 2(8)(a)). From that date the 1,140 include the universal 570 for children from the term after their third birthday and for eligible disadvantaged 2-year-olds, so for them the scheme adds 570 (reg 44(3)).
figures.2026-27: £2,643.68 (21+; £203.36 a week), £2,256.80 (18-20; £173.60 a week), £1,664 (under 18 or apprentice; £128 a week), confirmed on GOV.UK. £100,000 limit. Tax-year test for 21+: £10,574.72. Up to 1,140 hours a year, of which 570 are universal for a child from the term after their third birthday or on the disadvantaged 2-year-old offer.
figures.2027-28: Announced, not law: with the April 2027 NMW rates in Budget 2026 (£13.21 / £11.27 / £8.31), the 3-month minimum becomes £2,747.68 (21+; £211.36 a week), £2,344.16 (18-20; £180.32 a week) and £1,728.48 (under 18 or apprentice; £132.96 a week). Tax-year test for 21+: £10,990.72. Budget 2026 has no childcare measure, so the £100,000 limit and the 1,140 hours (including any universal 570) continue.

funding.status:
Law: Childcare Act 2016 s1 (s1(6)(a): universal hours count towards the 30) and the Childcare (Free of Charge for Working Parents) (England) Regulations 2022 (SI 2022/1134) regs 13-18, 31-33 and 44.
Amended by SI 2023/1330:
- 2-year-olds from 1 Apr 2024 and 9 months from 1 Sep 2024 (reg 2(5)(a)-(b));
- 1,140 hours from 1 Sep 2025 (reg 2(8)(a));
- a new reg 44(3), under which universal hours under Childcare Act 2006 s7 count towards them (reg 2(8)(b)).
The transitional sub-paragraphs reg 44(3)(a)-(b) were omitted from 1 Jan 2026 by SI 2025/1261 reg 5(4), as substituted by SI 2025/1287; reg 44(3) itself stays in force. Universal hours are 570 a year (SI 2014/2147 regs 3-4).
2026-27 thresholds are in force (NMW rates set by SI 2026/357). April 2027 NMW rates are announced in Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026) and not yet law. Budget 2026 has no childcare measure.
funding.relevance: For a child in England from 9 months until the term after their third birthday, all 30 funded hours a week in term time depend on passing the work and income tests, but from then until school only 15 do, because the other 15 are universal. The test uses expected profit, so the whole-year test can cover a quiet quarter, but the start-up exemption will not help an established freelancer.

funding.name: ScreenSkills bursaries (film, TV, animation, games)
funding.who: 18+, right to work in the UK, UK bank account, working in (or showing intent to work in) UK film, TV, animation or games (and, from the April 2026 renewal, film exhibition and distribution); not in full- or part-time education. Freelancers prioritised in film and TV.
funding.amount: Need-based and competitive; one bursary at a time; maximum £2,000. Entry up to £750 in any 12 months (100% of costs to £750); Early up to £1,500 (up to 80%); Experienced/Expert up to £2,000 (80% of the first £1,250 plus 50% above, so costs of £3,250+ for £2,000). Equipment caps £750 / £1,000 / £1,500 by stage; laptops 50% of cost; wet-weather gear £200; accommodation up to £165/night London, £135 elsewhere; care up to £75/day (max £1,500 a year); access costs up to £1,000 above the cap.
funding.how_taxed: Training, travel, accommodation, food, hire and software elements are revenue grants, normally trading receipts (BIM40451); net nil only if the cost is deductible (training must update existing skills, BIM35660; otherwise judgement needed). Equipment on the cash basis: deducted when paid; whether the grant is a s96A 'capital refund' is unclear. Equipment on accruals: capital allowances on cost net of grant (CAA s532, CA14100) where s532 applies (ScreenSkills' status under s536 not confirmed). Care costs and driving lessons: uncertain, flag for review. ITTOIA s776 scholarship exemption very unlikely to apply (applicants must not be in education).
funding.conditions: Apply before paying, at least 2 weeks and no more than 3 months before a course; decisions at least 4 weeks; CV, 500-word statement, evidence of stage and costs. Must show why support is needed, barriers and long-term benefit. Excluded: performers; video, music, branded or online content industries; own project development; costs already paid.
funding.risks: Corporate events and branded work do not count; eligibility rests on genuine film/TV credits. Covers only part of the cost above Entry level. Do not claim capital allowances on the grant-funded part of equipment where s532 applies.

figures.2025-26: null: guidelines in force before April 2026 not confirmed
figures.2026-27: Guidelines updated April 2026: as in amount field
figures.current: Maximum £2,000; one bursary at a time

funding.status: Operating discretionary charity grant, not law; guidelines updated April 2026 and changeable at any time; applications may close when budget runs short. BFI National Lottery funding of £1.575m renewed for April 2026 - March 2029 (announced 5 Oct 2026).
funding.relevance: Strongly relevant to the film/TV side: up to £2,000 a year towards courses or kit.

funding.name: Film and TV Charity Stop-Gap Grant
funding.who:
Individuals working behind the scenes in UK film, TV or cinema. They need either:
- at least 40 days of paid or funded film and TV work in the last 18 months; or
- at least 2 years in film and TV in the last 10 years, if returning after a career break.

Some experience may be unpaid, in proportion to career stage. The work must contribute to creating, distributing or commercially exploiting moving-image entertainment for UK broadcast or on-demand TV, paid-for original streaming services, or cinemas (a confirmed run of at least 10 screenings). Festival-only films may count at the charity's discretion.

Cinema staff (front of house, back office or technical) need at least 18 months full time (at least 20 hours a week) in the last 2 years.

These do not count: corporate videography, commercials, music videos, community or campaigning film, education or training content, and any front-of-camera role.
funding.amount: A one-off grant, generally no more than £500, with up to £750 at the charity's discretion. It may cover only part of the need. Only one application is allowed in any 12 months, and a repeat grant after 12 months is not guaranteed. The charity says it will process an application within 10 days and then confirm the outcome or ask for more information; that is not a promise of a decision within 10 days. The public web page says only 'up to £500'.
funding.how_taxed: HMRC has no guidance on this particular grant. It is a voluntary payment restricted to personal household costs, so it is likely not a trading receipt. BIM41810 says gifts are taxable only if they attach to a source such as a vocation, judged by the payment's character in the recipient's hands. On the other side, BIM41810 treats as a trading receipt a payment made to keep a business going, to preserve its solvency or to make good lost profit. Keep the award letter showing that the grant was for household need.
funding.status: Operating charity scheme, not law. The guidance is 'Stop Gap Grant application guidance' (file 'Stop-Gap-Grants-Guidance-June-2026-update', PDF created 10 June 2026). On 24 Nov 2026 the application form page was live (HTTP 200) and linked from the scheme page with no closure notice. The form loads by JavaScript, so whether it was accepting submissions could not be confirmed. The public web page says only 'up to £500', and its apply section wrongly tells applicants to read the Sir Horace Ové Grant criteria. The PDF is the fuller and more recent source.
funding.relevance: This applies only if the technician has at least 40 days of eligible behind-the-scenes TV, streaming or cinema work in the last 18 months, or 2 years in film and TV in the last 10 years and is returning after a break. Pure live-event and corporate days do not count. It is a one-off safety net of about £500 towards rent or bills in a quiet spell, not a tax-planning tool, and is probably not taxable.

funding.name: Film and TV Charity Sir Horace Ové Grant
funding.who:
People who identify as Black or Global Majority and work behind the camera in UK film, TV or professional cinema services. The guidance defines Black and Global Majority as people who are Black, Asian, Brown, dual-heritage, indigenous to the global south, and/or racialised as ethnic minorities.

The work-history test is the same as for the Stop-Gap Grant:
- at least 40 days of paid or funded film and TV work in the last 18 months; or
- at least 2 years in film and TV in the last 10 years, if returning after a career break.

Some experience may be unpaid, in proportion to career stage. Qualifying work contributes to moving-image entertainment for broadcast or on-demand TV, paid-for original streaming services, or cinemas (a confirmed run of at least 10 screenings). Allied services count, such as facilities and catering, or financial and administrative services. Festival-only films count at the charity's discretion.

These do not count: corporate videography, commercials, music videos, community or campaigning film, education or training content, and front-of-camera roles. So live-event and corporate work generally will not count.
funding.amount: Up to £500 per grant (capped). If the total cost is more than £500, the applicant must explain how the shortfall will be covered. The charity says it will be in touch within 10 days to confirm the outcome or ask for more information; that is not a guaranteed decision date.
funding.how_taxed:
Split the award by what it pays for.

Travel to events, memberships and courses: for a sole trader these are normally trading receipts (BIM40451; BIM50710 for awards that come as an incident of the profession). They net to nil only if the cost is deductible. A course is deductible only if it updates existing expertise or gives new expertise in the existing business area (BIM35660).

Child or adult care: a personal cost, not deductible (ITTOIA s34). Whether the grant for it is a trading receipt is unresolved. BIM41810 says the payment's character in the recipient's hands decides, and a payment that enables the business to carry on is a trading receipt. Because this grant is tied to taking up work, treat it as taxable by default and flag it.

Equipment on the accruals basis: a capital grant, not a trading receipt (BIM40451; Seaham Harbour Dock v Crook). It most likely does NOT reduce qualifying expenditure. The charity is not a public body, and paying from its own funds it gets no relief for a career grant: no contribution allowance, because s538(1)(b) needs the contribution to be for a trade or relevant activity of its own, and no deduction in a trade or relevant activity it carries on (CAA 2001 s536(2)-(5); CA14200 Example 2 is the closest example). So the full cost qualifies, unless the charity's money is in fact met directly or indirectly by a public body. No HMRC page names this charity.

Equipment on the cash basis (the default): the kit cost is deducted when paid (s33A). Whether the grant must then be brought in as a s96A 'capital refund' is unsettled. The conservative course is to include it as a receipt (see capital-grants-cash-basis).
funding.status:
Operating charity scheme, not law. The guidance, 'Sir Horace Ové Eligibility Criteria and Guidance June 2026' (PDF created 10 June 2026), calls it 'the new scheme'. On 24 Nov 2026 the application form page was live (HTTP 200) and linked from the scheme page with no closure notice. The form loads by JavaScript, so whether it was accepting submissions could not be confirmed.

The web page is unreliable in two ways:
- Its eligibility block is copied from the Stop-Gap page: it says 'To be eligible for a Stop-Gap Grant', and its 'full eligibility criteria' download is the Stop-Gap PDF.
- Its introduction says the grant can 'address immediate financial challenges', but the guidance excludes immediate needs such as rent and bills.

Use the Sir Horace Ové PDF instead. CAA 2001 ss532, 536 and 538 and ITTOIA 2005 ss33A, 34 and 96A are law.
funding.relevance: This applies only if the technician identifies as Black or Global Majority and has at least 40 days of eligible behind-the-camera TV, streaming or cinema work in the last 18 months, or 2 years in the last 10 if returning after a break. Live-event and corporate work does not count. It gives up to £500 towards kit, travel to festivals in Britain, memberships, courses or care, to take up a work opportunity.

funding.name: Arts Council England: Developing Your Creative Practice (DYCP)
funding.how_taxed:
ACE is an executive non-departmental public body (GOV.UK). For a self-employed practitioner, HMRC's default is that an award received as an incident of the profession is a taxable professional or trading receipt (BIM50710; see arts-council-awards-tax).

The 1978 Inland Revenue and Arts Council of Great Britain agreement has no statutory force, and HMRC does not reproduce it. BIM50710 says the Arts Council published it and tells HMRC staff to contact Business Profits (Technical) if they need a copy.

ACE's stated understanding of the agreement is in a DCMS written answer of 9 June 2020 (question 53581). Grants 'to support people to take time out to develop and explore their artistic and cultural practice' should not be taxable; grants for a specific project are taxable. That answer named ACE's Emergency Response Fund for Individuals as a non-taxable example. HMRC then ruled those grants taxable because they replaced lost revenue, and the answer was corrected (written statement HCWS717, 24 March 2022).

A DYCP award that includes a fee for the applicant's own time and develops the same work they trade in should be treated as taxable by default. A 'not taxable' position needs a documented develop-and-explore purpose and should be disclosed on the return. Deducting the funded costs as trade expenses while treating the grant as not taxable is hard to reconcile: if the activity is for the trade, the award is likely an incident of it (BIM50710).

Equipment part:
- On accruals it is a capital grant, not a trading receipt (BIM40451). CAA 2001 s532 removes the grant-funded part from qualifying expenditure (CA14100). The s536 exception does not apply, because ACE is treated as a public body: GOV.UK lists it as an executive NDPB and ACE calls itself a public authority, but no HMRC page names it, so this is an inference.
- On the cash basis, the kit is deducted under s33A, and the conservative course is to keep the equipment part in receipts (treatment unsettled; see capital-grants-cash-basis).
funding.risks: The fund is competitive: Round 24 had more than 3,350 applications and funded more than 1,150. It covers England only, rounds are infrequent, and applying again is restricted. A 'creative technician' must show creative practice in a supported discipline: corporate events work is unlikely to qualify, while theatre or live-music technical practice (for example lighting or sound design) might. The tax treatment is uncertain and should lean towards taxable.

figures.2025-26: Round 23 decisions emailed Monday 28 July 2025. On 30 Oct 2025 the next round was paused until April 2026, and the remaining £7.5m was moved into a time-limited NLPG research and development priority for individuals (£1,000 to £30,000, generally up to £12,000, no match funding), open until Thursday 26 Feb 2026.

funding.how_taxed: For a self-employed recipient normally a trading receipt (BIM50710; EIM50200 'more usually' trading income; revenue/undifferentiated grants BIM40451). The part specifically meeting capital expenditure (kit for the project) is normally a capital receipt, deducted from qualifying expenditure for capital allowances (CAA s532; CA14100); ACE is very likely a public body so the s536 exception will not apply. funding.name: The Theatrical Guild (TTG): support for backstage and front-of-house theatre workers
funding.who: People anywhere in the UK who have spent most of their career in a backstage or front-of-house theatre role. They need at least 3 full years' employment in such a role in the past 10 years, and theatre must be their principal career. TTG's sample list of roles includes: stage management; sound and lighting designers, engineers, technicians, operators and programmers; automation designers, technicians and operators; set construction (riggers, carpenters, flymen, electricians, technicians); stagehands; production, company and theatre managers; costume, props, front of house and box office. Actors, singers, dancers, comedians and musicians are not supported unless they also have relevant backstage or front-of-house experience. TTG notes that many backstage and front-of-house workers are self-employed or on short-term or zero-hours contracts.
funding.how_taxed:
No HMRC guidance deals directly with hardship grants from industry charities.
- Hardship grants: a grant given because of personal illness, injury or financial need (rent, bills, medical costs, childcare, counselling) is probably not a trading receipt. BIM41810 says voluntary payments are not taxable unless they can be attached to the trade (Beynon v Thorpe). But BIM41810 also says a payment that makes good a loss of profit (Rolfe v Nagel), or helps keep a business going (Smart v Lincolnshire Sugar), is a trading receipt. So a grant to replace lost day-rate income carries some risk.
- Training help paid straight to the course provider: nothing to record.
- Training help paid to you for a course that updates skills in your current trade: treat it as a receipt and deduct the course cost, so the net effect is nil (BIM40451; BIM42526).
- Training for a completely new specialisation or an unrelated qualification is unlikely to be deductible (BIM42526). A hardship grant towards that kind of course is probably personal, but this is not confirmed.
Keep the award letter.
funding.conditions:
- Apply using the form on ttg.org.uk. The General Manager then arranges a personal interview to go through your circumstances and the application.
- You must show eligible employment. The main test is financial hardship or welfare need.
- Trustees decide grants at monthly meetings, except in March and August. A sub-committee of 6 trustees can fast-track training grants only.
- Training funding must advance a theatre career, and is for people whose personal hardship may restrict their access to training.
- If you are not eligible, TTG points you to another charity.
funding.risks:
- Theatre must be your main career. Someone working mainly on corporate events, conferences, festivals, concerts or TV is unlikely to qualify; Backup Tech and Stage Hand cover live events more widely.
- Awards are discretionary and usually small.
- The tax treatment is not confirmed by HMRC (see how_taxed).
- Misstating your work history or hardship would be dishonest.

funding.name: Local Growth Hub and council business grants (England) and the GOV.UK finance and support finder
funding.who: Any UK business can search the GOV.UK 'Finance and support for your business' finder. It filters by region (the English regions, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland), business stage, industry, size and type of support (finance, equity, grant, loan, expertise and advice, recognition awards). Growth Hubs cover England only; there are 41. Each scheme sets its own rules on area, sector, size and stage, and some local grants are only for brand-new start-ups.
funding.amount:
No national figure; it depends on the area and the scheme.

An example of how narrow local grants can be is Test Valley Borough Council's Business Incentive Grant. The council's own page sets the rules:
- £750 for a genuinely new start-up located in that borough. A business under new management, a new name or a new governance structure that continues an existing business does not qualify.
- The owner must work in the business full time (at least 30 hours a week) as their only job.
- You must apply no later than 8 weeks after starting to trade.
- It is paid only after at least 6 months' trading (9 months if the business opens on a reduced-rent agreement).
The GOV.UK finder entry is tagged 'not yet trading' and says 'Available for businesses not yet trading', but it also gives the 8-week deadline, so read it as a grant for new start-ups. An established sole trader would not qualify.

Growth Hubs and the Business Support Service mainly give free advice and signposting, including routes to funding (GOV.UK: 'free advice and financial help through your local growth hub'). Any money comes through a specific grant or loan scheme with its own rules.
funding.how_taxed:
- Revenue grants, and grants not tied to a specific purpose, are normally trading receipts (BIM40451).
- Capital grants (towards kit or other capital assets) are normally not trading receipts.
- On the accruals basis with capital allowances, a grant from a public body such as a council is deducted from the qualifying cost, even if it arrives after the purchase (CAA 2001 s532; CA14100).
- On the cash basis (the default for sole traders from 2024-25), kit is usually deducted when paid. HMRC guidance does not say how a third-party capital grant is treated there. ITTOIA s96A may bring it into receipts as a 'capital refund', defined as an amount that is 'in substance a refund of capital expenditure' (BIM72020). Flag it for review, and never deduct the full cost while leaving the grant out.
funding.risks:
- Schemes open and close often and many are tied to one area. The finder's list changes; it showed 222 schemes on 24 November 2026.
- Missing a scheme's application window makes you ineligible.
- Leaving a revenue grant out of turnover understates profit. Claiming allowances on the full cost of grant-funded kit gives double relief.

traps.name: Goodwill when an individual incorporates (CTA 2009 s879K; TCGA s169LA; personal goodwill)
traps.why: Selling the sole trade's goodwill to the new company for a loan-account credit, then drawing it tax-free, is lawful only at genuine market value, and three rules limit it. (1) CT: for acquisitions from 1 April 2019, CTA 2009 s879K (FA 2019 Sch 9) blocks all amortisation and fixed-rate (6.5%, s879B) debits on goodwill and customer-related assets bought from a related individual or firm; a debit arises only on later realisation, as a non-trading debit that cannot be carried back (s879K(5); CIRD44083, CIRD44070); partial restriction where originally bought from a third party (s879N/879O). Earlier versions: s849B (3 Dec 2014 - 7 Jul 2015, omitted) and s816A (8 Jul 2015 - 31 Mar 2019). (2) CGT: goodwill sold to a close company where the seller meets the 5% personal company test is not a relevant business asset for BADR (TCGA s169LA; CG64006), save a 28-day exception if shares are sold on to a non-close company; main-purpose rule; gain taxed at 18%/24% after the £3,000 AEA; s162 relief reduced pro rata to loan-account consideration. (3) Value: in a business reliant on the proprietor's skill and personality goodwill is likely personal and must be excluded from business-goodwill value (SVM107070); for a freelance technician transferable goodwill is likely small or nil. Overpayment is a distribution (CTA 2010 s1020); CTA 2009 s864 avoidance rule applies. Overvaluation to create a large loan account is a known HMRC target.

figures.2024-25: CGT on goodwill outside BADR: 10%/20% to 29 Oct 2024; 18%/24% from 30 Oct 2024. AEA £3,000.
figures.2027-28: CGT 18%/24%; AEA £3,000 (Budget 2026 Annex A).

traps.status: Law: TCGA s169LA (FA 2015, amended FA 2016 and FA 2019); CTA 2009 s879K/879B (FA 2019 Sch 9, acquisitions from 1 Apr 2019); s849B omitted by F(No.2)A 2015 s33 (history only). AEA fixed by TCGA s1K(2).
