traps.name: Crewing agencies: agency legislation (ITEPA Part 2 Ch 7, s44) and umbrella company PAYE changes (6 April 2026)
traps.why: Where a worker personally provides services to a client under a contract with an agency, s44 treats the worker as an employee for tax unless the work is shown 'not subject to (or to the right of) supervision, direction or control by any person'. IR35 Chapter 8 does not override Chapter 7 (s48(2)(a)). Since 6 April 2026, where a worker is engaged through an umbrella company, the agency (or the end client if there is no agency) is jointly and severally liable for the umbrella's PAYE (FA 2026 s24); NIC equivalent SI 2026/388. Bookings through crewing agencies may be paid under PAYE whatever the user's structure; non-compliant or mini-umbrella arrangements appear on HMRC's named lists; loan-based 'umbrella' schemes do not work.

figures.2026-27: Umbrella PAYE liability shift effective 6 April 2026. HMRC estimate: about 700,000 umbrella workers affected.

traps.status: ITEPA s44 law since 2003; current text from 6 April 2014 (FA 2014 s16). Umbrella joint and several liability: FA 2026 s24 (Royal Assent 18 March 2026) for payments on or after 6 April 2026; NIC: SI 2026/388 (made 31 March 2026, in force 6 April 2026).
traps.relevance: Many events technicians take work through crewing agencies; neither sole trading nor a PSC changes the outcome where the client controls how the work is done.

traps.name: What IR35 means if this events technician incorporates
traps.why: Order of rules (ESM2051, updated 7 Oct 2026): (0) Agency rules first where the technician is subject to supervision, direction or control; HMRC treats the technician's own company as the 'agency' (ITEPA s44; ESM2032, ESM2051); they take precedence over MSC and IR35. (1) Small non-public clients: Chapter 8; the company decides status per engagement (s48); if inside, it computes a deemed employment payment treated as made at the tax year end (s50(3)) with PAYE and NIC: receipts less 5%, less employee-deductible expenses (incl. mileage allowance relief), s262 capital allowances, registered pension contributions, employer NIC actually paid, salary and benefits already taxed, and notional employer NIC on the remainder (s54); other company running costs not deductible. (2) Medium/large non-public and public-sector clients: Chapter 10; client must give an SDS (treated as fee-payer until it does, s61N(5)); if inside, fee-payer deducts income tax and employee NIC and pays employer NIC (and Apprenticeship Levy); only the part of a payment for the worker's services is a deemed direct payment (s61N(12)), so separately priced kit hire can be apportioned out. (3) Umbrella rules only if employed by an umbrella. (4) Evidence for 'outside': contract terms matching practice, substantial own kit required by contract without extra fee, multiple/overlapping clients, discrete per-production bookings, Hall v Lorimer factors, CEST outputs; ESM4115/ESM4120 are film/TV only, so indicative for live events (ESM0500 general principles). (5) Kit counts only if obtained entirely independently of the engager; disregarded where the engager underwrites it via increased rate, box payment or hire agreement (ESM4117); camera roles require kit 'without increased fee or other payment' (ESM4120). If most income is inside IR35 a company costs more than sole trading.

figures.current: null: depends on each engagement. Compare inside-IR35 outcome to sole trading using employer NIC 15% (2025-26 onward).

traps.status: Law: ITEPA Part 2 Ch 7, Ch 8 (ss48-61), Ch 10 (s61K onward). Guidance: off-payroll guidance (26 Feb 2026), ESM2051 (7 Oct 2026), ESM4115, ESM4117, ESM4120. Umbrella PAYE rules changed from 6 April 2026 (GOV.UK page updated 8 May 2026).
traps.relevance: Before recommending incorporation, ask the split of turnover between small and medium/large clients, how bookings are made (direct or agency), and whether substantial own kit is supplied under the contract.

traps.name: IR35: ITEPA 2003 Part 2 Chapter 8 (small or non-UK clients)
traps.why: Applies where the worker personally provides services through an intermediary (e.g. a PSC) to a non-public client that is small (ss60A-60G) or has no UK connection, and would be an employee 'if the services were provided under a contract directly between the client and the worker' (s49(1)(c)). The PSC, not the client, must compute a deemed employment payment for the tax year and pay PAYE and NIC: income less a 5% flat allowance, less employee-type expenses, plant capital allowances, employer pension contributions, employer NIC paid and salary already taxed; the balance less employer NIC on it is the deemed payment. The PSC decides status contract by contract; not relevant to a sole trader invoicing in their own name. A wrong 'outside' decision leaves the PSC liable for PAYE/NIC, interest and penalties. ESM4113: TV/radio workers in 'employed' grades who set up companies 'to avoid PAYE and Class 1 NICs' find 'such arrangements often fail'.

traps.status: Law. IR35 from 6 April 2000 (FA 2000 Sch 12), rewritten into ITEPA Part 2 Ch 8 from 2003-04. Public-authority clients removed by FA 2017 Sch 1 (from 6 April 2017); medium/large UK clients moved to Ch 10 by FA 2020 Sch 1 (2021-22 onwards). No IR35 change at Budget 2026. Higher Companies Act size thresholds (financial years from 6 April 2025) affect client size for IR35 from 2027-28 at the earliest (ESM10006A).
traps.relevance: Most event and production companies hiring the technician are likely 'small'; an incorporated technician must self-assess IR35 per engagement.

traps.name: Off-payroll working: ITEPA 2003 Part 2 Chapter 10 (public sector and medium/large clients)
traps.why: Where the client is a public authority or a medium/large UK-connected client (s61K), the client decides status and gives a Status Determination Statement with reasons. If deemed employed, the fee-payer (client or agency) deducts income tax and employee NIC from the fee and pays employer NIC and any Apprenticeship Levy; no Chapter 8 calculation for that engagement. HMRC stands by CEST results if inputs are accurate. Inside SDSs remove most of the benefit of a company; status can be disputed with the client; avoidance schemes to get round the rules are flagged by HMRC.

figures.2026-27: Employer NIC 15%.
figures.2027-28: Employer NIC 15%.

traps.status: Law. Public sector: deemed direct payments on or after 6 April 2017 (FA 2017 Sch 1 para 16). Medium/large: on or after 6 April 2021 (FA 2020 Sch 1 para 25). s61K up to date to 22 Nov 2026, no pending changes. No Budget 2026 change.
traps.relevance: Large broadcasters, studios, venue groups and big production houses are likely medium/large; many default to 'inside'.

traps.name: Small-client thresholds for IR35/off-payroll (ITEPA s60A; Companies Act 2006)
traps.why: This applies only if the technician works through their own company (PSC); a sole trader invoicing in their own name is under neither Chapter 8 nor Chapter 10. Chapter 10 (off-payroll) applies where the end client is a public authority, whatever its size, or is medium or large with a UK connection (ITEPA s61K(1), (3)). A UK connection means UK resident or with a UK permanent establishment (s60I). The client then decides status. The fee-payer is treated as making a deemed employment payment to the worker (s61N(2)-(3), subject to s61N(5)-(7)); a client that contracts directly with the worker's company is always the deemed employer (GOV.UK). Size is tested only on the end client: agencies in the chain do not need to consider size (ESM10006). For a small private-sector client, or one with no UK connection, the PSC must apply Chapter 8 (IR35) itself (ESM10006). A company client is small for a tax year in either of two cases. First, if its first financial year is not yet relevant, i.e. the filing period for its first accounts has not ended before the tax year begins (s60A(2), (4)). This can cover more than one tax year, and applies even if the company is part of a group (ESM10006). Second, if the Companies Act small companies regime applied for its last financial year whose filing period ended before the tax year began (s60A(3)-(4)). That regime means at least 2 of 3 limits are met, and a change of size counts only after two consecutive years (CA 2006 s382(2)). Some companies cannot be small under this second test: those excluded from the regime by CA 2006 s384 (e.g. public companies, banks, insurers, e-money issuers, members of ineligible groups), and a subsidiary whose group parent does not qualify as small (s60C(1); group limits in CA 2006 s383). LLPs, unregistered and overseas companies use the company test (s60D). Connected persons' turnover is aggregated (s60G). SI 2024/1303 raised the company limits for financial years beginning on or after 6 April 2025 (reg 2(2)), with a transitional re-test of earlier years (reg 3). HMRC says that for the usual 12-month financial year the earliest tax year affected is 2027-28 (ESM10006A). Other undertakings, such as ordinary partnerships, and individuals use a one-year turnover test only: partnerships look at their last financial year ending at least 9 months before the tax year (s60E), and individuals at the last calendar year before the tax year (s60F). Their limit is disputed (see figures_disputed). A client that stops being medium or large must withdraw its status determination statement before the tax year begins, or it is treated as still medium or large for that year (s61TA). The worker or the client's agent can require the client to say whether it considers itself small for a tax year, enforceable by injunction (s60H). Ask each client to confirm its size every tax year.

traps.relevance: This matters only if the technician works through their own company: for a small private-sector client, the company applies IR35 itself; a client may well be small, but ask each one (s60H gives the right to ask). For a medium or large client or a public body such as a council, the client decides status, and the fee-payer deducts income tax and NIC: the client itself if the company contracts with it directly, otherwise often the agency that pays the company.

traps.name: IR35 and off-payroll working for a personal service company working through one client (ITEPA Part 2 Ch 8 and Ch 10)
traps.why: If the user incorporates and works through a PSC for a client in an employment-like relationship: Chapter 10 for public authorities (since 6 April 2017) or medium/large private clients (since 6 April 2021): client decides and gives an SDS; deemed employer deducts income tax and employee NIC and pays employer NIC and Apprenticeship Levy; student loans via SA. Chapter 8 for small private clients: PSC decides and computes the s54 deemed payment (Step 1 less 5%, then expenses, capital allowances, pension contributions, employer NIC, actual salary). Contract by contract; CEST can help. Since 6 April 2024, where a deemed employer is assessed for a wrong 'outside' determination, HMRC can set off tax already paid by worker and PSC (ESM10037), not the deemed employer's own employer NIC. If inside, most company advantage is lost; under Chapter 8 HMRC can assess the PSC with interest and penalties; long single-client engagements under control are the classic IR35 case.

CA limits rose to £15m / £7.5m (50 employees) for financial years from 6 April 2025; earliest OPW effect 2027-28 (ESM10006A).

GOV.UK guidance 26 Feb 2026; ESM pages 7 Oct 2026. FA 2026 s24 added ITEPA Part 2 Ch 11 (umbrella joint liability) from 6 April 2026.

traps.name: IR35: deemed employment payment removes the salary/dividend advantage
traps.why: Trading through a company is lawful. But where the worker personally provides services through their own company, and the engagement would be employment if contracted directly (ITEPA s49), the intermediaries legislation stops the income being taken as dividends free of employment taxes. Chapter 8 applies where the client is not a public authority and is small or has no UK connection, or is a private individual buying services for non-business purposes (ss48, 50(5)). Medium or large UK clients and public authorities fall under Chapter 10 instead, where the client decides status and the fee-payer deducts PAYE and NIC. Under Chapter 8, two conditions trigger the charge. The company must meet the s51 conditions (for example, the worker has a material interest of more than 5%). And the worker or an associate must receive, or be entitled to, a payment or benefit that is not employment income, such as a dividend (s50(1)). The company is then treated as paying a deemed employment payment and must operate PAYE and NIC on it (s56; SI 2000/727 regs 6-8). The payment is treated as made on 5 April, or earlier if the company stops trading or the worker leaves (s57). s54(1) calculation: Step 1 takes the payments and benefits the company received for the relevant engagements, less 5%. Step 2 adds payments or benefits the worker received from others for those engagements that would be employment income. Step 3 deducts expenses an employee could deduct, including mileage allowance relief; a nil or negative result at this or any later step means no deemed payment. Step 4 deducts capital allowances an employee could claim. Step 5 deducts the company's registered pension contributions. Step 6 deducts employer Class 1 and Class 1A NIC already paid for the worker. Step 7 deducts salary and benefits already taxed as employment income, and tax-free mileage payments not deducted at Step 3 (s54(7)). Step 8 deducts the employer NIC that would be due on the deemed payment itself. NIC follows the same steps, including the 5% (SI 2000/727 reg 7). The company can deduct the deemed payment and its employer NIC for corporation tax in the period of account in which the payment is treated as made (CTA 2009 s139). It can also claim relief so that later dividends paid from the same money are not taxed twice (s58). Event and production companies often book technicians on near-employment terms. Dividends for inside-IR35 work therefore save nothing, and the deemed-payment liability falls on the company.

figures.current: Step 1 deduction: 5% of receipts (s54(1); SI 2000/727 reg 7). Step 8: let S = the secondary threshold not already used by salary in the year and r = the employer rate. Deemed payment = Step 7 result if that is no more than S; otherwise (Step 7 result + r x S) / (1 + r). At 15% with the threshold used up, this is Step 7 result / 1.15.

traps.name: Overdrawn director's loan accounts (CTA 2010 s455)
traps.why: If a close company lends to a participator or associate and the loan is not repaid by the s455 due date (the day after 9 months from the end of the accounting period, s455(3)), the company owes s455 tax at the dividend upper rate for the tax year of the loan: 33.75% for loans 6 April 2022 - 5 April 2026; 35.75% from 6 April 2026 (FA 2026 s4). Late-payment interest runs on unpaid s455. Repayment/release/write-off after the due date allows reclaim without interest, but not until 9 months after the end of the period of repayment (s458(5)); claim within 4 years (s458(3)). Separately, director loans over £10,000 at any time interest-free or below the official rate are a taxable benefit (ITEPA s180) on P11D with Class 1A. Release or write-off: dividend income for the participator (ITTOIA s415; ITA s19(2)(d)); HMRC says Class 1 NIC (not PAYE) is due if an employee/director. Anti-avoidance s464ZA-464ZB (FA 2025 s81, from 30 Oct 2024; replaced s464C-464D; s464B repealed): repayment matched to the new loan where (a) within 30 days repayments of £5,000+ and new loans of £5,000+ in a later period, or (b) £15,000+ owed and re-borrowing of £5,000+ already arranged; not where the repayment itself creates an income tax charge (dividend or bonus credited). Using the company as a bank account defers rather than saves tax.

figures.2026-27: 35.75% for loans made from 6 April 2026 (CTM61505); GOV.UK directors' loans page still shows 33.75%.
figures.current: BIK threshold £10,000 at any time in the year. Matching thresholds: £5,000 within 30 days; £15,000 with arrangements. Reclaim window 4 years.

traps.name: Bed-and-breakfasting a director's loan (CTA 2010 s464ZA)
traps.why: Repaying an overdrawn director's loan before the s455 due date (the day after 9 months from the end of the accounting period, CTA 2010 s455(3)) and borrowing it again shortly before or after does not secure s458 relief from s455 tax. The repayment is treated as repaying the new borrowing, so the original loan stays outstanding and s455 tax is due. There are two matching rules. The 30-day rule (s464ZA(1)-(2)) applies where, within any period of 30 days, there are repayments of £5,000 or more and new chargeable payments of £5,000 or more to the same participator or an associate, in either order. The new payments must be made in an accounting period later than the one in which the repaid loans were made; the repayment itself can fall before or after the end of that period. The new payments count only so far as they are not themselves repaid within the 30 days (CTM61630). The arrangements rule (s464ZA(3)) applies where £15,000 or more is owed just before a repayment and arrangements already exist for replacement chargeable payments of £5,000 or more. This rule has no time limit, and the 30-day rule takes priority (s464ZA(4); CTM61635). Not caught: a repayment that itself gives rise to an income tax charge on the participator (s464ZA(6)), for example a dividend credited to the loan account, or a bonus put through PAYE/NIC and then credited to it (CTM61642). Cash paid out and paid back in does not qualify, and nor does a dividend from another company (CTM61642). The same matching rules have applied to repayments since 20 March 2013 (former s464C, FA 2013 Sch 30 para 6). FA 2025 s81 re-enacted them as ss464ZA-464ZB from 30 October 2024, now limited to loans and advances charged under s455 (s464ZB(4)). Separately, it repealed s464B relief for return payments on s464A charges made on or after 30 October 2024, with no replacement (CTM61625). HMRC makes whatever assessments are needed (s464ZB(1)). A person whose filed return becomes incorrect because of these rules must notify HMRC within 3 months of becoming aware of it (s464ZB(2)-(3)).

CTA 2010 ss464ZA-464ZB were inserted by FA 2025 (c. 8) s81 and treated as in force from 30 October 2024 (s81(4)); s464B was repealed for payments on or after 30 October 2024 (s81(1)-(2)); Chapter 3B (ss464C-464D) was omitted. The same matching rules have applied since 20 March 2013 (FA 2013 Sch 30 para 6(2)). The Treasury may vary the £5,000 and £15,000 sums by order (s464ZA(7)); no change was announced at Budget 2026 (OOTLAR, 28 Oct 2026). s464ZA text checked on legislation.gov.uk on 24 Nov 2026 (shown as up to date with changes in force on or before 22 Nov 2026).
traps.relevance: This matters only if the technician incorporates and borrows from the company: an overdrawn director's loan cannot be 'cleared' at the year end with money that is borrowed again within about 30 days, before or after, or under an existing plan. Clear it with a genuine repayment that stays repaid, or with a dividend (only out of distributable profits, Companies Act 2006 s830) or a taxed bonus credited to the loan account.

traps.name: Dividends to a spouse: settlements legislation and the outright-gift exemption (ITTOIA ss619-648, s626; Jones v Garnett [2007] UKHL 35)
traps.why: Income from a 'settlement' (any disposition, trust, covenant, agreement, arrangement or transfer of assets with bounty; TSEM4105/4110) is taxed on the settlor where the settlor keeps an interest (s624), including where the settlor's spouse/civil partner may benefit (s625; s625(4)(d) excludes a future spouse). s626 exempts outright gifts between spouses carrying the whole income (Condition A) of property not wholly or substantially a right to income (Condition B); not outright if conditional or if it may benefit the giver (s626(4)). Jones v Garnett (78 TC 597): a settlement existed (share issued at par to the wife, bounty from the husband's expected conduct) but the exemption applied because an ordinary share carries capital rights; HMRC follows this (TSEM4205 Ex 6). Caught: B shares with no votes or winding-up rights (TSEM4205 Ex 5; Young v Pearce [1996] STC 743); dividend waivers (TSEM4225 Ex 12); dividends voted only on the spouse's class of equally ranking shares (Ex 13); income-only partnership shares (TSEM4215 Ex 10). Minor children: s629 unless £100 or less. Corrections: (1) shares to an unmarried partner are NOT generally caught (s624 needs a settlor interest; TSEM4320, TSEM4215); CGT/IHT not checked. (2) The distributions reform is announced only (draft legislation 2027, effect April 2028) and does not mention settlements or spouse shareholdings; no official source found for a separate HMRC campaign on 'tax-efficient profit extraction' (claim removed). Only works through a company or a partnership with a genuine full share; a sole trader cannot pay dividends.

figures.current: Uses the spouse's PA, basic-rate band and £500 dividend allowance; dividend rates as in the company item (10.75% / 35.75% / 39.35% from 2026-27).

traps.status: Law: ITTOIA ss624, 625, 626, 629 in force (s626 revised to 30 Jul 2026; only pending effect concerns s168). Jones v Garnett binding (HMRC applies it in TSEM4205, TSEM4105). Dividend rates 10.75%/35.75% from 2026-27 (FA 2026 s4). PA/BRB freeze to 2030-31 (FA 2026 s10). Distributions reform announced only (Budget 2026, 28 Oct 2026).
traps.relevance: Spousal ordinary shareholding is the main extra lever a company gives; can make incorporation worthwhile at lower profits if the spouse has unused allowances and bands.

traps.name: Alphabet shares and restricted share classes for family members
traps.why: HMRC attacks share-class planning three ways: (1) shares wholly or substantially a right to income fall outside s626 (TSEM4205 Ex 5: B shares with no votes or asset rights issued to wives, dividends taxed on husbands; Young v Pearce); (2) specially designed classes (TSEM4210 Ex 7: a £1 'U' share with rights only to the contractor's earnings and par repayment, extra share to spouse: bounteous, s626 fails); (3) equally ranking classes can still fail (TSEM4225 Ex 13: profits £25,000, £20,000 dividend voted only on B shares: £16,000 attributed to Mrs I under s624). TSEM4325 lists 'differing classes of shares enabling dividends to be paid only to shareholders paying lower rates of tax'. Lower-risk: spouse holds ordinary shares with full votes and capital rights outright, dividends at the same rate per share or per each class's genuine economic rights, with a documented commercial reason for any separate class. Different dividends on different classes are a settlement of income (TSEM4225 Ex 13; Donovan & McLaren). Minor children caught by s629 whatever the class. CGT/IHT consequences if value shifts. Budget 2026 (OOTLAR 2.44): close-company participator reporting 'will not be implemented at this time'.

figures.current: TSEM4225 Ex 13: profits £25,000; £20,000 dividend on B shares only; £16,000 attributed under s624.

traps.status: Law: ITTOIA Part 5 Ch 5 (ss620, 624, 626, 629). HMRC guidance current: TSEM4205 (14 Dec 2018), TSEM4210 (30 May 2024), TSEM4225 (7 Feb 2024), TSEM4325 (6 May 2021). Budget 2026 OOTLAR para 2.44 (28 Oct 2026).
traps.relevance: Only after incorporation: warn against alphabet-share 'dividend steering'; recommend plain ordinary shares with equal dividends per share.

traps.name: Settlements legislation as a trap for income-splitting (ITTOIA Part 5 Ch 5, ss619-648)
traps.why: A 'settlement' includes 'any disposition, trust, covenant, agreement, arrangement or transfer of assets' (s620), with bounty. Income from a settlement where the settlor or spouse retains an interest is the settlor's (s624); s626 exception for outright spouse gifts carrying the whole income, not wholly or substantially a right to income, unconditional, no reverter; parental settlement income paid to or for an unmarried minor child is the parent's unless £100 or less in the year (s629). Caught examples: dividend waivers letting the other spouse receive more than reserves would allow (TSEM4225); income-only shares (Young v Pearce, TSEM4205 Ex 5); non-working spouse taken into partnership with income share but no capital (TSEM4215 Ex 10); child admitted to a partnership on condition the share reverts (Ex 11); dividends diverted to minor children via a trust (Spotlight 62). Not caught: spouse with full-rights ordinary shares (Jones v Garnett; TSEM4205 Ex 6); spouse partner with full share of capital and profits (TSEM4215 Ex 9). Income is taxed on the settlor at their marginal rate plus interest and possibly penalties; excessive wages to a spouse or child also challengeable under wholly and exclusively (BIM47106); money returning to the settlor breaks the exception.

figures.current: s629(3): parental settlement income of a minor child not taxed on the parent if £100 or less in the year; minor = under 18 (s629(7)).
figures.2024-25: £100 limit
figures.2026-27: £100 limit

traps.status: Law. ITTOIA Part 5 Ch 5 in force (revised text modified 30 July 2026 incl. FA 2026); FA 2025 Sch 12 paras 6, 70(1) removed the s630A words from s629(5) for 2025-26 onwards. FA 2026 changed s636(7) and s643C only. TSEM4105, 4110, 4205, 4215, 4225, BIM47106 and Spotlight 62 (2 June 2023) live. 2027-28 announcements not checked (search budget).
traps.relevance: As a sole trader: only commercial wages for real work or a genuine partnership with capital and profit rights. With a company: ordinary shares gifted outright to a spouse can work; waivers, income-only shares and dividends for minor children are caught.

traps.name: TAAR on distributions in a winding up (phoenixism)
traps.why: A distribution in the winding up of a close company is taxed as income (dividend), not capital, if all four conditions hold: (A) the individual has at least a 5% interest; (B) the company is close or was in the two years before winding up; (C) within 2 years of the distribution the individual carries on a similar trade or activity (alone, in partnership, via a company or connected person); (D) it is reasonable to assume a main purpose was to avoid or reduce income tax. Amounts up to the no-gain amount and irredeemable share distributions are excluded (s396B(7)); meeting Condition C points to a main avoidance purpose. Liquidating to take reserves at BADR/CGT rates and then freelancing again within 2 years is the classic target.

figures.current: 2-year window after the distribution; 5% interest threshold
figures.2024-25: applies
figures.2026-27: applies
figures.2027-28: applies

traps.status: Law. ITTOIA s396B (FA 2016 s35(1)) for distributions on or after 6 April 2016 (s35(3)); up to date to 22 Nov 2026 with no pending amendment; s404A is the non-UK equivalent.
traps.relevance: If the user incorporates and later winds up, restarting the same work within 2 years loses capital treatment.

traps.name: 'Employing' a family member who does no real work
traps.why: Relatives' wages are deductible only if wholly and exclusively for the trade (ITTOIA s34; CTA 2009 s54). Pay at the rate for unconnected staff ('equal pay for equal value') is fine (BIM47105); pay set by the relationship or for a non-trade purpose is not; only an identifiable excessive part is disallowed (s34(2); Stott & Ingham v Trehearne [1924] 9 TC 69, BIM37707; Copeman v William Flood & Sons [1940/41] 24 TC 53, BIM37715; Earlspring Properties v Guest [1995] 67 TC 259, BIM37740). Must be genuine: Moschi v Kelly [1952] 33 TC 442 (BIM37735) disallowed a wife's 'wages' credited to the husband's drawings because they were not shown to be genuine (HMRC: 'not based on the mere fact of non-payment'). s36: remuneration unpaid 9 months after period end deductible only when paid. Dollar v Lyon [1981] 54 TC 459 (BIM37737): payments to children aged 7-14 were pocket money except £104 cash to the eldest; illegality does not by itself bar a deduction but the innocent explanation is preferred. Uncommercial pay to a spouse/minor child of a controlling director may also fall under the settlements rules or be taxed on the director (BIM47106). Claiming wages for someone doing no work, or 'paying' and taking it back, is a deliberate inaccuracy ('overstating your business expenses', CC/FS7a): up to 70%, or 100% if concealed (category 1; offshore higher, FA 2007 Sch 24 para 4); assessments up to 20 years (TMA s36(1A)); possible prosecution.

figures.current: Timing rule (s36): remuneration paid more than 9 months after the period end deductible only when paid. NMW: reg 58 family business exemption (family member living in the employer's home and participating in running the business); reg 57 family household. Deliberate inaccuracy up to 70%; deliberate and concealed up to 100%; 20-year assessment limit.

traps.status: Law: ITTOIA ss34, 36 (up to date 22-24 Nov 2026); BIM47105, 47106, 37707, 37715, 37735, 37737, 37740 current (some updated 4 Aug 2026). NMW Regs 2015 reg 58 unamended; reg 57 amended from 1 Apr 2024. FA 2007 Sch 24; TMA s36(1A).
traps.relevance: Genuine, documented, market-rate employment of a family member is allowed; paper wages are evasion.

traps.name: Tapered annual allowance
traps.why: The AA falls £1 for every £2 of adjusted income over £260,000, only if threshold income also exceeds £200,000; floor £10,000 (reached at £360,000); fractions rounded down. Threshold income starts from net income, adds back salary sacrificed after 8 July 2015, deducts gross relief-at-source contributions; adjusted income adds employer contributions back. Anti-avoidance s228ZB disregards arrangements mainly to reduce the taper. Only matters above roughly £200,000; relief-at-source contributions reduce threshold income.

figures.2024-25: Threshold income £200,000; adjusted income £260,000; minimum tapered AA £10,000
figures.2027-28: Adjusted income £260,000 (Budget 2026 Annex A); £200,000 threshold income not restated, no change announced

traps.status: Law: FA 2004 ss228ZA-228ZB (F(No.2)A 2015 Sch 4); F(No.2)A 2023 s22 (£260,000 and £10,000 from 2023-24); FA 2024 Sch 9 (lump sum death benefit deduction from 2024-25). Budget 2026 OOTLAR Annex A keeps £260,000 and AA £60,000 for 2027-28.
traps.relevance: Only at profits above about £200,000.

traps.name: Money purchase annual allowance (MPAA)
traps.why: After flexibly accessing a money-purchase pension (UFPLS or flexi-access drawdown income) further money-purchase contributions are limited to £10,000 a year; alternative AA for other savings £50,000. Taking only the tax-free lump sum does not trigger it. Unused allowance cannot be carried forward to increase the MPAA; recycling pension income while working is restricted.

figures.2026-27: MPAA £10,000; alternative £50,000

traps.name: Venture capital schemes: risk-to-capital, linked loans, linked sales and clawback
traps.why: For shares issued on or after 15 March 2018, EIS and SEIS relief requires the risk-to-capital condition (ITA ss157A, 257AAA): at issue it must be reasonable to conclude the company aims to grow its trade long term and there is a significant risk investors lose more capital than their net return (including relief). VCT equivalent (s286ZA) is a qualifying-holdings requirement on the VCT's own investment (investor relief not counted); failing it affects the VCT's approval conditions, not directly the investor. Principles-based, no bright lines (VCM8530); assured income or capital repayment and project-delivery SPVs unlikely to pass (VCM8540). No VCT relief with a linked loan to the individual or associate from the later of VCT incorporation or 2 years before issue until just before the 5th anniversary (s264). VCT relief reduced by linked sales of shares in the same/predecessor/successor VCT within 6 months either side or mutually conditional (s264A; reinvested dividends excluded). Clawback on disposals within 3 years (EIS/SEIS) or 5 years (VCT). Promoted low-risk or capital-protected products likely fail: relief withdrawn with interest, penalties possible.

figures.current: Holding periods: EIS and SEIS 3 years, VCT 5 years; VCT linked-sale window 6 months either side.

traps.status: Law: risk-to-capital FA 2018 s14 for shares issued on or after 15 March 2018 (SI 2018/931 reg 2); s264 (older); s264A (FA 2014 Sch 10, amended FA 2018 Sch 5). VCM8540 updated 29 October 2026.
traps.relevance: Warn against any capital-protected tax-relief investment pitched to freelancers.

traps.name: High Income Child Benefit Charge (£60,000 to £80,000 from 2024-25)
traps.why:
The charge applies to a person whose adjusted net income (ANI) for the tax year is over £60,000 (ITEPA s681B; F(No.2)A 2024 s5). It covers Child Benefit for each week in which either (A) the person is entitled to it and no partner living with them throughout that week has a higher ANI, or (B) their partner throughout that week is entitled to it and the person's ANI is the higher. So a single claimant pays on their own ANI, and in a couple the partner with the higher ANI pays. 'Partner' includes an unmarried partner living with the claimant as if married (s681G). Where Child Benefit goes to someone who contributes to the upkeep of a child who lives with another person, and nobody is charged on it under s681B, the person the child lives with can be charged instead (s681D; GOV.UK). The charge is 1% for every £200 of ANI over £60,000, and all of it at £80,000. The percentage, the Child Benefit total and the charge are each rounded down to whole numbers (s681C(3)). Before 2024-25 the band was £50,000 to £60,000, at 1% per £100.

ANI is net income less grossed-up Gift Aid (including gifts carried back under s426) and gross relief-at-source pension contributions (ITA s58), so those payments cut the charge. They do not reduce Class 4 NIC. A self-employed person must pay the charge through Self Assessment (GOV.UK). Opting out of Child Benefit payments while staying registered removes the charge for the weeks the opt-out covers and keeps the National Insurance credits (GOV.UK; s681E(1)(a)).

For a sole trader in the band in 2026-27, the marginal rate on extra profit is about 49% with one child and 54% with two (40% income tax + 2% Class 4 + about 7.2% or 11.9% charge). A pension contribution or Gift Aid saves about 47% to 52%, because there is no Class 4 saving.

Example, 2026-27, two children, 53 weeks: ANI of £70,000 gives a charge of 50% of £2,382 = £1,191. A £10,000 gross pension contribution (£8,000 paid; £2,000 more back through Self Assessment) brings ANI to £60,000 and removes the charge, so £10,000 in the pension costs about £4,809.

Announced, not law: Budget 2026 proposes that HMRC automatically offsets Child Benefit overpayments against the charge, backdated to January 2013 (Finance Bill 2026-27).

figures.2024-25: Band £60,000 to £80,000; 1% per £200. Child Benefit £25.60 a week (eldest or only child) and £16.95 (each other child) from 8 April 2024 (SI 2024/247). 52 charge weeks (Mondays 8 April 2024 to 31 March 2025): a full year is £1,331.20 and £881.40.
figures.2026-27: Band £60,000 to £80,000. £27.05 and £17.90 a week from 6 April 2026 (SI 2026/232). There are 53 charge weeks, beginning on Mondays from 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027 (s681H(3)). A full year is about £1,433.65 (eldest) and £948.70 (each other). Extra marginal rate in the band: about 7.2% with one child (£14.33 per £200, which is 1% of £1,433) and 11.9% with two (£23.82 per £200, 1% of £2,382).
figures.2027-28: Band £60,000 to £80,000 (no change announced at Budget 2026; no pending amendment to s681C). Child Benefit is announced at £28.00 and £18.55 a week (Budget 2026 OOTLAR Annex A), but this is not law until the 2027 up-rating order. 52 charge weeks (Mondays 12 April 2027 to 3 April 2028): about £1,456.00 and £964.60.

figures_disputed: 2026-27 53rd week (beginning Monday 5 April 2027): its rate depends on the 2027 up-rating order, which has not yet been made. The totals above assume the 2026-27 rates. If £28.00 / £18.55 applied to that week, the totals would be £1,434.60 and £949.35.
traps.status: Law: ITEPA 2003 Part 10 Ch 8 (ss681B-681H, including Conditions A and B in s681B(3)-(4) and the s681D extension where the child lives with someone other than the claimant); £60,000 and £200 for 2024-25 onwards (F(No.2)A 2024 s5); the opt-out disregard is s681E(1)(a) (election under SSAA 1992 s13A). Child Benefit rates in force: SI 2024/247, SI 2025/292, SI 2026/232. Announced, not law: 2027-28 Child Benefit of £28.00 / £18.55 (Budget 2026 OOTLAR Annex A), and automatic offset of Child Benefit overpayments against the charge (Budget 2026 document, 28 Oct 2026; OOTLAR 1.88: Finance Bill 2026-27, effective from Royal Assent and retrospective to January 2013).
traps.relevance: Applies if the user's adjusted net income is over £60,000 and the user or their partner gets Child Benefit; in a couple, whoever has the higher income pays. As profit moves through £60,000 to £80,000 it adds about 7% (one child) to 12% (two children) to the user's marginal rate in 2026-27. Personal pension contributions and Gift Aid reduce it, and opting out of payments avoids it.

traps.name: Capital grants and capital receipts under the cash basis (s96A, s105(2A) ITTOIA; BIM72020)
traps.why: Under the cash basis most capital spend on depreciating plant (lighting, audio, video kit) is deducted when paid (s33A, BIM72035). s96A then brings into profit disposal proceeds, any 'capital refund' (in substance a refund of capital expenditure) on a deducted asset, insurance/compensation, and market value when the asset leaves business use. Industrial Development Act grants are expressly taxable even if designated for capital (s105(2A)). HMRC's 2024-25 onwards guidance does not address other third-party capital grants (e.g. a charity bursary for kit). Safe treatment: deduct only net cost (cost minus grant), or deduct full cost and include the grant as a receipt; never deduct full cost and omit the grant. Selling hire kit later is a taxable receipt under s96A, not a capital gain (TCGA s47A). The 'capital refund' reading for third-party grants is not confirmed: flag for adviser review.

figures.current: null: no official figure or HMRC guidance on third-party capital grants under the cash basis

traps.status: Law: ITTOIA s96A (F(No.2)A 2017; amended FA 2024 Sch 10 from 6 April 2024); s105(2A) (FA 2013); s33A (F(No.2)A 2017); TCGA s47A. In force 2024-25 to 2026-27; no 2027-28 change announced. BIM72020 first published 7 April 2025.
traps.relevance: Directly relevant to grant-funded kit and later sales of hire kit.

traps.name: Unreported sales of business equipment (disposal values and balancing charges)
traps.why: Selling, giving away, swapping, scrapping, losing, or taking into private use kit whose cost got tax relief creates taxable income that must be reported, through whatever channel it is sold. (1) Cash basis (the default for sole traders from 2024-25 under ITTOIA 2005 s24A unless the trader elects out; no capital allowances except for cars): sale proceeds, insurance or other compensation for an asset whose cost was deducted are a trading receipt when received (s96A(3I)), reduced in proportion where only part of the cost was deducted (s96A(3J)). Stopping using it in the trade without selling it counts as a disposal at market value, and a material increase in private use counts as a disposal of that share (s96A(4)-(6)). (2) Accruals basis with capital allowances (AIA, FYA or WDA): the disposal value is brought into account in the period of the event (CAA 2001 s61) and deducted from the pool; any excess over the pool balance is a balancing charge. So kit fully relieved by the AIA gives a balancing charge equal to the whole price if the pool is nil. Disposal value is normally net sale proceeds plus any insurance or capital compensation. It is market value if the kit is given away or kept for non-business use (s61(2) item 7), or sold below market value to a buyer, connected or not, who cannot claim plant and machinery or R&D allowances, where there is no charge to tax under ITEPA 2003 (item 2, s61(4)). Where kit passes to an employee and an ITEPA charge arises, the disposal value is the net proceeds of a sale, or nil for a gift (item 1, s63(1)). It is nil for gifts of trade kit to charities, community amateur sports clubs, heritage bodies and museums listed in CTA 2010 s468, or for the purposes of a designated educational establishment (s63(2)). It is capped at the owner's qualifying cost or, after a chain of transfers between connected persons, the highest cost incurred by anyone in the chain (s62); this is the only place where connection matters. Proceeds cannot be netted against the cost of replacement kit (CA23086). The 40% main-rate first-year allowance (CAA s45U, FA 2026 s29, from 1 January 2026; open to sole traders) has no special disposal rule, so ordinary pool rules apply. The super-deduction, full expensing and the 50% special-rate FYA were for companies only and have their own balancing-charge rules. Business kit is not a 'personal possession' (an item for your own use), so HMRC's message that selling personal items from your home is unlikely to be taxed does not cover it. Online platforms report goods sellers with 30 or more sales, or more than 2,000 euros (about £1,700), in a calendar year; the low-value exclusion covers only sellers for whom the platform solely facilitated sales of goods (IEIM901630), so kit sold through a platform on which the person also offers services or rentals is reported at any level. Leaving out proceeds or a balancing charge is a careless or deliberate inaccuracy (FA 2007 Sch 24); deliberate omission is evasion.

figures.hs252_2026_example_pool_above_4000: no charge: deduct £4,000 from the pool before writing down allowances
figures.disposal_value_cap: owner's qualifying expenditure (CAA s62(1)); highest qualifying expenditure in a connected-person chain (s62(3))
figures.disposal_value_market_value_cases: gift or start of non-business use (s61(2) item 7); sale below market value to a buyer who cannot claim plant and machinery or R&D allowances, with no ITEPA 2003 charge (item 2, s61(4)), whether or not connected
figures.disposal_value_itepa_charge_case: net proceeds on a sale (item 1); nil on a gift (s63(1))
figures.gift_nil_disposal_value_recipients: charitable trusts and companies, community amateur sports clubs, CTA 2010 s468 heritage bodies and museums, designated educational establishments (CAA s63(2))

traps.status: Law: CAA 2001 ss61, 62, 63 and s45U (FA 2026 s29, expenditure from 1 Jan 2026); FA 2021 s12; ITTOIA 2005 s24A (cash basis default from 2024-25, FA 2024 Sch 10) and s96A; FA 2007 Sch 24 para 4. Text checked on legislation.gov.uk on 24 Nov 2026. Guidance: HS252 2026 edition (for 2025-26, published 6 April 2026); GOV.UK 'Capital allowances when you sell an asset' (13 Nov 2024); full expensing and 50% FYA disposal guidance (20 Mar 2024); super-deduction disposal guidance (24 Jul 2023); CA23086; CC/FS7a (21 Jul 2026); platform operator guidance (21 Jul 2026); IEIM901630 (excluded sellers).
traps.relevance: The technician buys, sells, trades in and hires out kit, so every sale, part-exchange, insurance payout or write-off of kit that got tax relief has to go in that year's accounts. On the default cash basis the whole sale price is usually taxable income.

traps.name: Contractor loan / disguised remuneration schemes and the GAAR
traps.why: Schemes paying most income to freelancers and PSC owners as 'loans' (often via offshore trusts, umbrellas or LLPs) do not work; HMRC 'has never approved these schemes and has always said they don't work'. Outstanding loans were taxed by the 2019 loan charge. The GAAR (FA 2013 Part 5) counteracts abusive arrangements failing the double reasonableness test, with just and reasonable adjustments and a 60% penalty (s212A). Warning signs: 'HMRC-approved' claims, pay structured as loans, take-home well above the norm, offers to get round IR35 or the loan charge. Tax, interest and penalties fall on the user, not the promoter; HMRC publishes named schemes and umbrella companies. Flag any 'contractor solution' offering more than about 80% take-home.

figures.current: GAAR penalty 60% of the counteracted advantage. Penalty up to 30% of tax avoided for failing to take reasonable care when using a defeated scheme. Loan Charge Review government response (Nov 2025): promoter fees of 18%-20% of contract value.

traps.status: GAAR in force from 17 July 2013 (NICs from 13 March 2014); 60% penalty for arrangements on or after 15 September 2016 (FA 2016 s158). Loan charge law (F(No.2)A 2017 Schs 11 and 12, amended FA 2020 ss15-17): loans made on or after 9 Dec 2010 outstanding at 5 April 2019. Settlement scheme law: FA 2026 ss25-27 (18 March 2026). GOV.UK overview updated 3 June 2026; named schemes list updated 19 Nov 2026.
traps.relevance: The assistant must refuse such schemes.

traps.name: Loan-based and contrived extraction schemes
traps.why: Paying an employee, director, contractor or self-employed person through 'loans', advances or other payments routed through a third party (offshore trusts, umbrella or similar arrangements), instead of taxed pay, profits or dividends, is disguised remuneration, and HMRC counteracts it. ITEPA Part 7A taxes employment income provided through third parties. ITTOIA ss23A-23H tax such benefits as trading profits of a self-employed person in the year they arise, including the principal of any loan (s23E). The 2019 loan charge (F(No.2)A 2017 Schs 11 and 12) taxed such loans still outstanding on 5 April 2019. For past users, FA 2026 s25 required the Treasury to create a loan charge settlement scheme, which it did by SI 2026/821 (made 14 July 2026, in force 5 August 2026). HMRC said on 7 September 2026 that it had started sending offers. Promoters face FA 2026 Part 6 (not Part 4, which is vaping products duty). Chapter 1 (ss159-165) prohibits promoting arrangements that are marketed for a tax advantage with no realistic prospect of delivering it (s159(1)(a)). It also prohibits promoting arrangements of a kind HMRC specifies in regulations as marketed for a tax advantage, unlikely to deliver it and likely to harm participants (s159(1)(b), (2)). Breaches carry civil penalties (s162) and a criminal offence (s163); s159(1) has been in force since 18 May 2026. Chapter 2 (ss166-176) covers promoter action notices, and Chapter 3 (ss177-208) anti-avoidance information notices. Announced, not law: a 'policy maintenance package' for the POTAS regime, first announced at Tax Update Day 2026, for Finance Bill 2026-27 and effective from its Royal Assent (OOTLAR 1.97). Proposed: a consultation announced at Budget 2026 and not yet published, on new powers against serious and serial users of avoidance schemes, earlier recovery of promoters' and certain individuals' liabilities, and a stronger POTAS regime (OOTLAR 2.35). Consequences for users: income tax and NIC as if the money were pay or profits, late payment interest and possible penalties. Where penalties for deliberate behaviour involve more than £50,000 of potential lost revenue, HMRC may also publish their details (FA 2009 s94). Announced, not law: Finance Bill 2026-27 will widen what HMRC can publish about deliberate defaulters and let it publish Personal Liability Notices (OOTLAR 1.90). Other contrived extraction schemes (remuneration trusts, 'loyalty point' advertising, share-class gifts) are covered under owner-managed-company-extraction-schemes. Do not use.

figures.current: No planning figures: do not use. For past users only, FA 2026 s25(6) sets the settlement amount. For each tax year, the starting amount is lowered (not below nil) by 10% of the first £50,000 and 5% of the next £100,000 of the total attributed to that year. The yearly results are added together and lowered by a further £5,000 (not below nil). The settlement amount cannot be more than £70,000 below the loan charge gross liability; if it would be, it is gross liability minus £70,000. Settlements agreed before 1 June 2021 are excluded (s25(4)). A settlement offer is open for 90 days from the day it is made, or any longer period HMRC reasonably decides (SI 2026/821 reg 9(8)). A further offer, made after an earlier one expired, was withdrawn, or was rejected or met with a counter-offer, is open for 30 days instead of 90 (reg 9(7)(c), (9)). HMRC may withdraw an offer or extend the time to accept it (reg 9(7)(a)-(b)); its guidance of 7 Sept 2026 says most customers will in practice have longer than 90 days. Publication of deliberate defaulters: potential lost revenue over £50,000 (FA 2009 s94(1)(b), threshold from 2 Oct 2026 under SI 2026/1000); no publication where the full reduction for disclosure was given (s94(10)).

traps.status: Law: ITEPA Part 7A; ITTOIA ss23A-23H (inserted by F(No.2)A 2017 s35, 16 Nov 2017); F(No.2)A 2017 Schs 11-12; FA 2026 (c.11, Royal Assent 18 March 2026) ss25-27 and Part 6 (s159(1) in force 18 May 2026 under s165(2)); SI 2026/821 (in force 5 Aug 2026); FA 2009 s94 (£50,000 threshold from 2 Oct 2026 under SI 2026/1000). Announced, not law: the OOTLAR 1.97 POTAS package for Finance Bill 2026-27 (Budget 2026 documents of 28 Oct 2026; OOTLAR updated 5 Nov 2026). Also announced, not law: OOTLAR 1.90 (first announced at Budget 2025) says Finance Bill 2026-27 will amend FA 2009 to widen the information HMRC can publish about deliberate defaulters and add a power to publish details of Personal Liability Notices, from Royal Assent. Separately, the Budget 2026 document says the government will strengthen the framework for publishing deliberate defaulters' details and 'will bring forward changes next year'. Proposed: the consultation in OOTLAR 2.35, 'Removing the Financial Incentives of Tax Avoidance' ('Tackling the tax avoidance market' in the Budget 2026 document). It was not on GOV.UK's list of open HMRC consultations on 24 Nov 2026. OOTLAR 2.35 is the avoidance consultation; the property income data consultation is a separate document ('Improving Property Income Data Reporting', 28 Oct 2026).
traps.relevance: Freelance crew are a target for 'contractor solutions' that pay most of a day rate as a loan or other 'non-taxable' payment. For a sole trader, any such payment linked to their work is taxed as trading profit anyway. The assistant must flag and refuse these offers and never model them as savings.

traps.name: Remuneration trusts and revenue service trusts marketed to the self-employed (HMRC Spotlights 51, 57, 61)
traps.why: Spotlight 51 (10 May 2019): the user (a self-employed person, partner, company or director) pays into an offshore 'remuneration trust'. The money, often minus a 10% scheme fee, goes to a personal management company the user controls and comes back as unsecured 'loans' or 'fiduciary receipts' that are rarely repaid. HMRC says that for self-employed users and partnerships the deductions are not allowable and Inheritance Tax is chargeable, with interest and possible penalties. HMRC is considering the GAAR (60% penalty for transactions after 14 September 2016). For transactions after 16 November 2017, an inaccurate return can attract a penalty for carelessness unless the user can show they took reasonable care. Spotlight 57 (17 December 2020, updated 26 May 2022): the business 'sells' a percentage of its future revenue to an offshore 'revenue service trust', leaves that revenue out of its accounts and does not disclose the transfer to HMRC. The money comes back through a personal management company or as 'loans' or 'fiduciary receipts'. HMRC says self-employed users still owe Income Tax, NIC and IHT, the trust may be taxed, and interest and penalties apply. Spotlight 57 also warns that 'Deliberately misleading, or concealing information from HMRC may result in criminal prosecution.' Spotlight 61 (22 December 2022): the First-tier Tribunal found the scheme was tax avoidance in Marlborough DP Ltd, Strategic Branding Ltd and CIA Insurance Services Ltd. All three were limited companies, not sole traders. Neither the trust contributions nor the 10% fees were allowable expenses. In Strategic Branding and CIA, the loans were disguised remuneration that needed PAYE and NIC. Spotlight 61's account of Marlborough, which says the contributions were distributions, is out of date. The Upper Tribunal ([2024] UKUT 98 (TCC)) allowed HMRC's appeal in part. It held that the loans to the director were not general earnings under ITEPA s62, but were employment income under ITEPA Part 7A, and that the contributions were not deductible. The Court of Appeal dismissed the company's appeal ([2025] EWCA Civ 796, 26 June 2025). For a sole trader the specific rule is ITTOIA 2005 ss23A-23H, which apply to relevant benefits arising on or after 6 April 2017. A loan or other benefit from such an arrangement is taxed as profit of the trade for the year it arises, and for a loan that means the whole principal (s23E). The 2019 loan charge (F(No.2)A 2017 Sch 12) only reached trading loans made between 9 December 2010 and 5 April 2017 that were still outstanding at 5 April 2019. It does not catch new schemes; ss23A-23H do. Since May 2026 a person must not promote arrangements that are marketed as a way to get a particular tax advantage where there is no realistic prospect that they will deliver it (FA 2026 s159(1)(a)). Doing so is a criminal offence (s163) and carries a civil penalty of up to £1,000,000 plus £5,000 for each participant (s162(2)). The ban is on promoters, not users. HMRC's guidance lists indicators of 'no realistic prospect'. These include users 'entering into a loan agreement which they do not genuinely expect to pay', and facts the same as, or substantially similar to, a scheme a court has already ruled ineffective. Never enter one. HMRC strongly advises users to withdraw and settle their tax affairs.

figures.careless_penalty_start: Spotlight 51: transactions after 16 November 2017. Spotlight 57: returns sent on or after 16 November 2017 for tax periods that begin on or after 6 April 2017 and end after 15 November 2017
figures.enablers_penalty_start: arrangements enabled and entered into on or after 16 November 2017 (Spotlight 57)
figures.sole_trader_rule: ITTOIA ss23A-23H apply to relevant benefits arising on or after 6 April 2017 (F(No.2)A 2017 s35(4)); a loan's full principal is taxed as trading profit (s23E(1), (2)(b))
figures.loan_charge_scope: trading loans made 9 December 2010 to 5 April 2017 and outstanding immediately before the end of 5 April 2019 (F(No.2)A 2017 Sch 12 para 1(2))
figures.fa2026_s159_commencement: 18 May 2026 per legislation.gov.uk (s165(2): two months after Royal Assent on 18 March 2026); HMRC guidance says 19 May 2026
figures.fa2026_s163_offence: on indictment up to 2 years' imprisonment, a fine or both; on summary conviction a fine (England and Wales) or a fine up to the statutory maximum (Scotland, Northern Ireland)
figures.fa2026_civil_penalty: maximum £1,000,000 plus £5,000 for each person who took part in the arrangements (FA 2026 s162(2)); repeated in HMRC guidance on the prohibition (published 30 October 2026, updated 6 November 2026)
figures.marlborough_dp: FTT [2021] UKFTT 0304 (TC). UT [2024] UKUT 98 (TCC), judgment dated 12 April 2024, released 16 April 2024: HMRC's appeal allowed in part (Ground 2, general earnings under ITEPA s62, dismissed; Ground 1, ITEPA Part 7A, allowed; Ground 3, contributions not deductible, allowed).
