traps.relevance: Freelance crew paid day rates by agencies and production companies are typical targets for 'keep more of your fees' trust offers. Sending fees or revenue to a trust and taking them back as loans leaves the full tax and NIC due, plus scheme fees, interest and penalties, so Expend should warn against it and never count it as a saving.

traps.name: Being paid in 'loans', 'grants' or 'annuities' through umbrella companies or trusts (disguised remuneration)
traps.why: Spotlights 33 and 60 warn contractors and freelancers about schemes paying most earnings as a 'loan', 'grant', 'annuity', 'capital advance' or other supposedly non-taxable payment via trusts, offshore companies or non-compliant umbrellas. They do not work: payments are taxable income; '80-90% take-home' is a warning sign; HMRC never approves schemes and a scheme reference number is not approval. Consequences: full tax and NIC, interest and penalties; accelerated payment notices; possible IHT where trusts used; HMRC can contact mortgage lenders; a third party may demand repayment of the 'loans'. FA 2026 ss25-27 legislate a settlement scheme for past users.

figures.current: Spotlight 33: HMRC wins around 9 out of 10 avoidance cases that reach court.

traps.status: Spotlight 33 (7 Jul 2016, updated 22 Dec 2022); Spotlight 60 (25 Aug 2022); Spotlight 71 (13 Jun 2025). Settlement scheme law: FA 2026 ss25-27 (18 Mar 2026); HMRC guidance 17 Jul 2026, updated 5 Nov 2026. Third-party repayment warning: GOV.UK overview updated 3 Jun 2026.
traps.relevance: Flag any pay split into a small salary plus a 'loan' or non-taxable payment.

traps.name: Disguised remuneration loan schemes and the loan charge (F(No.2)A 2017 Schs 11 and 12)
traps.why: Schemes that pay earnings as 'loans', 'advances', 'annuities', 'fiduciary receipts' or other credit through a third party (often an offshore trust, umbrella or 'contractor solution') rely on the money never being repaid and never being treated as income. They do not work. There are three layers of law, and which one applies depends on whether the person is employed (including by an umbrella) or self-employed for the work. (1) Employees: ITEPA 2003 Part 7A (employment income provided through third parties). The amount is employment income (s554A), PAYE applies to a payment of money (s687A), and it counts as earnings for Class 1 NIC (SS(C)R 2001 reg 22B). (2) Traders: ITTOIA 2005 ss23A-23H, inserted by F(No.2)A 2017 s35 (Royal Assent 16 Nov 2017), apply to relevant benefits arising on or after 6 April 2017, but only where all five conditions are met. Condition A: the person carries on a trade, alone or in partnership. Condition B: it is reasonable to suppose that an arrangement connected with the trade is in essence a means of providing relevant benefits. Condition C: a benefit arises to the trader or a connected person, or to someone else where an enjoyment condition is met. Condition D: it is reasonable to suppose the benefit is connected with a qualifying third-party payment, such as fees for the trader's services. Condition E: it is reasonable to suppose a tax advantage would be obtained. The benefit is taxed as trading profits of the tax year in which it arises, or of the year the trade ceased if that was earlier (s23E). For a loan, the amount taxed is the principal lent. A 'loan' includes any form of credit and any payment said to be a loan (s23B(5)). Because ss23A-23H sit in ITTOIA Part 2 Chapter 2, Class 4 NIC is also due (SSCBA 1992 s15(1)(b)). (3) The loan charge: loans and quasi-loans made on or after 9 Dec 2010 that were still outstanding immediately before the end of 5 April 2019 were taxed as 2018-19 income. Employment loans fall under Sch 11. Trading loans fall under Sch 12, but only if made before 6 April 2017. A trader who had already stopped trading is taxed on a post-cessation receipt (Sch 12 para 1(3)(b)). Repayments of principal made before 17 March 2016 (Sch 11) or before 5 December 2016 (Sch 12) reduce the outstanding amount whatever form they took. Later repayments count only if they were made in money and are not connected with another tax avoidance arrangement (Sch 11 paras 3-4; Sch 12 para 3(3)-(4)). FA 2020 added two things. First, an irrevocable election to spread the charge equally over 2018-19, 2019-20 and 2020-21, made before 1 October 2020 or later if an HMRC officer allows. Second, a reduction (not below nil) of the outstanding amount where the loan was reasonably disclosed on returns for 2015-16 or earlier and HMRC had taken no recovery steps by 6 April 2019 (Sch 11 paras 1A-1B; Sch 12 paras 1(3A)-(3D) and 1A). An unpaid loan charge can now be settled under the Loan Charge Settlement Scheme (FA 2026 ss25-27; SI 2026/821, in force 5 August 2026; see loan-charge-settlement-scheme). In Rangers ([2017] UKSC 45, 5 July 2017; HMRC Spotlight 41), the Supreme Court held that employment income paid to a third party is still taxable as employment income. HMRC's view is that this principle applies to a wide range of disguised remuneration schemes, including contractor loan schemes, and it says it will consider follower notices and accelerated payment notices in appropriate cases. In Spotlight 56 (1 Sept 2020), the GAAR Advisory Panel found a remuneration-trust loan arrangement 'contrived and abnormal' and not a reasonable course of action. HMRC may issue GAAR counteraction notices, which can carry a 60% penalty for arrangements entered into on or after 15 Sept 2016, and accelerated payment notices. There is no lawful way to take earnings as a tax-free 'loan'.

figures.trading_loan_window: Loans or quasi-loans made from 9 Dec 2010 to 5 April 2017 and outstanding immediately before the end of 5 April 2019 (F(No.2)A 2017 Sch 12 para 1(2))
figures.employment_loan_window: Loans or quasi-loans made on or after 9 Dec 2010 and outstanding immediately before the end of 5 April 2019 (Sch 11 para 1(1))
figures.charge_year: 2018-19 on the whole outstanding amount, or one third in each of 2018-19, 2019-20 and 2020-21 if the spreading election was made
figures.spreading_election_deadline: Before 1 October 2020, or later if an HMRC officer allows; cannot be revoked (Sch 11 para 1A(7),(9); Sch 12 para 1(3B),(3D))
figures.repayment_cut_off_dates: Sch 11: 17 March 2016; Sch 12: 5 December 2016. Repayments before these dates count in any form. From these dates, only payments in money count, and not if connected with another tax avoidance arrangement.
figures.disclosure_reduction: Qualifying tax years 2015-16 and earlier; reasonable disclosure on a return; no HMRC recovery steps by 6 April 2019; outstanding amount reduced, not below nil (Sch 11 para 1B; Sch 12 para 1A)
figures.ss23A_23H_start: Relevant benefits arising on or after 6 April 2017 (F(No.2)A 2017 s35(4)); taxed as trading profits of the tax year the benefit arises, a loan at the principal lent (ITTOIA s23E)
figures.settlement_amount_rules: A further £5,000 is deducted (not below nil), and the settlement amount is never more than £70,000 below the loan charge gross liability (SI 2026/821 reg 10, steps 8-11)
figures.settlement_offer_period: First offer: 90 days, or any longer period HMRC reasonably determines (reg 9(8)). Further offer, made after an earlier offer expired, was withdrawn or was rejected: 30 days in place of the 90 (reg 9(7)(c), (9)). HMRC may extend the time for acceptance, even after an offer has expired (reg 9(7)(b)).
figures.settlement_exclusions: Late payment interest and most penalties are left out (HMRC guidance, updated 5 Nov 2026). Unpaid IHT stops being payable only if it relates to the settled arrangements and has already arisen or arises within 3 months beginning with the day the offer was made (reg 15(1); the guidance says within 3 months of the date on the offer letter, or on a new offer letter). IHT arising after that must be paid when it arises.
figures.settlement_instalments: Up to 5 years, or longer depending on circumstances, with interest; agreed with the caseworker before accepting (HMRC guidance)

traps.status: Law: ITEPA 2003 Part 7A (employees); F(No.2)A 2017 s35 and Schs 11 and 12 (Royal Assent 16 Nov 2017; ITTOIA ss23A-23H for relevant benefits from 6 April 2017), amended by FA 2020 (Royal Assent 22 July 2020). Settlement scheme: FA 2026 ss25-27 (Royal Assent 18 March 2026) and SI 2026/821 (made 14 July 2026, in force 5 August 2026). HMRC guidance: 'The loan charge' and 'Find out about the Loan Charge Settlement Scheme' (first published 17 July 2026, updated 5 Nov 2026).
traps.relevance: If an agency, umbrella or 'contractor solution' offers to pay part of the user's day rate as a loan, advance or other 'non-taxable' payment, that money is still taxable: as trading profit of the year it arises if the user is self-employed for that work, or as employment income with PAYE and Class 1 NIC if the user is employed by the umbrella. The user can be left paying the tax, interest and penalties, and the loan charge itself matters only if the user took such loans between December 2010 and April 2019.

traps.name: Contractor 'tax-free', 'loan' and 'high take-home pay' schemes: HMRC warning signs
traps.why: HMRC's page 'Spot the signs of disguised remuneration tax avoidance schemes' (first published 26 Nov 2020, updated 14 Aug 2025) is written for people paid through umbrella companies. It lists seven warning signs. (1) The scheme or umbrella claims to be 'HMRC approved'. This should raise concern, because HMRC never approves avoidance schemes or any umbrella company's compliance. Reassuring checks are accreditation by an independent body that audits payroll companies, a Companies House check and reviews from other contractors. (2) The scheme or promoter is on HMRC's list of named schemes, promoters, enablers and suppliers. Absence from the list is not approval. (3) The umbrella company or its directors are outside the UK. For tax purposes the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands are outside the UK, and a UK phone number proves nothing. (4) You receive more than the 'net pay after tax' on your payslip. That cannot be right: it means full income tax and NICs are not being paid. An agency should give you a Key Information Document showing the deductions and fees. (5) You are asked to sign another agreement, such as an annuity, as well as your employment contract. Other signs are a choice of 'standard' or 'enhanced' arrangements, or a contract without full terms or a breakdown of deductions. (6) Your payslip shows only PAYE pay, while other money arrives described as 'loans, annuities, bonuses, shares, fiduciary receipts, credit facility, capital payments/advances or something similar'. (7) The umbrella charges a higher fee or margin. HMRC gives £25 to £30 a week as an example of a fixed weekly fee, which you should have been told about when you signed the contract. It says to compare the fee with other companies' fees, to make sure you are not paying more than the normal fees, and warns that a fee set at a level similar to the tax or NICs you would expect can make the deductions look right. HMRC's payslip guidance (updated 3 Dec 2025) adds that umbrellas running avoidance schemes often charge higher fees than legitimate ones. It also lists labels to watch for: loans, annuities, bonuses, profit shares, fiduciary receipts, credit facilities, capital payments and pay advances. Such payments can be legitimate if they are taxed through PAYE. Otherwise they are still taxable: for an umbrella employee, as employment income (the Rangers principle, Spotlight 41; ITEPA Part 7A where a third party is used); for a self-employed person paid outside PAYE, as trading profit under ITTOIA 2005 ss23A-23H. Loans still outstanding at 5 April 2019 were also caught by the loan charge (F(No.2)A 2017 Schs 11 and 12). A DOTAS scheme reference number (FA 2004 s311) only identifies the user to HMRC and is not approval (Spotlight 33), and leaving it off a tax return brings extra penalties. Consequences for users: the tax, NICs and interest; possible inaccuracy penalties; follower notices and accelerated payment notices (FA 2014 Part 4); GAAR counteraction, with a 60% penalty for arrangements entered into on or after 15 September 2016; and HMRC publishing the scheme and its promoters. Promoter fees are lost. To leave a scheme, email CAGetHelpOutOfTaxAvoidance@hmrc.gov.uk. To report one, use the Report Tax Fraud online form with the code 'TAC' in 'Other information', or phone 0800 788 887 (+44 (0)203 080 0871 from outside the UK). Working through an umbrella makes the user its employee for that work. For payments made on or after 6 April 2026, the agency that contracts with the client (and in some cases the client) is jointly and severally liable for the umbrella's PAYE (FA 2026 s24, ITEPA Part 2 Ch 11; see umbrella-jsl-april-2026).

figures.tax_saving: None: the amounts remain taxable, with interest and possibly penalties, on top of promoter fees
figures.umbrella_fixed_fee_example: £25 to £30 a week: HMRC's example of a fixed weekly fee, which should be disclosed in the contract. HMRC does not call this level normal or high; it says to compare with other umbrellas' fees.
figures.follower_notice_penalty: 30% of the denied advantage (FA 2014 s209(1), as amended by FA 2021 Sch 28 para 3(3) for s208 penalties assessed on or after 10 June 2021; previously 50%)
figures.follower_notice_penalty_floor: Can be reduced for co-operation, but not below 10% of the denied advantage (FA 2014 s210(4))
figures.follower_notice_additional_penalty: A further 20% of the denied advantage (s208A, s209(1A)), only if the tribunal appeal is struck out or the tribunal declares it unreasonable; combined maximum 50%
figures.accelerated_payment_period: 90 days from the notice. If representations were made, the later of that and 30 days after HMRC's determination (FA 2014 s223(5))
figures.gaar_penalty: 60% of the value of the counteracted advantage (FA 2013 s212A(2)). Only for tax arrangements entered into on or after 15 September 2016 (FA 2016 s158(15)), and only where a GAAR counteraction notice has been given, a return or other tax document relied on the advantage, and the advantage has been counteracted (s212A(1)).

traps.status: HMRC guidance: 'Spot the signs' (26 Nov 2020, updated 14 Aug 2025); payslip guidance (18 Nov 2021, updated 3 Dec 2025); named schemes list (updated 19 Nov 2026); Spotlights 33 and 41. Law: ITEPA 2003 Part 7A; ITTOIA 2005 ss23A-23H; F(No.2)A 2017 Schs 11 and 12; FA 2014 Part 4 as amended by FA 2021 Sch 28 (Royal Assent 10 June 2021; no separate commencement provision found); FA 2013 s212A (inserted by FA 2016 s158, for arrangements entered into from 15 Sept 2016); FA 2004 Part 7 (s311); FA 2026 s24 (umbrella joint and several liability for payments from 6 April 2026).
traps.relevance: Events crew are often asked by agencies to work through an umbrella or 'contractor solution'. The assistant should run these checks whenever the user mentions one. Any promise of more take-home pay than a normal payslip or normal self-employed profit would give is a red flag.

traps.name: Non-compliant umbrella companies (HMRC guidance; Spotlights 45, 55, 60, 64, 71)
traps.why: A legitimate umbrella employs the worker under PAYE, deducting its margin, employer NIC, employer pension, holiday pay and any Apprenticeship Levy from the assignment rate, then income tax, employee NIC, employee pension and student loan from gross pay. Warning signs: a separate 'non-taxable' payment (e.g. a loan), being paid more than the payslip shows, payment from someone other than the umbrella, extra agreements; Spotlight 71 adds being moved between umbrellas at short notice, changes of PAYE reference or employer name, and payment by a similarly named or overseas company. Unpaid tax and NIC fall back on the worker; lower pension and benefits; damage to employment history and mortgages; HMRC endorses no umbrella. IR35 rules are unlikely to apply to someone employed by an umbrella. Working through an umbrella changes the user's status for that work from self-employed to employee. FA 2026 s24 (ITEPA Part 2 Ch 11, ss61Y-61Z2) makes agencies/clients jointly liable for umbrella PAYE from 6 April 2026.

figures.current: No tax advantage. HMRC's 'Work out pay from an umbrella company' tool updated for 2026-27 rates on 6 April 2026.

traps.status: HMRC guidance 'Working through an umbrella company' (29 Apr 2021, updated 17 Sep 2025); payslip guidance 3 Dec 2025; Spotlights 45, 55, 60 (25 Aug 2022), 64, 71 (13 Jun 2025) live. Law: FA 2026 s24 (ITEPA ss61Y-61Z2) for payments on or after 6 April 2026; HMRC page updated 19 June 2026 ('now in force'); ESM2420 updated 7 Oct 2026.
traps.relevance: When an agency asks the user to work 'inside IR35' via a preferred umbrella, check payslips against the personal tax account and warn about any extra 'loan' or 'bonus' outside PAYE.

traps.name: Agency and client joint and several liability for umbrella company PAYE from 6 April 2026 (ITEPA Part 2 Ch 11, ss61Y-61Z2)
traps.why: FA 2026 s24 makes each 'relevant party' jointly and severally liable with the umbrella for PAYE on a qualifying umbrella company payment; SI 2026/388 adds Class 1 NIC (relevant party not treated as secondary contributor). Relevant party (s61Z): the person contracting with the end client where the umbrella contracts with someone else (normally the agency); the client where it contracts directly with the umbrella, or alongside the agency where that agency is connected with the umbrella or non-UK resident; where client and that agency are non-UK and others are in the chain, the UK-resident person closest to the client. s61Z1 'purported umbrella companies' (Case 1: impression of employing but not; Case 2: contracts directly with client, engages worker as self-employed so agency rules would otherwise apply, no work-finding services; Case 3: a company in which the worker has a material interest gives the impression a substantial proportion of receipts will be paid as earnings but does not): worker treated as employed by it; all remuneration is earnings; Chapters 7-10 and ITTOIA s863A disapplied. s61Z2: HMRC may disclose to potentially liable parties. Strict liability (HMRC need not show knowledge). If the user hires crew via an umbrella with no agency, the user as end client becomes jointly liable. Styling one's own company as an 'umbrella' is caught by Case 3.

figures.current: Applies to payments on or after 6 April 2026 (FA 2026 s24(11)), new and existing chains. Umbrella outside s61Y if the worker has a 'material interest': more than 5% of share capital, distributions or assets on a winding up.

traps.status: Law. FA 2026 (c.11) s24, Royal Assent 18 March 2026; payments on or after 6 April 2026. SI 2026/388 (made 31 Mar, laid 1 Apr, in force 6 Apr 2026). GOV.UK guidance updated 19 June 2026; ESM2400-ESM2445 (ESM2440 updated 7 Oct 2026). No outstanding amendments.
traps.relevance: Relevant if paid via agencies, and if the business grows to subcontracting crew.

traps.name: Mini umbrella company (MUC) fraud
traps.why: Organised crime groups split an umbrella workforce across many small companies each claiming the Employment Allowance and using the VAT Flat Rate Scheme (charging 20% VAT, accounting at the lower flat rate); MUCs build tax debts and close. Workers are moved between MUCs unknowingly and may have deductions never paid over. Warning signs: unusual or similar company names created together, unrelated Companies House activity, foreign national directors with no industry history, frequent moves, short-lived companies. HMRC denies input tax and transfers penalties to officers where a business in the chain knew or should have known. Criminal and civil action by HMRC's Fraud Investigation Service; workers lose employment rights and NIC credits (check the personal tax account and NI record). Agencies jointly liable for PAYE from 6 April 2026.

figures.current: HMRC has deregistered 'tens of thousands' of MUCs; in Elphysic HMRC said the scheme involved over 18,000 MUCs; limited cost trader VAT rules from 2017.

traps.status: Law and current guidance. 'Mini umbrella company fraud' first published 10 May 2021, updated 4 Aug 2025 (after the 17 July 2025 Upper Tribunal decision). Joint liability: ITEPA ss61Y-61Z2 (FA 2026 s24, 18 March 2026) for payments on or after 6 April 2026; the guidance page still calls it 'draft legislation published 21 July 2025'.
traps.relevance: If paid via an agency or umbrella and the employer name or PAYE reference changes on payslips, check the HMRC app or personal tax account.

traps.name: Managed Service Company (MSC) schemes (Spotlight 67; ITEPA 2003 Part 2 Ch 9)
traps.why: Managed Service Company (MSC) providers sell mass-marketed, 'off-the-shelf' structures: personal service companies, partnerships, or composite companies with several worker-shareholders. They are often presented as accountancy services and promise higher take-home pay, usually through a low salary and high dividends. Under ITEPA 2003 s61B, a company is an MSC if all four of the following conditions are met. For this purpose 'company' includes a partnership (s61C(3)). (a) Its business consists wholly or mainly of providing an individual's services to others. (b) Payments equal to 'the greater part or all' of the consideration for those services are made to the individual or associates. HMRC's Spotlight 67 paraphrases this as 'at least 50%', but the statute gives no percentage, and ESM3510 applies the test cumulatively each time a payment is made. (c) The way the payments are made leaves the individual better off, net of tax and NICs, than if every payment were employment income. (d) An MSC provider is involved with the company. An MSC provider is a person carrying on a business of promoting or facilitating the use of companies to provide individuals' services. It is involved if it, or an associate, does any of the following (s61B(2)): benefits financially on an ongoing basis from the services; influences or controls how the services are provided; influences or controls how the individual is paid; influences or controls the company's finances or activities; or gives or promotes an undertaking to make good any tax loss. A firm is not an MSC provider merely because it provides legal or accountancy services in a professional capacity (s61B(3)). A business that only places workers with clients is not one unless it also does something listed in s61B(5) (s61B(4)-(5)). Where the rules apply, any payment or benefit that the worker or an associate receives from anyone for the services, other than earnings paid to the worker directly by the MSC, is treated as a 'deemed employment payment' made by the MSC (s61D(1)-(2)). Salary the MSC already runs through PAYE stays ordinary earnings. Dividends, 'loans', other distributions and payments from third parties become deemed employment payments. The amount is worked out under s61E: the payment or benefit, less expenses that would have been deductible had the worker been employed by the client, less the employer NIC treated as included in what remains. It bears PAYE and, from 6 August 2007, Class 1 NICs, with the MSC as secondary contributor (ESM3530). If an HMRC officer considers that PAYE or Class 1 NIC owed by the MSC (the 'specified amount') cannot be recovered from the MSC within a reasonable period, HMRC can direct that it be recovered from the persons listed in s688A(2) (PAYE Regs 2003 reg 97C; SS(C)R 2001 Sch 4 para 29C). ESM3620 treats about three months as normally a reasonable time. Those persons are: the MSC's directors, office-holders and associates; the MSC provider and its directors, office-holders and associates; and anyone who has encouraged or been actively involved in the MSC providing the worker's services, and their directors, office-holders and associates. Merely giving legal or accountancy advice in a professional capacity, or placing the worker with clients, does not put someone in that last group (s688A(3)). For debts after 6 January 2008, and only where recovery from the first two groups is impracticable, HMRC can transfer the debt to that last group (ESM3625). HMRC normally treats a worker-shareholder of an MSC as part of that group, unless the worker genuinely did not know they had been made a shareholder. A debt cannot pass to a director's spouse. The MSC rules do not apply where the off-payroll rules (Chapter 10) apply to an engagement with a public authority, or with a medium or large client with a UK connection (s61D(4A)). Spotlight 67 says traditional bespoke tax advice or accountancy, and ordinary bookkeeping software, are outside the rules. Its own example is caught by them: a worker who registers a company and runs it through a provider's portal for a variable fee. The signs of an MSC product it lists are pop-up adverts promising maximum take-home pay, a push to take a small salary and the rest as dividends, standardised software that picks the most tax-advantageous result, and a fee that rises when you work and falls when you do not.

figures.condition_b_threshold: 'the greater part or all of the consideration' (ITEPA s61B(1)(b)), read as more than half. Spotlight 67 says 'at least 50%'. ESM3510 gives no percentage and compares the totals cumulatively each time a payment is made (its example: £550 paid out of £900 received meets the test).
figures.rules_start_dates: Income tax on deemed employment payments from 6 April 2007 (FA 2007 s25 and Sch 3); Class 1 NICs from 6 August 2007 (ESM3530)
figures.debt_transfer_trigger: PAYE or Class 1 NIC that an HMRC officer considers irrecoverable from the MSC within a reasonable period (PAYE Regs 2003 reg 97C(1)(b); SS(C)R 2001 Sch 4 para 29C(1)(b)); ESM3620: within three months is normally a reasonable time
figures.debt_transfer_to_others: Only for debts after 6 January 2008, and only where recovery from the MSC's directors and associates and from the provider is impracticable (ESM3625)

traps.status: Law: ITEPA 2003 Part 2 Chapter 9 (ss61A-61J) and s688A, inserted by FA 2007 s25 and Sch 3 with effect from 6 April 2007; PAYE Regs 2003 (SI 2003/2682) reg 97C; SS(C)R 2001 (SI 2001/1004) Sch 4 para 29C. s61D(4A)-(4C) were substituted by FA 2020 Sch 1. legislation.gov.uk (data revised to 22 Sept 2026) shows no outstanding changes to s61B or s688A; the outstanding FA 2026 effects listed on those pages concern other ITEPA sections. HMRC guidance: Spotlight 67 (21 Nov 2024, updated 15 Jan 2025); ESM3510, ESM3530, ESM3620, ESM3625. The Budget 2026 OOTLAR (28 Oct 2026, updated 5 Nov 2026) contains no MSC measure.
traps.relevance: This matters only if the user incorporates, or joins a 'limited company' or partnership 'solution'. A company set up with an independent accountant is not an MSC. A provider-run, off-the-shelf company or partnership that pays out most of the day rate as dividends can be one, which puts PAYE and NIC on everything and can make the user personally liable for unpaid debts. IR35 still needs checking for an ordinary company of the user's own.

traps.name: Owner-managed company profit extraction schemes (Spotlights 56, 61, 62, 66, 68)
traps.why: Spotlight 68 (31 Mar 2025): company buys 'advertising' from a promoter, claims CT and VAT relief; at least 80% returns to directors as 'loyalty points' converting 1:1 onto prepaid cards: taxable income, CT deduction and VAT recovery may be denied. Spotlight 56 (1 Sep 2020): offshore remuneration trusts with tiny director loans to qualify as beneficiary, uncommercial 'tax-free' loans back; GAAR Advisory Panel (7 April 2020) said 'not a reasonable course of action', 'contrived and abnormal'; GAAR counteraction then APNs; 60% penalty for arrangements on or after 15 Sep 2016; loan charge and Part 7A also apply. Spotlight 61 (22 Dec 2022): trust contributions with a 10% fee and loans back; tribunal decided Marlborough DP, Strategic Branding, CIA Insurance Services: contributions and fees not deductible; distributions (Marlborough) or disguised remuneration (others). Spotlight 62 (2 June 2023): new share class bought below value by a grandparent/sibling and gifted to a trust for the owner's minor children; defeated by ITTOIA s619 onwards (s629). Spotlight 66 (23 Oct 2024): 'The Partnership Model' converting employees to LLP members with compensation treated as capital contributions; HMRC says they remain employees. Promoters face DOTAS penalties (now FA 2004 ss315-315E from 18 March 2026), enablers penalties and POTAS. Legitimate extraction: salary, dividends, pension contributions and properly documented expenses.

figures.current: Spotlight 68: at least 80% of 'advertising' spend returned at £1 per point. DOTAS promoter penalties up to £600 a day initially, up to £1 million.

traps.status: All five Spotlights listed on GOV.UK (checked Nov 2026). Law in force: ITEPA Part 7A, ITTOIA Part 5 Ch 5, GAAR (FA 2013 Part 5; s212A), wholly and exclusively. DOTAS promoter penalties moved from TMA s98C (omitted 18 March 2026) to FA 2004 ss315-315E (FA 2026 s216); old proceedings continue (FA 2026 s219).

traps.name: Accelerated Payment Notices and follower notices (FA 2014 Part 4)
traps.why: Two HMRC enforcement tools that remove the cash-flow 'benefit' avoidance promoters sell ('it will take HMRC years'). Accelerated payment notice (APN, FA 2014 s219): HMRC may give one where (A) an enquiry into the person's return or claim is open, or their tax appeal has not been decided or disposed of; (B) the return, claim or appeal relies on a tax advantage from particular arrangements; and (C) a follower notice has been given for the same advantage, or the arrangements are DOTAS arrangements (given a scheme reference number by HMRC, or substantially the same, s219(5)), or a GAAR final counteraction notice (including pooling and generic-referral notices under FA 2013 Schs 43A and 43B, added by FA 2016 s157) has been given where at least two members of the GAAR Advisory Panel sub-panel said entering into the arrangements was not a reasonable course of action. The tax stated must be paid within 90 days, or, if representations were made, by the later of that and 30 days after HMRC's decision (s223(5) in enquiry cases; TMA 1970 s55(8D) in appeal cases). There is no right of appeal against an APN, only written representations within 90 days (s222). In an enquiry case the payment counts as a payment on account of the tax in dispute (s223(3)); in an appeal case the disputed tax simply stops being postponed (s224, inserting TMA 1970 s55(8B)-(8D)). Either way the enquiry or appeal continues. HMRC says it will normally repay the amount, with any interest due, if the person finally wins, but if it appeals further it may in some cases ask the court for permission not to repay in the meantime (HMRC factsheet CC/FS25a). Paying late brings penalties in both kinds of case: s226 penalties for enquiry-case APNs, and ordinary late-payment penalties for appeal-case APNs (CC/FS25a). Follower notice (s204): HMRC may give one during an open enquiry or appeal where it considers that a final ruling of any court or tribunal (s205; it need not be in another taxpayer's case or about the same scheme) has principles or reasoning that would deny the advantage. It cannot be given more than 12 months after the later of the ruling becoming final and the return or claim being received or the appeal being made (s204(6)). No appeal, only representations within 90 days (s207). The person must take corrective action (amend the return or claim, or in an appeal case take all necessary steps to agree in writing to give up the advantage, and tell HMRC) within 90 days; if representations were made and the notice confirmed, by the later of that and 30 days after HMRC's decision (s208(8)). Otherwise a penalty of 30% of the denied advantage (s209(1)), which HMRC may reduce for co-operation but not below 10% (s210), plus a further 20% (s208A, s209(1A)) only if a tribunal appeal is struck out or the tribunal declares the person's conduct of it unreasonable. Other penalties on the same tax (for example inaccuracy, failure-to-notify, late-return, GAAR or serial-avoidance penalties) can be charged as well; together with the follower penalties they are capped at normally 100% of the tax, higher in deliberate-and-concealed or offshore cases (s212). Part 4 also applies to Class 4 NICs (SSCBA 1992 s16(1)(d), inserted by NICA 2015 Sch 2).

figures.apn_payment_period_if_representations: later of 90 days from the notice and 30 days from HMRC's decision on the representations (s223(5); TMA 1970 s55(8D) for appeal cases)
figures.apn_penalty_scope: s226 penalties apply only to APNs given while an enquiry is open (s219(2)(a)); the penalty day is the day after the payment period ends. Appeal-case APNs: see apn_appeal_case_late_payment_penalties
figures.apn_appeal_case_late_payment_penalties: income tax and CGT for 2010-11 onwards: 5% of the amount still unpaid at a penalty date 31 days after the APN due date, a further 5% at 5 months and another 5% at 11 months from the penalty date (FA 2009 Sch 56 para 3; HMRC CC/FS25a); surcharges instead for 2009-10 and earlier
figures.apn_interest: no interest on the APN as such; late-payment interest on the tax runs from its original due date until paid (CC/FS25a)
figures.corrective_action_deadline_if_representa: later of 90 days from the notice and 30 days from HMRC's decision confirming it (s208(8))
figures.aggregate_cap_with_other_penalties_pct_o: 100 normally (s212(5)(e)); 125 where one penalty is at the 100% deliberate-and-concealed rate in FA 2007 Sch 24 para 4(2)(c) or the FA 2008 Sch 41 or FA 2009 Sch 55 provisions listed in s212(5)(ba); 105, 140, 150 or 200 where an offshore-category rate applies (s212(5)(a)-(d))

traps.status: Law: FA 2014 Part 4, amended by FA 2016 s157 (GAAR routes in s219(4)(d)-(e)) and FA 2021 s119 and Sch 28 (30% rate, s208A and s209(1A), and s212 changes), which apply to s208 penalties assessed on or after the day Sch 28 came into force; FA 2021 sets no separate date, so that is Royal Assent, 10 June 2021 (earlier assessments: 50%). Aggregate cap: FA 2014 s212. Appeal-case postponement ends under TMA 1970 s55(8B)-(8D) (inserted by FA 2014 s224); late-payment penalties under FA 2009 Sch 56. Applies to Class 4 NICs via SSCBA 1992 s16(1)(d) (NICA 2015, from 12 April 2015). Text checked on legislation.gov.uk on 24 Nov 2026. Guidance: HMRC factsheet CC/FS25a (last updated 29 Sept 2022), used for appeal-case late-payment penalties and repayment practice; it still says 50% for the follower penalty and is out of date on that rate: follow the Act.
traps.relevance: If anyone offers the technician a scheme, umbrella or loan arrangement promising lower tax, HMRC can demand the disputed tax within 90 days with no right of appeal, and where a court has already defeated a similar scheme it can add a penalty of normally 30% of the tax (10% to 50%), with other penalties able to take the total to 100% of the tax or more. Ordinary planning such as claiming expenses, capital allowances or pension contributions is not affected.

traps.name: Promoters of Tax Avoidance Schemes (POTAS) and stop notices (FA 2014 Part 5, ss234-283; Schs 33A-36)
traps.why: POTAS targets high-risk promoters: conduct notices, monitoring notices, publication. Stop notices (ss236A-236K, inserted by FA 2021 Sch 30 para 1 from 10 June 2021): an authorised officer (HMRC policy: senior officer outside the counter-avoidance unit) gives one when suspecting promotion of arrangements meeting Condition A plus B or C, or B plus D (A: similar to loan-charge, DOTAS/DASVOIT-numbered, follower-notice or specified arrangements; B: marketed advantage more likely than not undeliverable; C: reference number allocated and information notice not complied with or tribunal application; D: recipient under a conduct or monitoring notice). The recipient must not promote such arrangements or similar ones (s236B(1)). Criminal offence (ss277A-277B, FA 2024 s34) for failures on or after 22 Feb 2024, including officers whose consent, connivance or neglect contributed. HMRC publishes named schemes, promoters, enablers and suppliers (FA 2022 s86, amended FA 2026 s214(3)); list updated 19 Nov 2026. FA 2026 Part 6 Ch 1 (ss159-165, in force 18 May 2026) bans promoting arrangements with no realistic prospect of success; Ch 2 (ss166-176) promoter action notices. Rules hit promoters; users should not join or should leave named schemes; absence from the list is not approval.

figures.current: Stop notice breach civil penalty: up to £100,000 plus up to £5,000 per person to whom promoted; with a monitoring notice up to £250,000 (or £1,000,000 if £250,000 inappropriately low) plus £10,000 per person. Criminal offence (s277A): unlimited fine, up to 2 years' imprisonment, or both. Daily default penalties for information failures. FA 2026 s162 civil penalty up to £1,000,000 plus £5,000 per participant; s163 offence up to 2 years on indictment.

traps.status: Law: FA 2014 Part 5 as amended by FA 2015, FA 2016, F(No.2)A 2017, FA 2021 (stop notices from 10 June 2021), FA 2024 (offence from 22 Feb 2024) and FA 2026 (s218; s214(3) from 18 March 2026; ss159-165 with s159(1) from 18 May 2026; ss166-176). POTAS guidance 22 April 2025 (predates FA 2026). Named list 19 Nov 2026.
traps.relevance: Check any named adviser or scheme against HMRC's current list of named schemes, promoters, enablers and suppliers.

traps.name: Statutory prohibition on promoting 'no realistic prospect' schemes and promoter action notices (FA 2026 Part 6 Chs 1-2, ss159-176)
traps.why: Finance Act 2026 Part 6 Chapter 1 (ss159-165) makes it unlawful to promote either of two kinds of arrangement. The first is arrangements that have been, or are likely to be, marketed as a way to get a particular tax advantage when there is no realistic prospect of getting it (s159(1)(a)). The second is arrangements specified in HMRC regulations (s159(1)(b)). Regulations under s159(2) can specify only arrangements that, in HMRC's reasonable opinion, are marketed for a tax advantage, are unlikely to deliver it and are likely to harm participants. s159(3) gives examples of signs of harm: many participants; participants who are not independently advised or whose tax affairs are otherwise straightforward; mass-marketing; standardised documents; and promoters whom participants cannot identify or contact. Such regulations lapse after 28 days unless the House of Commons approves them (s161). It does not matter whether the promoter knows the arrangements are caught (s159(5)). 'Promotion' (s160) means doing any of the following in the course of a business or with a view to monetary gain: communicating information to encourage others to implement the arrangements, making them available, organising or managing them, or arranging for others to do these things. It excludes supplying goods or services on commercial terms without knowing, or being reasonably expected to know, what they are used for, and it excludes legally privileged advice. The sanctions are a civil penalty (s162), a criminal offence (s163) and criminal liability for responsible officers of companies and partnerships where the offence involves their consent, connivance or neglect (s164). Under Chapter 2 (ss166-176), an authorised HMRC officer can certify that a person is promoting in breach of a stop notice (FA 2014 s236B) or of s159(1) (s166). The promoter must be given a copy and 30 days for representations. HMRC can then issue a promoter action notice to a business suspected of supplying goods or services used in that promotion (s167), after an optional preliminary notice (s168). The notice can require the business to stop supplying, to supply only on conditions, or to take specified steps, and must give it at least 30 days to comply. It cannot require monitoring, restrict internet access services, or restrict legal or auditing services (s167(6)). Recipients can appeal (s170). Failing to comply without reasonable excuse can lead to penalties (s171), publication for up to 12 months (s172) and reporting to regulators or trade bodies (s173). These rules target promoters and their suppliers. Anyone who uses such a scheme still owes the tax, interest and any penalties, and may face the GAAR. Announced, not yet law: a Finance Bill 2026-27 'policy maintenance package' was announced at Tax Update 2026 (23 June 2026) and confirmed at Budget 2026 (28 Oct 2026; OOTLAR 1.97 and the TIIN 'Changes to the promoters of tax avoidance scheme legislation'). It will: bring VAT and indirect taxes fully into POTAS by amending FA 2014 ss234, 281A and 283 and Sch 34, which allows publication under FA 2022 s86, wider stop notices, and conduct and monitoring notices; allow earlier publication of promoters and schemes under stop notices (FA 2014 s236H); require publication of the fact that an appeal has been made against a refusal to lift a stop notice, or a later appeal; and correct FA 2026 s209(6). Proposed only: Budget 2026 announced a consultation on new powers against serious and serial users of avoidance schemes, earlier recovery of promoters' and certain individuals' liabilities, and a stronger POTAS regime (OOTLAR 2.35).

figures.s162_civil_penalty_max: £1,000,000 plus £5,000 for each person who participated; 30 days for representations; interest under FA 2009 s101
figures.s163_offence: Summary conviction: a fine (England and Wales), or a fine not exceeding the statutory maximum (Scotland, NI). On indictment: up to 2 years' imprisonment, a fine, or both
figures.s171_promoter_action_notice_penalty_max: £1,000 for each day of non-compliance without reasonable excuse; 30 days for representations
figures.publication_max_period: Withdrawn no later than 12 months after publication (s172(4))
figures.s159_1_in_force: 18 May 2026 (s165(2): two months after Royal Assent)
figures.finance_bill_2026_27_package: No new penalty figures; Exchequer impact nil for 2026-27 to 2031-32; takes effect from Royal Assent to Finance Bill 2026-27 (date not yet known)

traps.status: Law: FA 2026 (c.11), Royal Assent 18 March 2026. s159(1) has been in force since 18 May 2026 (s165(2)). The rest of Chapter 1 and all of Chapter 2 have no separate commencement provision, and legislation.gov.uk dates them from 18 March 2026. A title search of 2026 SIs on legislation.gov.uk (24 Nov 2026) found no regulations under s159(2). Announced, not enacted: the Finance Bill 2026-27 POTAS package (Tax Update 2026, 23 June 2026; Budget 2026, 28 Oct 2026, OOTLAR 1.97 and TIIN), effective from Royal Assent to that Bill. Proposed: consultation announced at Budget 2026 (OOTLAR 2.35).
traps.relevance: It is now unlawful for anyone, the user included, to promote a scheme marketed as giving a tax advantage that has no realistic prospect of working, for example by passing it to other crew in the course of business or for a referral fee, even without knowing it fails (FA 2026 ss159-160, 162-163). The rules protect the user only indirectly, because anyone who joins such a scheme still owes all the tax, and a user who supplies goods or services to a certified promoter must comply with any promoter action notice they receive.

traps.name: Disclosure of Tax Avoidance Schemes (DOTAS) (FA 2004 Part 7)
traps.why: Promoters must disclose notifiable arrangements within 5 days (excluding weekends and bank holidays) of making them available, a firm approach, or implementation. Notifiable if a tax advantage is expected and is a main benefit and a hallmark applies (IT/CGT/CT: confidentiality 1a/1b and 2, premium fee 3, standardised tax products 5, loss schemes 6, leasing 7, employment income 8, financial products 9; IHT hallmark SI 2017/1172; SDLT and ATED own tests). Users must disclose where the only promoter is offshore and does not (5 days), legal privilege prevents disclosure (5 days), or there is no promoter (30 days). HMRC issues an SRN; from 10 June 2021 HMRC can give a s310D notice (30 days to show not notifiable) and allocate an SRN (s311(3)). Promoters pass SRNs to clients (AAG6); users report on the return or AAG4. An SRN does not mean HMRC accepts the scheme; DOTAS-notifiable schemes expose users to APNs (pay within 90 days). FA 2026 s216 replaced TMA s98C and FA 2004 s315 with ss315-315E (penalty table, daily penalties, penalties set by an authorised officer, time limits, reasonable excuse, Treasury power to change amounts); s217 removed the one-year publication limits (s316C(6A)-(6B)). VAT and indirect taxes under DASVOIT (from 1 Jan 2018).

figures.current: User failing to report an SRN: £5,000 first failure; £7,500 if one other failure in the previous 36 months; £10,000 if two or more. Promoter failing to disclose: up to £600 a day initial, up to £1 million if inappropriately low; after an s306A/s314A order: £600 a day for 10 days then £5,000 a day. Promoter failing to give an SRN to a client: £5,000 per client plus up to £600 a day. Employer failing to report employees: £5,000 per employee plus up to £600 a day.

traps.status: Law: FA 2004 Part 7, amended by FA 2021 (from 10 June 2021) and FA 2026 ss216-219 (from 18 March 2026; earlier proceedings under the old rules, s219). HMRC guidance updated 31 July 2026.
traps.relevance: Treat any mention of an SRN, AAG4 or AAG6 as notifiable avoidance; SRN reporting penalties feed the fines estimator.

traps.name: General Anti-Abuse Rule (GAAR) and its 60% penalty (FA 2013 Part 5, ss206-215, s212A)
traps.why: HMRC can make just and reasonable adjustments to counteract advantages from abusive tax arrangements. Tax arrangements: obtaining a tax advantage reasonably a main purpose (s207(1)). Abusive: cannot reasonably be regarded as a reasonable course of action (s207(2), double reasonableness), considering consistency with principles and policy, contrived or abnormal steps, exploiting shortcomings. Indicators of abuse (s207(4)) and against (s207(5), HMRC-accepted established practice). A 3-member GAAR Advisory Panel sub-panel opinion is needed first (members independent of HMRC); pooling/binding notices (Sch 43A) and generic referrals (Sch 43B) extend opinions. Penalty 60% of the counteracted advantage (s212A(2)) for arrangements on or after 15 Sept 2016 where a final counteraction notice was given, the advantage counteracted under s209, and a tax document relied on it. Applies from 17 July 2013; NICs from 13 March 2014 (NICA 2014 s10; NIC penalty s10A). Taxes covered (s206(3)): income tax incl. PAYE, CT (incl. the FA 2026 charge on unassessed transfer pricing profits), CGT, PRT, apprenticeship levy, IHT, SDLT, ATED, multinational and domestic top-up taxes; diverted profits tax removed for periods from 1 Jan 2026 (FA 2026 s46). Recent opinions: 29 July 2026 (DR dual payments, published 25 Aug 2026); 30 Jan 2026 (two, IHT gifts of shares to employee trusts, published 22 July 2026); 7 Aug and 29 Oct 2024 (unfunded pensions, added to Spotlight 58 on 18 Nov 2025). Ordinary statutory choices on normal terms (sole trader v company, capital allowances, pension contributions) are not abusive.

traps.name: Offshore schemes: trusts, overseas 'employers' and moving income abroad
traps.why: A UK-resident sole trader (not using the FIG regime) is taxed on worldwide income; routing fees through an overseas company or trust, an offshore umbrella, or an Isle of Man/Channel Islands vehicle does not remove UK tax (transfer of assets abroad ITA s720, disguised remuneration rules, loan charge; Spotlight 60: IoM and Channel Islands are outside the UK). Spotlight 52 (15 May 2019): Hyrax and Curzon offshore-trust loan schemes found DOTAS-notifiable. Rangers ([2017] UKSC 45; Spotlight 41): earnings paid to a third party are still taxable. HMRC receives offshore account data under CRS (SI 2015/878). Offshore non-compliance: penalties up to 100/150/200% by territory category; asset-move penalty 50% of the underlying penalty (moves after 26 Mar 2015); asset-based penalty where offshore tax at stake exceeds £25,000 a year (lower of 10% of asset value and 10 x the tax); 12-year assessment limit (TMA s36A); strict-liability offences. Enablers: higher of 100% of PLR and £3,000 (offshore evasion) or 50% and £3,000 (asset move) (FA 2016 Sch 20; CC/FS17a), reducible to the higher of 10% and £1,000 for unprompted disclosure. Hiding income offshore is evasion; offshore remuneration-trust and umbrella schemes are targeted avoidance. Lawful declared foreign work (e.g. a European tour) is fine, with possible foreign tax credit relief.

figures.current: Offshore time limit up to 12 years from the end of the tax year (from 2015-16 where reasonable care taken; from 2013-14 where careless).

traps.status: Law in force: TMA s36A (FA 2019 s80); TMA s36(1)/(1A); FA 2015 Sch 21; FA 2016 Schs 20, 22; ITA s720 (amended to 20 Mar 2025); SI 2015/878. Guidance CC/FS17 (11 Jan 2022), CC/FS17a (10 Jan 2022), Spotlights 52, 60, 41. 2027-28 announcements not checked (search budget).

traps.name: Offshore non-disclosure: penalties up to 200% and strict-liability offences
traps.why: Offshore non-compliance is evasion. Penalties for inaccuracies (FA 2007 Sch 24), failure to notify (FA 2008 Sch 41) and deliberate withholding (FA 2009 Sch 55; for MTD ITSA users from 1 April 2026 FA 2021 Sch 25, same rates, £300 minimum) are graded by territory category: maximum 100% (cat 1), 150% (cat 2), 200% (cat 3) of PLR; higher minimums for deliberate offshore cases from 2016-17 (FA 2016 Sch 21). Asset-move penalty +50% (FA 2015 Sch 21) where a deliberate original penalty and an asset moved mainly to prevent or delay discovery. Asset-based penalty (FA 2016 Sch 22) only where the underlying penalty is deliberate or FTC, the tax is CGT, IHT or asset-based income tax (not trading income), and offshore tax at stake exceeds £25,000 in a year. Failure to Correct (F(No.2)A 2017 Sch 18): pre-6 April 2017 offshore non-compliance not corrected by 30 Sept 2018, 200% (statutory floor 100%; HMRC policy 150% minimum where prompted). Strict-liability offences (TMA ss106B-106D, FA 2016 s166, from 2017-18) for failing to notify, failing to file, or filing an inaccurate return, only where offshore income tax and CGT for the year exceed £25,000 (SI 2017/988); defences reasonable excuse/reasonable care; CRS/DAC2-reportable income excluded; trustees and executors excluded. Other risks: publication as a deliberate defaulter; 12-year offshore or 20-year deliberate look-back.

figures.current: Maximum penalties: cat 1 100%, cat 2 150%, cat 3 200% of PLR. Deliberate and concealed cat 3: 70-200% unprompted, 110-200% prompted. Failure to Correct: standard 200%; minimum 100% voluntary / 150% not. Asset-move penalty 50% of the underlying penalty. Asset-based penalty: lower of 10% of asset value or 10 x offshore tax at stake (where over £25,000). Strict-liability threshold £25,000 a year (SI 2017/988). Sentence: E&W up to 6 months (51 weeks once CJA 2003 s281(5) commences) and an unlimited fine per guidance; Scotland and NI up to 6 months and/or level 5 fine (£5,000).

traps.status: Law in force: TMA ss106B-106H (FA 2016 s166; from 7 Oct 2017 for 2017-18 onwards, SI 2017/970); threshold and CRS exclusion SI 2017/988 (3 Nov 2017); FTC F(No.2)A 2017 Sch 18. Offences guidance 13 Sept 2023; CC/FS17 11 Jan 2022.
traps.relevance: If the user has overseas bank or payment accounts (e.g. Revolut multi-currency), overseas clients or foreign kit-hire income, all must be declared.

traps.name: Cash-in-hand jobs, unrecorded hire income and other undeclared receipts
traps.why: Every receipt of the trade is taxable and must be recorded, however it is paid: cash or bank transfers from private clients, kit-hire fees (taxable as trading or miscellaneous income), 'mates' rates' jobs (the amount actually received), tips and other voluntary extras paid for the work (BIM41810), and the value of goods, services or other money's worth received instead of money (ITTOIA 2005 s28A; HMRC's online-income guidance says to use what they would have cost). A benefit that cannot be turned into money, such as a non-transferable reward holiday from a supplier, is not a receipt (BIM40051). Leaving receipts out deliberately is evasion and can be a crime (TMA 1970 s106A); leaving them out carelessly is a civil matter with penalties and interest, not a crime. Online platforms have collected seller details since 1 January 2024 and report each calendar year to HMRC by the following 31 January (first reports by 31 January 2025). The only exclusion relevant to an individual is for a seller for whom the platform solely facilitated sales of goods, fewer than 30 of them, for total consideration of not more than 2,000 euros (about £1,700) in the year; both tests must be met (IEIM901630). There is no such exclusion for services or for rental of transport or property, so technician work booked and paid through a platform is reported whatever the amount, and so are goods sales by someone who also provides services through the same platform. Putting it right: current-year income goes on that year's return; the previous year's on its return, or an amendment within 12 months of the filing date; earlier years (currently up to 2024-25) through HMRC's Digital Disclosure Service: notify, then disclose and pay (or have a payment arrangement agreed) within 90 days of HMRC's acknowledgement (not for VAT). But if HMRC has sent a return for 2024-25, or any year from 2022-23 onwards, that is still outstanding, that return must be filed and the year left out of the disclosure. Deliberate cases use the Contractual Disclosure Facility, the only route that gives an assurance of no criminal investigation into what is completely and accurately disclosed. Someone who has not been sent a return must tell HMRC they are chargeable within 6 months of the end of the tax year (TMA s7(1A), (1C)). The trading allowance (£1,000; £3,000 from 2027-28 announced at Budget 2026, not yet law) is measured against total receipts of all the person's relevant trades plus miscellaneous income (ITTOIA s783AC). Above that, it can only be claimed as a fixed deduction instead of all actual expenses, so it cannot shelter selected cash jobs on top of a trade. It is lost for the whole year if relevant income includes payments from the person's employer or their spouse's or civil partner's employer, from a firm in which the person is, or is connected with, a partner, or from a close company in which the person is a participator or an associate of a participator (ss783AO-783AQ). Business kit is not a 'personal possession' (an item for your own use), so selling it is not covered by HMRC's message that selling personal items is usually not taxed.

traps.relevance: Every payment for work or kit hire, including small cash or bank-transfer jobs for private clients and tips, belongs in the books and on the tax return, and work booked through an online platform is reported to HMRC whatever the amount. If anything has been missed, telling HMRC first (on the return or by disclosure) keeps penalties much lower than waiting to be found.

cases.name: Hall (HM Inspector of Taxes) v Lorimer
cases.citation: [1994] 1 WLR 209; (1993) 66 TC 349 (CA: Nolan LJ, Dillon and Roch LJJ agreeing), on appeal from Mummery J [1992] 1 WLR 939. Neutral citation [1993] EWCA Civ 25 and judgment date 5 November 1993: null (not verified; BAILII blocked, Find Case Law covers CA only from 2001).
cases.principle: A freelance vision mixer (over 800 days between 2 Feb 1985 and 5 April 1989; 120-150 engagements a year, longest 10 days, most 1-2 days; about 20-22 clients; work at studios on studio-supplied equipment; phone bookings to his home office, no formal written terms) was self-employed under contracts for services. Status is not a mechanical checklist: 'paint a picture from the accumulation of detail' and make a qualitative appreciation of the whole. With many short engagements, the worker's wider business is relevant: exposure to bad debts, time and money organising and getting work, length of engagements, number of other engagers (ESM7160). Not providing 'very expensive equipment' pointed towards employment but was not fatal; casual work can still be employment. Later: Atholl House [2022] EWCA Civ 501 (HMRC did not challenge Hall v Lorimer; RMC and Hall v Lorimer are not separate tests; the worker's business counts only so far as known or reasonably available to both parties at contracting); PGMOL [2024] UKSC 29 cited it with approval (para 30) and held each engagement is assessed on its own. ESM4120 Column A uses 'the conditions in Hall v Lorimer' only for some roles (e.g. sound, vision mixer); electrician, gaffer, lighting electrician and rigger roles need provision of necessary substantial equipment; Column B (specific production, finite period, ESM4115) is an alternative.
cases.status: Case law in force; Court of Appeal, binding on tribunals and the High Court; cited with approval in PGMOL [2024] UKSC 29 para 30; referenced in ESM7160 and ESM4120.
cases.relevance: Leading case for freelance crew: many short bookings for many production companies give a strong analogy, even using the client's kit.

figures.current: No monetary figures.

cases.name: HMRC v Professional Game Match Officials Ltd
cases.citation: [2024] UKSC 29 (Supreme Court, 16 September 2024, unanimous; on appeal from [2021] EWCA Civ 1370; press summary 15 October 2024)
cases.principle: For single engagements, mutuality of obligation need not exist before the engagement starts; a right to cancel without penalty does not remove mutuality while the contract exists; control need not include a right to intervene in every aspect and can come from a framework of obligations and sanctions. These are necessary minimum conditions, not sufficient; the whole picture still decides. Remitted to the FTT for an overall assessment applying Atholl House. Weakens 'no mutuality' arguments for day-booked crew; status should rest on own kit, multiple clients, business risk and ESM4120 criteria.
cases.status: Binding Supreme Court authority (case law, not legislation).
cases.relevance: Each booking is assessed on its own; short bookings alone do not prove self-employment.

figures.current: No monetary figures.

cases.name: HMRC Employment Status Manual: film and TV 'Lists of Roles' (ESM4120, Appendix 1)
cases.citation: HMRC ESM4120 (Appendix 1, 'TV and radio workers - behind camera workers'); guidance, not law
cases.principle: Lists roles HMRC 'regards as normally self-employed for tax purposes where the specified conditions are met' (new contracts and extensions) if Column A (role criteria), Column B (specific production for a finite period, re-engagements discrete; ESM4115; all roles except Safety diver), or both are met. Relevant roles and Column A: Electrician, Gaffer, Lighting electrician, Lighting hand (best boy/girl): contract requires provision of the necessary, substantial equipment. Rigger, Advanced rigger, Gaffer rigger, Construction rigger, Senior/HoD rigger: provision of substantial equipment. Rigger driver: provides vehicle and holds HGV C+E licence, EU digital tachograph card and Driver CPC. Console, Lighting desk, Rigging desk and Shooting dimmer operators: multiple and/or overlapping clients and no right to switch tasks. Lighting designer and Lighting director: responsible for designing lighting or photography (designer must also work off the engager's premises). Sound mixer, supervisor, recordist, boom operator, designer, maintenance engineer; Vision controller/engineer, supervisor, mixer; Live graphics operator: substantial equipment OR Hall v Lorimer conditions. Video technician: substantial equipment only. Stagehands (chargehand, HoD, standby, supervisor), Floor manager (only with no senior floor manager), Senior floor manager: multiple/overlapping clients and no right to switch tasks. Unit manager and OB (technical) manager: contract requires the individual to provide facilities. List 'not exhaustive'; unlisted roles use ESM0500 and CEST (HMRC stands by CEST if inputs accurate; re-run on contract change). ESM4116: short engagements (10 days or less) with many clients can be self-employed on Hall v Lorimer principles; engagements of 7 days or less allow NI-only deductions. ESM4117: 'substantial' = major items of significant value playing a fundamental role, generally owned by the worker; hired kit counts only if obtained entirely independently of the engager (disregarded if underwritten via increased rate, box payment or hire agreement); tools of the trade disregarded; no numerical threshold. Written for film/TV, so persuasive only by analogy for live events; separately invoiced kit hire may not count as provision of substantial equipment.
cases.status: HMRC guidance, not law. 7 June 2023 Appendix 1 replaced (then ESM4118); 22 July 2026 roles added; 7 October 2026 ESM4118 withdrawn and replaced by ESM4120 (page 'Updated: 7 October 2026'; first published 19 June 2026 per metadata). ESM4115 and ESM4116 updated 7 Oct 2026; ESM4117 last updated 20 Dec 2019.
cases.relevance: Strongest official support for treating lighting, rigging, sound and video technicians as self-employed on productions; keep contracts showing own substantial kit, multiple clients and discrete per-production bookings.

figures.current: No monetary figures; no numerical threshold for 'substantial' equipment (ESM4117).

cases.name: Jones v Garnett (Arctic Systems)
cases.citation: [2007] UKHL 35; 78 TC 597 (House of Lords, 25 July 2007; on appeal from [2005] EWCA Civ 1553)
cases.principle: Mr Jones (IT consultant) and his wife each bought one of two £1 subscriber shares in Arctic Systems Ltd (her share transferred 11 Aug 1992); he was sole director, she secretary doing 4-5 hours a week of admin. 1999-2000: receipts £78,355; salaries £6,520 (his, below market) and £3,600 (hers, reasonable); taxable profits £26,372; CT £4,927 (reported dividends of £25,767.25 each 'may be a mistake' per Lord Hoffmann: do not use). Unanimous dismissal of HMRC's appeal. (1) By a majority (Baroness Hale with reservations, not dissenting) there was an 'arrangement' with bounty, so a settlement: 'The decisions were tax driven and not commercially driven'. (2) The outright-gift exception between spouses (then ICTA s660A(6), now ITTOIA s626) applied: consent to her acquiring a share for £1 with expected dividends was a gift; an ordinary share is not 'wholly or substantially a right to income' because it carries votes, capital on winding up, power to block special resolutions and the right to petition (Lord Hoffmann at [30]). Distinguished Young v Pearce (1996) 70 TC 331 (preference shares with 30% of distributed profits, par on winding up, no votes). Lord Neuberger at [75]: a principal purpose of s660A is to defeat non-arm's-length arrangements between spouses equalising income.
cases.status: Binding House of Lords authority, current; HMRC applies it in TSEM4205 Example 6; s626 in force; dividend rates 10.75%/35.75% from 2026-27 (FA 2026 s4) reduce the benefit.
cases.relevance: Only after incorporation: a spouse owning ordinary shares outright can receive dividends at their own rates; does not protect minor children (s629), income-only or restricted classes, dividend waivers or MSC arrangements; IR35 still applies.

figures.current: Judgment 25 July 2007. 1999-2000: receipts £78,355; salaries £6,520 and £3,600; taxable profits £26,372; CT £4,927.

cases.name: Donovan & McLaren v HMRC
cases.citation: [2014] UKFTT 48 (TC), TC03188 (First-tier Tribunal, Judge Jennifer Blewitt and Ms Ruth Watts Davies; heard 12 Dec 2013, released 6 Jan 2014)
cases.principle: Victory Fire Ltd: husbands 40% each, wives 10% each. For the period to 31 March 2010, £130,000 of dividends via two interim dividends with one-day reciprocal waivers: 6 April 2009 husbands waived, £3,200 a share, each wife £32,000; 8 April 2009 wives waived, £825 a share, each husband £33,000 (pro rata would have been £52,000 / £13,000); similar waivers in many earlier years. Following Jones v Garnett and Buck v HMRC: the waivers were part of a plan to equalise income and use the wives' basic rate bands, an 'arrangement' and so a 'settlement' (s620); bounty (no commercial purpose; not at arm's length, conceded by the couples' accountant); distributable reserves not conclusive, but counting earlier waivers the same rate could not have been paid on every share; husbands kept an interest via s625 (spouses), so s624 applied; s626 did not apply (no evidence the 2001 allotments were gifts; a waiver is not an outright gift of property). Discovery assessments for 2007-08 and 2008-09 valid because returns did not disclose waivers, dividends voted or shareholdings. Upheld extra tax: Mr Donovan £4,749.98 (2009-10), £3,689.77 (2008-09), £5,350.85 (2007-08); Mr McLaren £4,731.07, £3,715.20, £5,350.85. TSEM4225 signs: reserves too low to pay the same rate on all shares; successive waivers over years exceeding accumulated realised profits; other evidence; non-waiving holders are people the waiver wishes to benefit; non-waiving holder pays less tax. TSEM4225 Ex 12: Mrs H 80 shares, Mr H 20, profit £25,000; she waives; £1,000/share gives Mr H £20,000; £16,000 treated as hers. TSEM4220: waivers benefiting a spouse caught by s624, a minor child by s629; others (e.g. adult child) not unless money returns to the settlor or spouse.
cases.status: FTT decision (does not bind other tribunals; no appeal found). ITTOIA ss619-626 in force. TSEM4220 and TSEM4225 current.
cases.relevance: Only if incorporated with family shareholders: never use dividend waivers to steer dividends to a spouse or children.

figures.current: Dividends £130,000; waivers produced £32,000 per wife and £33,000 per husband; extra tax upheld per year as listed.

cases.name: RFC 2012 Plc (Rangers) v Advocate General for Scotland
cases.citation: [2017] UKSC 45 (Supreme Court, 5 July 2017; UKSC 2016/0073; on appeal from [2015] CSIH 77; heard 15-16 March 2017; Lord Hodge, unanimous)
cases.principle: Money paid into an employee benefit trust as part of footballers' and executives' remuneration was taxable earnings when paid to the trust, even though employees took it as 'loans' from sub-trusts. General rule (para 41): the employment income charge covers money the employee is entitled to have paid as remuneration, whether paid to the employee or to a third party such as a trustee; the payer should have operated PAYE. Exceptions noted: benefits in kind under the benefits rules and payments giving only a contingent interest. Undermines every 'redirect your pay to a trust or third party' scheme; same purposive reasoning used against trading-income variants. HMRC Spotlight 41 (29 Sept 2017).
cases.status: Binding Supreme Court authority; appeal dismissed; nothing found suggesting it has been departed from (fresh 2026 check not possible).
cases.relevance: Authority to cite when the user is offered schemes paying part of fees to a trust, third party or 'employee benefit' vehicle.

figures.current: Judgment 5 July 2017.

cases.name: Elphysic Ltd and others v HMRC
cases.citation: [2025] UKUT 00236 (TCC) (Upper Tribunal, Mr Justice Rajah and Judge Andrew Scott; heard 20 and 23 May 2025; released 17 July 2025; UT/2024/000069 and UT/2024/000082)
cases.principle: HMRC was entitled to deregister mini umbrella companies for VAT under the Ablessio principle without showing that nominee directors knew or should have known of the fraud, where the company's own VAT number was the means of fraud; a deregistration decision can rest on sound objective evidence that fraudulent use of the VAT number is probable, inferred from the evidence as a whole. Lead appellants used the VAT Flat Rate Scheme and claimed the Employment Allowance. HMRC's appeal succeeded; the companies' grounds dismissed. Confirms MUC models are fraudulent; businesses in the chain risk losing input tax.
cases.status: Upper Tribunal decision; cited in HMRC 'Mini umbrella company fraud' guidance (updated 4 Aug 2025) and the August 2025 Employer Bulletin; any onward appeal not checked (search budget).
cases.relevance: Background authority for the MUC warning when working via umbrellas.
